anopheles: 1. A genus of mosquitoes which are secondary hosts of the malaria parasites, and whose bite is the usual, if not the only, means of infecting human beings with malaria. Several species are found in the United States. They may be distinguished from the ordinary mosquitoes of the genus Culex by the long slender palpi, nearly equaling the beak in length, while those of the female Culex are very short. They also assume different positions when resting, Culex usually holding the body parallel to the surface on which it rests and keeping the head and beak bent at an angle, while Anopheles holds the body at an angle with the surface and the head and beak in line with it. Unless they become themselves infected by previously biting a subject affected with malaria, the insects cannot transmit the disease

prothetic: 1. Of or pertaining to prothesis | 2. As, a prothetic apparatus
contriver: 1. One who contrives, devises, plans, or schemas. Swift
conditionality: 1. The quality of being conditional, or limited | 2. Limitation by certain terms
untaste: 1. To deprive of a taste for a thing.  Daniel
wharp: 1. A kind of fine sand from the banks of the Trent, used as a polishing powder
dame: 1. A mistress of a family, who is a lady | 2. A womam in authority | 3. Especially, a lady. Then shall these lords do vex me half so much, As that proud dame, the lord protector's wife. Shak
hoddydoddy: 1. An awkward or foolish person.  B. Jonson
sport: 1. That which diverts, and makes mirth | 2. Pastime | 3. Amusement. It is as sport a fool do mischief. prov. x
impostrous: 1. Characterized by imposture | 2. Deceitful. "Impostrous pretense of knowledge." Grote
verruculose: 1. Minutely verrucose | 2. As, a verruculose leaf or stalk
horsewhip:
1. A whip for horses.

To flog or chastise with a horsewhip
prostration: 1. The act of prostrating, throwing down, or laying fiat | 2. As, the prostration of the body | 3. The act of falling down, or of bowing in humility or adoration

homeopathic: 1. Of or pertaining to homeopathy | 2. According to the principles of homeopathy
volution: 1. A spiral turn or wreath | 2. A whorl of a spiral shell

negativeness: 1. The quality or state of being negative

spitted: 1. Put upon a spit | 2. Pierced as if by a spit | 3. Shot out long
supraspinal: 1. Situated above the vertebral column. Situated above a spine or spines | 2. Supraspinate | 3. Supraspinous
intercurrent:
1. Running between or among | 2. Intervening. Boyle. Bp. Fell | 3. Not belonging to any particular season. Said of diseases occurring in the course of another disease. Dunglison.

Something intervening. Holland
inebriant:
1. Intoxicating.

Anything that intoxicates, as opium, alcohol, etc | 2. An intoxicant. Smart
decarbonization: 1. The action or process of depriving a substance of carbon
quamoclit: 1. Formerly, a genus of plants including the cypress vine. The genus is now merged in Ipomoea
palmister: 1. One who practices palmistry Bp. Hall
flathead:
1. Characterized by flatness of head, especially that produced by artificial means, as a certain tribe of American Indians.

A Chinook Indian. See Chinook, n.,
paramere: 1. One of the symmetrical halves of any one of the radii, or spheromeres, of a radiate animal, as a starfish
scum: 1. The extraneous matter or impurities which rise to the surface of liquids in boiling or fermentation, or which form on the surface by other means | 2. Also, the scoria of metals in a molten state | 3. Dross. Some to remove the scum it did rise. Spenser
telescopy: 1. The art or practice of using or making telescopes
rename: 1. To give a new name to
oreosoma: 1. A genus of small oceanic fishes, remarkable for the large conical tubercles which cover the under surface
impenetrably: 1. In an impenetrable manner or state | 2. Imperviously. "Impenetrably armed." Milton. "Impenetrably dull." Pope

enmesh: 1. To catch or entangle in, or as in, meshes. Shak. My doubts enmesh me if I try | 2. Lowell
decease: 1. Departure, especially departure from this life | 2. Death. His decease, which he should accomplish at Jerusalem. Luke ix | 3. And I, the whilst you mourn for his decease, Will with my mourning plaints your plaint increase. Spenser. Syn. -- Death
amplitude: 1. State of being ample | 2. Extent of surface or space | 3. Largeness of dimensions
freely: 1. In a free manner | 2. Without restraint or compulsion | 3. Abundantly
mohr: 1. A West African gazelle, having horns on which are eleven or twelve very prominent rings. It is one of the species which produce bezoar
unruffle: 1. To cease from being ruffled or agitated. Dryden
hanse:
1. That part of an elliptical or many-centered arch which has the shorter radius and immediately adjoins the impost.

An association | 2. A league or confederacy. Hanse towns, certain commercial cities in Germany which associated themselves for the protection and enlarging of their commerce. The confederacy, called also Hansa and Hanseatic league, held its first diet in 1260, and was maintained for nearly four hundred years. At one time the league comprised eighty-five cities. Its remnants, Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen, are free cities, and are still frequently called Hanse towns
sloggy: 1. Sluggish.  Somnolence that is sloggy slumbering Chaucer
brogue: 1. A stout, coarse shoe | 2. A brogan. Note: In the Highlands of Scotland, the ancient brogue was made of horsehide or deerskin, untanned or tenned with the hair on, gathered round the ankle with a thong. The name was afterward given to any shoe worn as a part of the Highland costume. Clouted brogues, patched brogues | 3. Also, brogues studded with nails. See under Clout, v. t
cornstarch: 1. Starch made from Indian corn, esp | 2. A fine white flour used for puddings, etc
necroscopical: 1. Or or relating to post-mortem examinations
sixpenny: 1. Of the value of, or costing, sixpence | 2. As, a sixpenny loaf
disassiduity: 1. Want of as siduity or care.  Sir H. Wotton
misrecollect: 1. To have an erroneous remembrance of | 2. To suppose erroneously that one recollects. Hitchcock
synoptical: 1. Affording a general view of the whole, or of the principal parts of a thing | 2. As, a synoptic table | 3. A synoptical statement of an argument. "The synoptic Gospels." Alford. -- Syn*op"tic*al*ly, adv
vakeel: 1. A native attorney or agent | 2. Also, an ambassador
concinnity: 1. Internal harmony or fitness | 2. Mutual adaptation of parts | 3. Elegance
crystal: 1. The regular form which a substance tends to assume in solidifying, through the inherent power of cohesive attraction. It is bounded by plane surfaces, symmetrically arranged, and each species of crystal has fixed axial ratios. See Crystallization | 2. The material of quartz, in crystallization transparent or nearly so, and either colorless or slightly tinged with gray, or the like | 3. - - called also rock crystal. Ornamental vessels are made of it. Cf. Smoky quartz, Pebble
voltaism: 1. That form of electricity which is developed by the chemical action between metals and different liquids | 2. Voltaic electricity | 3. Also, the science which treats of this form of electricity
announcement: 1. The act of announcing, or giving notice | 2. That which announces | 3. Proclamation
bonnet: 1. A headdress for men and boys | 2. A cap | 3. Milton. Shak
tannigen: 1. A compound obtained as a yellowish gray powder by the action of acetyl chloride or acetic anhydride or ordinary tannic acid. It is used as an intestinal astringent, and locally in rhinitis and pharyngitis
blatteroon: 1. A senseless babbler or boaster.  "I hate such blatteroons." Howell
concertante: 1. A concert for two or more principal instruments, with orchestral accompaniment. Also adjectively | 2. As, concertante parts
quadrennial: 1. Comprising four years | 2. As, a quadrennial period | 3. Occurring once in four years, or at the end of every four years
bluefin: 1. A species of whitefish found in Lake Michigan
broach: 1. A spit.  He turned a broach that had worn a crown. Bacon | 2. An awl | 3. A bodkin
trafficker: 1. One who traffics, or carries on commerce | 2. A trader | 3. A merchant
row:
1. Rough | 2. Stern | 3. Angry.  "Lock he never so row." Chaucer.

A noisy, turbulent quarrel or disturbance
accurately: 1. In an accurate manner | 2. Exactly | 3. Precisely

jockeyship: 1. The art, character, or position, of a jockey | 2. The personality of a jockey. Go flatter Sawney for his jockeyship. Chatterton. Where can at last his jockeyship retire Cowper
latitat: 1. A writ based upon the presumption that the person summoned was hiding. Blackstone
injection: 1. The act of injecting or throwing in | 2. -- applied particularly to the forcible throwing in of a liquid, or aëriform body, by means of a syringe, pump, etc | 3. That which is injected
willet: 1. A large North American snipe | 2. -- called also pill-willet, will-willet, semipalmated tattler, or snipe, duck snipe, and stone curlew. Carolina willet, the Hudsonian godwit
postulatory: 1. Of the nature of a postulate. Sir T. Browne
lanseh: 1. The small, whitish brown fruit of an East Indian tree. It has a fleshy pulp, with an agreeable subacid taste. Balfour
trifoliate: 1. Having three leaves or leaflets, as clover. See Illust. of Shamrock
apse: 1. A projecting part of a building, esp | 2. Of a church, having in the plan a polygonal or semicircular termination, and, most often, projecting from the east end | 3. In early churches the Eastern apse was occupied by seats for the bishop and clergy. Hence: The bishop's seat or throne, in ancient churches
convergence: 1. The condition or quality of converging | 2. Tendency to one point. The convergence or divergence of the rays falling on the pupil. Berkeley
papilionaceous: 1. Resembling the butterfly | 2. Having a winged corolla somewhat resembling a butterfly, as in the blossoms of the bean and pea | 3. Belonging to that suborder of leguminous plants which includes the bean, pea, vetch, clover, and locust
piation: 1. The act of making atonement | 2. Expiation
laudation: 1. The act of lauding | 2. Praise | 3. High commendation

manage: 1. The handling or government of anything, but esp | 2. Of a horse | 3. Management
negligent: 1. Apt to neglect | 2. Customarily neglectful | 3. Characterized by negligence
cassolette: 1. A box, or vase with a perforated cover to emit perfumes

bamboozler: 1. A swindler | 2. One who deceives by trickery.  Arbuthnot
glossal: 1. Of or pertaining to the tongue | 2. Lingual
ortolan: 1. A European singing bird, about the size of the lark, with black wings. It is esteemed delicious food when fattened. Called also bunting. In England, the wheatear. In America, the sora, or Carolina rail. See Sora

skylarking: 1. The act of running about the rigging of a vessel in sport | 2. Hence, frolicking | 3. Scuffing
loof:
1. The spongelike fibers of the fruit of a cucurbitaceous plant | 2. Called also vegetable sponge. Formerly, some appurtenance of a vessel which was used in changing her course | 3. -- probably a large paddle put over the lee bow to help bring her head nearer to the wind. The part of a ship's side where the planking begins to curve toward bow and stern.

See Luff
zaffer: 1. A pigment obtained, usually by roasting cobalt glance with sand or quartz, as a dark earthy powder. It consists of crude cobalt oxide, or of an impure cobalt arseniate. It is used in porcelain painting, and in enameling pottery, to produce a blue color, and is often confounded with smalt, from which, however, it is distinct, as it contains no potash. The name is often loosely applied to mixtures of zaffer proper with silica, or oxides of iron, manganese, etc
alcoholometrical: 1. Relating to the alcoholometer or alcoholometry. The alcoholometrical strength of spirituous liquors. Ure
azotic: 1. Pertaining to azote, or nitrogen | 2. Formed or consisting of azote | 3. Nitric
berth: 1. Convenient sea room. A room in which a number of the officers or ship's company mess and reside. The place where a ship lies when she is at anchor, or at a wharf | 2. An allotted place | 3. An appointment
prod: 1. A pointed instrument for pricking or puncturing, as a goad, an awl, a skewer, etc | 2. A prick or stab which a pointed instrument | 3. A light kind of crossbow
primy: 1. Being in its prime.  "The youth of primy nature." Shak
sternson: 1. The end of a ship's keelson, to which the sternpost is bolted | 2. -- called also stern knee
caesural: 1. Of or pertaining to a cæsura. Cæsural pause, a pause made at a cæsura
electroplate: 1. To plate or cover with a coating of metal, usually silver, nickel, or gold, by means of electrolysis
profane: 1. Not sacred or holy | 2. Not possessing peculiar sanctity | 3. Unconsecrated
circumstantiable: 1. Capable of being circumstantiated.  Jer Taylor
suppositive:
1. Including or implying supposition, or hypothesis | 2. Supposed. -- Sup*pos"i*tive*ly, adv | 3. Hammond.

A word denoting or implying supposition, as the words if, granting, provided, etc
spancel:
1. A rope used for tying or hobbling the legs of a horse or cow | 2. Grose.

To tie or hobble with a spancel.  Malone
laureled: 1. Crowned with laurel, or with a laurel wreath | 2. Laureate
polypean: 1. Of or pertaining to a polyp, or polyps
liberalistic: 1. Pertaining to, or characterized by, liberalism | 2. As, liberalistic opinions
function: 1. The act of executing or performing any duty, office, or calling | 2. Per formance. "In the function of his public calling." Swift | 3. The appropriate action of any special organ or part of an animal or vegetable organism
matchable: 1. Capable of being matched | 2. Comparable on equal conditions | 3. Adapted to being joined together
sparteine: 1. A narcotic alkaloid extracted from the tops of the common broom, as a colorless oily liquid of aniline-like odor and very bitter taste
acinaceous: 1. Containing seeds or stones of grapes, or grains like them
glonoine: 1. Same as Nitroglycerin | 2. -- called also oil of glonoin | 3. A dilute solution of nitroglycerin used as a neurotic
mail: 1. A spot | 2. A small piece of money | 3. Especially, an English silver half-penny of the time of Henry V
narrowly: 1. With little breadth | 2. In a narrow manner | 3. Without much extent
taupie: 1. A foolish or thoughtless young person, esp | 2. A slothful or slovenly woman.   Burns
pro: 1. A Latin preposition signifying for, before, forth. Pro confesso Etym:, taken as confessed. The action of a court of equity on that portion of the pleading in a particular case which the pleading on the other side does not deny. -- Pro rata. Etym:  In proportion | 2. Proportion. -- Pro re nata Etym:, for the existing occasion | 3. As matters are
saltwort: 1. A name given to several plants which grow on the seashore, as the Batis maritima, and the glasswort. See Glasswort. Black saltwort, the sea milkwort
thrombosis: 1. The obstruction of a blood vessel by a clot formed at the site of obstruction | 2. -- distinguished from embolism, which is produced by a clot or foreign body brought from a distance. -- Throm*bot"ic, a
bombilation: 1. A humming sound | 2. A booming. To . . . silence the bombilation of guns. Sir T. Browne
beaumontague: 1. A cement used in making joints, filling cracks, etc | 2. For iron, the principal constituents are iron borings and sal ammoniac | 3. For wood, white lead or litharge, whiting, and linseed oil
desirableness: 1. The quality of being desirable. The desirableness of the Austrian alliance. Froude
tormenting: 1. Causing torment | 2. As, a tormenting dream. -- Tor*ment"ing*ly, adv
clout: 1. A cloth | 2. A piece of cloth or leather | 3. A patch
gambogic: 1. Pertaining to, resembling, or containing, gamboge
nighted: 1. Darkness | 2. Clouded.  Shak | 3. Overtaken by night
umbery: 1. Of or pertaining to umber | 2. Like umber | 3. As, umbery gold
bookkeeper: 1. One who keeps accounts | 2. One who has the charge of keeping the books and accounts in an office
rowable: 1. That may be rowed, or rowed upon. "That long barren fen, once rowable." B. Jonson
thing: 1. Whatever exists, or is conceived to exist, as a separate entity, whether animate or inanimate | 2. Any separable or distinguishable object of thought. God made . . . every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind. Gen. i | 3. He sent after this manner
gressorious: 1. Adapted for walking | 2. Anisodactylous | 3. As the feet of certain birds and insects. See Illust. under Aves
turgid: 1. Distended beyond the natural state by some internal agent or expansive force | 2. Swelled | 3. Swollen
dementate:
1. Deprived of reason. Arise, thou dementate sinner! Hammond.

To deprive of reason | 2. To dement.  Burton
coarctate: 1. To press together | 2. To crowd | 3. To straiten
welldoer: 1. One who does well | 2. One who does good to another | 3. A benefactor
alexipyretic: 1. Serving to drive off fever | 2. Antifebrile. -- n.  A febrifuge
calicular: 1. Relating to, or resembling, a cup | 2. Also improperly used for calycular, calyculate
certes: 1. Certainly | 2. In truth | 3. Verily.  Certes it great pity was to see Him his nobility so foul deface. Spenser
photophony: 1. The art or practice of using the photophone
capable: 1. Possessing ability, qualification, or susceptibility | 2. Having capacity | 3. Of sufficient size or strength
succedaneous: 1. Pertaining to, or acting as, a succedaneum | 2. Supplying the place of something else | 3. Being, or employed as, a substitute for another. Sir T. Browne
tracheata: 1. An extensive division of arthropods comprising all those which breathe by tracheæ, as distinguished from Crustacea, which breathe by means of branchiæ

spoutshell: 1. Any marine gastropod shell of the genus Apporhais having an elongated siphon. See Illust. under Rostrifera

check: 1. A word of warning denoting that the king is in danger | 2. Such a menace of a player's king by an adversary's move as would, if it were any other piece, expose it to immediate capture. A king so menaced is said to be in check, and must be made safe at the next move | 3. A condition of interrupted or impeded progress
ceterach: 1. A species of fern with fronds
prosecution: 1. The act or process of prosecuting, or of endeavoring to gain or accomplish something | 2. Pursuit by efforts of body or mind | 3. As, the prosecution of a scheme, plan, design, or undertaking
feebleness: 1. The quality or condition of being feeble | 2. Debility | 3. Infirmity. That shakes for age and feebleness. Shak
poverty: 1. The quality or state of being poor or indigent | 2. Want or scarcity of means of subsistence | 3. Indigence
safety: 1. The condition or state of being safe | 2. Freedom from danger or hazard | 3. Exemption from hurt, injury, or loss. Up led by thee, Into the heaven I have presumed, An earthly guest . . . With like safety guided down, Return me to my native element. Milton
transportant: 1. Transporting | 2. As, transportant love.  Dr. H. More

agist: 1. To take to graze or pasture, at a certain sum | 2. -- used originally of the feeding of cattle in the king's forests, and collecting the money for the same. Blackstone
navvy: 1. Originally, a laborer on canals for internal navigation | 2. Hence, a laborer on other public works, as in building railroads, embankments, etc
deliberative: 1. Pertaining to deliberation | 2. Proceeding or acting by deliberation, or by discussion and examination | 3. Deliberating
halometer: 1. An instrument for measuring the forms and angles of salts and crystals | 2. A goniometer
leachy: 1. Permitting liquids to pass by percolation | 2. Not capable of retaining water | 3. Porous

associationist: 1. One who explains the higher functions and relations of the soul by the association of ideas | 2. G., Hartley, J. C. Mill
bastile: 1. A tower or an elevated work, used for the defense, or in the siege, of a fortified place. The high bastiles . . . which overtopped the walls. Holland | 2. "The Bastille", formerly a castle or fortress in Paris, used as a prison, especially for political offenders | 3. Hence, a rhetorical name for a prison
immigrate: 1. To come into a country of which one is not a native, for the purpose of permanent residence. See Emigrate
hexametrist: 1. One who writes in hexameters. "The Christian hexametrists." Milman
tressed: 1. Having tresses | 2. Formed into ringlets or braided | 3. Braided
quotation: 1. The act of quoting or citing | 2. That which is quoted or cited | 3. A part of a book or writing named, repeated, or adduced as evidence or illustration. Locke
ronyon: 1. A mangy or scabby creature. "Aroint thee, with!" the rump-fed ronyon cries. Shak
retrogradation: 1. The act of retrograding, or moving backward | 2. The state of being retrograde | 3. Decline
elutriation: 1. The process of elutriating | 2. A decanting or racking off by means of water, as finer particles from heavier
unknit: 1. To undo or unravel what is knitted together. Fie, fie! unknit that threatening unkind brow. Shak
exsertile: 1. Capable of being thrust out or protruded. J. Fleming
irradiate: 1. To throw rays of light upon | 2. To illuminate | 3. To brighten
sendal: 1. A light thin stuff of silk.  Chaucer. Wore she not a veil of twisted sendal embroidered with silver Sir W. Scott
woodsy: 1. Of or pertaining to the woods or forest.  It  is woodsy, and savors of trees. J. Burroughs
cordite: 1. A smokeless powder composed of nitroglycerin, guncotton, and mineral jelly, and used by the British army and in other services. A variety containing less nitroglycerin than the original is known  as cordite M. D
corpus: 1. A body, living or dead | 2. The corporeal substance of a thing. Corpus callosum (k | 3. Pl. Corpora callosa, the great band of commissural fibers uniting the cerebral hemispheries. See Brain. -- Corpus Christi, a festival in honor of the eucharist, observed on the Thursday after Trinity Sunday. -- Corpus Christi cloth. Same as Pyx cloth, under Pyx. -- Corpus delicti, the substantial and fundamental fact of the comission of a crime
misemploy: 1. To employ amiss | 2. As, to misemploy time, advantages, talents, etc | 3. Their frugal father's gains they misemploy. Dryden
contraversion: 1. A turning to the opposite side | 2. Antistrophe. Congreve
alineeation: 1. Alignment | 2. Position in a straight line, as of two planets with the sun | 3. Whewell. The allineation of the two planets. C. A. Young
cycadaceous: 1. Pertaining to, or resembling, an order of plants like the palms, but having exogenous wood. The sago palm is an example
fluxibility: 1. The quality of being fluxible. Hammond
allemande: 1. A dance in moderate twofold time, invented by the French in the reign of Louis XIV | 2. -- now mostly found in suites of pieces, like those of Bach and Handel | 3. A figure in dancing
brimless: 1. Having no brim | 2. As, brimless caps
cadaver: 1. A dead human body | 2. A corpse
pliform: 1. In the form of a ply, fold, or doubling.  Pennant
endosmometer: 1. An instrument for measuring the force or amount of endosmotic action
overthwart: 1. Having a transverse position | 2. Placed or situated across | 3. Hence, opposite. "Our overthwart neighbors." Dryden
designate: 1. Designated | 2. Appointed | 3. Chosen.  Sir G. Buck

else: 1. Other | 2. One or something beside | 3. As, Who else is coming What else shall I give Do you expect anything else "Bastards and else." Shak. Note: This word always follows its noun. It is usual to give the possessive form to else rather than to the substantive
fico: 1. A fig | 2. An insignificant trifle, no more than the snap of one's thumb | 3. A sign of contempt made by the fingers, expressing. A fig for you

isagon: 1. A figure or polygon whose angles are equal
uraniscoplasty: 1. The process of forming an artificial palate
tollman: 1. One who receives or collects toll | 2. A toll gatherer. Cowper
coronis: 1. In Greek grammar, a sign  sometimes placed over a contracted syllable. W. W. Goodwin | 2. The curved line or flourish at the end of a book or chapter | 3. Hence, the end
flanch: 1. A flange. .  A bearing consisting of a segment of a circle encroaching on the field from the side. Note: Flanches are always in pairs. A pair of flanches is considered one of the subordinaries
infamize: 1. To make infamous | 2. To defame.  Coleridge
existence: 1. The state of existing or being | 2. Actual possession of being | 3. Continuance in being
conscientiously: 1. In a conscientious manner | 2. As a matter of conscience | 3. Hence
viscin: 1. A clear, viscous, tasteless substance extracted from the mucilaginous sap of the mistletoe, holly, etc., and constituting an essential ingredient of birdlime

notebook: 1. A book in which notes or memorandums are written | 2. A book in which notes of hand are registered

A civil office, or a civil process  To serve in a civility. Latimer

gnu: 1. One of two species of large South African antelopes of the genus Catoblephas, having a mane and bushy tail, and curved horns in both sexes. 1. To anneal.  Chaucer.

gland: 1. An organ for secreting something to be used in, or eliminated from, the body | 2. As, the sebaceous glands of the skin | 3. The salivary glands of the mouth. An organ or part which resembles a secreting, or true, gland, as the ductless, lymphatic, pineal, and pituitary glands, the functions of which are very imperfectly known. Note: The true secreting glands are, in principle, narrow pouches of the mucous membranes, or of the integument, lined with a continuation of the epithelium, or of the epidermis, the cells of which produce the secretion from the blood. In the larger glands, the pouches are tubular, greatly elongated, and coiled, as in the sweat glands, or subdivided and branched, making compound and racemose glands, such as the pancreas

tea: 1. The prepared leaves of a shrub, or small tree. The shrub is a native of China, but has been introduced to some extent into some other countries. Note: Teas are classed as green or black, according to their color or appearance, the kinds being distinguished also by various other characteristic differences, as of taste, odor, and the like. The color, flavor, and quality are dependent upon the treatment which the leaves receive after being gathered. The leaves for green tea are heated, or roasted slightly, in shallow pans over a wood fire, almost immediately after being gathered, after which they are rolled with the hands upon a table, to free them from a portion of their moisture, and to twist them, and are then quickly dried. Those intended for black tea are spread out in the air for some time after being gathered, and then tossed about with the hands until they become soft and flaccid, when they are roasted for a few minutes, and rolled, and having then been exposed to the air for a few hours in a soft and moist state, are finally dried slowly over a charcoal fire. The operation of roasting and rolling is sometimes repeated several times, until the leaves have become of the proper color. The principal sorts of green tea are Twankay, the poorest kind | 2. Hyson skin, the refuse of Hyson | 3. Hyson, Imperial, and Gunpowder, fine varieties

anticous: 1. Facing toward the axis of the flower, as in the introrse anthers of the water lily

beaconage: 1. Money paid for the maintenance of a beacon | 2. Also, beacons, collectively
seemingly: 1. In appearance | 2. In show | 3. In semblance
devil: 1. The Evil One | 2. Satan, represented as the tempter and spiritual of mankind.  being forty days tempted of the devil. Luke iv | 3. That old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world. Rev. xii
willow: 1. Any tree or shrub of the genus Salix, including many species, most of which are characterized often used as an emblem of sorrow, desolation, or desertion. "A wreath of willow to show my forsaken plight." Sir W. Scott. Hence, a lover forsaken by, or having lost, the person beloved, is said to wear the willow. And I must wear the willow garland For him that's dead or false to me. Campbell | 2. A machine in which cotton or wool is opened and cleansed by the action of long spikes projecting from a drum which revolves within a box studded with similar spikes | 3. -- probably so called from having been originally a cylindrical cage made of willow rods, though some derive the term from winnow, as denoting the winnowing, or cleansing, action of the machine. Called also willy, twilly, twilly devil, and devil. Almond willow, Pussy willow, Weeping willow. See under Almond, Pussy, and Weeping. -- Willow biter the blue tit
delegacy: 1. The act of delegating, or state of being delegated | 2. Deputed power.  By way of delegacy or grand commission. Sir W. Raleigh | 3. A body of delegates or commissioners
gige: 1. The leather strap by which the shield of a knight was slung across the shoulder, or across the neck and shoulder. Meyrick
phoronomics: 1. The science of motion | 2. Kinematics.  Weisbach
interfascicular: 1. Between fascicles or bundles | 2. As, the interfascicular spaces of connective tissue
scortatory: 1. Pertaining to lewdness or fornication | 2. Lewd
eyeball: 1. The ball or globe of the eye
feria: 1. A week day, esp | 2. A day which is neither a festival nor a fast. Shipley
misprint:
1. To print wrong.

A mistake in printing | 2. A deviation from the copy | 3. As, a book full of misprints
ferricyanic: 1. Pertaining to, or derived from, a ferricyanide. Ferricyanic acid, a brown crystalline substance, H612Fe2, obtained from potassium ferricyanide, and regarded as the type of the ferricyanides | 2. -- called also hydro-ferricyanic acid, hydrogen ferricyanide, etc
ticketing: 1. A periodical sale of ore in the English mining districts | 2. -- so called from the tickets upon which are written the bids of the buyers
petrohyoid: 1. Pertaining to petrous, oe periotic, portion of the skull and the hyoid arch | 2. As, the petrohyoid muscles of the frog
bolus: 1. A rounded mass of anything, esp | 2. A large pill
hutch: 1. To place in huts | 2. To live in huts | 3. As, to hut troops in winter quarters. The troops hutted among the heights of Morristown. W. Irving
dice: 1. Small cubes used in gaming or in determining by chance | 2. Also, the game played with dice. See Die, n. Dice coal, a kind of coal easily splitting into cubical fragments. Brande & C | 3. To play games with dice. I . . . diced not above seven times a week. Shak
come: 1. To move hitherward | 2. To draw near | 3. To approach the speaker, or some place or person indicated
faintish: 1. Slightly faint | 2. Somewhat faint. -- Faint"ish*ness, n
triliteralness: 1. The quality of being triliteral | 2. As, the triliterality of Hebrew roots. W. D. Whitney
novaculite: 1. A variety of siliceous slate, of which hones are made | 2. Razor stone | 3. Turkey stone
thy: 1. Of thee, or belonging to thee | 2. The more common form of thine, possessive case of thou | 3. -- used always attributively, and chiefly in the solemn or grave style, and in poetry. Thine is used in the predicate
equibalance:
1. Equal weight | 2. Equiponderance.

To make of equal weight | 3. To balance equally
irpe: 1. A fantastic grimace or contortion of the body.  Smirks and irps and all affected humors. B. Jonson
ugrian: 1. A Mongolian race, ancestors of the Finns
filing: 1. A fragment or particle rubbed off by the act of filing | 2. As, iron filings
antinational: 1. Antagonistic to one's country or nation, or to a national government
sagittate: 1. Shaped like an arrowhead | 2. Triangular, with the two basal angles prolonged downward
proverbialist: 1. One who makes much use of proverbs in speech or writing | 2. One who composes, collects, or studies proverbs
brooklime: 1. A plant, with flowers, usually blue, in axillary racemes. The American species is V. Americana
unalienable: 1. Inalienable | 2. As, unalienable rights. Swift. -- Un*al"ien*a*bly, adv
tripodian: 1. An ancient stringed instrument | 2. -- so called because, in form, it resembled the Delphic tripod
defend: 1. To ward or fend off | 2. To drive back or away | 3. To repel.  Th' other strove for to defend The force of Vulcan with his might and main. Spenser
accommodating: 1. Affording, or disposed to afford, accommodation | 2. Obliging | 3. As an accommodating man, spirit, arrangement
gazetteer: 1. A writer of news, or an officer appointed to publish news by authority. Johnson | 2. A newspaper | 3. A gazette.  Burke
chainlet: 1. A small chain. Sir W. Scott
indiscerptible: 1. Not discerpible | 2. Inseparable.  Bp. Butler. -- In`dis*cerp"i*ble*ness, n., In`dis*cerp"ti*ble*ness, n.  -- In`dis*cerp"ti*bly, adv
laryngotracheal: 1. Pertaining to both larynx and trachea | 2. As, the laryngotracheal cartilage in the frog
bicostate: 1. Having two principal ribs running longitudinally, as a leaf
photosphere: 1. A sphere of light | 2. Esp., the luminous envelope of the sun
squatter: 1. One who squats | 2. Specifically, one who settles unlawfully upon land without a title. In the United States and Australia the term is sometimes applied also to a person who settles lawfully upon government land under permission and restrictions, before acquiring title. In such a tract, squatters and trespassers were tolerated to an extent now unknown. Macaulay | 3. See Squat snipe, under Squat. Squatter sovereignty, the right claimed by the squatters, or actual residents, of a Territory of the United States to make their own laws.  Bartlett
blur: 1. To render obscure by making the form or outline of confused and uncertain, as by soiling | 2. To smear | 3. To make indistinct and confused
ransomless: 1. Incapable of being ransomed | 2. Without ransom. Shak
swashbuckler: 1. A bully or braggadocio | 2. A swaggering, boastful fellow | 3. A swaggerer. Milton
coot: 1. A wading bird with lobate toes, of the genus Fulica. The common European or bald coot is F. atra | 2. The American is F. Americana. The surf duck or scoter. In the United States all the species of (Edemia are called coots. See Scoter. "As simple as a coot." Halliwell | 3. A stupid fellow
tripartite: 1. Divided into three parts | 2. Triparted | 3. As, a tripartite leaf
uxorial: 1. Dotingly fond of, or servilely submissive to, a wife | 2. Uxorious | 3. Also, becoming a wife
chute: 1. A framework, trough, or tube, upon or through which objects are made to slide from a higher to a lower level, or through which water passes to a wheel | 2. See Shoot
common: 1. Belonging or relating equally, or similary, to more than one | 2. As, you and I have a common interest in the property. Though life and sense be common to men and brutes. Sir M. Hale | 3. Belonging to or shared by, affecting or serving, all the members of a class, consired together
rasp: 1. To rub or file with a rasp | 2. To rub or grate with a rough file | 3. As, to rasp wood to make it smooth
dorse:
1. Same as dorsal, n | 2. The back of a book.  Books, all richly bound, with gilt dorses. Wood.

The Baltic or variable cod, by some believed to be the young of the common codfish
arbuscular: 1. Of or pertaining to a dwarf tree | 2. Shrublike. Da Costa
sphincter:
1. A muscle which surrounds, and by its contraction tends to close, a natural opening | 2. As, the sphincter of the bladder.

Of, pertaining to, or designating, a sphincter | 3. As, a sphincter muscle
pelvis: 1. The pelvic arch, or the pelvic arch together with the sacrum. See Pelvic arch, under Pelvic, and Sacrum | 2. The calyx of a crinoid. Pelvis of the kidney, the basinlike cavity into which the ureter expands as it joins the kidney
kingbird: 1. A small American bird, noted for its courage in attacking larger birds, even hawks and eagles, especially when they approach its nest in the breeding season. It is a typical tyrant flycatcher, taking various insects upon the wing. It is dark ash above, and blackish on the bead and tail. The quills and wing coverts are whitish at the edges. It is white beneath, with a white terminal band on the tail. The feathers on the head of the adults show a bright orange basal spot when erected. Called also bee bird, and bee martin. Several Southern and Western species of Tyrannus are also called king birds | 2. The king tody. See under King
hyalescence: 1. The process of becoming, or the state of being, transparent like glass
deadly: 1. Capable of causing death | 2. Mortal | 3. Fatal
changeless: 1. That can not be changed | 2. Constant | 3. As, a changeless purpose. -- Change"less*ness, n
moira: 1. The deity who assigns to every man his lot
instructible: 1. Capable of being instructed | 2. Teachable | 3. Docible. Bacon
linguiform: 1. Having the form of the tongue | 2. Tongue-shaped
diurna: 1. A division of Lepidoptera, including the butterflies | 2. -- so called because they fly only in the daytime
soliloquize: 1. To utter a soliloquy | 2. To talk to one's self
lethargic: 1. Pertaining to, affected with, or resembling, lethargy | 2. Morbidly drowsy | 3. Dull
goatish: 1. Characteristic of a goat | 2. Goatlike. Give your chaste body up to the embraces Of goatish lust. Massinger. -- Goat"ish*ly, adv | 3. -- Goat"ish*ness, n
proboscidian: 1. Pertaining to the Proboscidea. -- n.  One of the Proboscidea
kibed: 1. Chapped | 2. Cracked with cold | 3. Affected with chilblains
numerary: 1. Belonging to a certain number | 2. Counting as one of a collection or body. A supernumerary canon, when he obtains a prebend, becomes a numerary canon. Ayliffe
pun:
1. To pound.  He would pun thee into shivers with his fist. Shak.

A play on words which have the same sound but different meanings | 2. An expression in which two different applications of a word present an odd or ludicrous idea | 3. A kind of quibble or equivocation. Addison. A better put on this word was made on the Beggar's Opera, which, it was said, made Gay rich, and Rich gay
gowdnook: 1. The saury pike | 2. -- called also gofnick
fantom: 1. See Phantom. Fantom corn, phantom corn. Grose
alkaloid:
1. An organic base, especially one of a class of substances occurring ready formed in the tissues of plants and the bodies of animals. Note: Alcaloids all contain nitrogen, carbon, and hydrogen, and many of them also contain oxygen. They include many of the active principles in plants | 2. Thus, morphine and narcotine are alkaloids found in opium.

Pertaining to, resembling, or containing, alkali
yestern: 1. Of or pertaining to yesterday | 2. Relating to the day last past
productus: 1. An extinct genus of brachiopods, very characteristic of the Carboniferous rocks
bulb: 1. A spheroidal body growing from a plant either above or below the ground, which is strictly a bud, consisting of a cluster of partially developed leaves, and producing, as it grows, a stem above, and roots below, as in the onion, tulip, etc | 2. It differs from a corm in not being solid | 3. A name given to some parts that resemble in shape certain bulbous roots
cheirotherium: 1. A genus of extinct animals, so named from fossil footprints rudely resembling impressions of the human hand, and believed to have been made by labyrinthodont reptiles. See Illustration in Appendix
unspilt: 1. Not spilt or wasted | 2. Not shed
alguazil: 1. An inferior officer of justice in Spain | 2. A warrant officer | 3. A constable. Prescott
lawbreaker: 1. One who disobeys the law | 2. A criminal. -- Law"break`ing, n. & a
leafed: 1. Having a leaf or leaves | 2. -- used in composition | 3. As, broad-leafed
seise: 1. See Seize. Spenser. Note: This is the common spelling in the law phrase to be seised of
unappropriated: 1. Not specially appropriate | 2. Having not special application. J. Warton | 3. Not granted to any person, corporation, or the like, to the exclusion of others
centrebit: 1. An instrument turning on a center, for boring holes. See Bit, n.,
epure: 1. A draught or model from which to build | 2. Especially, one of the full size of the work to be done | 3. A detailed drawing
egotize: 1. To talk or write as an egotist. Cowper
absterge: 1. To make clean by wiping | 2. To wipe away | 3. To cleanse
transcript: 1. That which has been transcribed | 2. A writing or composition consisting of the same words as the original | 3. A written copy. The decalogue of Moses was but a transcript. South
algometer: 1. An instrument for measuring sensations of pain due to pressure. It has a piston rod with a blunted tip which is pressed against the skin. -- Al*gom"e*try, n. -- Al`go*met"ric, *met"ric*al, a. --Al`go*met"ric*al*ly, adv
parelectronomy: 1. A condition of the muscles induced by exposure to severe cold, in which the electrical action of the muscle is reversed
triplite: 1. A mineral of a dark brown color, generally with a fibrous, massive structure. It is a fluophosphate of iron and manganese
gaul: 1. The Anglicized form of Gallia, which in the time of the Romans included France and Upper Italy | 2. A native or inhabitant of Gaul
unfool: 1. To restore from folly, or from being a fool.  Shak
illimitable: 1. Incapable of being limited or bounded | 2. Immeasurable | 3. Limitless
piccadil: 1. A high, stiff collar for the neck | 2. Also, a hem or band about the skirt of a garment, -- worn by men in the 17th century
rhinoplastic: 1. Of or pertaining to rhinoplasty | 2. As, a rhinoplastic operation
turndown: 1. Capable of being turned down | 2. Specif., designating, or pertaining to, an incandescent lamp with a small additional filament which can be made incandescent when only a small amount of light is required | 3. Made to wear with the upper part turned down
verily: 1. In very truth | 2. Beyond doubt or question | 3. In fact
determinative: 1. Having power to determine | 2. Limiting | 3. Shaping
treenail: 1. A long wooden pin used in fastening the planks of a vessel to the timbers or to each other
foreread: 1. To tell beforehand | 2. To signify by tokens | 3. To predestine.  Spenser
delusional: 1. Of or pertaining to delusions | 2. As, delusional monomania
rigel: 1. A fixed star of the first magnitude in the left foot of the constellation Orion
chouka: 1. The Indian four-horned antelope | 2. The chikara
unio: 1. Any one of numerous species of fresh-water mussels belonging to Unio and many allied genera
venulose: 1. Full of venules, or small veins
carling: 1. A short timber running lengthwise of a ship, from one transverse desk beam to another | 2. Also, one of the cross timbers that strengthen a hath | 3. -- usually in pl
whimsical: 1. Full of, or characterized by, whims | 2. Actuated by a whim | 3. Having peculiar notions
ennead: 1. The number nine or a group of nine. The Enneads, the title given to the works of the philosopher Plotinus, published by his pupil Porphyry | 2. -- so called because each of the six books into which it is divided contains nine chapters
noncontent: 1. One who gives a negative vote | 2. -- sometimes abridged into noncon. or non con
sedum: 1. A genus of plants, mostly perennial, having succulent leaves and cymose flowers | 2. Orpine | 3. Stonecrop. Gray
zumbooruk: 1. A small cannon supported by a swiveled rest on the back of a camel, whence it is fired, -- used in the East
fernticle: 1. A freckle on the skin, resembling the seed of fern
clatter: 1. To make a rattling sound by striking hard bodies together | 2. To make a succession of abrupt, rattling sounds. Clattering loud with clamk. Longfellow | 3. To talk fast and noisily
stalagmitical: 1. Having the form or structure of stalagmites. -- Stal`ag*mit"ic*al*ly, adv
innocent: 1. Not harmful | 2. Free from that which can injure | 3. Innoxious
aecidium: 1. A form of fruit in the cycle of development of the Rusts or Brands, an order of fungi, formerly considered independent plants
lyrie: 1. A European fish, having the body covered with bony plates, and having three spines projecting in front of the nose | 2. -- called also noble, pluck, pogge, sea poacher, and armed bullhead
bridestake: 1. A stake or post set in the ground, for guests at a wedding to dance round. Divide the broad bridecake Round about the bridestake. B. Jonson
ottawas: 1. A tribe of Indians who, when first known, lived on the Ottawa River. Most of them subsequently migrated to the southwestern shore of Lake Superior
speediness: 1. The quality or state of being speedy
miscredent: 1. A miscreant, or believer in a false religious doctrine.  Holinshed
impressive: 1. Making, or tending to make, an impression | 2. Having power to impress | 3. Adapted to excite attention and feeling, to touch the sensibilities, or affect the conscience
formula: 1. A prescribed or set form | 2. An established rule | 3. A fixed or conventional method in which anything is to be done, arranged, or said
enecate: 1. To kill off | 2. To destroy.  Harvey
jesus: 1. The Savior | 2. The name of the Son of God as announced by the angel to his parents | 3. The personal name of Our Lord, in distinction from Christ, his official appellation. Luke i
stereochromy: 1. A style of painting on plastered walls or stone, in which the colors are rendered permanent by sprinklings of water, in which is mixed a proportion of soluble glass
tubful: 1. As much as a tub will hold | 2. Enough to fill a tub
circulatory: 1. Circular | 2. As, a circulatory letter. Johnson | 3. Circulating, or going round. T. Warton
measle:
1. A leper.   Wyclif (Matt. x | 2. ).

A tapeworm larva. See 2d Measles,
republican: 1. Of or pertaining to a republic. The Roman emperors were republican magistrates named by the senate. Macaulay | 2. Consonant with the principles of a republic | 3. As, republican sentiments or opinions
lichenic: 1. Of, pertaining to, or obtained from, lichens. Lichenic acid. An organic acid, C14H24O3 obtained from Iceland moss. An old name of fumaric acid
rumkin: 1. A popular or jocular name for a drinking vessel
cage: 1. A box or inclosure, wholly or partly of openwork, in wood or metal, used for confining birds or other animals. In his cage, like parrot fine and gay | 2. Cowper | 3. A place of confinement for malefactors Shak. Stone walls do not a prison make, Nor iron bars a cage. Lovelace
syphilodermatous: 1. Of or pertaining to the cutaneous manifestations of syphilis
fangle: 1. Something new-fashioned | 2. A foolish innovation | 3. A gewgaw
aggressor: 1. The person who first attacks or makes an aggression | 2. He who begins hostility or a quarrel | 3. An assailant. The insolence of the aggressor is usually proportioned to the tameness of the sufferer. Ames
incorrupt: 1. Not affected with corruption or decay | 2. Unimpaired | 3. Not marred or spoiled
bantling: 1. A young or small child | 2. An infant.  In what out of the way corners genius produces her bantlings. W. Irving
chestnut: 1. The edible nut of a forest tree of Europe and America. Commonly two or more of the nuts grow in a prickly bur | 2. The tree itself, or its light, coarse-grained timber, used for ornamental work, furniture, etc | 3. A bright brown color, like that of the nut
wedge: 1. A piece of metal, or other hard material, thick at one end, and tapering to a thin edge at the other, used in splitting wood, rocks, etc., in raising heavy bodies, and the like. It is one of the six elementary machines called the mechanical powers. See Illust. of Mechanical powers, under Mechanical | 2. A solid of five sides, having a rectangular base, two rectangular or trapezoidal sides meeting in an edge, and two triangular ends | 3. A mass of metal, especially when of a wedgelike form. "Wedges of gold." Shak
bronchotome: 1. An instrument for cutting into the bronchial tubes
demilance: 1. A light lance | 2. A short spear | 3. A half pike
besmoke: 1. To foul with smoke | 2. To harden or dry in smoke. Johnson
contrapuntal: 1. Pertaining to, or according to the rules of, counterpoint
liberality: 1. The quality or state of being liberal | 2. Liberal disposition or practice | 3. Freedom from narrowness or prejudice
commonwealth: 1. A state | 2. A body politic consisting of a certain number of men, united, by compact or tacit agreement, under one form of government and system of laws. The trappings of a monarchy would set up an ordinary commonwealth. Milton. Note: This term is applied to governments which are considered as free or popular, but rarely, or improperly, to an absolute government. The word signifies, strictly, the common well-being or happiness | 3. And hence, a form of government in which the general welfare is regarded rather than the welfare of any class
hawaiian: 1. Belonging to Hawaii or the Sandwich Islands, or to the people of Hawaii. -- n.  A native of Hawaii
uprising: 1. Act of rising | 2. Also, a steep place | 3. An ascent. "The steep uprising of the hill." Shak
lignite: 1. Mineral coal retaining the texture of the wood from which it was formed, and burning with an empyreumatic odor. It is of more recent origin than the anthracite and bituminous coal of the proper coal series. Called also brown coal, wood coal
luminiferous: 1. Producing light | 2. Yielding light | 3. Transmitting light
hydrocephalus: 1. An accumulation of liquid within the cavity of the cranium, especially within the ventricles of the brain | 2. Dropsy of the brain. It is due usually to tubercular meningitis. When it occurs in infancy, it often enlarges the head enormously
emmew: 1. To mew or coop up.  Shak
entity: 1. A real being, whether in thought or in fact | 2. Being | 3. Essence
unfounded: 1. Not founded | 2. Not built or established. Milton | 3. Having no foundation
fornicator: 1. An unmarried person, male or female, who has criminal intercourse with the other sex | 2. One guilty of fornication
malic: 1. Pertaining to, or obtained from, apples | 2. As, malic acid. Malic acid, a hydroxy acid obtained as a substance which is sirupy or crystallized with difficulty, and has a strong but pleasant sour taste. It occurs in many fruits, as in green apples, currants, etc | 3. It is levorotatory or dextrorotatory according to the temperature and concentration. An artificial variety is a derivative of succinic acid, but has no action on polarized light, and thus malic acid is a remarkable case of physical isomerism
bibber: 1. One given to drinking alcoholic beverages too freely | 2. A tippler | 3. -- chiefly used in composition
croupous: 1. Relating to or resembling croup | 2. Especially, attended with the formation of a deposit or membrance like that found in membranous croup | 3. As, croupous laryngitis. Croupous pneumonia, pneumonia attended with deposition of fibrinous matter in the air vesicles of the lungs
rontgenize: 1. To render conducting by the passage of Röntgen rays
smuggle: 1. To import or export secretly, contrary to the law | 2. To import or export without paying the duties imposed by law | 3. As, to smuggle lace
clasper: 1. One who, or that which, clasps, as a tendril. "The claspers of vines." Derham | 2. One of a pair of organs used by the male for grasping the female among many of the Crustacea. One of a pair of male copulatory organs, developed on the anterior side of the ventral fins of sharks and other elasmobranchs. See Illust. of Chimæra
igasurine: 1. An alkaloid found in nux vomica, and extracted as a white crystalline substance
disennoble: 1. To deprive of that which ennobles | 2. To degrade. An unworthy behavior degrades and disennobles a man | 3. Guardian
delibrate: 1. To strip off the bark | 2. To peel.  Ash
priming: 1. The powder or other combustible used to communicate fire to a charge of gunpowder, as in a firearm | 2. The first coating of color, size, or the like, laid on canvas, or on a building, or other surface | 3. The carrying over of water, with the steam, from the boiler, as into the cylinder. Priming of the tide. See Lag of the tide, under 2d Lag. -- Priming tube, a small pipe, filled with a combustible composition for firing cannon. -- Priming valve, a spring safety valve applied to the cylinder of a steam engine for discharging water carried into the cylinder by priming. -- Priming wire, a pointed wire used to penetrate the vent of a piece, for piercing the cartridge before priming
subcontracted: 1. Contracted after a former contract | 2. Betrothed for the second time.  Shak
calculary:
1. Of or pertaining to calculi.

A congeries of little stony knots found in the pulp of the pear and other fruits
cargo: 1. The lading or freight of a ship or other vessel | 2. The goods, merchandise, or whatever is conveyed in a vessel or boat | 3. Load
troublous: 1. Full of trouble | 2. Causing trouble. "In doubtful time of troublous need." Byron. A tall ship tossed in troublous seas. Spenser
tonicity: 1. The state of healty tension or partial contraction of muscle fibers while at rest | 2. Tone | 3. Tonus
brokenness: 1. The state or quality of being broken | 2. Unevenness. Macaulay | 3. Contrition
gleeman: 1. A name anciently given to an itinerant minstrel or musician
hortative:
1. Giving exhortation | 2. Advisory | 3. Exhortative. Bullokar.

An exhortation
turpitude: 1. Inherent baseness or vileness of principle, words, or actions | 2. Shameful wickedness | 3. Depravity. Shak
generality: 1. The state of being general | 2. The quality of including species or particulars. Hooker | 3. That which is general
adeniform: 1. Shaped like a gland | 2. Adenoid. Dunglison
pleasantness: 1. The state or quality of being pleasant
unparadise: 1. To deprive of happiness like that of paradise | 2. To render unhappy.  Young
wren: 1. Any one of numerous species of small singing birds belonging to Troglodytes and numerous allied of the family Troglodytidæ. Note: Among the species best known are the house wren common in both Europe and America, and the American winter wren. See also Cactus wren, Marsh wren, and Rock wren, under Cactus, Marsh, and Rock | 2. Any one of numerous species of small singing birds more or less resembling the true wrens in size and habits. Note: Among these are several species of European warblers | 3. As, the reed wren, under Reed), the sedge wren, the willow wren, the golden-crested wren, and the ruby-crowned wren. Ant wren, any one of numerous South American birds of the family Formicaridæ, allied to the ant thrushes. -- Blue wren, a small Australian singing bird, the male of which in the breeding season is bright blue. Called also superb warbler. -- Emu wren. See in the Vocabulary. -- Wren babbler, any one of numerous species of small timaline birds belonging to Alcippe, Stachyris, Timalia, and several allied genera. These birds are common in Southern Asia and the East Indies. -- Wren tit
strangely: 1. As something foreign, or not one's own | 2. In a manner adapted to something foreign and strange.  Shak | 3. In the manner of one who does not know another
besieger: 1. One who besieges | 2. -- opposed to the besieged
bebirine: 1. An alkaloid got from the bark of the bebeeru, or green heart of Guiana. It is a tonic, antiperiodic, and febrifuge, and is used in medicine as a substitute for quinine
dataria: 1. Formerly, a part of the Roman chancery | 2. Now, a separate office from which are sent graces or favors, cognizable in foro externo, such as appointments to benefices. The name is derived from the word datum, given or dated
spiracular: 1. Of or pertaining to a spiracle
unruliment: 1. Unruliness.  "Breaking forth with rude unruliment." Spenser
chitterlings: 1. The smaller intestines of swine, etc., fried for food
tidings: 1. Account of what has taken place, and was not before known | 2. News. I shall make my master glad with these tidings. Shak. manograph: 1. An optical device for making an indicator diagram for high- speed engines. The mirror is pivoted so that it can be moved in one direction by a small plunger operated by an elastic metal diaphragm which closes a tube connected with the engine cylinder. It is also moved at right angles to this direction by a reducing motion, called a reproducer, so as to copy accurately on a smaller scale the motion of the engine piston. The resultant of these two movements imparts to the reflected beam of light a motion similar to that of the pencil of the ordinary indicator, and this can be traced on the sheet of ground glass, or photographed

oxygen: 1. Note: It occurs combined in immense quantities, forming eight ninths by weight of water, and probably one half by weight of the entire solid crust of the globe, being an ingredient of silica, the silicates, sulphates, carbonates, nitrates, etc | 3. Oxygen combines with all elements, forming oxides, bases, oxyacid anhydrides, etc., the process in general being called oxidation, of which combustion is only an intense modification. At ordinary temperatures with most substances it is moderately active, but at higher temperatures it is one of the most violent and powerful chemical agents known. It is indispensable in respiration, and in general is the most universally active and efficient element. It may be prepared in the pure state by heating potassium chlorate. This element was named oxygen by Lavoisier because he supposed it to be a constituent of all acids. This is not so in the case of a very few acids, but these do contain elements analogous to oxygen in property and action. Moreover, the fact that most elements approach the nearer to acid qualities in proportion as they are combined with more oxygen, shows the great accuracy and breadth of Lavoisier's conception of its nature

Garnet berry, the red currant | 2. -- so called from its transparent red color. -- Garnet brown, an artificial dyestuff, produced as an explosive brown crystalline substance with a green or golden luster. Radium was discovered by M. and Mme. Curie, of Paris, who in 1902 separated compounds of it by a tedious process from pitchblende. Its compounds color flames carmine and give a characteristic spectrum. It resembles barium chemically. Radium preparations are remarkable for maintaining themselves at a higher temperature than their surroundings, and for their radiations, which are of three kinds: alpha rays, beta rays, and gamma rays. By reason of these rays they ionize gases, affect photographic plates, cause sores on the skin, and produce many other striking effects. Their degree of activity depends on the proportion of radium present, but not on its state of chemical combination or on external conditions.The radioactivity of radium is therefore an atomic property, and is explained as result from a disintegration of the atom. This breaking up occurs in at least seven stages

had: 1. See Have. Had as lief, Had rather, Had better, Had as soon, etc., with a nominative and followed by the infinitive without to, are well established idiomatic forms. The original construction was that of the dative with forms of be, followed by the infinitive. See Had better, under Better. And lever me is be pore and trewe.  C. Mundi. Him had been lever to be syke.  Fabian. For him was lever have at his bed's head Twenty bookes, clad in black or red, . . . Than robes rich, or fithel, or gay sawtrie. Chaucer. Note: Gradually the nominative was substituted for the dative, and had for the forms of be. During the process of transition, the nominative with was or were, and the dative with had, are found. Poor lady, she were better love a dream. Shak. You were best hang yourself. Beau. & Fl. Me rather had my heart might feel your love Than my unpleased eye see your courtesy. Shak. I hadde levere than my scherte, That ye hadde rad his legende, as have I. Chaucer. I had as lief not be as live to be In awe of such a thing as I myself. Shak. I had rather be a dog and bay the moon, Than such a Roman. Shak. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness. Ps. lxxxiv

Revolt is a casting off the authority of a government, with a view to put it down by force, or to substitute one ruler for another. Rebellion is an extended insurrection and revolt.
