telephotographic: 1. Designating, or pertaining to, the process of telephotography
brushwood: 1. Brush | 2. A thicket or coppice of small trees and shrubs | 3. Small branches of trees cut off
myrobalan: 1. A dried astringent fruit much resembling a prune. It contains tannin, and was formerly used in medicine, but is now chiefly used in tanning and dyeing. Myrobolans are produced by various species of Terminalia of the East Indies, and of Spondias of South America
haunter: 1. One who, or that which, haunts
blackstrap: 1. A mixture of spirituous liquor and molasses. No blackstrap to-night | 2. Switchel, or ginger pop | 3. Judd
goff:
1. A silly clown.  Halliwell.

A game. See Golf.  Halliwell
sned:
1. To lop | 2. To snathe. 

See Snath
balkingly: 1. In manner to balk or frustrate
fainthearted: 1. Wanting in courage | 2. Depressed by fear | 3. Easily discouraged or frightened
extend: 1. To stretch out | 2. To prolong in space | 3. To carry forward or continue in length
island: 1. A tract of land surrounded by water, and smaller than a continent. Cf. Continent | 2. Anything regarded as resembling an island | 3. As, an island of ice
iatromathematical: 1. Of or pertaining to iatromathematicians or their doctrine
incensed: 1. Angered | 2. Enraged | 3. Represented as enraged, as any wild creature depicted with fire issuing from mouth and eyes
plantigrada: 1. A subdivision of Carnivora having plantigrade feet. It includes the bears, raccoons, and allied species
aline: 1. To range or place in a line | 2. To bring into line | 3. To align. Evelyn
can: 1. An obs | 2. Form of began, imp | 3. & p. p. of Begin, sometimes used in old poetry. Note:  With gentle words he can faile gree. Spenser
whitsunday: 1. The seventh Sunday, and the fiftieth day, after Easter | 2. A festival of the church in commemoration of the descent of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost | 3. Pentecost
fairyland: 1. The imaginary land or abode of fairies
metastatic: 1. Of, pertaining to, or caused by, metastasis | 2. As, a metastatic abscess | 3. The metastatic processes of growth
desultoriness: 1. The quality of being desultory or without order or method | 2. Unconnectedness. The seeming desultoriness of my method. Boyle
hyporhachis: 1. The stem of an aftershaft or hypoptilum
erythronium: 1. A name originally given to the metal vanadium
lazyback: 1. A support for the back, attached to the seat of a carriage
restaurateur: 1. The keeper of an eathing house or a restaurant
analemma: 1. An orthographic projection of the sphere on the plane of the meridian, the eye being supposed at an infinite distance, and in the east or west point of the horizon | 2. An instrument of wood or brass, on which this projection of the sphere is made, having a movable horizon or cursor | 3. -- formerly much used in solving some common astronomical problems
burg: 1. A fortified town | 2. A borough.  See 1st Borough
calumniation: 1. False accusation of crime or offense, or a malicious and false representation of the words or actions of another, with a view to injure his good name. The calumniation of her principal counselors. Bacon
mangrove: 1. The name of one or two trees of the genus Rhizophora inhabiting muddy shores of tropical regions, where they spread by emitting aërial roots, which fasten in the saline mire and eventually become new stems. The seeds also send down a strong root while yet attached to the parent plant. Note: The fruit has a ruddy brown shell, and a delicate white pulp which is sweet and eatable. The bark is astringent, and is used for tanning leather. The black and the white mangrove have much the same habit | 2. The mango fish
tetraptote: 1. A noun that has four cases only. Andrews
vestibular: 1. Of or pertaining to a vestibule | 2. Like a vestibule
botuliform: 1. Having the shape of a sausage. Henslow
spooler: 1. One who, or that which, spools
cyma: 1. A member or molding of the cornice, the profile of which is wavelike in form | 2. A cyme. See Cyme. Cyma recta, or Cyma, a cyma, hollow in its upper part and swelling below. -- Cyma reversa, or Ogee, a cyma swelling out on the upper part and hollow below
toff: 1. A fop | 2. A beau | 3. A swell.   Kipling
coloboma: 1. A defect or malformation | 2. Esp., a fissure of the iris supposed to be a persistent embryonic cleft
nitty:
1. Full of nits. B. Jonson.

Shining | 2. Elegant | 3. Spruce.  "O sweet, nitty youth." Marston
trimmer: 1. One who trims, arranges, fits, or ornaments | 2. One who does not adopt extreme opinions in politics, or the like | 3. One who fluctuates between parties, so as to appear to favor each
amazedness: 1. The state of being amazed, or confounded with fear, surprise, or wonder. Bp. Hall
append: 1. To hang or attach to, as by a string, so that the thing is suspended | 2. As, a seal appended to a record | 3. The inscription was appended to the column
housework: 1. The work belonging to housekeeping | 2. Especially, kitchen work, sweeping, scrubbing, bed making, and the like
crotalum: 1. A kind of castanet used by the Corybantes
spotted: 1. Marked with spots | 2. As, a spotted garment or character. "The spotted panther." Spenser. Spotted fever, a name applied to various eruptive fevers, esp | 3. To typhus fever and cerebro-spinal meningitis. -- Spotted tree, an Australian tree
shortage: 1. Amount or extent of deficiency, as determined by some requirement or standard | 2. As, a shortage in money accounts
incivilization: 1. The state of being uncivilized | 2. Want of civilization | 3. Barbarism
powderflask: 1. A flask in which gunpowder is carried, having a charging tube at the end
rasse: 1. A carnivore allied to the civet but smaller, native of China and the East Indies. It furnishes a perfume resembling that of the civet, which is highly prized by the Javanese. Called also Malacca weasel, and lesser civet
rocking: 1. Having a swaying, rolling, or back-and-forth movement | 2. Used for rocking. Rocking shaft. See Rock shaft
receptary:
1. Generally or popularly admitted or received.  Sir T. Browne.

That which is received.  "Receptaries of philosophy." Sir T. Browne
thereafter: 1. After that | 2. Afterward | 3. According to that
inexist: 1. To exist within | 2. To dwell within.  Substances inexisting within the divine mind. A. Tucker
synpelmous: 1. Having the two main flexor tendons of the toes blended together
tormentress: 1. A woman who torments. Fortune ordinarily cometh after to whip and punish them, as the scourge and tormentress of glory and honor. Holland
wonderstruck: 1. Struck with wonder, admiration, or surprise. Dryden
silversmith: 1. One whose occupation is to manufacture utensils, ornaments, etc., of silver | 2. A worker in silver
nares: 1. The nostrils or nasal openings, -- the anterior nares being the external or proper nostrils, and the posterior nares, the openings of the nasal cavities into the mouth or pharynx
subhyoidean: 1. Situated or performed beneath the hyoid bone | 2. As, subhyoidean laryngotomy
mister:
1. A title of courtesy prefixed to the name of a man or youth. It is usually written in the abbreviated form Mr. To call your name, inquire your where, Or whet you think of Mister Some-one's book, Or Mister Other's marriage or decease. Mrs. Browning.

To address or mention by the title Mr | 2. As, he mistered me in a formal way | 3. A trade, art, or occupation.  In youth he learned had a good mester. Chaucer
jeopardize: 1. To expose to loss or injury | 2. To risk | 3. To jeopard. That he should jeopardize his willful head Only for spite at me. H. Taylor
perfection: 1. The quality or state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing requisite is wanting | 2. Entire development | 3. Consummate culture, skill, or moral excellence
vivacity: 1. The quality or state of being vivacious. Specifically: -- Tenacity of life | 2. Vital force | 3. Natural vigor.  The vivacity of some of these pensioners is little less than a miracle, they lived so long. Fuller. Life
forewarn: 1. To warn beforehand | 2. To give previous warning, admonition, information, or notice to | 3. To caution in advance. We were forewarned of your coming. Shak
midweek: 1. The middle of the week. Also used adjectively
cymar: 1. A sight covering | 2. A scarf. See Simar. Her body shaded with a light cymar. Dryden
liquescency: 1. The quality or state of being liquescent. Johnson
flyte: 1. Strife | 2. Dispute | 3. Abusive or upbraiding talk, as in fliting
soot:
1. A black substance formed by combustion, or disengaged from fuel in the process of combustion, which rises in fine particles, and adheres to the sides of the chimney or pipe conveying the smoke | 2. Strictly, the fine powder, consisting chiefly of carbon, which colors smoke, and which is the result of imperfect combustion. See Smoke.

To cover or dress with soot | 3. To smut with, or as with, soot
rationality: 1. The quality or state of being rational | 2. Agreement with reason | 3. Possession of reason
natant: 1. Floating in water, as the leaves of water lilies, or submersed, as those of many aquatic plants | 2. Placed horizontally across the field, as if swimmimg toward the dexter side | 3. Said of all sorts of fishes except the flying fish
estafet: 1. A courier who conveys messages to another courier | 2. A military courier sent from one part of an army to another
inveigle: 1. To lead astray as if blind | 2. To persuade to something evil by deceptive arts or flattery | 3. To entice
intently: 1. In an intent manner | 2. As, the eyes intently fixed. Syn. -- Fixedly | 3. Steadfastly
logos: 1. A word | 2. Reason | 3. Speech. H. Bushell
easter: 1. An annual church festival commemorating Christ's resurrection, and occurring on Sunday, the second day after Good Friday. It corresponds to the pasha or passover of the Jews, and most nations still give it this name under the various forms of pascha, pasque, pâque, or pask | 2. The day on which the festival is observed | 3. Easter day
qualified: 1. Fitted by accomplishments or endowments | 2. Modified | 3. Limited
aphrodisian: 1. Pertaining to Aphrodite or Venus. "Aphrodisian dames" . C. Reade
tolerant: 1. Inclined to tolerate | 2. Favoring toleration | 3. Forbearing
mathematics: 1. That science, or class of sciences, which treats of the exact relations existing between quantities or magnitudes, and of the methods by which, in accordance with these relations, quantities sought are deducible from other quantities known or supposed | 2. The science of spatial and quantitative relations. Note: Mathematics embraces three departments, namely: | 3. Arithmetic
maintop: 1. The platform about the head of the mainmast in square-rigged vessels
phylactery: 1. Any charm or amulet worn as a preservative from danger or disease | 2. A small square box, made either of parchment or of black calfskin, containing slips of parchment or vellum on which are written the scriptural passages Exodus xiii. 2-10, and 11-17, Deut. vi. 4-9, 13- | 3. They are worn by Jews on the head and left arm, on week-day mornings, during the time of prayer. Schaff-Herzog Encyc
incapsulate: 1. To inclose completely, as in a membrane
witing: 1. Knowledge.  "Withouten witing of any other wight." Chaucer
cephalosome: 1. The anterior region or head of insects and other arthropods. Packard
weaver: 1. One who weaves, or whose occupation is to weave. "Weavers of linen." P. Plowman | 2. A weaver bird | 3. An aquatic beetle of the genus Gyrinus. See Whirling. Weaver bird, any one of numerous species of Asiatic, Fast Indian, and African birds belonging to Ploceus and allied genera of the family Ploceidæ. Weaver birds resemble finches and sparrows in size, colors, and shape of the bill. They construct pensile nests composed of interlaced grass and other similar materials. In some of the species the nest is retort-shaped, with the opening at the bottom of the tube. -- Weavers' shuttle, an East Indian marine univalve shell
xylotomist: 1. One versed or engaged in xylotomy
shallow: 1. Not deep | 2. Having little depth | 3. Shoal. "Shallow brooks, and rivers wide." Milton
scarmage: 1. A slight contest | 2. A skirmish. See Skirmish.  Such cruel game my scarmoges disarms. Spenser
aster: 1. A genus of herbs with compound white or bluish flowers | 2. Starwort | 3. Michaelmas daisy
classis: 1. A class or order | 2. Sort | 3. Kind.  His opinion of that classis of men
diagnostic:
1. Pertaining to, or furnishing, a diagnosis | 2. Indicating the nature of a disease.

The mark or symptom by which one disease is known or distinguished from others
smallsword: 1. A light sword used for thrusting only | 2. Especially, the sword worn by civilians of rank in the eighteenth century
sludger:
1. A bucket for removing mud from a bored hole | 2. A sand pump.

A shovel for sludging out drains, etc
foreshorten: 1. To represent on a plane surface, as if extended in a direction toward the spectator or nearly so | 2. To shorten by drawing in perspective | 3. Fig.: To represent pictorially to the imagination. Songs, and deeds, and lives that lie Foreshortened in the tract of time. Tennyson
smuggler: 1. One who smuggles | 2. A vessel employed in smuggling
terete: 1. Cylindrical and slightly tapering | 2. Columnar, as some stems of plants
attenuation: 1. The act or process of making slender, or the state of being slender | 2. Emaciation | 3. The act of attenuating
magenta: 1. An aniline dye obtained as an amorphous substance having a green bronze surface color, which dissolves to a shade of red | 2. Also, the color | 3. -- so called from Magenta, in Italy, in allusion to the battle fought there about the time the dye was discovered. Called also fuchsine, roseïne, etc
detectable: 1. Capable of being detected or found out | 2. As, parties not detectable. "Errors detectible at a glance." Latham
quizzism: 1. The act or habit of quizzing
drub:
1. To beat with a stick | 2. To thrash | 3. To cudgel. Soundly Drubbed with a good honest cudgel. L'Estrange.

A blow with a cudgel
wafer: 1. A thin cake made of flour and other ingredients. Wafers piping hot out of the gleed. Chaucer. The curious work in pastry, the fine cakes, wafers, and marchpanes. Holland. A woman's oaths are wafers -- break with making B. Jonson | 2. A thin cake or piece of bread used in the Eucharist, as in the Roman Catholic Church | 3. An adhesive disk of dried paste, made of flour, gelatin, isinglass, or the like, and coloring matter, -- used in sealing letters and other documents. Wafer cake, a sweet, thin cake. Shak. -- Wafer irons, or Wafer tongs, a pincher-shaped contrivance, having flat plates, or blades, between which wafers are baked. -- Wafer woman, a woman who sold wafer cakes
posting: 1. The act of traveling post | 2. The act of transferring an account, as from the journal to the ledger. Posting house, a post house
outfitter: 1. One who furnishes outfits for a voyage, a journey, or a business
profundity: 1. The quality or state of being profound | 2. Depth of place, knowledge, feeling, etc | 3. "The vast profundity obscure." Milton
aqua: 1. Water | 2. -- a word much used in pharmacy and the old chemistry, in various signification, determined by the word or words annexed. Aqua ammoniæ, the aqueous solution of ammonia | 3. Liquid ammonia
tryster: 1. One who makes an appointment, or tryst | 2. One who meets with another
supercilium: 1. The eyebrow, or the region of the eyebrows
blore: 1. The act of blowing | 2. A roaring wind | 3. A blast.  A most tempestuous blore. Chapman
ten: 1. One more than nine | 2. Twice five. With twice ten sail I crossed the Phrygian Sea. Dryden. Note: Ten is often used, indefinitely, for several, many, and other like words. There 's proud modesty in merit, Averse from begging, and resolved to pay Ten times the gift it asks. Dryden | 3. The number greater by one than nine
lister:
1. A spear armed with three or more prongs, for striking fish. 

One who makes a list or roll.

Same as Leister
mouth: 1. The opening through which an animal receives food | 2. The aperture between the jaws or between the lips | 3. Also, the cavity, containing the tongue and teeth, between the lips and the pharynx
bilboquet: 1. The toy called cup and ball
caned: 1. Filled with white flakes | 2. Mothery | 3. -- said vinegar when containing mother.  Halliwell
incompetent: 1. Not competent | 2. Wanting in adequate strength, power, capacity, means, qualifications, or the like | 3. Incapable
purl: 1. To decorate with fringe or embroidery. "Nature's cradle more enchased and purled." B. Jonson | 2. An embroidered and puckered border | 3. A hem or fringe, often of gold or silver twist
positive: 1. Having a real position, existence, or energy | 2. Existing in fact | 3. Real
attagen: 1. A species of sand grouse found in Asia and rarely in southern Europe
mise: 1. The issue in a writ of right | 2. Expense | 3. Cost
brawl: 1. To quarrel noisily and outrageously. Let a man that is a man consider that he is a fool that brawleth openly with his wife. Golden Boke | 2. To complain loudly | 3. To scold
parrel: 1. The rope or collar by which a yard or spar is held to the mast in such a way that it may be hoisted or lowered at pleasure. Totten | 2. A chimney-piece. Halliwell
equator: 1. The imaginary great circle on the earth's surface, everywhere equally distant from the two poles, and dividing the earth's surface into two hemispheres | 2. The great circle of the celestial sphere, coincident with the plane of the earth's equator | 3. -- so called because when the sun is in it, the days and nights are of equal length
ambush: 1. A disposition or arrangement of troops for attacking an enemy unexpectedly from a concealed station. Hence: Unseen peril | 2. A device to entrap | 3. A snare. Heaven, whose high walls fear no assault or siege Or ambush from the deep. Milton
ephod: 1. A part of the sacerdotal habit among Jews, being a covering for the back and breast, held together on the shoulders by two clasps or brooches of onyx stones set in gold, and fastened by a girdle of the same stuff as the ephod. The ephod for the priests was of plain linen | 2. That for the high priest was richly embroidered in colors. The breastplate of the high priest was worn upon the ephod in front. Exodus xxviii. 6-
dijudicate: 1. To make a judicial decision | 2. To decide | 3. To determine.  Hales
swimming: 1. That swims | 2. Capable of swimming | 3. Adapted to, or used in, swimming
revealability: 1. The quality or state of being revealable | 2. Revealableness
crustation: 1. An adherent crust | 2. An incrustation. Pepys
ruination: 1. The act of ruining, or the state of being ruined
windrow:
1. A row or line of hay raked together for the purpose of being rolled into cocks or heaps | 2. Sheaves of grain set up in a row, one against another, that the wind may blow between them | 3. The green border of a field, dug up in order to carry the earth on other land to mend it. 

To arrange in lines or windrows, as hay when newly made. Forby
acquaint: 1. Acquainted | 2. To furnish or give experimental knowledge of | 3. To make to know
grangerism: 1. The practice of illustrating a particular book by engravings collected from other books
hylozoism: 1. The doctrine that matter possesses a species of life and sensation, or that matter and life are inseparable.  Cudworth
risen: 1. P. & a. from Rise. "Her risen Son and Lord." Keble | 2. Obs. imp | 3. Pl. of Rise. Chaucer
merlon: 1. One of the solid parts of a battlemented parapet | 2. A battlement. See Illust. of Battlement
vitelline: 1. Of or pertaining to the yolk of eggs | 2. As, the vitelline membrane, a smooth, transparent membrane surrounding the vitellus
ferric: 1. Pertaining to, derived from, or containing iron. Specifically, denoting those compounds in which iron has a higher valence than in the ferrous compounds | 2. As, ferric oxide | 3. Ferric acid. Ferric acid, an acid, H2FeO4, which is not known in the free state, but forms definite salts, analogous to the chromates and sulphates. -- Ferric oxide, sesquioxide of iron, Fe2O3
intelligential: 1. Of or pertaining to the intelligence | 2. Exercising or implying understanding | 3. Intellectual. "With act intelligential." Milton
adamantine: 1. Made of adamant, or having the qualities of adamant | 2. Incapable of being broken, dissolved, or penetrated | 3. As, adamantine bonds or chains
tiling: 1. A surface covered with tiles, or composed of tiles. They . . . let him down through the tiling. Luke v | 2. Tiles, collectively
gula: 1. The upper front of the neck, next to the chin | 2. The upper throat. A plate which in most insects supports the submentum | 3. A capping molding. Same as Cymatium
puncticular: 1. Comprised in, or like, a point | 2. Exact.  Sir T. Browne
despeed: 1. To send hastily.  Despeeded certain of their crew. Speed
weeder: 1. One who, or that which, weeds, or frees from anything noxious
moonglade: 1. The bright reflection of the moon's light on an expanse of water
grasper: 1. One who grasps or seizes | 2. One who catches or holds
presentiality: 1. State of being actually present.  South
valetudinous: 1. Valetudinarian.  "The valetudinous condition of King Edward." Fuller
primigenous: 1. First formed or generated | 2. Original | 3. Primigenial. Bp. Hall
paxwax: 1. The strong ligament of the back of the neck in quadrupeds. It connects the back of the skull with dorsal spines of the cervical vertebræ, and helps to support the head. Called also paxywaxy and packwax
manteau: 1. A woman's cloak or mantle | 2. A gown worn by women
pitheci: 1. A division of mammals including the apes and monkeys. Sometimes used in the sense of Primates
magnificent: 1. Doing grand things | 2. Admirable in action | 3. Displaying great power or opulence, especially in building, way of living, and munificence. A prince is never so magnificent As when he's sparing to enrich a few With the injuries of many. Massinger
strabismus: 1. An affection of one or both eyes, in which the optic axes can not be directed to the same object, -- a defect due either to undue contraction or to undue relaxation of one or more of the muscles which move the eyeball | 2. Squinting | 3. Cross-eye
triumvir: 1. One of tree men united in public office or authority. Note: In later times the triumvirs of Rome were three men who jointly exercised sovereign power. Julius Cæsar, Crassus, and Pompey were the first triumvirs | 2. Octavianus, Antony, and Lepidus were the second and last
ettle: 1. To earn.  See Addle, to earn. Boucher
innixion: 1. Act of leaning upon something | 2. Incumbency.  Derham
this: 1. As a demonstrative pronoun, this denotes something that is present or near in place or time, or something just mentioned, or that is just about to be mentioned. When they heard this, they were pricked in their heart. Acts ii | 2. But know this, that if the good man of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched. Matt. xxiv | 3. As an adjective, this has the same demonstrative force as the pronoun, but is followed by a noun
misstep:
1. A wrong step | 2. An error of conduct.

To take a wrong step | 3. To go astray
superjacent: 1. Situated immediately above | 2. As, superjacent rocks
achlamydate: 1. Not possessing a mantle | 2. -- said of certain gastropods
relieving: 1. Serving or tending to relieve. Relieving arch, a discharging arch. See under Discharge, v. t. -- Relieving tackle. A temporary tackle attached to the tiller of a vessel during gales or an action, in case of accident to the tiller ropes. A strong tackle from a wharf to a careened vessel, to prevent her from going over entirely, and to assist in righting her | 2. Totten. Craig
immanence: 1. The condition or quality of being immanent | 2. Inherence | 3. An indwelling.  is mainly concerned in enforcing the immanence of God. Christ is everywhere presented by him as Deity indwelling in the world. A. V. G. Allen
serrifera: 1. A division of Hymenoptera comprising the sawflies
verine: 1. An alkaloid obtained as a yellow amorphous substance by the decomposition of veratrine
cops: 1. The connecting crook of a harrow
unsay: 1. To recant or recall, as what has been said | 2. To refract | 3. To take back again
abolitionism: 1. The principles or measures of abolitionists. Wilberforce
costiveness: 1. An unnatural retention of the fecal matter of the bowels | 2. Constipation | 3. Inability to express one's self
intime: 1. Inward | 2. Internal | 3. Intimate.  Sir K. Digby
invisibility: 1. The state or quality of being invisible | 2. Also, that which is invisible. "Atoms and invisibilities." Landor
underlying: 1. Lying under or beneath | 2. Hence, fundamental | 3. As, the underlying strata of a locality
deprivation: 1. The act of depriving, dispossessing, or bereaving | 2. The act of deposing or divesting of some dignity | 3. The state of being deprived
miscreancy: 1. The quality of being miscreant | 2. Adherence to a false religion | 3. False faith.  Ayliffe
plagiocephaly: 1. Oblique lateral deformity of the skull
quacksalver: 1. One who boasts of his skill in medicines and salves, or of the efficacy of his prescriptions | 2. A charlatan | 3. A quack
cyamelide: 1. A white amorphous substance, regarded as a polymeric modification of isocyanic acid
herr: 1. A title of respect given to gentlemen in Germany, equivalent to the English Mister
gigue: 1. A piece of lively dance music, in two strains which are repeated | 2. Also, the dance
inheritable: 1. Capable of being inherited | 2. Transmissible or descendible | 3. As, an inheritable estate or title. Blackstone
infraposition: 1. A situation or position beneath. Kane
parmesan: 1. Of or pertaining to Parma in Italy. Parmesan cheese, a kind of cheese of a rich flavor, though from skimmed milk, made in Parma, Italy
enucleate: 1. To bring or peel out, as a kernel from its enveloping husks its enveloping husks or shell | 2. To remove without cutting | 3. To bring to light
siesta: 1. A short sleep taken about the middle of the day, or after dinner | 2. A midday nap
conjurement: 1. Serious injunction | 2. Solemn demand or entreaty.  Milton
domesticate: 1. To make domestic | 2. To habituate to home life | 3. As, to domesticate one's self
topical: 1. Of or pertaining to a place | 2. Limited | 3. Logical application
morus: 1. A genus of trees, some species of which produce edible fruit | 2. The mulberry. See Mulberry. Note: Morus alba is the white mulberry, a native of India or China, the leaves of which are extensively used for feeding silkworms, for which it furnishes the chief food. -- Morus multicaulis, the many-stemmed or Chinese mulberry, is only a form of white mulberry, preferred on account of its more abundant leaves. -- Morus nigra, the black mulberry, produces a dark-colored fruit, of an agreeable flavor
disinthrallment: 1. A releasing from thralldom or slavery | 2. Disenthrallment
denounce: 1. To make known in a solemn or official manner | 2. To declare | 3. To proclaim.  Denouncing wrath to come. Milton. I denounce unto you this day, that ye shall surely perish. Deut. xxx
embracery: 1. An attempt to influence a court, jury, etc., corruptly, by promises, entreaties, money, entertainments, threats, or other improper inducements
rant:
1. To rave in violent, high-sounding, or extravagant language, without dignity of thought | 2. To be noisy, boisterous, and bombastic in talk or declamation | 3. As, a ranting preacher. Look where my ranting host of the Garter comes! Shak.

High-sounding language, without importance or dignity of thought
subsphenoidal: 1. Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the body of the sphenoid bone
malapropism: 1. A grotesque misuse of a word | 2. A word so used
stillhouse: 1. A house in which distillation is carried on | 2. A distillery
rimple:
1. A fold or wrinkle. See Rumple.

To rumple | 2. To wrinkle
crafty: 1. Relating to, or characterized by, craft or skill | 2. Dexterous.  "Crafty work." Piers Plowman | 3. Possessing dexterity
zinnia: 1. Any plant of the composite genus Zinnia, Mexican herbs with opposite leaves and large gay-colored blossoms. Zinnia elegans is the commonest species in cultivation
conclavist: 1. One of the two ecclesiastics allowed to attend a cardinal in the conclave
landscape: 1. A portion of land or territory which the eye can comprehend in a single view, including all the objects it contains | 2. To change by introducing novelties

1. To concert or arrange beforehand | 2. To settle by previous agreement.

The earth that casteth up from the plow a great clod, is not so good as that which casteth up a smaller clod. Bacon | 2. The ground | 3. The earth
orthoceratite: 1. An orthoceras | 2. Also, any fossil shell allied to Orthoceras
ejector: 1. One who, or that which, ejects or dispossesses | 2. A jet jump for lifting water or withdrawing air from a space. Ejector condenser, a condenser in which the vacuum is maintained by a jet pump
gangliform: 1. Having the form of a ganglion
colonist: 1. A member or inhabitant of a colony
vilayet: 1. One of the chief administrative divisions or provinces of the Ottoman Empire | 2. -- formerly called eyalet
dairymaid: 1. A female servant whose business is the care of the dairy
scratcher: 1. One who, or that which, scratches | 2. Specifically, any rasorial bird
shuttle: 1. An instrument used in weaving for passing or shooting the thread of the woof from one side of the cloth to the other between the threads of the warp. Like shuttles through the loom, so swiftly glide My feathered hours. Sandys | 2. The sliding thread holder in a sewing machine, which carries the lower thread through a loop of the upper thread, to make a lock stitch | 3. A shutter, as for a channel for molten metal.  Shuttle box, a case at the end of a shuttle race, to receive the shuttle after it has passed the thread of the warp
immorality: 1. The state or quality of being immoral | 2. Vice. The root of all immorality. Sir W. Temple | 3. An immoral act or practice. Luxury and sloth and then a great drove of heresies and immoralities broke loose among them. Milton
subrogation: 1. The act of subrogating. Specifically:  The substitution of one person in the place of another as a creditor, the new creditor succeeding to the rights of the former | 2. kendal: 1. A cloth colored green by dye obtained from the woad-waxen, formerly used by Flemish weavers at Kendal, in Westmoreland, England. J. Smith. How couldst thou know these men in Kendal green Shak
shearer: 1. One who shears. Like a lamb dumb before his shearer. Acts viii | 2. A reaper.  Jamieson
seemly: 1. Suited to the object, occasion, purpose, or character | 2. Suitable | 3. Fit
incrassate: 1. To make thick or thicker | 2. To thicken | 3. Especially, in pharmacy, to thicken by the mixture of another substance, or by evaporating the thinner parts. Acids dissolve or attenuate
peristyle: 1. A range of columns with their entablature, etc | 2. Specifically, a complete system of columns, whether on all sides of a court, or surrounding a building, such as the cella of a temple. taking: 1. Apt to take | 2. Alluring | 3. Attracting. Subtile in making his temptations most taking. Fuller
trivalve: 1. Anything having three valves, especially a shell
panurgic: 1. Skilled in all kinds of work. "The panurgic Diderot." J. Morley
tipple: 1. To drink spirituous or strong liquors habitually | 2. To indulge in the frequent and improper used of spirituous liquors | 3. Especially, to drink frequently in small quantities, but without absolute drunkeness. Few of those who were summoned left their homes, and those few generally found it more agreeable to tipple in alehouses than to pace the streets. Macaulay
writative: 1. Inclined to much writing | 2. -- correlative to talkative.  Pope
carucate: 1. A plowland | 2. As much land as one team can plow in a year and a day | 3. -- by some said to be about 100 acres. Burrill
shiner: 1. That which shines. Specifically: A luminary. A bright piece of money.  Has she the shiners, d' ye think Foote. black eye | 2. Any one of numerous species of small freshwater American cyprinoid fishes, belonging to Notropis, or Minnilus, and allied genera | 3. As the redfin, and the golden shiner of the Eastern United States
slope: 1. An oblique direction | 2. A line or direction including from a horizontal line or direction | 3. Also, sometimes, an inclination, as of one line or surface to another
leontodon: 1. A genus of liguliflorous composite plants, including the fall dandelion, and formerly the true dandelion | 2. -- called also lion's tooth
autophony: 1. An auscultatory process, which consists in noting the tone of the observer's own voice, while he speaks, holding his head close to the patient's chest. Dunglison
thallus: 1. A solid mass of cellular tissue, consisting of one or more layers, usually in the form of a flat stratum or expansion, but sometimes erect or pendulous, and elongated and branching, and forming the substance of the thallogens
isoperimetry: 1. The science of figures having equal perimeters or boundaries
lactobutyrometer: 1. An instrument for determining the amount of butter fat contained in a given sample of milk
separate: 1. To disunite | 2. To divide | 3. To disconnect
interpubic: 1. Between the pubic bones or cartilages | 2. As, the interpubic disk
pavonine: 1. Like, or pertaining to, the genus Pavo | 2. Characteristic of a peacock | 3. Resembling the tail of a peacock, as in colors
volti: 1. Turn, that is, turn over the leaf. Volti subito Etym:, turn over quickly
photochemical: 1. Of or pertaining to chemical action of light, or produced by it | 2. As, the photochemical changes of the visual purple of the retina
prolicide: 1. The crime of destroying one's offspring, either in the womb or after birth. Bouvier

evincement: 1. The act of evincing or proving, or the state of being evinced
kernel: 1. The essential part of a seed | 2. All that is within the seed walls | 3. The edible substance contained in the shell of a nut
blindness: 1. State or condition of being blind, literally or figuratively. Darwin. Color blindness, inability to distinguish certain color. See Daltonism
polander: 1. A native or inhabitant of Poland | 2. A Pole
anabranch: 1. A branch of a river that reënters, or anastomoses with, the main stream | 2. Also, less properly, a branch which loses itself in sandy soil.  Such branches of a river as after separation reunite, I would term anastomosing branches | 3. Or, if a word might be coined, anabranches, and the islands they form branch islands. Col. Jackson
fast: 1. To abstain from food | 2. To omit to take nourishment in whole or in part | 3. To go hungry. Fasting he went to sleep, and fasting waked. Milton
clangous: 1. Making a clang, or a ringing metallic sound
heartener: 1. One who, or that which, heartens, animates, or stirs up. W. Browne
garniture: 1. That which garnishes | 2. Ornamental appendage | 3. Embellishment

sauerkraut: 1. Cabbage cut fine and allowed to ferment in a brine made of its own juice with salt, -- a German dish
safely: 1. In a safe manner | 2. Danger, injury, loss, or evil consequences
conicalness: 1. State or quality of being conical
spatial: 1. Of or pertaining to space. "Spatial quantity and relations." L. H. Atwater

fossane: 1. A species of civet resembling the genet
neuron: 1. The brain and spinal cord | 2. The cerebro-spinal axis | 3. Myelencephalon. B. G. Wilder
arthrodynia: 1. An affection characterized by pain in or about a joint, not dependent upon structural disease

prick: 1. That which pricks, penetrates, or punctures | 2. A sharp and slender thing | 3. A pointed instrument

liberate: 1. To release from restraint or bondage | 2. To set at liberty | 3. To free

It is sometimes found native, but usually combined with silver, cobalt, nickel, iron, antimony, or sulphur. Orpiment and realgar are two of its sulphur compounds, the first of which is the true arsenticum of the ancients. The element and its compounds are active poisons. Specific gravity from | 2. 7 to | 3. Atomic weight. Symbol As
gutwort: 1. A plant, Globularia Alypum, a violent purgative, found in Africa
exceptioner: 1. One who takes exceptions or makes objections.  Milton
trapeze: 1. A trapezium. See Trapezium, | 2. A swinging horizontal bar, suspended at each end by a rope | 3. -- used by gymnasts
coleperch: 1. A kind of small black perch
frenzied: 1. Affected with frenzy | 2. Frantic | 3. Maddened. -- Fren"zied-ly, adv
extrusive: 1. Forced out at the surface | 2. As, extrusive rocks | 3. -- contrasted with intrusive
clubbish: 1. Rude | 2. Clownish | 3. Disposed to club together
cisleithan: 1. On the Austrian side of the river Leitha | 2. Austrian
ametropia: 1. Any abnormal condition of the refracting powers of the eye | 2. -- Am`e*trop"ic, a
tralatitiously: 1. , adv | 2. In a tralatitious manner | 3. Metephorically. Holder
tuner: 1. One who tunes | 2. Especially, one whose occupation is to tune musical instruments
ultroneous: 1. Spontaneous | 2. Voluntary.  Jer. Taylor. -- Ul*tro"ne*ous*ly, adv | 3. -- Ul*tro"ne*ous*ness, n
decision: 1. Cutting off | 2. Division | 3. Detachment of a part.  Bp. Pearson
taskwork: 1. Work done as a task | 2. Also, work done by the job | 3. Piecework
malkin: 1. Originally, a kitchenmaid | 2. A slattern. Chaucer | 3. A mop made of clouts, used by the kitchen servant

sonant: 1. Of or pertaining to sound | 2. Sounding | 3. Uttered, as an element of speech, with tone or proper vocal sound, as distinguished from mere breath sound
paralogism: 1. A reasoning which is false in point of form, that is, which is contrary to logical rules or formulæ | 2. A formal fallacy, or pseudo- syllogism, in which the conclusion does not follow from the premises
femme: 1. A woman. See Feme, n. Femme de chambre. Etym:  A lady's maid | 2. A chambermaid

photozincography: 1. A process, analogous to photolithography, for reproducing photographed impressions transferred to zinc plate

alatern: 1. An ornamental evergreen shrub belonging to the buckthorns
kinepox: 1. See Cowpox. Kin"e*scope (, n.  See Kinetoscope

commencement: 1. The first existence of anything | 2. Act or fact of commencing | 3. Rise

interfusion: 1. The act of interfusing, or the state of being interfused. Coleridge

apocalyptic:
1. Of or pertaining to a revelation, or, specifically, to the Revelation of St. John | 2. Containing, or of the nature of, a prophetic revelation. Apocolyptic number, the number 666, mentioned in Rev. xiii | 3. It has been variously interpreted.

The writer of the Apocalypse
interviewer: 1. One who interviews | 2. Especially, one who obtains an interview with another for the purpose of eliciting his opinions or obtaining information for publication. It would have made him the prince of interviewers in these days. Leslie Stephen
corsak: 1. A small foxlike mammal, found in Central Asia
redfish: 1. The blueback salmon of the North Pacific | 2. -- called also nerka. See Blueback.. The rosefish. A large California labroid food fish | 3. -- called also fathead. The red bass, red drum, or drumfish. See the Note under Drumfish
carbonatation: 1. The saturation of defecated beet juice with carbonic acid gas | 2. Knight
trimyarian: 1. A lamellibranch which has three muscular scars on each valve
rhopalic: 1. Applied to a line or verse in which each successive word has one more syllable than the preceding

lengthiness: 1. The state or quality of being lengthy | 2. Prolixity
impersonate: 1. To invest with personality | 2. To endow with the form of a living being | 3. To ascribe the qualities of a person to
uppertendom: 1. The highest class in society | 2. The upper ten | 3. See Upper ten, under Upper
bristol: 1. A seaport city in the west of England. Bristol board, a kind of fine pasteboard, made with a smooth but usually unglazed surface. -- Bristol brick, a brick of siliceous matter used for polishing cultery | 2. -- originally manufactured at Bristol. -- Bristol stone, rock crystal, or brilliant crystals of quartz, found in the mountain limestone near Bristol, and used in making ornaments, vases, etc | 3. When polished, it is called Bristol diamond
wishedly: 1. According to wish | 2. Conformably to desire.  Chapman
mnemosyne: 1. The goddess of memory and the mother of the Muses

A small discolored place in or on anything, or a small place of a color different from that of the main substance

desquamative: 1. Of, pertaining to, or attended with, desquamation

imposthume:
1. A collection of pus or purulent matter in any part of an animal body | 2. An abscess.

Same as Imposthumate
subtilty: 1. The quality or state of being subtile | 2. Thinness | 3. Fineness
underthing: 1. Something that is inferior and of little worth.  Beau. & Fl

A solid figure generated by the revolution of an ellipse about one of its axes. It is called a prolate spheroid, or prolatum, when the ellipse is revolved about the major axis, and an oblate spheroid, or oblatum, when it is revolved about the minor axis.

Upon the whole, it will be necessary to avoid that perpetual repetition of the same epithets which we find in Homer. Pope. He had abandoned the frontiers, retiring upon Glasgow. Sir. W. Scott. Wheat is not known to exist as a wild native plant, and all statements as to its origin are either incorrect or at best only guesses. Buck wheat. See Buckwheat. -- German wheat. See 2d Spelt. -- Guinea wheat, a name for Indian corn. -- Indian wheat, or Tartary wheat, a grain much like buckwheat, but only half as large. -- Turkey wheat, a name for Indian corn. -- Wheat aphid, or Wheat aphis, any one of several species of Aphis and allied genera, which suck the sap of growing wheat. -- Wheat beetle. A very small, reddish brown, oval beetle whose larvæ eat the interior of grains of wheat. -- Wheat duck, the American widgeon.  -- Wheat fly | 2. Same as Wheat midge, below. -- Wheat grass, a kind of grass somewhat resembling wheat. It grows in the northern parts of Europe and America. -- Wheat jointworm. See Jointworm. -- Wheat louse, any wheat aphid. -- Wheat maggot, the larva of a wheat midge. -- Wheat midge. A small two-winged fly which is very destructive to growing wheat, both in Europe and America. The female lays her eggs in the flowers of wheat, and the larvæ suck the juice of the young kernels and when full grown change to pupæ in the earth. The Hessian fly | 3. See under Hessian. -- Wheat moth, any moth whose larvæ devour the grains of wheat, chiefly after it is harvested

horse: 1. A hoofed quadruped of the genus Equus | 2. Especially, the domestic horse, which was domesticated in Egypt and Asia at a very early period. It has six broad molars, on each side of each jaw, with six incisors, and two canine teeth, both above and below. The mares usually have the canine teeth rudimentary or wanting. The horse differs from the true asses, in having a long, flowing mane, and the tail bushy to the base. Unlike the asses it has callosities, or chestnuts, on all its legs. The horse excels in strength, speed, docility, courage, and nobleness of character, and is used for drawing, carrying, bearing a rider, and like purposes. Note: Many varieties, differing in form, size, color, gait, speed, etc., are known, but all are believed to have been derived from the same original species. It is supposed to have been a native of the plains of Central Asia, but the wild species from which it was derived is not certainly known. The feral horses of America are domestic horses that have run wild | 3. And it is probably true that most of those of Asia have a similar origin. Some of the true wild Asiatic horses do, however, approach the domestic horse in several characteristics. Several species of fossil are known from the later Tertiary formations of Europe and America. The fossil species of other genera of the family Equidæ are also often called horses, in general sense

1. This word is properly an adjective, but is commonly called the indefinite article. It is used before nouns of the singular number only, and signifies one, or any, but somewhat less emphatically. Note: An is used before a word beginning with a vowel sound | 2. As, an enemy, an hour. It in also often used before h sounded, when the accent of the word falls on the second syllable | 3. As, an historian, an hyena, an heroic deed. Many writers use a before h in such positions. Anciently an was used before consonants as well as vowels.

mastodon: 1. An extinct genus of mammals closely allied to the elephant, but having less complex molar teeth, and often a pair of lower, as well as upper, tusks, which are incisor teeth. The species were mostly larger than elephants, and their romains occur in nearly all parts of the world in deposits ranging from Miocene to late Quaternary time
than: 1. A particle expressing comparison, used after certain adjectives and adverbs which express comparison or diversity, as more, better, other, otherwise, and the like. It is usually followed by the object compared in the nominative case. Sometimes, however, the object compared is placed in the objective case, and than is then considered by some grammarians as a preposition. Sometimes the object is expressed in a sentence, usually introduced by that | 2. As, I would rather suffer than that you should want. Behold, a greater than Solomon is here. Matt. xii | 3. Which when Beelzebub perceived, than whom, Satan except, none higher sat
descensory: 1. A vessel used in alchemy to extract oils
polemoscope: 1. An opera glass or field glass with an oblique mirror arranged for seeing objects do not lie directly before the eye | 2. -- called also diagonal, or side, opera glass
syntonin: 1. A proteid substance formed from the albuminous matter of muscle by the action of dilute acids | 2. -- formerly called musculin. See Acid albumin, under Albumin
apron: 1. An article of dress, of cloth, leather, or other stuff, worn on the fore part of the body, to keep the clothes clean, to defend them from injury, or as a covering. It is commonly tied at the waist by strings | 2. Something which by its shape or use suggests an apron | 3. As, The fat skin covering the belly of a goose or duck.  Halliwell. A piece of leather, or other material, to be spread before a person riding on an outside seat of a vehicle, to defend him from the rain, snow, or dust
endemiology: 1. The science which treats of endemic affections
livingly: 1. In a living state. Sir T. Browne
telemetrograph: 1. A combination of the camera lucida and telescope for drawing and measuring distant objects. -- Tel`e*me*trog"ra*phy, n. -- Tel`e*met`ro*graph"ic, a
totemic: 1. Of or pertaining to a totem, or totemism
rideau: 1. A small mound of earth | 2. Ground slightly elevated | 3. A small ridge
morulation: 1. The process of cleavage, or segmentation, of the ovum, by which a morula is formed
hematinon: 1. A red consisting of silica, borax, and soda, fused with oxide of copper and iron, and used in enamels, mosaics, etc
swelling: 1. The act of that which swells | 2. As, the swelling of rivers in spring | 3. The swelling of the breast with pride. Rise to the swelling of the voiceless sea
osteology: 1. The science which treats of the bones of the vertebrate skeleton
foliar: 1. Consisting of, or pertaining to, leaves | 2. As, foliar appendages. Foliar gap, an opening in the fibrovascular system of a stem at the point of origin of a leaf. -- Foliar trace, a particular fibrovascular bundle passing down into the stem from a leaf
kingtruss: 1. A truss, framed with a king-post | 2. -- used in roofs, bridges, etc
aaronical: 1. Pertaining to Aaron, the first high priest of the Jews. AARON'S ROD Aar"on's rod`. Etym: [See Exodus vii | 2. 9 and Numbers xvii. 8] | 3. A rod with one serpent twined around it, thus differing from the caduceus of Mercury, which has two
cureall: 1. A remedy for all diseases, o
graduate: 1. To mark with degrees | 2. To divide into regular steps, grades, or intervals, as the scale of a thermometer, a scheme of punishment or rewards, etc | 3. To admit or elevate to a certain grade or degree
multiplication: 1. The act or process of multiplying, or of increasing in number | 2. The state of being multiplied | 3. As, the multiplication of the human species by natural generation. The increase and multiplication of the world. Thackeray
ulna: 1. The postaxial bone of the forearm, or branchium, corresponding to the fibula of the hind limb. See Radius | 2. An ell | 3. Also, a yard. Burrill
transfiguration: 1. A change of form or appearance | 2. Especially, the supernatural change in the personal appearance of our Savior on the mount | 3. A feast held by some branches of the Christian church on the 6th of August, in commemoration of the miraculous change above mentioned
caladium: 1. A genus of aroideous plants, of which some species are cultivated for their immense leaves, and others for food
ceroplastics: 1. The art of modeling in wax
dejeration: 1. The act of swearing solemnly.  Bp. Hall
exemptitious: 1. Separable.  "Exemptitious from matter." Dr. H. More
recompense: 1. To render an equivalent to, for service, loss, etc | 2. To requite | 3. To remunerate
tensity: 1. The quality or state of being tense, or strained to stiffness | 2. Tension | 3. Tenseness
herculean: 1. Requiring the strength of Hercules | 2. Hence, very great, difficult, or dangerous | 3. As, an Herculean task
pterosauria: 1. An extinct order of flying reptiles of the Mesozoic age | 2. The pterodactyls | 3. -- called also Pterodactyli, and Ornithosauria. Note: The wings were formed, like those of bats, by a leathery expansion of the skin, principally supported by the greatly enlarged outer or " little" fingers of the hands. The American Cretaceous pterodactyls had no teeth. See Pteranodontia, and Pterodactyl
centesimo: 1. A copper coin of Italy and Spain equivalent to a centime
consecration: 1. The act or ceremony of consecrating | 2. The state of being consecrated | 3. Dedication. Until the days of your consecration be at an end
electrographic: 1. Of or pertaining to an electrograph or electrography
convincible: 1. Capable of being convinced or won over | 2. Capable of being confuted and disproved by argument | 3. Refutable.  Sir T. Browne
thornbird: 1. A small South American bird allied to the ovenbirds of the genus Furnarius). It builds a very large and complex nest of twigs and thorns in a bush or tree
flabile: 1. Liable to be blown about. Bailey
epicondyle: 1. A projection on the inner side of the distal end of the numerus | 2. The internal condyle
deadness: 1. The state of being destitute of life, vigor, spirit, activity, etc | 2. Dullness | 3. Inertness
lacturamic: 1. Pertaining to, or designating, an organic amido acid, which is regarded as a derivative of lactic acid and urea
seron: 1. Same as Ceroon. Note: This word as expressing a quantity or weight has no definite signification. McElrath
bolognian: 1. Bolognese. Bolognian stone. See Bologna stone, under Bologna
asbestic: 1. Of, pertaining to, or resembling asbestus | 2. Inconsumable | 3. Asbestine
degerm: 1. To extract the germs from, as from wheat grains
syrtic: 1. Of or pertaining to a syrt | 2. Resembling syrt, or quicksand.  Ed. Rev
devolvement: 1. The act or process of devolving | 2. Devolution
actinic: 1. Of or pertaining to actinism | 2. As, actinic rays
constructional: 1. Pertaining to, or deduced from, construction or interpretation
driftage: 1. Deviation from a ship's course due to leeway | 2. Anything that drifts
calendrical: 1. Of or pertaining to a calendar
phosphatic: 1. Pertaining to, or containing, phosphorus, phosphoric acid, or phosphates | 2. As, phosphatic nodules. Phosphatic diathesis, a habit of body which leads to the undue excretion of phosphates with the urine
ecclesiastically: 1. In an ecclesiastical manner | 2. According ecclesiastical rules
syrinx: 1. A wind instrument made of reeds tied together | 2. -- called also pandean pipes | 3. The lower larynx in birds. Note: In birds there are two laringes, an upper or true, but voiceless, larynx in the usual position behind the tongue, and a lower one, at or near the junction of the trachea and bronchi, which is the true organ of the voice
reduce: 1. To bring or lead back to any former place or condition.  And to his brother's house reduced his wife. Chapman. The sheep must of necessity be scattered, unless the great Shephered of souls oppose, or some of his delegates reduce and direct us. Evelyn | 2. To bring to any inferior state, with respect to rank, size, quantity, quality, value, etc | 3. To diminish
supplicate: 1. To entreat for | 2. To seek by earnest prayer | 3. To ask for earnestly and humbly
zeitgeist: 1. The spirit of the time | 2. The general intellectual and moral state or temper characteristic of any period of time
cacodyl: 1. Alkarsin | 2. A colorless, poisonous, arsenical liquid, As24, spontaneously inflammable and possessing an intensely disagreeable odor. It is the type of a series of compounds analogous to the nitrogen compounds called hydrazines
commensality: 1. Fellowship at table | 2. The act or practice of eating at the same table.  "Promiscuous commensality." Sir T. Browne
drummer: 1. One whose office is to best the drum, as in military exercises and marching | 2. One who solicits custom | 3. A commercial traveler.  Bartlett
stirless: 1. Without stirring | 2. Very quiet | 3. Motionless. "Lying helpless and stirless." Hare
wayment:
1. To lament | 2. To grieve | 3. To wail.   Thilke science . . . maketh a man to waymenten. Chaucer. For what boots it to weep and wayment, When ill is chanced Spenser.

Grief
maneh: 1. A Hebrew weight for gold or silver, being one hundred shekels of gold and sixty shekels of silver. Ezek. xlv
degender: 1. To degenerate.  "Degendering to hate." Spenser. He degenereth into beastliness. Joye
ronion: 1. A mangy or scabby creature. "Aroint thee, with!" the rump-fed ronyon cries. Shak
decivilize: 1. To reduce from civilization to a savage state.  Blackwood's Mag
appreciate: 1. To set a price or value on | 2. To estimate justly | 3. To value. To appreciate the motives of their enemies. Gibbon
micrometry: 1. The art of measuring with a micrometer
historic: 1. Of or pertaining to history, or the record of past events | 2. As, an historical poem | 3. The historic page. -- His*tor"ic*al*ness, n. -- His*to*ric"i*ty, n. There warriors frowning in historic brass. Pope. Historical painting, that branch of painting which represents the events of history. -- Historical sense, that meaning of a passage which is deduced from the circumstances of time, place, etc., under which it was written. -- The historic sense, the capacity to conceive and represent the unity and significance of a past era or age
indiscerpible: 1. Not discerpible | 2. Inseparable.  Bp. Butler. -- In`dis*cerp"i*ble*ness, n., In`dis*cerp"ti*ble*ness, n.  -- In`dis*cerp"ti*bly, adv
diastasis: 1. A forcible of bones without fracture
kobellite: 1. A blackish gray mineral, a sulphide of antimony, bismuth, and lead
wanty: 1. A surcingle, or strap of leather, used for binding a load upon the back of a beast | 2. Also, a leather tie | 3. A short wagon rope
fleury: 1. Finished at the ends with fleurs-de-lis | 2. -- said esp | 3. A cross so decorated
hymnologist: 1. A composer or compiler of hymns | 2. One versed in hymnology. Busby
caution: 1. A careful attention to the probable effects of an act, in order that failure or harm may be avoided | 2. Prudence in regard to danger | 3. Provident care
brelan: 1. A French gambling game somewhat like poker. In French games, a pair royal, or triplet
tilth: 1. The state of being tilled, or prepared for a crop | 2. Culture | 3. As, land is good tilth. The tilth and rank fertility of its golden youth. De Quincey
bocking: 1. A coarse woolen fabric, used for floor cloths, to cover carpets, etc | 2. -- so called from the town of Bocking, in England, where it was first made
wavellite: 1. A hydrous phosphate of alumina, occurring usually in hemispherical radiated forms varying in color from white to yellow, green, or black
down: 1. Fine, soft, hairy outgrowth from the skin or surface of animals or plants, not matted and fleecy like wool | 2. Esp.: The soft under feathers of birds. They have short stems with soft rachis and bards and long threadlike barbules, without hooklets. The pubescence of plants | 3. The hairy crown or envelope of the seeds of certain plants, as of the thistle. The soft hair of the face when beginning to appear. And the first down begins to shade his face. Dryden
hammock: 1. A swinging couch or bed, usually made of netting or canvas about six feet wide, suspended by clews or cords at the ends | 2. A piece of land thickly wooded, and usually covered with bushes and vines. Used also adjectively | 3. As, hammock land.  Bartlett. Hammock nettings, formerly, nets for stowing hammocks
pouchong: 1. A superior kind of souchong tea | 2. De Colange
hautboy: 1. A wind instrument, sounded through a reed, and similar in shape to the clarinet, but with a thinner tone. Now more commonly called oboe. See Illust. of Oboe | 2. A sort of strawberry
tallyho: 1. The huntsman's cry to incite or urge on his hounds | 2. A tallyho coach. Tallyho coach, a pleasure coach. See under Coach
collection: 1. The act or process of collecting or of gathering | 2. As, the collection of specimens | 3. That which is collected
ladylikeness: 1. The quality or state of being ladylike
protagonist: 1. One who takes the leading part in a drama | 2. Hence, one who takes lead in some great scene, enterprise, conflict, or the like. Shakespeare, the protagonist on the great of modern poetry. De Quincey
angustation: 1. The act or making narrow | 2. A straitening or contacting. Wiseman
snowplough: 1. An implement operating like a plow, but on a larger scale, for clearing away the snow from roads, railways, etc
lacinia: 1. One of the narrow, jagged, irregular pieces or divisions which form a sort of fringe on the borders of the petals of some flowers. A narrow, slender portion of the edge of a monophyllous calyx, or of any irregularly incised leaf | 2. The posterior, inner process of the stipes on the maxillæ of insects
vegetarianism: 1. The theory or practice of living upon vegetables and fruits
streamer: 1. An ensign, flag, or pennant, which floats in the wind | 2. Specifically, a long, narrow, ribbonlike flag. Brave Rupert from afar appears, Whose waving streamers the glad general knows. Dryden | 3. A stream or column of light shooting upward from the horizon, constituting one of the forms of the aurora borealis. Macaulay. While overhead the North's dumb streamers shoot. Lowell
klipspringer: 1. A small, graceful South African antelope, which, like the chamois, springs from one crag to another with great agility | 2. -- called also kainsi
trayful: 1. As much as a tray will hold | 2. Enough to fill a tray
steinkirk:
1. A kind of neckcloth worn in a loose and disorderly fashion.

Same as Steenkirk
phatagin: 1. The long-tailed pangolin | 2. -- called also ipi
unbreathed: 1. Not breathed | 2. Not exercised | 3. Unpracticed.  "Their unbreathed memories." Shak
aphemia: 1. Loss of the power of speaking, while retaining the power of writing | 2. -- a disorder of cerebral origin
mare:
1. The female of the horse and other equine quadrupeds.

Sighing, suffocative panting, intercepted utterance, with a sense of pressure across the chest, occurring during sleep | 2. The incubus | 3. -- obsolete, except in the compound nightmare. I will ride thee o' nights like the mare. Shak
eighteenth: 1. Next in order after the seventeenth | 2. Consisting of one of eighteen equal parts or divisions of a thing | 3. The quotient of a unit divided by eighteen
arytenoid: 1. Ladle-shaped | 2. -- applied to two small cartilages of the larynx, and also to the glands, muscles, etc., connected with them. The cartilages are attached to the cricoid cartilage and connected with the vocal cords
regressive: 1. Passing back | 2. Returning | 3. Characterized by retrogression
organogenesis: 1. The origin and development of organs in animals and plants | 2. The germ history of the organs and systems of organs, -- a branch of morphogeny. Haeckel
magnesic: 1. Pertaining to, or containing, magnesium | 2. As, magnesic oxide
cheeringly: 1. In a manner to cheer or encourage
indubitable: 1. Not dubitable or doubtful | 2. Too evident to admit of doubt | 3. Unquestionable
charta: 1. Material on which instruments, books, etc., are written | 2. Parchment or paper. A charter or deed | 3. A writing by which a grant is made. See Magna Charta
surangular: 1. Above the angular bone | 2. Supra-angular | 3. -- applied to a bone of the lower jaw in many reptiles and birds. -- n.  The surangular bone
triton: 1. A fabled sea demigod, the son of Neptune and Amphitrite, and the trumpeter of Neptune. He is represented by poets and painters as having the upper part of his body like that of a man, and the lower part like that of a fish. He often has a trumpet made of a shell. Have sight of Proteus rising from the sea, Or hear old Triton blow his wreathed horn. Wordsworth | 2. Any one of many species of marine gastropods belonging to Triton and allied genera, having a stout spiral shell, often handsomely colored and ornamented with prominent varices. Some of the species are among the largest of all gastropods. Called also trumpet shell, and sea trumpet | 3. Any one of numerous species of aquatic salamanders. The common European species are Hemisalamandra cristata, Molge palmata, and M. alpestris, a red-bellied species common in Switzerland. The most common species the United States is Diemyctylus viridescens. See Illust. under Salamander
pitch: 1. A thick, black, lustrous, and sticky substance obtained by boiling down tar | 2. It is used in calking the seams of ships | 3. Also in coating rope, canvas, wood, ironwork, etc., to preserve them. He that toucheth pitch shall be defiled therewith. Ecclus. xiii
grandaunt: 1. The aunt of one's father or mother
interpoint: 1. To point | 2. To mark with stops or pauses | 3. To punctuate.  Her sighs should interpoint her words. Daniel
spirituosity: 1. The quality or state of being spirituous | 2. Spirituousness
obvious: 1. Opposing | 2. Fronting.  To the evil turn My obvious breast. Milton | 3. Exposed
megapode: 1. Any one of several species of large-footed, gallinaceous birds of the genera Megapodius and Leipoa, inhabiting Australia and other Pacific islands. See Jungle fowl under Jungle, and Leipoa
demonship: 1. The state of a demon. Mede
coctile: 1. Made by baking, or exposing to heat, as a brick
bonhomie: 1. Good nature | 2. Pleasant and easy manner

prolificness: 1. The quality or state of being prolific | 2. Fruitfulness | 3. Prolificacy
taffeta: 1. A fine, smooth stuff of silk, having usually the wavy luster called watering. The term has also been applied to different kinds of silk goods, from the 16th century to modern times. Lined with taffeta and with sendal. Chaucer
scrofulide: 1. Any affection of the skin dependent on scrofula
pigtailed: 1. Having a tail like a pig's | 2. As, the pigtailed baboon
chalybeate:
1. Impregnated with salts of iron | 2. Having a taste like iron | 3. As, chalybeate springs.

Any water, liquid, or medicine, into which iron enters as an ingredient
auf: 1. A changeling or elf child, -- that is, one left by fairies | 2. A deformed or foolish child | 3. A simpleton
bridesmaid: 1. A female friend who attends on a bride at her wedding
meloplastic: 1. Of or pertaining to meloplasty, or the artificial formation of a new cheek
unbred: 1. Not begotten | 2. Unborn.  "Thou age unbred." Shak | 3. Not taught or trained
wound: 1. Imp | 2. & p. p. of Wind to twist, and Wind to sound by blowing | 3. A hurt or injury caused by violence
catelectrode: 1. The negative electrode or pole of a voltaic battery. Faraday
organum: 1. An organ or instrument | 2. Hence, a method by which philosophical or scientific investigation may be conducted | 3. -- a term adopted from the Aristotelian writers by Lord Bacon, as the title of part of his treatise on philosophical method. Sir. W. Hamilton
archness: 1. The quality of being arch | 2. Cleverness | 3. Sly humor free from malice
falconine: 1. Like a falcon or hawk | 2. Belonging to the Falconidæ
repossess: 1. To possess again | 2. As, to repossess the land. Pope. To repossess one's self of, to acquire again
smudge: 1. A suffocating smoke. Grose | 2. A heap of damp combustibles partially ignited and burning slowly, placed on the windward side of a house, tent, or the like, in order, by the thick smoke, to keep off mosquitoes or other insects.  Bartlett | 3. That which is smeared upon anything
dipsy: 1. Deep-sea | 2. As, a dipsey line | 3. A dipsy lead
pleurapophysis: 1. One of the ventral processes of a vertebra, or the dorsal element in each half of a hemal arch, forming, or corresponding to, a vertebral rib | 2. -- Pleu*rap`o*phys"i*al, a. Owen
paytine: 1. An alkaloid obtained from a white bark resembling that of the cinchona, first brought from Payta, in Peru
intercolumnar: 1. Between columns or pillars | 2. As, the intercolumnar fibers of Poupart's ligament | 3. An intercolumnar statue
bluff: 1. Having a broad, flattened front | 2. As, the bluff bows of a ship. "Bluff visages." Irving | 3. Rising steeply with a flat or rounded front. "A bluff or bold shore." Falconer. Its banks, if not really steep, had a bluff and precipitous aspect. Judd
adduction: 1. The act of adducing or bringing forward. An adduction of facts gathered from various quarters. I. Taylor | 2. The action by which the parts of the body are drawn towards its axis] | 3. -- opposed to abduction. Dunglison
ecbasis: 1. A figure in which the orator treats of things according to their events consequences
saki:
1. Any one of several species of South American monkeys of the genus Pithecia. They have large ears, and a long hairy tail which is not prehensile. Note: The black saki, the white-headed, and the red-backed, or hand-drinking, saki, are among the best-known.

The alcoholic drink of Japan. It is made from rice.sake
entreative: 1. Used in entreaty | 2. Pleading.  "Entreative phrase." A. Brewer
ponderosity: 1. The quality or state of being ponderous | 2. Weight | 3. Gravity
weka: 1. A New Zealand rail which has wings so short as to be incapable of flight
rheae: 1. A suborder of struthious birds including the rheas
filament: 1. A thread or threadlike object or appendage | 2. A fiber | 3. Esp
rakel: 1. Hasty | 2. Reckless | 3. Rash.  Chaucer. -- Ra"kel*ness, n.  Chaucer
moule: 1. To contract mold | 2. To grow moldy | 3. To mold.  Let us not moulen thus in idleness. Chaucer
mange: 1. The scab or itch in cattle, dogs, and other beasts. Mange insect, any one of several species of small parasitic mites, which burrow in the skin of cattle. horses, dogs, and other animals, causing the mange. The mange insect of the horse, and that of cattle are the most important species. See Acarina
wield: 1. To govern | 2. To rule | 3. To keep, or have in charge
endure: 1. To continue in the same state without perishing | 2. To last | 3. To remain. Their verdure still endure. Shak. He shall hold it  fast, but it shall not endure. Job viii
distillery: 1. The building and works where distilling, esp | 2. Of alcoholic liquors, is carried on | 3. The act of distilling spirits.  Todd
degraded: 1. Reduced in rank, character, or reputation | 2. Debased | 3. Sunken
tithonicity: 1. The state or property of being tithonic | 2. Actinism
poinder: 1. The keeper of a cattle pound | 2. A pinder.  T. Adams | 3. One who distrains property.  Jamieson

defectionist: 1. One who advocates or encourages defection
indent: 1. To notch | 2. To jag | 3. To cut into points like a row of teeth

It has several long, slender filaments below the pectoral fins. It appears about the same time with the mango fruit, in April and May, whence the name. -- Mango tree, an East Indian tree of the genus Mangifera, related to the cashew and the sumac. minimization: 1. The act or process of minimizing. Bentham
accuser: 1. One who accuses | 2. One who brings a charge of crime or fault

satiny: 1. Like or composed of satin | 2. Glossy | 3. As, to have a satiny appearance
elsewhere: 1. In any other place | 2. As, these trees are not to be found elsewhere | 3. In some other place

alienor: 1. One who alienates or transfers property to another. Blackstone

eminently: 1. In an eminent manner | 2. In a high degree | 3. Conspicuously
nutrication: 1. The act or manner of feeding.  Sir T. Browne

accumulative: 1. Characterized by accumulation | 2. Serving to collect or amass | 3. Cumulative
daguerreotypy: 1. The art or process of producing pictures by method of Daguerre
falsifier: 1. One who falsifies, or gives to a thing a deceptive appearance | 2. A liar
decoloration: 1. The removal or absence of color. Ferrand

mantologist: 1. One who is skilled in mantology | 2. A diviner
coinhere: 1. To inhere or exist together, as in one substance. Sir W. Hamilton
cyclops: 1. One of a race of giants, sons of Neptune and Amphitrite, having but one eye, and that in the middle of the forehead. They were fabled to inhabit Sicily, and to assist in the workshops of Vulcan, under Mt. Etna. Note: Pope, in his translation of the "Odyssey," uniformly spells this word Cyclop, when used in the singular | 2. A genus of minute Entomostraca, found both in fresh and salt water. See Copepoda | 3. A portable forge, used by tinkers, etc
dhow: 1. A coasting vessel of Arabia, East Africa, and the Indian Ocean. It has generally but one mast and a lateen sail

interchange: 1. To put each in the place of the other | 2. To give and take mutually | 3. To exchange
wariangle: 1. The red-backed shrike | 2. -- called also würger, worrier, and throttler
evocative: 1. Calling forth | 2. Serving to evoke | 3. Developing. Evocative power over all that is eloquent and expressive in the better soul of man

handmaid: 1. A maid that waits at hand | 2. A female servant or attendant
neurosensiferous: 1. Pertaining to, or forming, both nerves and sense organs
antasthmatic: 1. Opposing, or fitted to relieve, asthma. -- n.  A remedy for asthma

zayat: 1. A public shed, or portico, for travelers, worshipers, etc

centrifugal:
1. Tending, or causing, to recede from the center | 2. Expanding first at the summit, and later at the base, as a flower cluster. Having the radicle turned toward the sides of the fruit, as some embryos. Centrifugal force, a force whose direction is from a center. Note: When a body moves in a circle with uniform velocity, a force must act on the body to keep it in the circle without change of velocity. The direction of this force is towards the center of the circle. If this force is applied by means of a string to the body, the string will be in a state of tension. To a person holding the other end of the string, this tension will appear to be directed toward the body as if the body had a tendency to move away from the center of the circle which it is describing. Hence this latter force is often called centrifugal force. The force which really acts on the body being directed towards the center of the circle is called centripetal force, and in some popular treatises the centripetal and centrifugal forces are described as opposing and balancing each other. But they are merely the different aspects of the same stress. Clerk Maxwell. Centrifugal impression, an impression sent from a nerve center outwards to a muscle or muscles by which motion is produced. -- Centrifugal machine, A machine for expelling water or other fluids from moist substances, or for separating liquids of different densities by centrifugal action | 3. A whirling table. -- Centrifugal pump, a machine in which water or other fluid is lifted and discharged through a pipe by the energy imparted by a wheel or blades revolving in a fixed case. Some of the largest and most powerful pumps are of this kind.

Note: A distinction is carefully made, by English writers, between escheat to the lord of the fee and forfeiture to the crown. hery: 1. To worship | 2. To glorify | 3. To praise.  Chaucer. Spenser

1. See Aghast.

The F or bass clef, and the G or treble clef, are fixed in their positions upon the staff. The C clef may have three positions. It may be placed upon the first or lower line of the staff, in which case it is called soprano clef, upon the third line, in which case it called alto clef, or upon the fourth line, in which case tenor clef.
