congestion: 1. The act of gathering into a heap or mass | 2. Accumulation.  The congestion of dead bodies one upon another. Evelyn | 3. Overfullness of the capillary and other blood vessels, etc., in any locality or organ
organization: 1. The act of organizing | 2. The act of arranging in a systematic way for use or action | 3. As, the organization of an army, or of a deliberative body. "The first organization of the general government." Pickering
esopian:
1. Of or pertaining to Æsop, or in his manner.

Same as Æsopian, Æsopic
lymphoma: 1. A tumor having a structure resembling that of a lymphatic gland | 2. -- called also lymphadenoma. Malignant lymphoma, a fatal disease characterized by the formation in various parts of the body of new growths resembling lymphatic glands in structure
scholium: 1. Marginal anotation | 2. An explanatory remark or comment | 3. Specifically, an explanatory comment on the text of a classic author by an early grammarian
extinction: 1. The act of extinguishing or making extinct | 2. A putting an end to | 3. The act of putting out or destroying light, fire, life, activity, influence, etc
swarmspore: 1. One of innumerable minute, motile, reproductive bodies, produced asexually by certain algæ and fungi | 2. A zoöspore | 3. One of the minute flagellate germs produced by the sporulation of a protozoan
provender: 1. Dry food for domestic animals, as hay, straw, corn, oats, or a mixture of ground grain | 2. Feed. "Hay or other provender." Mortimer. Good provender laboring horses would have. Tusser | 3. Food or provisions
alluvion: 1. Wash or flow of water against the shore or bank | 2. An overflowing | 3. An inundation
demonstrator: 1. One who demonstrates | 2. One who proves anything with certainty, or establishes it by indubitable evidence | 3. A teacher of practical anatomy
spaghetti: 1. A variety or macaroni made in tubes of small diameter
sepulture: 1. The act of depositing the dead body of a human being in the grave | 2. Burial | 3. Interment. Where we may royal sepulture prepare. Dryden
exasperation: 1. The act of exasperating or the state of being exasperated | 2. Irritation | 3. Keen or bitter anger. Extorted from him by the exasperation of his spirits. South
weakfish: 1. Any fish of the genus Cynoscion | 2. A squeteague | 3. -- so called from its tender mouth. See Squeteague. Spotted weakfish, the spotted squeteague
underplay:
1. To play in a subordinate, or in an inferior manner | 2. To underact a part | 3. To play a low card when holding a high one, in the hope of a future advantage.

The act of underplaying
idiosyncratical: 1. Of peculiar temper or disposition | 2. Belonging to one's peculiar and individual character
outreason: 1. To excel or surpass in reasoning | 2. To reason better than. South
intertexture: 1. The act of interweaving, or the state of being interwoven | 2. That which is interwoven. "Knit in nice intertexture." Coleridge. Skirted thick with intertexture firm Of thorny boughs. Cowper
anisol: 1. Methyl phenyl ether, C6H5OCH3, got by distilling anisic acid or by the action of methide on potassium phenolate
endopleura: 1. The inner coating of a seed. See Tegmen
decylic: 1. Allied to, or containing, the radical decyl
incontestable: 1. Not contestable | 2. Not to be disputed | 3. That cannot be called in question or controverted
oxyacetic: 1. Hydroxyacetic | 2. Designating an acid called also glycolic acid
misnurture: 1. To nurture or train wrongly | 2. As, to misnurture children. Bp. Hall
earlock: 1. A lock or curl of hair near the ear | 2. A lovelock. See Lovelock
spermic: 1. Of or pertaining to sperm, or semen
chromogenic: 1. Containing, or capable of forming, chromogen | 2. As, chromogenic bacteria
uncinata: 1. A division of marine chætopod annelids which are furnished with uncini, as the serpulas and sabellas
potale: 1. The refuse from a grain distillery, used to fatten swine
allocatur: 1. "Allowed." The word allocatur expresses the allowance of a proceeding, writ, order, etc., by a court, judge, or judicial officer
turner: 1. One who turns | 2. Especially, one whose occupation is to form articles with a lathe | 3. A variety of pigeon
sesquipedal: 1. Measuring or containing a foot and a half | 2. As, a sesquipedalian pygmy | 3. -- sometimes humorously applied to long words
onerous: 1. Burdensome | 2. Oppressive. "Too onerous a solicitude." I. Taylor. Onerous cause, a good and legal consideration | 3. -- opposed to gratuitous
shrag: 1. A twig of a tree cut off | 2. To trim, as trees | 3. To lop
petrology: 1. The department of science which is concerned with the mineralogical and chemical composition of rocks, and with their classification: lithology | 2. A treatise on petrology
foreordination: 1. Previous ordination or appointment | 2. Predetermination | 3. Predestination
lepidodendron: 1. A genus of fossil trees of the Devonian and Carboniferous ages, having the exterior marked with scars, mostly in quincunx order, produced by the separation of the leafstalks
clergyable: 1. Entitled to, or admitting, the benefit of clergy | 2. As, a clergyable felony. Blackstone
hypnotize: 1. To induce hypnotism in | 2. To place in a state of hypnotism
pesky: 1. Pestering | 2. Vexatious | 3. Troublesome. Used also as an intensive.  Judd
disinterment: 1. The act of disinterring, or taking out of the earth | 2. Exhumation
hydraemia: 1. An abnormally watery state of the blood | 2. Anæmia
pronominalize: 1. To give the effect of a pronoun to | 2. As, to pronominalize the substantives person, people, etc | 3. Early
badge: 1. A distinctive mark, token, sign, or cognizance, worn on the person | 2. As, the badge of a society | 3. The badge of a policeman. "Tax gatherers, recognized by their official badges. " Prescott
outwit:
1. To surpass in wisdom, esp | 2. In cunning | 3. To defeat or overreach by superior craft. They did so much outwit and outwealth us ! Gauden.

The faculty of acquiring wesdom by observation and experience, or the wisdom so acquired
deep: 1. Extending far below the surface | 2. Of great perpendicular dimension | 3. Far to the bottom
perineorrhaphy: 1. The operation of sewing up a ruptured perineum
digenesis: 1. The faculty of multiplying in two ways | 2. -- by ova fecundated by spermatic fluid, and asexually, as by buds. See Parthenogenesis
ethological: 1. Treating of, or pertaining to, ethnic or morality, or the science of character. J. S. Mill
scylla: 1. A dangerous rock on the Italian coast opposite the whirpool Charybdis on the coast of Sicily, -- both personified in classical literature as ravenous monsters. The passage between them was formerly considered perilous | 2. Hence, the saying "Between Scylla and Charybdis," signifying a great peril on either hand
dedecorate: 1. To bring to shame | 2. To disgrace.  Bailey
griffin: 1. An Anglo-Indian name for a person just arrived from Europe. H. Kingsley | 2. A fabulous monster, half lion and half eagle. It is often represented in Grecian and Roman works of art | 3. A representation of this creature as an heraldic charge
interspersion: 1. The act of interspersing, or the state of being interspersed
datura: 1. A genus of solanaceous plants, with large funnel-shaped flowers and a four-celled, capsular fruit. Note: The commonest species are the thorn apple, with a prickly capsule, white flowers and green stem, and D. tatula, with a purplish tinge of the stem and flowers. Both are narcotic and dangerously poisonous
septuary: 1. Something composed of seven | 2. A week.  Ash
dragonnade: 1. The severe persecution of French Protestants under Louis XIV., by an armed force, usually of dragoons | 2. Hence, a rapid and devastating incursion | 3. Dragoonade. He learnt it as he watched the dragonnades, the tortures, the massacres of the Netherlands. C. Kingsley. DRAGON'S BLOOD
darn:
1. To mend as a rent or hole, with interlacing stitches of yarn or thread by means of a needle | 2. To sew together with yarn or thread. He spent every day ten hours in his closet, in darning his stockins. Swift. Darning last. See under Last. -- Darning needle. A long, strong needle for mending holes or rents, especially in stockings. Any species of dragon fly, having a long, cylindrical body, resembling a needle. These flies are harmless and without stings. Note:  Called also devil's darning-needle.

A place mended by darning.

A colloquial euphemism for Damn
contend: 1. To strive in opposition | 2. To contest | 3. To dispute
cot: 1. A small house | 2. A cottage or hut | 3. The sheltered cot, the cultivated farm. Goldsmith
horde: 1. A wandering troop or gang | 2. Especially, a clan or tribe of a nomadic people migrating from place to place for the sake of pasturage, plunder, etc | 3. A predatory multitude. Thomson
cooperation: 1. The act of coöperating, or of operating together to one end | 2. Joint operation | 3. Concurrent effort or labor. Not holpen by the coöperation of angels. Bacon
drawspring: 1. The spring to which a drawbar is attached
jobation: 1. A scolding | 2. A hand, tedious reproof.  Grose
showbread: 1. Bread of exhibition | 2. Loaves to set before God | 3. -- the term used in translating the various phrases used in the Hebrew and Greek to designate the loaves of bread which the priest of the week placed before the Lord on the golden table in the sanctuary. They were made of fine flour unleavened, and were changed every Sabbath. The loaves, twelve in number, represented the twelve tribes of Israel. They were to be eaten by the priests only, and in the Holy Place.  Mark ii
panderism: 1. The employment, arts, or practices of a pander. Bp. Hall
dephlegmate: 1. To deprive of superabundant water, as by evaporation or distillation | 2. To clear of aqueous matter | 3. To rectify
bilinguous: 1. Having two tongues, or speaking two languages
secco: 1. Dry. Secco painting, or Painting in secco, painting on dry plaster, as distinguished from fresco painting, which is on wet or fresh plaster
scherzo: 1. A playful, humorous movement, commonly in 3-4 measure, which often takes the place of the old minuet and trio in a sonata or a symphony
occlude: 1. To shut up | 2. To close. Sir T. Browne | 3. To take in and retain
pursuable: 1. Capable of being, or fit to be, pursued, followed, or prosecuted. Sherwood
smew: 1. Small European merganser which has a white crest | 2. -- called also smee, smee duck, white merganser, and white nun | 3. The hooded merganser
genian: 1. Of or pertaining to the chin | 2. Mental | 3. As, the genian prominence
punctual: 1. Consisting in a point | 2. Limited to a point | 3. Unextended.  "This punctual spot." Milton. The theory of the punctual existence of the soul. Krauth
tame: 1. To broach or enter upon | 2. To taste, as a liquor | 3. To divide
stable: 1. Firmly established | 2. Not easily moved, shaken, or overthrown | 3. Fixed
bosky: 1. Woody or bushy | 2. Covered with boscage or thickets. Milton | 3. Caused by boscage. Darkened over by long bosky shadows. H. James
stomapoda: 1. An order of Crustacea including the squillas. The maxillipeds are leglike in form, and the large claws are comblike. They have a large and elongated abdomen, which contains a part of the stomach and heart | 2. The abdominal appendages are large, and bear the gills. Called also Gastrula, Stomatopoda, and Squilloidea
enharmonic: 1. Of or pertaining to that one of the three kinds of musical scale recognized by the ancient Greeks, which consisted of quarter tones and major thirds, and was regarded as the most accurate | 2. Pertaining to a change of notes to the eye, while, as the same keys are used, the instrument can mark no difference to the ear, as the substitution of A for G#. Pertaining to a scale of perfect intonation which recognizes all the notes and intervals that result from the exact tuning of diatonic scales and their transposition into other keys
dazzle: 1. To overpower with light | 2. To confuse the sight of by brilliance of light. Those heavenly shapes Will dazzle now the earthly, with their blaze Insufferably bright. Milton. An unreflected light did never yet Dazzle the vision feminine. Sir H. Taylor | 3. To bewilder or surprise with brilliancy or display of any kind. "Dazzled and drove back his enemies." Shak
inertia: 1. That property of matter by which it tends when at rest to remain so, and when in motion to continue in motion, and in the same straight line or direction, unless acted on by some external force | 2. - - sometimes called vis inertiæ | 3. Inertness
dilluing: 1. A process of sorting ore by washing in a hand sieve
subaid: 1. To aid secretly | 2. To assist in a private manner, or indirectly.  Daniel
pteron: 1. The region of the skull, in the temporal fossa back of the orbit, where the great wing of the sphenoid, the temporal, the parietal, and the frontal hones approach each other
subway: 1. An underground way or gallery | 2. Especially, a passage under a street, in which water mains, gas mains, telegraph wires, etc., are conducted
saltire: 1. A St. Andrew's cross, or cross in the form of an X, -- one of the honorable ordinaries
rebaptize: 1. To baptize again or a second time
complainable: 1. That may be complained of.  Feltham
displeasure: 1. The feeling of one who is displeased | 2. Irritation or uneasiness of the mind, occasioned by anything that counteracts desire or command, or which opposes justice or a sense of propriety | 3. Disapprobation
boatable: 1. Such as can be transported in a boat | 2. Navigable for boats, or small river craft. The boatable waters of the Alleghany. J. Morse
blizzard: 1. A gale of piercingly cold wind, usually accompanied with fine and blinding snow | 2. A furious blast
fomalhaut: 1. A star of the first magnitude, in the constellation Piscis Australis, or Southern Fish
calker: 1. One who calks | 2. A calk on a shoe. See Calk, n.,
countersink: 1. To chamfer or form a depression around the top of for the reception of the head of a screw or bolt below the surface, either wholly or in part | 2. As, to countersink a hole for a screw | 3. To cause to sink even with or below the surface
notodontian: 1. Any one of several species of bombycid moths belonging to Notodonta, Nerice, and allied genera. The caterpillar of these moths has a hump, or spine, on its back
synartesis: 1. A fastening or knitting together | 2. The state of being closely jointed | 3. Close union.  Coleridge
duebill: 1. A brief written acknowledgment of a debt, not made payable to order, like a promissory note. Burrill
hires: 1. Hers | 2. Theirs. See Here, pron.  Chaucer
mangostan: 1. A tree of the East Indies of the genus Garcinia. The tree grows to the height of eighteen feet, and bears fruit also called mangosteen, of the size of a small apple, the pulp of which is very delicious food
praesternum: 1. Same as Preoral, Prepubis, Prescapula, etc
gnathostegite: 1. One of a pair of broad plates, developed from the outer maxillipeds of crabs, and forming a cover for the other mouth organs
spang:
1. To spangle. 

To spring | 2. To bound | 3. To leap.  But when they spang o'er reason's fence, We smart for't at our own expense. Ramsay.

A bound or spring.  Sir W. Scott.

A spangle or shining ornament.  With glittering spangs that did like stars appear. Spenser
alcyonaria: 1. One of the orders of Anthozoa. It includes the Alcyonacea, Pennatulacea, and Gorgonacea
ypsiloid: 1. In the form of the letter Y | 2. Y-shaped
indorsement: 1. The act of writing on the back of a note, bill, or other written instrument | 2. That which is written on the back of a note, bill, or other paper, as a name, an order for, or a receipt of, payment, or the return of an officer, etc | 3. A writing, usually upon the back, but sometimes on the face, of a negotiable instrument, by which the property therein is assigned and transferred. Story. Byles. Burrill
foolhardihood: 1. The state of being foolhardy | 2. Foolhardiness
anthobian: 1. A beetle which feeds on flowers
interstratification: 1. Stratification among or between other layers or strata | 2. Also, that which is interstratified
rayonnant: 1. Darting forth rays, as the sun when it shines out
pressor: 1. Causing, or giving rise to, pressure or to an increase of pressure | 2. As, pressor nerve fibers, stimulation of which excites the vasomotor center, thus causing a stronger contraction of the arteries and consequently an increase of the arterial blood pressure | 3. -- opposed to depressor. Landois & Stirling
atmospherology: 1. The science or a treatise on the atmosphere
impart: 1. To bestow a share or portion of | 2. To give, grant, or communicate | 3. To allow another to partake in
anion: 1. An electro-negative element, or the element which, in electro- chemical decompositions, is evolved at the anode | 2. -- opposed to cation. Faraday
sensorial: 1. Of or pertaining to the sensorium | 2. As, sensorial faculties, motions, powers. A. Tucker
butcherly: 1. Like a butcher | 2. Without compunction | 3. Savage
demonomania: 1. A form of madness in which the patient conceives himself possessed of devils
nothing: 1. Not anything | 2. No thing | 3. -- opposed to Ant: anything and Ant: something. Yet had his aspect nothing of severe. Dryden
multigranulate: 1. Having, or consisting of, many grains
fossa: 1. A pit, groove, cavity, or depression, of greater or less depth | 2. As, the temporal fossa on the side of the skull | 3. The nasal fossæ containing the nostrils in most birds
ciliograde: 1. Moving by means of cilia, or cilialike organs | 2. As, the ciliograde Medusæ
quiddany: 1. A confection of quinces, in consistency between a sirup and marmalade
dogfish: 1. A small shark, of many species, of the genera Mustelus, Scyllium, Spinax, etc | 2. Note: The European spotted dogfishes are very abundant | 3. The American smooth, or blue dogfish is Mustelus canis
crepitate: 1. To make a series of small, sharp, rapidly repeated explosions or sounds, as salt in fire | 2. To crackle | 3. To snap
deserve: 1. To earn by service | 2. To be worthy of | 3. To merit
thrillant: 1. Piercing | 2. Sharp | 3. Thrilling.  "His thrillant spear." Spenser
winding:
1. A call by the boatswain's whistle.

Twisting from a direct line or an even surface | 2. Circuitous. Keble.

A turn or turning | 3. A bend
yielding: 1. Inclined to give way, or comply | 2. Flexible | 3. Compliant
mixtilinear: 1. Containing, or consisting of, lines of different kinds, as straight, curved, and the like | 2. As, a mixtilinear angle, that is, an angle contained by a straight line and a curve
wesleyanism: 1. The system of doctrines and church polity inculcated by John Wesley (b. 1703 | 2. 1791), the founder of the religious sect called Methodist | 3. Methodism. See Methodist, n.,
anaseismic: 1. Moving up and down | 2. -- said of earthquake shocks
underpart: 1. A subordinate part. It should be lightened with underparts of mirth. Dryden
nutant: 1. Nodding | 2. Having the top bent downward
antisocial: 1. Tending to interrupt or destroy social intercourse | 2. Averse to society, or hostile to its existence | 3. As, antisocial principles
mackintosh: 1. A waterproof outer garment | 2. -- so called from the name of the inventor
feoff: 1. , v. t. [imp | 2. & p. p. Feoffed | 3. Pr. & vb. n.. Feoffing.] Etym: [OE. feffen, OF. feffer, fieffer, F. fieffer, fr. fief fief
microcline: 1. A mineral of the feldspar group, like orthoclase or common feldspar in composition, but triclinic in form
estuary: 1. A place where water boils up | 2. A spring that wells forth.  Boyle | 3. A passage, as the mouth of a river or lake, where the tide meets the current
intelligencer: 1. One who, or that which, sends or conveys intelligence or news | 2. A messenger. All the intriguers in foreign politics, all the spies, and all the intelligencers . . . acted solely upon that principle. Burke
avatar: 1. The descent of a deity to earth, and his incarnation as a man or an animal | 2. -- chiefly associated with the incarnations of Vishnu | 3. Incarnation
protectingly: 1. By way of protection | 2. In a protective manner
carbonarism: 1. The principles, practices, or organization of the Carbonari
hysteranthous: 1. Having the leaves expand after the flowers have opened. Henslow
jester: 1. A buffoon | 2. A merry-andrew | 3. A court fool. This . . . was Yorick's skull, the king's jester. Shak. Dressed in the motley garb that jesters wear. Longfellow
viperoidea: 1. A division of serpents which includes the true vipers of the Old World and the rattlesnakes and moccasin snakes of America | 2. -- called also Viperina
aruspicy: 1. Prognostication by inspection of the entrails of victims slain sacrifice
fortissimo: 1. Very loud | 2. With the utmost strength or loudness
husbandry: 1. Care of domestic affairs | 2. Economy | 3. Domestic management
sternothyroid: 1. Of or pertaining to the sternum and the thyroid cartilage
diverticle: 1. A turning | 2. A byway | 3. A bypath.  Hales
carthamin: 1. A red coloring matter obtained from the safflower, or Carthamus tinctorius
cupping: 1. The operation of drawing blood to or from the surface of the person by forming a partial vacuum over the spot. Also, sometimes, a similar operation for drawing pus from an abscess. Cupping glass, a glass cup in which a partial vacuum is produced by heat, in the process of cupping. -- Dry cupping, the application of a cupping instrument without scarification, to draw blood to the surface, produce counter irritation, etc | 2. -- Wet cupping, the operation of drawing blood by the application of a cupping instrument after scarification
declass: 1. To remove from a class | 2. To separate or degrade from one's class.  North Am. Rev
demephitize: 1. To purify from mephitic. -- De*meph`i*ti*za"tion, n
clamminess: 1. State of being clammy or viscous
weeping: 1. The act of one who weeps | 2. Lamentation with tears | 3. Shedding of tears
fearsome: 1. Frightful | 2. Causing fear  "This fearsome wind." Sir W. Scott 2  . Easily frightened | 3. Timid
pat: 1. To strike gently with the fingers or hand | 2. To stroke lightly | 3. To tap
dilatable: 1. Capable of expansion | 2. That may be dilated | 3. -- opposed to contractible
tormentry: 1. Anything producing torment, annoyance, or pain.  Chaucer
mutuation: 1. The act of borrowing or exchanging.  Bp. Hall
achromatic: 1. Free from color | 2. Transmitting light without decomposing it into its primary colors | 3. Uncolored
drugget: 1. A coarse woolen cloth dyed of one color or printed on one side | 2. Generally used as a covering for carpets. By extension, any material used for the same purpose
firk: 1. To beat | 2. To strike | 3. To chastise.  I'll fer him, and firk him, and ferret him
chiminage: 1. A toll for passage through a forest.  Cowell
marker: 1. One who or that which marks. Specifically: One who keeps account of a game played, as of billiards. A counter used in card playing and other games. The soldier who forms the pilot of a wheeling column, or marks the direction of an alignment. An attachment to a sewing machine for marking a line on the fabric by creasing it
peculation: 1. The act or practice of peculating, or of defrauding the public by appropriating to one's own use the money or goods intrusted to one's care for management or disbursement | 2. Embezzlement. Every British subject . . . active in the discovery of peculations has been ruined. Burke
sentencer: 1. One who pronounced a sentence or condemnation
divorce: 1. A legal dissolution of the marriage contract by a court or other body having competent authority. This is properly a divorce, and called, technically, divorce a vinculo matrimonii. "from the bond of matrimony." The separation of a married woman from the bed and board of her husband -- divorce a mensa et toro, "from bed board." | 2. The decree or writing by which marriage is dissolved | 3. Separation
thermotical: 1. Of or pertaining to heat | 2. Produced by heat | 3. As, thermotical phenomena. Whewell
legislatorial: 1. Of or pertaining to a legislator or legislature
goth: 1. One of an ancient Teutonic race, who dwelt between the Elbe and the Vistula in the early part of the Christian era, and who overran and took an important part in subverting the Roman empire. The former inhabiting countries on the Black Sea up to the Danube, and the latter on this river generally. Some of them took possession of the province of Moesia, and hence were called Moesogoths. Others, who made their way to Scandinavia, at a time unknown to history, are sometimes styled Suiogoths | 3. One who is rude or uncivilized
enfever: 1. To excite fever in.  A. Seward
supperless: 1. Having no supper | 2. Deprived of supper | 3. As, to go supperless to bed
gentlemanhood: 1. The qualities or condition of a gentleman.  Thackeray
sinistrin: 1. A mucilaginous carbohydrate, resembling achroödextrin, extracted from squill as a colorless amorphous substance | 2. -- so called because it is levorotatory
butteris: 1. A steel cutting instrument, with a long bent shank set in a handle which rests against the shoulder of the operator. It is operated by a thrust movement, and used in paring the hoofs of horses
ginglymus: 1. A hinge joint | 2. An articulation, admitting of flexion and extension, or motion in two directions only, as the elbow and the ankle
exarillate: 1. Having no aril | 2. -- said of certain seeds, or of the plants producing them
sperm:
1. The male fecundating fluid | 2. Semen. See Semen. Sperm cell, one of the cells from which the spermatozoids are developed. -- Sperm morula. Same as Spermosphere.

Spermaceti. Sperm oil, a fatty oil found as a liquid, with spermaceti, in the head cavities of the sperm whale. -- Sperm whale. See in the Vocabulary
concerning: 1. Pertaining to | 2. Regarding | 3. Having relation to
alkaline: 1. Of or pertaining to an alkali or to alkalies | 2. Having the properties of an alkali. Alkaline earths, certain substances, as lime, baryta, strontia, and magnesia, possessing some of the qualities of alkalies. -- Alkaline metals, potassium, sodium, cæsium, lithium, rubidium. -- Alkaline reaction, a reaction indicating alkalinity, as by the action on limits, turmeric, etc
millepore: 1. Any coral of the genus Millepora, having the surface nearly smooth, and perforated with very minute unequal pores, or cells. The animals are hydroids, not Anthozoa. See Hydrocorallia
ocarina: 1. A kind of small simple wind instrument
wagonry: 1. Conveyance by means of a wagon or wagons.  Milton
centricity: 1. The state or quality of being centric | 2. Centricalness
clootie: 1. A little hoof | 2. The Devil. "Satan, Nick, or Clootie."  Burns
prorector: 1. An officer who presides over the academic senate of a German university. Heyse
inshaded: 1. Marked with different shades. W. Browne
phalangist: 1. Any arboreal marsupial of the genus Phalangista. The vulpine phalangist is the largest species, the full grown male being about two and a half feet long. It has a large bushy tail
thomsonian: 1. Of or pertaining to Thomsonianism. -- n.  A believer in Thomsonianism | 2. One who practices Thomsonianism
strictness: 1. Quality or state of being strict
legislatrix: 1. A woman who makes laws. Shaftesbury
repentance: 1. The act of repenting, or the state of being penitent | 2. Sorrow for what one has done or omitted to do | 3. Especially, contrition for sin
handiwork: 1. Work done by the hands | 2. Hence, any work done personally. The firmament showeth his handiwork. Ps. xix
mateology: 1. A vain, unprofitable discourse or inquiry
sparterie: 1. Articles made of the blades or fiber of the Lygeum Spartum and Stipa tenacissima, kinds of grass used in Spain and other countries for making ropes, mats, baskets, nets, and mattresses. Loudon
willying: 1. The process of cleansing wool, cotton, or the like, with a willy, or willow. Willying machine. Same as 1st Willow, 2
retribute: 1. To pay back | 2. To give in return, as payment, reward, or punishment | 3. To requite
alfilaria: 1. The pin grass, a weed in California
saker: 1. A falcon native of Southern Europe and Asia, closely resembling the lanner. Note: The female is called chargh, and the male charghela, or sakeret. The peregrine falcon | 2. To pour down particles of ice, or frozen vapors.

To pour forcibly down, as hail. Shak.

Healthy. See Hale | 3. To call loudly to, or after

Note: The chancellor was originally a chief scribe or secretary under the Roman emperors, but afterward was invested with judicial powers, and had superintendence over the other officers of the empire. From the Roman empire this office passed to the church, and every bishop has his chancellor, the principal judge of his consistory. In later times, in most countries of Europe, the chancellor was a high officer of state, keeper of the great seal of the kingdom, and having the supervision of all charters, and like public instruments of the crown, which were authenticated in the most solemn manner. In France a secretary is in some cases called a chancellor. In Scotland, the appellation is given to the foreman of a jury, or assize. In the present German empire, the chancellor is the president of the federal council and the head of the imperial administration. In the United States, the title is given to certain judges of courts of chancery or equity, established by the statutes of separate States. Blackstone. Wharton. Chancellor of a bishop, or of a diocese, a law officer appointed to hold the bishop's court in his diocese, and to assist him in matter of ecclesiastical law | 2. -- Chancellor of a cathedral, one of the four chief dignitaries of the cathedrals of the old foundation, and an officer whose duties are chiefly educational, with special reference to the cultivation of theology. -- Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, an officer before whom, or his deputy, the court of the duchy chamber of Lancaster is held. The latter are also called soluble or chemical ferments, and enzymes. Ferments of the first class are as a rule simple microscopic vegetable organisms, and the fermentations which they engender are due to their growth and development | 2. As, the acetic ferment, the butyric ferment, etc | 3. See Fermentation. Ferments of the second class, on the other hand, are chemical substances, as a rule soluble in glycerin and precipitated by alcohol. In action they are catalytic and, mainly, hydrolytic. Good examples are pepsin of the dastric juice, ptyalin of the salvia, and disease of malt. globular proteins, capable of catalyzing a wide variety of chemical reactions, not merely hydrolytic. pulse: 1. Leguminous plants, or their seeds, as beans, pease, etc | 2. If all the world Should, in a pet of temperance, feed on pulse. Milton | 3. The beating or throbbing of the heart or blood vessels, especially of the arteries. Note: In an artery the pulse is due to the expansion and contraction of the elastic walls of the artery by the action of the heart upon the column of blood in the arterial system. On the commencement of the diastole of the ventricle, the semilunar valves are closed, and the aorta recoils by its elasticity so as to force part of its contents into the vessels farther onwards. These, in turn, as they already contain a certain quantity of blood, expand, recover by an elastic recoil, and transmit the movement with diminished intensity. Thus a series of movements, gradually diminishing in intensity, pass along the arterial system. For the sake of convenience, the radial artery at the wrist is generally chosen to detect the precise character of the pulse. The pulse rate varies with age, position, sex, stature, physical and psychical influences, etc

type: 1. The mark or impression of something; stamp; impressed sign; emblem. The faith they have in tennis, and tall stockings, Short blistered breeches, and those types of travel. Shak. 2. Form or character impressed; style; semblance. Thy father bears the type of king of Naples. Shak. 3. A figure or representation of something to come; a token; a sign; a symbol; -- correlative to antitype. A type is no longer a type when the thing typified comes to be actually exhibited. South. 4. That which possesses or exemplifies characteristic qualities; the representative. Specifically:  A general form or structure common to a number of individuals; hence, the ideal representation of a species, genus, or other group, combining the essential characteristics; an animal or plant possessing or exemplifying the essential characteristics of a species, genus, or other group. Also, a group or division of animals having a certain typical or characteristic structure of body maintained within the group. Since the time of Cuvier and Baer . . . the whole animal kingdom has been universally held to be divisible into a small number of main divisions or types. Haeckel.  The original object, or class of objects, scene, face, or conception, which becomes the subject of a copy; esp., the design on the face of a medal or a coin. A simple compound, used as a mode or pattern to which other compounds are conveniently regarded as being related, and from which they may be actually or theoretically derived. Note: The fundamental types used to express the simplest and most essential chemical relations are hydrochloric acid, HCl; water, H2O; ammonia, NH3; and methane, CH4. 5. A raised letter, figure, accent, or other character, cast in metal or cut in wood, used in printing. Such letters or characters, in general, or the whole quantity of them used in printing, spoken of collectively; any number or mass of such letters or characters, however disposed. Note: Type are mostly made by casting type metal in a mold, though some of the larger sizes are made from maple, mahogany, or boxwood. In the cut, a is the body; b, the face, or part from which the impression is taken; c, the shoulder, or top of the body; d, the nick, designed to assist the compositor in distinguishing the bottom of the face from the top; e, the groove made in the process of finishing, -- each type as cast having attached to the bottom of the body a jet, or small piece of metal, which, when broken off, leaves a roughness that requires to be removed. The fine lines at the top and bottom of a letter are technically called ceriphs, and when part of the face projects over the body, as in the letter f, the projection is called a kern. The type which compose an ordinary book font consist of Roman CAPITALS, small capitals, and lower-case letters, and Italic CAPITALS and lower-case letters, with accompanying figures, points, and reference marks, -- in all about two hundred characters. Including the various modern styles of fancy type, some three or four hundred varieties of face are made. Besides the ordinary Roman and Italic, some of the most important of the varieties are -- Old English. Black Letter. Old Style. French Elzevir. Boldface. Antique. Clarendon. Gothic. Typewriter. Script. Agate, however, is called ruby, in England, where, also, a size intermediate between nonpareil and minion is employed, called emerald. Point system of type bodies, a system adopted by the type founders of the United States by which the various sizes of type have been so modified and changed that each size bears an exact proportional relation to every other size. The system is a modification of a French system, and is based on the pica body. This pica body is divided into twelfths, which are termed "points," and every type body consist of a given number of these points. Many of the type founders indicate the new sizes of type by the number of points, and the old names are gradually being done away with. polarization: 1. The act of polarizing | 2. The state of being polarized, or of having polarity | 3. A peculiar affection or condition of the rays of light or heat, in consequence of which they exhibit different properties in different directions. Note: If a beam of light, which has been reflected from a plate of unsilvered glass at an angle of about 56°, be received upon a second plate of glass similar to the former, and at the same angle of incidence, the light will be readily reflected when the two planes of incidence are parallel to each other, but will not be reflected when the two planes of incidence are perpendicular to each other. The light has, therefore, acquired new properties by reflection from the first plate of glass, and is called polarized light, while the modification which the light has experienced by this reflection is called polarization. The plane in which the beam of light is reflected from the first mirror is called the plane of polarization. The angle of polarization is the angle at which a beam of light must be reflected, in order that the polarization may be the most complete. The term polarization was derived from the theory of emission, and it was conceived that each luminous molecule has two poles analogous to the poles of a magnet

1. An instrument for reproducing sounds, especially articulate speech, at a distance. Note: The ordinary telephone consists essentially of a device by which currents of electricity, produced by sounds through the agency of certain mechanical devices and exactly corresponding in duration and intensity to the vibrations of the air which attend them, are transmitted to a distant station, and there, acting on suitable mechanism, reproduce similar sounds by repeating the vibrations. The necessary variations in the electrical currents are usually produced by means of a microphone attached to a thin diaphragm upon which the voice acts, and are intensified by means of an induction coil. In the magnetic telephone, or magneto-telephone, the diaphragm is of soft iron placed close to the pole of a magnet upon which is wound a coil of fine wire, and its vibrations produce corresponding vibrable currents in the wire by induction. The mechanical, or string, telephone is a device in which the voice or sound causes vibrations in a thin diaphragm, which are directly transmitted along a wire or string connecting it to a similar diaphragm at the remote station, thus reproducing the sound. quadragene: 1. An indulgence of forty days, corresponding to the forty days of ancient canonical penance
monogynian: 1. Pertaining to the Monogynia | 2. Monogynous. -- n.  One of the Monogynia
fortition: 1. Casual choice | 2. Fortuitous selection | 3. Hazard.  No mode of election operating in the spirit of fortition or rotation can be generally good. Burke
tanyard: 1. An inclosure where the tanning of leather is carried on | 2. A tannery
traverse: 1. Lying across | 2. Being in a direction across something else | 3. As, paths cut with traverse trenches. Oak . . . being strong in all positions, may be better trusted in cross and traverse work. Sir H. Wotton. The ridges of the fallow field traverse. Hayward. Traverse drill, a machine tool for drilling slots, in which the work or tool has a lateral motion back and forth
hyperbole: 1. A figure of speech in which the expression is an evident exaggeration of the meaning intended to be conveyed, or by which things are represented as much greater or less, better or worse, than they really are | 2. A statement exaggerated fancifully, through excitement, or for effect. Our common forms of compliment are almost all of them extravagant hyperboles. Blair. Somebody has said of the boldest figure in rhetoric, the hyperbole, that it lies without deceiving. Macaulay
sulphuret: 1. A sulphide | 2. As, a sulphuret of potassium
explode: 1. To become suddenly expanded into a great volume of gas or vapor | 2. To burst violently into flame | 3. As gunpowder explodes
coigny: 1. The practice of quartering one's self as landlord on a tenant | 2. A quartering of one's self on anybody.  Spenser
cripple: 1. One who creeps, halts, or limps | 2. One who has lost, or never had, the use of a limb or limbs | 3. A lame person
thwack:
1. To strike with something flat or heavy | 2. To bang, or thrash: to thump. "A distant thwacking sound." W. Irving | 3. To fill to overflow.  Stanyhurst.

A heavy blow with something flat or heavy
armgaunt: 1. With gaunt or slender legs. "An armgaunt steed." Shak. Note: This word is peculiar to Shakespeare. Its meaning has not yet been satisfactorily explained
catadioptric: 1. Pertaining to, produced by, or involving, both the reflection and refraction of light | 2. As, a catadioptric light. Hutton
muggins:
1. A game of dominoes in which the object is to make the sum of the two ends of the line some multiple of five | 2. A game at cards which depends upon building in suits or matching exposed cards, the object being to get rid of one's cards.

In certain games, to score against, or take an advantage over, as for an error, announcing the act by saying "muggins."
melolonthidian: 1. A beetle of the genus Melolontha, and allied genera. See May beetle, under May
solver: 1. One who, or that which, solves
euphony: 1. A pleasing or sweet sound | 2. An easy, smooth enunciation of sounds | 3. A pronunciation of letters and syllables which is pleasing to the ear
anthropopathism: 1. The ascription of human feelings or passions to God, or to a polytheistic deity. In its recoil from the gross anthropopathy of the vulgar notions, it falls into the vacuum of absolute apathy. Hare
condensible: 1. Capable of being condensed | 2. As, a gas condensible to a liquid by cold
plitt: 1. An instrument of punishment or torture resembling the knout, used in Russia
agasp: 1. In a state of gasping. Coleridge
reconvert:
1. To convert again. Milton.

A person who has been reconverted. Gladstone
garnishee: 1. One who is garnished | 2. A person upon whom garnishment has been served in a suit by a creditor against a debtor, such person holding property belonging to the debtor, or owing him money. Note: The order by which warning is made is called a garnishee order. To make a garnishee | 3. To warn by garnishment
sake: 1. Final cause | 2. End | 3. Purpose of obtaining
yelting: 1. The Florida and West Indian red snapper | 2. Also, sometimes, one of certain other allied species, as L. caxis
hippocampus: 1. A fabulous monster, with the head and fore quarters of a horse joined to the tail of a dolphin or other fish, -- seen in Pompeian paintings, attached to the chariot of Neptune. Fairholt | 2. A genus of lophobranch fishes of several species in which the head and neck have some resemblance to those of a horse | 3. -- called also sea horse. Note: They swim slowly, in an erect position, and often cling to seaweeds by means of the incurved prehensile tail. The male has a ventral pouch, in which it carries the eggs till hatched
proscribe: 1. To doom to destruction | 2. To put out of the protection of law | 3. To outlaw
seljuckian: 1. A member of the family of Seljuk | 2. An adherent of that family, or subject of its government | 3. The dynasty of Turkish sultans sprung from Seljuk
excruciating: 1. Torturing | 2. Racking. "Excruciating pain." V. Knox. "Excruciating fears." Bentley -- Ex*cru"ci*a`ting*ly, adv
babylonian: 1. Of or pertaining to the real or to the mystical Babylon, or to the ancient kingdom of Babylonia | 2. Chaldean | 3. An inhabitant of Babylonia
academicals: 1. The articles of dress prescribed and worn at some colleges and universities
embolismal: 1. Pertaining to embolism | 2. Intercalary | 3. As, embolismal months
acrolithan: 1. Pertaining to, or like, an acrolith
javelinier: 1. A soldier armed with a javelin. Holland
pomegranate: 1. The fruit of the tree Punica Granatum | 2. Also, the tree itself, which is native in the Orient, but is successfully cultivated in many warm countries, and as a house plant in colder climates. The fruit is as large as an orange, and has a hard rind containing many rather large seeds, each one separately covered with crimson, acid pulp | 3. A carved or embroidered ornament resembling a pomegranate. Ex. xxviii
franking: 1. A method of forming a joint at the intersection of window-sash bars, by cutting away only enough wood to show a miter
detergent: 1. Cleansing | 2. Purging. -- n.  A substance which cleanses the skin, as water or soap | 3. A medicine to cleanse wounds, ulcers, etc
preach: 1. To proclaim or publish tidings | 2. Specifically, to proclaim the gospel | 3. To discourse publicly on a religious subject, or from a text of Scripture
earn: 1. See Ern, n. Sir W. Scott | 2. To merit or deserve, as by labor or service | 3. To do that which entitles one to. The high repute Which he through hazard huge must earn. Milton
eclectically: 1. In an eclectic manner | 2. By an eclectic method
rasores: 1. An order of birds | 2. The Gallinæ. Note: Formely, the word Rasores was used in a wider sense, so as to include other birds now widely separated in classification
sorbic: 1. Pertaining to, or obtained from, the rowan tree, or sorb | 2. Specifically, designating an acid, C
mulada:
1. A moor.  Lockhart.

A drove of mules
gymnosomata: 1. One of the orders of Pteropoda. They have no shell
needment: 1. Something needed or wanted. pl.  Outfit | 2. Necessary luggage.  Spenser. Carrying each his needments. Wordsworth
chelonian: 1. Of or pertaining to animals of the tortoise kind. -- n.  One of the Chelonia
ordinant:
1. Ordaining | 2. Decreeing.  Shak.

One who ordains. F. G. Lee
insatiate: 1. Insatiable | 2. As, insatiate thirst. The insatiate greediness of his desires. Shak. And still insatiate, thirsting still for blood. Hook
vinaigrette: 1. A sauce, made of vinegar, oil, and other ingredients, -- used esp | 2. For cold meats | 3. A small perforated box for holding aromatic vinegar contained in a sponge, or a smelling bottle for smelling salts
cazique: 1. A chief or petty king among some tribes of Indians in America
oxheart: 1. A large heart-shaped cherry, either black, red, or white
seclusive: 1. Tending to seclude | 2. Keeping in seclusion | 3. Secluding
infratrochlear: 1. Below a trochlea, or pulley | 2. -- applied esp | 3. To one of the subdivisions of the trigeminal nerve
maudle: 1. To throw onto confusion or disorder | 2. To render maudlin
coffee: 1. The "beans" or "berries" obtained from the drupes of a small evergreen tree of the genus Coffea, growing in Abyssinia, Arabia, Persia, and other warm regions of Asia and Africa, and also in tropical America | 2. The coffee tree. Note: There are several species of the coffee tree, as, Coffea Arabica, C. occidentalis, and C. Liberica. The white, fragrant flowers grow in clusters at the root of the leaves, and the fruit is a red or purple cherrylike drupe, with sweet pulp, usually containing two pyrenes, commercially called "beans" or "berries" | 3. The beverage made from the roasted and ground berry. They have in Turkey a drink called coffee . . . This drink comforteth the brain and heart, and helpeth digestion. Bacon. Note: The use of coffee is said to have been introduced into England about 1650, when coffeehouses were opened in Oxford and London. Coffee bug, a species of scale insect, often very injurious to the coffee tree. -- Coffee rat See Musang
ceria: 1. Cerium oxide, CeO2, a white infusible substance constituting about one per cent of the material of the common incandescent mantle
confirmative: 1. Tending confirm or establish. Sherwood. -- Con*firm"a*tive*ly, adv
grave: 1. To clean, as a vessel's bottom, of barnacles, grass, etc., and pay it over with pitch | 2. -- so called because graves or greaves was formerly used for this purpose | 3. Of great weight
bicaudal: 1. Having, or terminating in, two tails
passager: 1. A passenger | 2. A bird or boat of passage.  Ld. Berners
goltschut: 1. A small ingot of gold | 2. A silver ingot, used in Japan as money
karma: 1. One's acts considered as fixing one's lot in the future existence. The doctrine of fate as the inflexible result of cause and effect | 2. The theory of inevitable consequence
waif: 1. Goods found of which the owner is not known | 2. Originally, such goods as a pursued thief threw away to prevent being apprehended, which belonged to the king unless the owner made pursuit of the felon, took him, and brought him to justice. Blackstone | 3. Hence, anything found, or without an owner
quercite: 1. A white crystalline substance, C6H75, found in acorns, the fruit of the oak. It has a sweet taste, and is regarded as a pentacid alcohol
recreate: 1. To give fresh life to | 2. To reanimate | 3. To revive
saucepan: 1. A small pan with a handle, in which sauce is prepared over a fire | 2. A stewpan
pentacrostic: 1. A set of verses so disposed that the name forming the subject of the acrostic occurs five times -- the whole set of verses being divided into five different parts from top to bottom
windstorm: 1. A storm characterized by high wind with little or no rain
obviate: 1. To meet in the way | 2. Not to stir a step to obviate any of a different religion. Fuller | 3. To anticipate
indicant:
1. Serving to point out, as a remedy | 2. Indicating.

That which indicates or points out | 3. As, an indicant of the remedy for a disease
disarticulator: 1. One who disarticulates and prepares skeletons
jigging: 1. The act or using a jig | 2. The act of separating ore with a jigger, or wire-bottomed sieve, which is moved up and down in water. Jigging machine. A machine for separating ore by the process of jigging. A machine with a rotary milling cutter and a templet by which the action of the cutter is guided or limited | 3. -- used for forming the profile of an irregularly shaped piece
bimetallism: 1. The legalized use of two metals in the currency of a country, at a fixed relative value | 2. -- in opposition to monometallism. Note: The words bimétallisme and monométallisme are due to M. Cernuschi . Littré
wildwood: 1. A wild or unfrequented wood. Also used adjectively | 2. As, wildwood flowers | 3. Wildwood echoes. Burns
outplay: 1. To excel or defeat in a game | 2. To play better than | 3. As, to be outplayed in tennis or ball
isatogen: 1. A complex nitrogenous radical, C8H4NO2, regarded as the essential residue of a series of compounds, related to isatin, which easily pass by reduction to indigo blue. -- I*sat`o*gen"ic, a
mouldery: 1. Covered or filled with mold | 2. Consisting of, or resembling, mold
revolt: 1. To turn away | 2. To abandon or reject something | 3. Specifically, to turn away, or shrink, with abhorrence. But this got by casting pearl to hogs, That bawl for freedom in their senseless mood, And still revolt when trith would set them free. Milton. HIs clear intelligence revolted from the dominant sophisms of that time. J. Morley
portraiture: 1. A portrait | 2. A likeness | 3. A painted resemblance
overjump: 1. To jump over | 2. Hence, to omit | 3. To ignore. Marston
spurt:
1. To gush or issue suddenly or violently out in a stream, as liquor from a cask | 2. To rush from a confined place in a small stream or jet | 3. To spirt. Thus the small jet, which hasty hands unlock, Spurts in the gardener's eyes who turns the cock. Pope.

To throw out, as a liquid, in a stream or jet
tristigmatic: 1. Having, or consisting of, three stigmas. Gray
redtail: 1. The red-tailed hawk. The European redstart
tropist: 1. One who deals in tropes | 2. Specifically, one who avoids the literal sense of the language of Scripture by explaining it as mere tropes and figures of speech
readjustment: 1. A second adjustment | 2. A new or different adjustment
douar: 1. A village composed of Arab tents arranged in streets
abies: 1. A genus of coniferous trees, properly called Fir, as the balsam fir and the silver fir | 2. The spruces are sometimes also referred to this genus
milling: 1. The act or employment of grinding or passing through a mill | 2. The process of fulling | 3. The process of making a raised or intented edge upon coin, etc
fructed: 1. Bearing fruit | 2. -- said of a tree or plant so represented upon an escutcheon. Cussans
dense: 1. Having the constituent parts massed or crowded together | 2. Close | 3. Compact
vindication: 1. The act of vindicating, or the state of being vindicated | 2. Defense | 3. Justification against denial or censure
ejaculatory: 1. Casting or throwing out | 2. Fitted to eject | 3. As, ejaculatory vessels
engorged: 1. Swallowed with greediness, or in large draughts | 2. Filled to excess with blood or other liquid | 3. Congested
apsis: 1. One of the two points of an orbit, as of a planet or satellite, which are at the greatest and least distance from the central body, corresponding to the aphelion and perihelion of a planet, or to the apogee and perigee of the moon. The more distant is called the higher apsis | 2. The other, the lower apsis | 3. And the line joining them, the line of apsides
marcasitic: 1. Containing, or having the nature of, marcasite
poke: 1. A large North American herb of the genus Phytolacca, bearing dark purple juicy berries | 2. -- called also garget, pigeon berry, pocan, and pokeweed. The root and berries have emetic and purgative properties, and are used in medicine. The young shoots are sometimes eaten as a substitute for asparagus, and the berries are said to be used in Europe to color wine | 3. A bag
boxthorn: 1. A plant of the genus Lycium, esp | 2. Lycium barbarum
traducianism: 1. The doctrine that human souls are produced by the act of generation | 2. -- opposed to creationism, and infusionism
commaterial: 1. Consisting of the same material.  Bacon
neoclassic: 1. Belonging to, or designating, the modern revival of classical, esp | 2. Greco-Roman, taste and manner of work in architecture, etc
invalidness: 1. Invalidity | 2. As, the invalidness of reasoning
tangram: 1. A Chinese toy made by cutting a square of thin wood, or other suitable material, into seven pieces, as shown in the cut, these pieces being capable of combination in various ways, so as to form a great number of different figures. It is now often used in primary schools as a means of instruction
geminate: 1. In pairs or twains | 2. Two together | 3. Binate
thermoelectricity: 1. Electricity developed in the action of heat. See the Note under Electricity
pseudonym: 1. A fictitious name assumed for the time, as by an author | 2. A pen name
fossores: 1. A group of hymenopterous insects including the sand wasps. They excavate cells in earth, where they deposit their eggs, with the bodies of other insects for the food of the young when hatched
leucopathy: 1. The state of an albino, or of a white child of black parents
affrightment: 1. Affright | 2. The state of being frightened | 3. Sudden fear or alarm.  Passionate words or blows . . . fill the child's mind with terror and affrightment. Locke
compellation: 1. Style of address or salutation | 2. An appellation. "Metaphorical compellations." Milton. He useth this endearing compellation, "My little children." Bp. Beveridge. The peculiar compellation of the kings in France is by "Sire," which is nothing else but father. Sir W. Temple
gelt:
1. Trubute, tax | 2. All these the king granted unto them . . . free from all gelts and payments, in a most full and ample manner. Fuller.

A gelding.  Mortimer.

Gilding | 3. Tinsel.  Spenser
orthodoxy: 1. Soundness of faith | 2. A belief in the doctrines taught in the Scriptures, or in some established standard of faith | 3. -- opposed to heterodoxy or to heresy. Basil himself bears full and clear testimony to Gregory's orthodoxy. Waterland
condylar: 1. Of or pertaining to a condyle. Condylar foramen, a formen in front of each condyle of the occipital bone | 2. -- sometimes called the anterior condylar foramen when a second, or posterior, foramen is present behind the condyle, as often happens in man
azoturia: 1. Excess of urea or other nitrogenous substances in the urine
mammiform: 1. Having the form of a mamma or mammæ
spathe: 1. A special involucre formed of one leaf and inclosing a spadix, as in aroid plants and palms. See the Note under Bract, and Illust. of Spadix. Note: The name is also given to the several-leaved involucre of the iris and other similar plants
trundlehead: 1. One of the disks forming the ends of a lantern wheel or pinion | 2. The drumhead of a capstan | 3. Especially, the drumhead of the lower of two capstans on the sane axis
dagoba: 1. A dome-shaped structure built over relics of Buddha or some Buddhist saint
shore:
1. Imp | 2. Of Shear. Chaucer.

A sewer. 

A prop, as a timber, placed as a brace or support against the side of a building or other structure | 3. A prop placed beneath anything, as a beam, to prevent it from sinking or sagging. 

To support by a shore or shores
collier: 1. One engaged in the business of digging mineral coal or making charcoal, or in transporting or dealing in coal | 2. A vessel employed in the coal trade
treachetour: 1. A traitor.  "Treachour full of false despite." Spenser
naphthene: 1. A peculiar hydrocarbon occuring as an ingredient of Caucasian petroleum
mendelian: 1. Pert. to Mendel, or to Mendel's law | 2. -- Men*de"li*an*ism, Men*del"ism, n
nonruminant: 1. Not ruminating | 2. As, a nonruminant animal
algerian: 1. Of or pertaining to Algeria. -- n.  A native of Algeria
ophthalmologist: 1. One skilled in ophthalmology | 2. An oculist
sweven: 1. A vision seen in sleep | 2. A dream.  Wycliff. I defy both sweven and dream. Chaucer
acetonaemia: 1. A morbid condition characterized by the presence of acetone in the blood, as in diabetes
bergstock: 1. A long pole with a spike at the end, used in climbing mountains | 2. An alpenstock
urostege: 1. One of the plates on the under side of the tail of a serpent
casuistical: 1. Of or pertaining to casuists or casuistry
unware: 1. Unaware | 2. Not foreseeing | 3. Being off one's guard.  Chaucer. Fairfax
antimonarchic: 1. Opposed to monarchial government. Bp. Benson. Addison
saxicavous: 1. Boring, or hollowing out, rocks | 2. -- said of certain mollusks which live in holes which they burrow in rocks. See Illust. of Lithodomus
yerne: 1. Eagerly | 2. Briskly | 3. Quickly.  Piers Plowman. My hands and my tongue go so yerne. Chaucer
genet: 1. One of several species of small Carnivora of the genus Genetta, allied to the civets, but having the scent glands less developed, and without a pouch. Note: The common genet of Southern Europe, Asia Minor, and North Africa, is dark gray, spotted with black. The long tail is banded with black and white. The Cape genet, and the berbe, are related African species | 2. The fur of the common genet | 3. Also, any skin dressed in imitation of this fur
sequoia: 1. A genus of coniferous trees, consisting of two species, Sequoia Washingtoniana, syn | 2. Gigantea, the "big tree" of California, and S. sempervirens, the redwood, both of which attain an immense height
ventriloquist: 1. One who practices, or is skilled in, ventriloquism. Ventriloquist monkey, the onappo | 2. -- so called from the character of its cry
melanochroic: 1. Having a dark complexion | 2. Of or pertaining to the Melanochroi
metasome: 1. One of the component segments of the body of an animal
heterotropous: 1. Having the embryo or ovule oblique or transverse to the funiculus | 2. Amphitropous. Gray
bystander: 1. One who stands near | 2. A spectator | 3. One who has no concern with the business transacting. He addressed the bystanders and scattered pamphlets among them. Palfrey. Syn. -- Looker on
clique:
1. A narrow circle of persons associated by common interests or for the accomplishment of a common purpose | 2. -- generally used in a bad sense.

To To associate together in a clannish way | 3. To act with others secretly to gain a desired end
legist: 1. One skilled in the laws | 2. A writer on law | 3. Milman. J. Morley
suiting: 1. Among tailors, cloth suitable for making entire suits of clothes
thanedom: 1. The property or jurisdiction of a thane | 2. Thanage. Sir W. Scott
protamin: 1. An amorphous nitrogenous substance found in the spermatic fluid of salmon. It is soluble in water, which an alkaline reaction, and unites with acids and metallic bases
spectroheliogram: 1. A photograph of the sun made by monochromatic light, usually of the calcium line, and showing the sun's faculæ and prominences
obtrusive: 1. Disposed to obtrude | 2. Inclined to intrude or thrust one's self or one's opinions upon others, or to enter uninvited | 3. Forward
perverseness: 1. The quality or state of being perverse. "Virtue hath some perverseness." Donne
hurried: 1. Urged on | 2. Hastened | 3. Going or working at speed
wealthful: 1. Full of wealth | 2. Wealthy | 3. Prosperous.  Sir T. More. -- Wealth"ful*ly, adv
september: 1. The ninth month of the year, containing thurty days
brachycephalism: 1. The state or condition of being brachycephalic | 2. Shortness of head
littleness: 1. The state or quality of being little | 2. As, littleness of size, thought, duration, power, etc | 3. Syn. -- Smallness
crateriform: 1. Having the form of a shallow bowl | 2. -- said of a corolla
feticide: 1. The act of killing the fetus in the womb | 2. The offense of procuring an abortion
derringer: 1. A kind of short-barreled pocket pistol, of very large caliber, often carrying a half-ounce ball
vibraculum: 1. One of the movable, slender, spinelike organs or parts with which certain bryozoans are furnished. They are regarded as specially modified zooids, of nearly the same nature as Avicularia
intumesce: 1. To enlarge or expand with heat | 2. To swell | 3. Specifically, to swell up or bubble up under the action of heat, as before the blowpipe. In a higher heat, it intumesces, and melts into a yellowish black mass. Kirwan
chigre: 1. A species of flea, common in the West Indies and South America, which often attacks the feet or any exposed part of the human body, and burrowing beneath the skin produces great irritation. When the female is allowed to remain and breed, troublesome sores result, which are sometimes dangerous. See Jigger.  Note: The name is sometimes erroneously given to certain mites or ticks having similar habits
unburiable: 1. Not ready or not proper to be buried. Tennyson
physiocrat: 1. One of the followers of Quesnay of France, who, in the 18th century, founded a system of political economy based upon the supremacy of natural order. F. A. Walker. -- Phys`i*o*crat"ic, a
shampoo:
1. To press or knead the whole surface of the body of, and at the same time to stretch the limbs and joints, in connection with the hot bath | 2. To wash throughly and rub the head of, with the fingers, using either soap, or a soapy preparation, for the more thorough cleansing.

The act of shampooing
parenticide: 1. The act of one who kills one's own parent | 2. One who kills one's own parent | 3. A parricide
preexistent: 1. Existing previously | 2. Preceding existence | 3. As, a preëxistent state. Pope
cist: 1. A box or chest. Specifically: A bronze receptacle, round or oval, frequently decorated with engravings on the sides and cover, and with feet, handles, etc., of decorative castings. A cinerary urn | 2. See Illustration in Appendix | 3. See Cyst
pavise: 1. A large shield covering the whole body, carried by a pavisor, who sometimes screened also an archer with it.  Fairholt
steganography: 1. The art of writing in cipher, or in characters which are not intelligible except to persons who have the key | 2. Cryptography
phrasing: 1. Method of expression | 2. Association of words | 3. The act or method of grouping the notes so as to form distinct musical phrases
sortilege: 1. The act or practice of drawing lots | 2. Divination by drawing lots. A woman infamous for sortileges and witcheries. Sir W. Scott
hymnology: 1. The hymns or sacred lyrics composed by authors of a particular country or period | 2. As, the hymnology of the eighteenth century | 3. Also, the collective body of hymns used by any particular church or religious body
inane: 1. Without contents | 2. Empty | 3. Void of sense or intelligence
extravagantness: 1. The state of being extravagant or in excess | 2. Excess | 3. Extravagance
unthinker: 1. A person who does not think, or does not think wisely
nasturtium: 1. A genus of cruciferous plants, having white or yellowish flowers, including several species of cress. Any plant of the genus Tropæolum, geraniaceous herbs, having mostly climbing stems, peltate leaves, and spurred flowers, and including the common Indian cress, the canary-bird flower, and about thirty more species, all natives of South America. bongo: 1. Either of two large antelopes of a reddish or chestnut-brown color with narrow white stripes on the body. Their flesh is especially esteemed as food
cresylic: 1. Pertaining to, or derived from, cresol, creosote, etc | 2. Cresylic acid. See Cresol
poorliness: 1. The quality or state of being poorly | 2. Ill health
skimmer: 1. One who, or that which, skims | 2. Esp., a utensil with which liquids are skimmed | 3. Any species of longwinged marine birds of the genus Rhynchops, allied to the terns, but having the lower mandible compressed and much longer than the upper one
nummary: 1. Of or relating to coins or money
antitypy: 1. Opposition or resistance of matter to force.  Sir W. Hamilton
immitigable: 1. Not capable of being mitigated, softened, or appeased. Coleridge
laterality: 1. The state or condition of being lateral
umbrel: 1. An umbrella.  Each of them besides bore their umbrels. Shelton
egest: 1. To cast or throw out | 2. To void, as excrement | 3. To excrete, as the indigestible matter of the food
haustorium: 1. One of the suckerlike rootlets of such plants as the dodder and ivy | 2. Brown
recaptor: 1. One who recaptures | 2. One who takes a prize which had been previously taken
countercheck: 1. To oppose or check by some obstacle | 2. To check by a return check | 3. A check
lurchline: 1. The line by which a fowling net was pulled over so as to inclose the birds
regularly: 1. In a regular manner | 2. In uniform order | 3. Methodically
humpback: 1. A crooked back | 2. A humped back. Tatler | 3. A humpbacked person

v: 1. V, the twenty-second letter of the English alphabet, is a vocal consonant. V and U are only varieties of the same character, U being the cursive form, while V is better adapted for engraving, as in stone. The two letters were formerly used indiscriminately, and till a comparatively recent date words containing them were often classed together in dictionaries and other books of reference. The letter V is from the Latin alphabet, where it was used both as a consonant and as a vowel. The Latin derives it from it from a form of the Greek vowel UPSILON, this Greek letter being either from the same Semitic letter as the digamma F, or else added by the Greeks to the alphabet which they took from the Semitic. tooth: 1. One of the hard, bony appendages which are borne on the jaws, or on other bones in the walls of the mouth or pharynx of most vertebrates, and which usually aid in the prehension and mastication of food. Note: The hard parts of teeth are principally made up of dentine, or ivory, and a very hard substance called enamel. These are variously combined in different animals. Each tooth consist of three parts, a crown, or body, projecting above the gum, one or more fangs imbedded in the jaw, and the neck, or intermediate part. In some animals one or more of the teeth are modified into tusks which project from the mouth, as in both sexes of the elephant and of the walrus, and in the male narwhal. In adult man there are thirty-two teeth, composed largely of dentine, but the crowns are covered with enamel, and the fangs with a layer of bone called cementum. Of the eight teeth on each half of each jaw, the two in front are incisors, then come one canine, cuspid, or dog tooth, two bicuspids, or false molars, and three molars, or grinding teeth. The milk, or temporary, teeth are only twenty in number, there being two incisors, one canine, and two molars on each half of each jaw | 2. hysteria: 1. A nervous affection, occurring almost exclusively in women, in which the emotional and reflex excitability is exaggerated, and the will power correspondingly diminished, so that the patient loses control over the emotions, becomes the victim of imaginary sensations, and often falls into paroxism or fits. Note: The chief symptoms are convulsive, tossing movements of the limbs and head, uncontrollable crying and laughing, and a choking sensation as if a ball were lodged in the throat. The affection presents the most varied symptoms, often simulating those of the gravest diseases, but generally curable by mental treatment alone

There are now recognized about three hundred species, of which nearly fifty occur in the United States, the rest in Europe, Asia, and the other parts of North America, a very few barely reaching the northern parts of South America and Africa. Many of the oaks form forest trees of grand proportions and live many centuries. The wood is usually hard and tough, and provided with conspicuous medullary rays, forming the silver grain | 2. The strong wood or timber of the oak | 3. Note: Among the true oaks in America are: Barren oak, or Black-jack, Q. nigra. -- Basket oak, Q. U, the twenty-first letter of the English alphabet, is a cursive form of the letter V, with which it was formerly used interchangeably, both letters being then used both as vowels and consonants. The true primary vowel sound of U, in Anglo-Saxon, was the sound which it still retains in most of the languages of Europe, that of long oo, as in tool, and short oo, as in wood, answering to the French ou in tour. contango: 1. The premium or interest paid by the buyer to the seller, to be allowed to defer paying for the stock purchased until the next fortnightly settlement day | 2. The postponement of payment by the buyer of stock on the payment of a premium to the seller. See Backwardation. N. Biddle
impone: 1. To stake | 2. To wager | 3. To pledge.  Against the which he has imponed, as I take it, six French rapiers and poniards. Shak
hinder: 1. Of or belonging to that part or end which is in the rear, or which follows | 2. As, the hinder part of a wagon | 3. The hinder parts of a horse. He was in the hinder part of the ship. Mark iv
differentiation: 1. The act of differentiating. Further investigation of the Sanskrit may lead to differentiation of the meaning of such of these roots as are real roots. J. Peile | 2. The act of distinguishing or describing a thing, by giving its different, or specific difference | 3. Exact definition or determination
cerussite: 1. Native lead carbonate | 2. A mineral occurring in colorless, white, or yellowish transparent crystals, with an adamantine, also massive and compact
broadcloth: 1. A fine smooth-faced woolen cloth for men's garments, usually of double width | 2. -- so called in distinction from woolens three quarters of a yard wide
cholagogue: 1. Promoting the discharge of bile from the system. -- n.  An agent which promotes the discharge of bile from the system
pyrus: 1. A genus of rosaceous trees and shrubs having pomes for fruit. It includes the apple, crab apple, pear, chokeberry, sorb, and mountain ash
tileseed: 1. Any plant of the genus Geissois, having seeds overlapping like tiles on a roof
eft:
1. A European lizard of the genus Seps. A salamander, esp | 2. The European smooth newt.

Again | 3. Afterwards
spurrier: 1. One whose occupation is to make spurs. B. Jonson. "The saddlers and spurriers would be ruined by thousands." Macaulay
tatch: 1. A spot or stain | 2. Also, a trick.  Sir T. Elyot
diffidence: 1. The state of being diffident | 2. Distrust | 3. Want of confidence
salute: 1. To adress, as with expressions of kind wishes and courtesy | 2. To greet | 3. To hail. I salute you with this kingly title. Shak
quint: 1. A set or sequence of five, as in piquet | 2. The interval of a fifth
