muxy: 1. Soft | 2. Sticky, and dirty.  See Mucky
introreception: 1. The act of admitting into or within. Hammond
vermiculate: 1. To form or work, as by inlaying, with irregular lines or impressions resembling the tracks of worms, or appearing as if formed by the motion of worms | 2. Wormlike in shape | 3. Covered with wormlike elevations
crystalline: 1. Consisting, or made, of crystal. Mount, eagle, to my palace crystalline. Shak | 2. Formed by crystallization | 3. Like crystal in texture. Their crystalline structure. Whewell
hexapodous: 1. Having six feet | 2. Belonging to the Hexapoda
socialize: 1. To render social | 2. To subject to, or regulate by, socialism
quartation: 1. The act, process, or result of alloying a button of nearly pure gold with enough silver to reduce the fineness so as to allow acids to attack and remove all metals except the gold | 2. -- called also inquartation. Compare Parting
enneatic: 1. Occurring once in every nine times, days, years, etc | 2. Every ninth. Enneatical day, every ninth day of a disease. -- Enneatical year, every ninth year of a man's life
terrel: 1. A spherical magnet so placed that its poles, equator, etc., correspond to those of the earth.  Chambers
vively: 1. In a lively manner.  If I see a thing vively represented on the stage. B. Jonson
misunderstanding: 1. Mistake of the meaning | 2. Error | 3. Misconception. Bacon
holily: 1. Piously | 2. With sanctity | 3. In a holy manner
swingebuckler: 1. A swashbuckler | 2. A bully | 3. A roiserer.  Shak
starchness: 1. Of or pertaining to starched or starch | 2. Stiffness of manner | 3. Preciseness
surveillant: 1. One who watches over another | 2. An overseer | 3. A spy
flesher: 1. A butcher. A flesher on a block had laid his whittle down. Macaulay | 2. A two-handled, convex, blunt-edged knife, for scraping hides | 3. A fleshing knife
aversely: 1. Backward | 2. In a backward direction | 3. As, emitted aversely
forcer: 1. One who, or that which, forces or drives | 2. The solid piston of a force pump | 3. The instrument by which water is forced in a pump. A small hand pump for sinking pits, draining cellars, etc
iambize: 1. To satirize in iambics | 2. To lampoon
margay: 1. An American wild cat, ranging from Mexico to Brazil. It is spotted with black. Called also long-tailed cat
bryology: 1. That part of botany which relates to mosses
punnet: 1. A broad, shallow basket, for displaying fruit or flowers
heteroscian: 1. One who lives either north or south of the tropics, as contrasted with one who lives on the other side of them | 2. -- so called because at noon the shadows always fall in opposite directions
kangaroo: 1. Any one of numerous species of jumping marsupials of the family Macropodidæ. They inhabit Australia, New Guinea, and adjacent islands, They have long and strong hind legs and a large tail, while the fore legs are comparatively short and feeble. The giant kangaroo is the largest species, sometimes becoming twelve or fourteen feet in total length. The tree kangaroos, belonging to the genus Dendrolagus, live in trees | 2. The rock kangaroos, of the genus Petrogale, inhabit rocky situations | 3. And the brush kangaroos, of the genus Halmaturus, inhabit wooded districts. See Wallaby. Kangaroo apple, the edible fruit of the Tasmanian plant Solanum aviculare. -- Kangaroo grass, a perennial Australian forage grass. -- Kangaroo hare, the jerboa kangaroo. See under Jerboa. -- Kangaroo mouse. See Jumping mouse, under Jumping. -- Kangaroo rat, the potoroo
callot:
1. A plant coif or skullcap. Same as Calotte. B. Jonson.

A close cap without visor or brim. Especially: Such a cap, worn by English serjeants at law | 2. Such a cap, worn by the French cavalry under their helmets. Such a cap, worn by the clergy of the Roman Catholic Church. To assume the calotte, to become a priest
statehouse: 1. The building in which a State legislature holds its sessions | 2. A State capitol
denticulation: 1. The state of being set with small notches or teeth. Grew | 2. A diminutive tooth | 3. A denticle
thornbill: 1. Any one of several species of small, brilliantly colored American birds of the genus Rhamphomicron. They have a long, slender, sharp bill, and feed upon honey, insects, and the juice of the sugar cane
unrivet: 1. To take out, or loose, the rivets of | 2. As, to unrivet boiler plates
apposite: 1. Very applicable | 2. Well adapted | 3. Suitable or fit
islamitic: 1. Of or pertaining to Islam | 2. Mohammedan
sonata: 1. An extended composition for one or two instruments, consisting usually of three or four movements | 2. As, Beethoven's sonatas for the piano, for the violin and piano, etc | 3. Note: The same general structure prevails in symphonies, instrumental trios, quartets, etc., and even in classical concertos. The sonata form, distinctively, characterizes the quick opening movement, which may have a short, slow introduction
caliculate: 1. Relating to, or resembling, a cup | 2. Also improperly used for calycular, calyculate
preterition: 1. The act of passing, or going past | 2. The state of being past. Bp. Hall | 3. A figure by which, in pretending to pass over anything, a summary mention of it is made
nummulation: 1. The arrangement of the red blood corpuscles in rouleaux, like piles of coins, as when a drop of human blood is examined under the microscope
bundle: 1. A number of things bound together, as by a cord or envelope, into a mass or package convenient for handling or conveyance | 2. A loose package | 3. A roll
homoousian:
1. One of those, in the 4th century, who accepted the Nicene creed, and maintained that the Son had the same essence or substance with the Father | 2. -- opposed to homoiousian.

Of or pertaining to the Homoousians, or to the doctrines they held
aetiological: 1. Pertaining to ætiology | 2. Assigning a cause. -- Æ`ti*o*log"ic*al*ly, adv
guitguit: 1. One of several species of small tropical American birds of the family Coerebidæ, allied to the creepers | 2. -- called also quit. See Quit
dory:
1. A European fish. See Doree, and John Doree | 2. The American wall-eyed perch | 3. -- called also doré. See Pike perch.

A small, strong, flat-bottomed rowboat, with sharp prow and flaring sides
imbar: 1. To bar in | 2. To secure.  To imbar their crooked titles. Shak
resenter: 1. One who resents. Sir H. Wotton
magnetotherapy: 1. The treatment of disease by the application of magnets to the surface of the body
chippeways: 1. A tribe of Indians formerly inhabiting the northern and weastern shores of Lake Superior | 2. -- called also Objibways
inflationist: 1. One who favors an increased or very large issue of paper money
kiosk: 1. A Turkish open summer house or pavilion, supported by pillars
glucina: 1. A white or gray tasteless powder, the oxide of the element glucinum | 2. -- formerly called glucine
zax: 1. A tool for trimming and puncturing roofing states
grater: 1. One who, or that which, grates | 2. Especially, an instrument or utensil with a rough, indented surface, for rubbing off small particles of any substance | 3. As a grater for nutmegs
hectoliter: 1. A measure of liquids, containing a hundred liters | 2. Equal to a tenth of a cubic meter, nearly 26
belate: 1. To retard or make too late. Davenant
interjacence: 1. The state of being between | 2. A coming or lying between or among | 3. Intervention
shake: 1. Obs | 2. P. of Shake. Chaucer | 3. To cause to move with quick or violent vibrations
auriga: 1. The Charioteer, or Wagoner, a constellation in the northern hemisphere, situated between Perseus and Gemini. It contains the bright star Capella
adversifoliate: 1. Having opposite leaves, as plants which have the leaves so arranged on the stem
vasculose: 1. One of the substances of which vegetable tissue is composed, differing from cellulose in its solubility in certain media
clerisy: 1. The literati, or well educated class | 2. The clergy, or their opinions, as opposed to the laity
azole: 1. Any of a large class of compounds characterized by a five- membered ring which contains an atom of nitrogen and at least one other noncarbon atom. The prefixes furo-, thio, and pyrro-are used to distinguish three subclasses of azoles, which may be regarded as derived respectively from furfuran, thiophene, and pyrrol by replacement of the CH group by nitrogen | 2. As, furo-monazole. Names exactly analogous to those for the azines are also used | 3. As, oxazole, diazole, etc
shortening: 1. The act of making or becoming short or shorter | 2. That which renders pastry short or friable, as butter, lard, etc
emperor: 1. The sovereign or supreme monarch of an empire | 2. -- a title of dignity superior to that of king | 3. As, the emperor of Germany or of Austria
rhabdopleura: 1. A genus of marine Bryozoa in which the tubular cells have a centralchitinous axis and the tentacles are borne on a bilobed lophophore. It is the type of the order Pterobranchia, or Podostomata
electrifiable: 1. Capable of receiving electricity, or of being charged with it
vinosity: 1. The quality or state of being vinous
beaucatcher: 1. A small flat curl worn on the temple by women
prooetic: 1. In front of the auditory capsule | 2. -- applied especially to a bone, or center of ossification, in the periotic capsule. -- n.  A proötic bone
coronium: 1. The principal gaseous substance forming the solar corona, characterized by a green line in the coronal spectrum
endostosis: 1. A process of bone formation in which ossification takes place within the substance of the cartilage
freck: 1. To checker | 2. To diversify.  The painted windows, frecking gloom with glow. Lowell
argentiferous: 1. Producing or containing silver | 2. As, argentiferous lead ore or veins
wreck: 1. See 2d & 3d Wreak | 2. The destruction or injury of a vessel by being cast on shore, or on rocks, or by being disabled or sunk by the force of winds or waves | 3. Shipwreck. Hard and obstinate As is a rock amidst the raging floods, 'Gainst which a ship, of succor desolate, Doth suffer wreck, both of herself and goods. Spenser
galenic:
1. Pertaining to, or containing, galena.

Relating to Galen or to his principles and method of treating diseases. Dunglison. Galenic pharmacy, that branch of pharmacy which relates to the preparation of medicines by infusion, decoction, etc., as distinguished from those which are chemically prepared
anomy: 1. Disregard or violation of law | 2. Glanvill
counterirritant: 1. See Counter irritant, etc., under Counter, a
carbonate: 1. A salt or carbonic acid, as in limestone, some forms of lead ore, etc
plainness: 1. The quality or state of being plain
argal:
1. Crude tartar. See Argol.

A ludicrous corruption of the Latin word ergo, therefore. Shak.

A species of wild sheep, remarkable for its large horns. It inhabits the mountains of Siberia and central Asia. Note: The bearded argali is the aoudad. See Aoudad. The name is also applied to the bighorn sheep of the Rocky Mountains. See Bighorn
otherwhiles: 1. At another time, or other times | 2. Sometimes | 3. Weighing otherwhiles ten pounds and more. Holland
saturn: 1. One of the elder and principal deities, the son of Coelus and Terra, anf the father of Jupiter. The corresponding Greek divinity was Kro`nos, later CHro`nos, Time | 2. One of the planets of the solar system, next in magnitude to Jupiter, but more remote from the sun | 3. Its diameter is seventy thousand miles, its mean distance from the sun nearly eight hundred and eighty millions of miles, and its year, or periodical revolution round the sun, nearly twenty-nine years and a half. It is surrounded by a remarkable system of rings, and has eight satellites
monocular: 1. Having only one eye | 2. With one eye only | 3. As, monocular vision
epileptogenous: 1. Producing epilepsy or epileptoid convulsions | 2. -- applied to areas of the body or of the nervous system, stimulation of which produces convulsions
uniserial: 1. Having only one row or series
cherubical: 1. Of or pertaining to cherubs | 2. Angelic. "The cherubic host." Milton
germane: 1. Literally, near akin | 2. Hence, closely allied | 3. Appropriate or fitting
surbase: 1. A cornice, or series of moldings, on the top of the base of a pedestal, podium, etc | 2. See Illust. of Column | 3. A board or group of moldings running round a room on a level with the tops of the chair backs. Knight
washing: 1. The act of one who washes | 2. The act of cleansing with water | 3. Ablution
purgery: 1. The part of a sugarhouse where the molasses is drained off from the sugar
rhapsody: 1. A recitation or song of a rhapsodist | 2. A portion of an epic poem adapted for recitation, or usually recited, at one time | 3. Hence, a division of the Iliad or the Odyssey
remorse: 1. The anguish, like gnawing pain, excited by a sense of guilt | 2. Compunction of conscience for a crime committed, or for the sins of one's past life. "Nero will be tainted with remorse." Shak | 3. Sympathetic sorrow
bombazette: 1. A sort of thin woolen cloth. It is of various colors, and may be plain or twilled
unbid: 1. Not bidden | 2. Not commanded. Thorns also and thistles it shall bring thee forth Unbid | 3. And thou shalt eat the herb of the field. Milton
layship: 1. The condition of being a layman.  Milton
illegibility: 1. The state or quality of being illegible
inestimably: 1. In a manner, or to a degree, above estimation | 2. As, things inestimably excellent
reprobation: 1. The act of reprobating | 2. The state of being reprobated | 3. Strong disapproval or censure. The profligate pretenses upon which he was perpetually soliciting an increase of his disgraceful stipend are mentioned with becoming reprobation. Jeffrey. Set a brand of reprobation on clipped poetry and false coin. Dryden
swollen:
1. P. of Swell.

Enlarged by swelling | 2. Immoderately increased | 3. As, swollen eyes
conflagration: 1. A fire extending to many objects, or over a large space | 2. A general burning. Till one wide conflagration swallows all | 3. Pope
interhyal: 1. Of or pertaining to a segment sometimes present at the proximal end of the hyoidean arch. -- n.  An interhyal ligament or cartilage
wastage: 1. Loss by use, decay, evaporation, leakage, or the like | 2. Waste
barege: 1. A gauzelike fabric for ladies' dresses, veils, etc | 2. Of worsted, silk and worsted, or cotton and worsted
dairyman: 1. A man who keeps or takes care of a dairy
wisly: 1. Certainly.  "God so wisly have mercy on me." Chaucer
conchoidal: 1. Having elevations or depressions in form like one half of a bivalve shell | 2. -- applied principally to a surface produced by fracture
pentarchy: 1. A government in the hands of five persons | 2. Five joint rulers. P. Fletcher. "The pentarchy of the senses." A. Brewer
stipple:
1. To engrave by means of dots, in distinction from engraving in lines. The interlaying of small pieces can not altogether avoid a broken, stippled, spotty effect. Milman | 2. To paint, as in water colors, by small, short touches which together produce an even or softly graded surface.

A mode of execution which produces the effect by dots or small points instead of lines | 3. A mode of execution in which a flat or even tint is produced by many small touches
megaphyton: 1. An extinct genus of tree ferns with large, two-ranked leaves, or fronds
syrphian: 1. Of or pertaining to the syrphus flies. -- n.  A syrphus fly
eviction: 1. The act or process of evicting | 2. Or state of being evicted | 3. The recovery of lands, tenements, etc., from another's possession by due course of law
counterclaim: 1. A claim made by a person as an offset to a claim made on him
spermary: 1. An organ in which spermatozoa are developed | 2. A sperm gland | 3. A testicle
examinable: 1. Capable of being examined or inquired into. Bacon
discruciate: 1. To torture | 2. To excruciate.  Discruciate a man in deep distress. Herrick
gallicize: 1. To conform to the French mode or idiom
staid:
1. Imp | 2. & p. p. of Stay.

Sober | 3. Grave
solidarity: 1. An entire union or consolidation of interests and responsibilities | 2. Fellowship | 3. Community. Solidarity , signifies a fellowship in gain and loss, in honor and dishonor, in victory and defeat, a being, so to speak, all in the same boat. Trench. The solidarity . . . of Breton and Welsh poetry. M. Arnold
peritricha: 1. A division of ciliated Infusoria having a circle of cilia around the oral disk and sometimes another around the body. It includes the vorticellas. See Vorticella
whine: 1. To utter a plaintive cry, as some animals | 2. To mean with a childish noise | 3. To complain, or to tell of sorrow, distress, or the like, in a plaintive, nasal tone
hopscotch: 1. A child's game, in which a player, hopping on one foot, drives a stone from one compartment to another of a figure traced or scotched on the ground | 2. -- called also hoppers
teleocephial: 1. An extensive order of bony fishes including most of the common market species, as bass, salmon, cod, perch, etc
platinocyanide: 1. A double cyanide of platinum and some other metal or radical | 2. A salt of platinocyanic acid
mitrailleuse: 1. A breech-loading machine gun consisting of a number of barrels fitted together, so arranged that the barrels can be fired simultaneously, or successively, and rapidly
misconceive: 1. To conceive wrongly | 2. To interpret incorrectly | 3. To receive a false notion of
emotioned: 1. Affected with emotion.  "The emotioned soul." Sir W. Scott
malthusian:
1. Of or pertaining to the political economist, the Rev. T. R. Malthus, or conforming to his views | 2. As, Malthusian theories. Note: Malthus held that population tends to increase faster than its means of subsistence can be made to do, and hence that the lower classes must necessarily suffer more or less from lack of food, unless an increase of population be checked by prudential restraint or otherwise.

A follower of Malthus
cafileh: 1. A caravan of travelers | 2. A military supply train or government caravan | 3. A string of pack horses
tetractinellida: 1. A division of Spongiæ in which the spicules are siliceous and have four branches diverging at right angles. Called also Tetractinellinæ
skinch: 1. To give scant measure | 2. To squeeze or pinch in order to effect a saving
fermentation: 1. The process of undergoing an effervescent change, as by the action of yeast | 2. In a wider sense, the transformation of an organic substance into new compounds by the action of a ferment, either formed or unorganized. It differs in kind according to the nature of the ferment which causes it | 3. A state of agitation or excitement, as of the intellect or the feelings. It puts the soul to fermentation and activity. Jer. Taylor. A univesal fermentation of human thought and faith. C. Kingsley. Acetous, or Acetic, fermentation, a form of oxidation in which alcohol is converted into vinegar or acetic acid by the agency of a specific fungus or ferment. The process involves two distinct reactions, in which the oxygen of the air is essential. An intermediate product, aldehyde, is formed in the first process
hypoderma: 1. A layer of tissue beneath the epidermis in plants, and performing the physiological function of strengthening the epidermal tissue. In phanerogamous plants it is developed as collenchyma | 2. An inner cellular layer which lies beneath the chitinous cuticle of arthropods, annelids, and some other invertebrates
bescummer: 1. To discharge ordure or dung upon.  B. Jonson
urania: 1. One of the nine Muses, daughter of Zeus by Mnemosyne, and patron of astronomy | 2. A genus of large, brilliantly colored moths native of the West Indies and South America. Their bright colored and tailed hind wings and their diurnal flight cause them to closely resemble butterflies
conservancy: 1. Conservation, as from injury, defilement, or irregular use | 2. Passed in 1866, for vesting in the Conservators of the River Thames the conservancy of the Thames and Isis. Mozley & W
eddaic: 1. Relating to the Eddas | 2. Resembling the Eddas
repellence: 1. The principle of repulsion | 2. The quality or capacity of repelling | 3. Repulsion
marseillaise:
1. Of or pertaining to Marseilles, in France, or to its inhabitants. Marseillaise hymn, or The Marseillaise, the national anthem of France, popularly so called. It was composed in 1792, by Rouget de l'Isle, an officer then stationed at Strasburg. In Paris it was sung for the first time by the band of men who came from Marseilles to aid in the revolution of August 10, 1792 | 2. Whence the name.

A native or inhabitant of Marseilles
figulate: 1. Made of potter's clay | 2. Molded | 3. Shaped.  Johnson
scullery: 1. A place where dishes, kettles, and culinary utensils, are cleaned and kept | 2. Also, a room attached to the kitchen, where the coarse work is done | 3. A back kitchen
redact: 1. To reduce to form, as literary matter | 2. To digest and put in shape | 3. To edit
spermospore: 1. The male germinal or seminal cell, from the breaking up of which the spermoblasts are formed and ultimately the spermatozoids | 2. A spermatospore. Balfour
foin:
1. The beech marten. See Marten | 2. A kind of fur, black at the top on a whitish ground, taken from the ferret or weasel of the same name. He came to the stake in a fair black gown furred and faced with foins. Fuller.

To thrust with a sword or spear | 3. To lunge.  He stroke, he soused, he foynd, he hewed, he lashed. Spenser. They lash, they foin, they pass, they strive to bore Their corselets, and the thinnest parts explore. Dryden.

To prick
marlstone: 1. A sandy calcareous straum, containing, or impregnated with, iron, and lying between the upper and lower Lias of England
pinocle:
1. A game at cards, played with forty-eight cards, being all the cards above the eight spots in two packs.

See Penuchle
bifold: 1. Twofold | 2. Double | 3. Of two kinds, degrees, etc
pipelaying: 1. The laying of conducting pipes underground, as for water, gas, etc | 2. The act or method of making combinations for personal advantage secretly or slyly | 3. -- in this sense, usually written as one word
auspicate: 1. Auspicious.  Holland | 2. To foreshow | 3. To foretoken.  B. Jonson
ellagic: 1. Pertaining to, or derived from, gallnuts or gallic acid | 2. As, ellagic acid. Ellagic acid, a white crystalline substance, C14H8O9, found in bezoar stones, and obtained by the oxidation of gallic acid
gaddish: 1. Disposed to gad | 2. -- Gad"dish*nes, n. "Gaddishness and folly." Abp. Leighton
egg: 1. The oval or roundish body laid by domestic poultry and other birds, tortoises, etc | 2. It consists of a yolk, usually surrounded by the "white" or albumen, and inclosed in a shell or strong membrane | 3. A simple cell, from the development of which the young of animals are formed
subprehensile: 1. Somewhat prehensile | 2. Prehensile in an inferior degree
repaganize: 1. To paganize anew | 2. To bring back to paganism
healful: 1. Tending or serving to heal | 2. Healing.  Ecclus. xv
cherokees: 1. An Appalachian tribe of Indians, formerly inhabiting the region about the head waters of the Tennessee River. They are now mostly settled in the Indian Territory, and have become one of the most civilized of the Indian Tribes
ditokous: 1. Having two kinds of young, as certain annelids. Producing only two eggs for a clutch, as certain birds do
pubescence: 1. The quality or state of being pubescent, or of having arrived at puberty. Sir T. Browne | 2. A covering of soft short hairs, or down, as one some plants and insects | 3. Also, the state of being so covered
basal: 1. Relating to, or forming, the base. Basal cleavage. See under Cleavage. -- Basal plane, one parallel to the lateral or horizontal axis
makebate: 1. One who excites contentions and quarrels
timocratic: 1. Belonging to, or constituted by, timocracy. Sir G. C. Lewis
myeloidin: 1. A substance, present in the protoplasm of the retinal epithelium cells, and resembling, if not identical with, the substance forming the medullary sheaths of nerve fibers
balder: 1. The most beautiful and beloved of the gods | 2. The god of peace | 3. The son of Odin and Freya
assonant: 1. Having a resemblance of sounds | 2. Pertaining to the peculiar species of rhyme called assonance | 3. Not consonant
silurus: 1. A genus of large malacopterygious fishes of the order Siluroidei. They inhabit the inland waters of Europe and Asia
sleeky: 1. Of a sleek, or smooth, and glossy appearance. Thomson | 2. Fawning and deceitful | 3. Sly
licheniform: 1. Having the form of a lichen
cloistered: 1. Dwelling in cloisters | 2. Solitary. "Cloistered friars and vestal nuns." Hudibras. In cloistered state let selfish sages dwell, Proud that their heart is narrow as their cell. Shenstone | 3. Furnished with cloisters. Sir H. Wotton
designful: 1. Full of design | 2. Scheming.  -- De*sign"ful*ness, n.  Barrow
garter: 1. A band used to prevent a stocking from slipping down on the leg | 2. The distinguishing badge of the highest order of knighthood in Great Britain, called the Order of the Garter, instituted by Edward III | 3. Also, the Order itself
mandarinate: 1. The collective body of officials or persons of rank in China. S. W. Williams
arabical: 1. Relating to Arabia | 2. Arabic. -- A*rab"ic*al*ly, adv
lochia: 1. The discharge from the womb and vagina which follows childbirth
reviction: 1. Return to life.  Sir T. Browne
ordonnant: 1. Of or pertaining to ordonnance. Dryden
belomancy: 1. A kind of divination anciently practiced by means of marked arrows drawn at random from a bag or quiver, the marks on the arrows drawn being supposed to foreshow the future. Encyc. Brit
infecter: 1. One who, or that which, infects
jungle: 1. A dense growth of brushwood, grasses, reeds, vines, etc | 2. An almost impenetrable thicket of trees, canes, and reedy vegetation, as in India, Africa, Australia, and Brazil. The jungles of India are of bamboos, canes, and other palms, very difficult to penetrate. Balfour. Jungle bear, the aswail or sloth bear. -- Jungle cat, the chaus. -- Jungle cock, the male of a jungle fowl. -- Jungle fowl. extinguishment: 1. The act of extinguishing, putting out, or quenching, or the state of being extinguished | 2. Extinction | 3. Suppression
jaspilite: 1. A compact siliceous rock resembling jasper
sondeli: 1. The musk shrew. See under Musk
tubman: 1. One of the two most experienced barristers in the Court of Exchequer. Cf. Postman,
centrosome: 1. A peculiar rounded body lying near the nucleus of a cell. It is regarded as the dynamic element by means of which the machinery of cell division is organized
tweezers: 1. Small pinchers used to pluck out hairs, and for other purposes
aeolotropy: 1. Difference of quality or property in different directions
kakapo: 1. A singular nocturnal parrot, native of New Zealand. It lives in holes during the day, but is active at night. It resembles an owl in its colors and general appearance. It has large wings, but can fly only a short distance. Called also owl parrot, night parrot, and night kaka
spectral: 1. Of or pertaining to a specter | 2. Ghosty. He that feels timid at the spectral form of evil is not the man to spread light. F. W. Robertson | 3. Of or pertaining to the spectrum
bombard: 1. A piece of heavy ordnance formerly used for throwing stones and other ponderous missiles. It was the earliest kind of cannon. They planted in divers places twelve great bombards, wherewith they threw huge stones into the air, which, falling down into the city, might break down the houses. Knolles | 2. A bombardment.  J. Barlow | 3. A large drinking vessel or can, or a leather bottle, for carrying liquor or beer.  Yond same black cloud, yond huge one, looks like a foul bombard that would shed his liquor. Shak
peregrination: 1. A traveling from one country to another | 2. A wandering | 3. Sojourn in foreign countries. "His peregrination abroad." Bacon
insular: 1. Of or pertaining to an island | 2. Of the nature, or possessing the characteristics, of an island | 3. As, an insular climate, fauna, etc
everywhere: 1. In every place | 2. In all places | 3. Hence, in every part
grief: 1. Pain of mind on account of something in the past | 2. Mental suffering arising from any cause, as misfortune, loss of friends, misconduct of one's self or others, etc | 3. Sorrow
miliola: 1. A genus of Foraminifera, having a porcelanous shell with several longitudinal chambers
keta: 1. A small salmon of inferior value, which in the autumn runs up all the larger rivers between San Francisco and Kamchatka
rabbiting: 1. The hunting of rabbits.  T. Hughes
communism: 1. A scheme of equalizing the social conditions of life | 2. Specifically, a scheme which contemplates the abolition of inequalities in the possession of property, as by distributing all wealth equally to all, or by holding all wealth in common for the equal use and advantage of all | 3. Note: At different times, and in different countries, various schemes pertaining to socialism in government and the conditions of domestic life, as well as in the distribution of wealth, have been called communism
versify: 1. To make verses. I'll versify in spite, and do my best. Dryden | 2. To relate or describe in verse | 3. To compose in verse. I'll versify the truth, not poetize. Daniel
ganja: 1. The dried hemp plant, used in India for smoking. It is extremely narcotic and intoxicating
estate: 1. Settled condition or form of existence | 2. State | 3. Condition or circumstances of life or of any person
dismettled: 1. Destitute of mettle, that is, or fire or spirit.  Llewellyn
blitheness: 1. The state of being blithe. Chaucer
zincous: 1. Of, pertaining to, or containing, zinc | 2. Zincic | 3. As, zincous salts. Hence, formerly, basic, basylous, as opposed to chlorous
potassamide: 1. A yellowish brown substance obtained by heating potassium in ammonia
testicle: 1. One of the essential male genital glands which secrete the semen
crux: 1. Anything that is very puzzling or difficult to explain. Dr. Sheridan. The perpetual crux of New Testament chronologists. Strauss
acuminose: 1. Terminating in a flat, narrow end | 2. Lindley
toothleted: 1. Having a toothlet or toothlets | 2. As, a toothleted leaf
descendant:
1. Descendent.

One who descends, as offspring, however remotely | 2. -- correlative to ancestor or ascendant. Our first parents and their descendants. Hale. The descendant of so many kings and emperors. Burke
fourhanded: 1. Having four hands | 2. Quadrumanous. Goldsmith | 3. Requiring four "hands" or players
zenithal: 1. Of or pertaining to the zenith. "The deep zenithal blue." Tyndall
desirable: 1. Worthy of desire or longing | 2. Fitted to excite desire or a wish to possess | 3. Pleasing
be: 1. To exist actually, or in the world of fact | 2. To have ex To be contents his natural desire. Pope. To be, or not to be: that is the question. Shak | 3. To exist in a certain manner or relation, -- whether as a reality or as a product of thought
beseech: 1. To ask or entreat with urgency | 2. To supplicate | 3. To implore. I beseech you, punish me not with your hard thoughts. Shak. But Eve . . . besought his peace. Milton. Syn. -- To beg
pasticcio: 1. A medley | 2. An olio.  H. Swinburne | 3. A work of art imitating directly the work of another artist, or of more artists than one
hareld: 1. The long-tailed duck. See Old Squaw
deficient: 1. Wanting, to make up completeness | 2. Wanting, as regards a requirement | 3. Not sufficient
diplomatically: 1. According to the rules of diplomacy | 2. In the manner of a diplomatist | 3. Artfully
chilognath: 1. A myriapod of the order Chilognatha
pinaster: 1. A species of pine growing in Southern Europe
retrench: 1. To cut off | 2. To pare away. Thy exuberant parts retrench. Denham | 3. To lessen
meconic: 1. Pertaining to, or obtained from, the poppy or opium | 2. Specif., designating an acid related to aconitic acid, found in opium and extracted as a white crystalline substance
nutrition: 1. In the broadest sense, a process or series of processes by which the living organism as a whole is maintained in its normal condition of life and growth. Note: In this wide sense it comprehends digestion, absorption, circulation, assimilation, etc., in fact all of the steps by which the nutritive matter of the food is fitted for incorporation with the different tissues, and the changes which it undergoes after its assimilation, prior to its excretion. See Metabolism | 2. In a more limited sense, the process by which the living tissues take up, from the blood, matters necessary either for their repair or for the performance of their healthy functions | 3. That which nourishes
scotching: 1. Dressing stone with a pick or pointed instrument
southward:
1. Toward the south, or toward a point nearer the south than the east or west point | 2. As, to go southward.

Toward the south.

The southern regions or countries | 3. The south. Sir W. Raleigh
terminist: 1. One of a class of theologians who maintain that God has fixed a certain term for the probation of individual persons, during which period, and no longer, they have the offer to grace. Murdock
beast: 1. Any living creature | 2. An animal | 3. -- including man, insects, etc
traveler: 1. One who travels | 2. One who has traveled much | 3. A commercial agent who travels for the purpose of receiving orders for merchants, making collections, etc
veratrol: 1. A liquid hydrocarbon obtained by the decomposition of veratric acid, and constituting the dimethyl ether of pyrocatechin
ambulatory: 1. Of or pertaining to walking | 2. Having the faculty of walking | 3. Formed or fitted for walking
hypophosphoric: 1. Pertaining to, or derived from, or containing, phosphorus in a lower state of oxidation than in phosphoric compounds | 2. As, hypophosphoric acid. Hypophosphoric acid, an acid, P2H4O6, produced by the slow oxidation of moist phosphorus, and isolated only as a solution in water. It is regarded as a condensation product of one molecule of phosphoric acid with one of phosphorous acid, by partial dehydration
antinephritic: 1. Counteracting, or deemed of use in, diseases of the kidneys. -- n.  An antinephritic remedy
annunciator: 1. One who announces. Specifically: An officer in the church of Constantinople, whose business it was to inform the people of the festivals to be celebrated | 2. An indicator which designates the room where attendance is wanted
tredille: 1. A game at cards for three
courap: 1. A skin disease, common in India, in which there is perpetual itching and eruption, esp | 2. Of the groin, breast, armpits, and face
harquebuse: 1. A firearm with match holder, trigger, and tumbler, made in the second half of the 15th century. the barrel was about forty inches long. A form of the harquebus was subsequently called arquebus with matchlock
princewood: 1. The wood of two small tropical American trees. It is brownish, veined with lighter color
pleuritic: 1. Of or pertaining to pleurisy | 2. As, pleuritic symptoms. Suffering from pleurisy
choice: 1. Act of choosing | 2. The voluntary act of selecting or separating from two or more things that which is preferred | 3. The determination of the mind in preferring one thing to another
flatus: 1. A breath | 2. A puff of wind. Clarke | 3. Wind or gas generated in the stomach or other cavities of the body. Quincy
rambooze: 1. A beverage made of wine, ale, sugar, etc | 2. Blount
tricuspidate: 1. Three-pointed | 2. Ending in three points | 3. As, a tricuspidate leaf
switchman: 1. One who tends a switch on a railway
jabot: 1. Originally, a kind of ruffle worn by men on the bosom of the shirt | 2. An arrangement of lace or tulle, looped ornamentally, and worn by women on the front of the dress
glires: 1. An order of mammals | 2. The Rodentia. -- Gli"rine, a
coherence: 1. A sticking or cleaving together | 2. Union of parts of the same body | 3. Cohesion
confiscation: 1. The act or process of taking property or condemning it to be taken, as forfeited to the public use | 2. The confiscations following a subdued rebellion. Hallam
vallar:
1. Of or pertaining to a rampart. Vallar crown, a circular gold crown with palisades, bestowed upon the soldier who first surmounted the rampart and broke into the enemy's camp.

A vallar crown
autophoby: 1. Fear of one's self | 2. Fear of being egotistical.  Hare
cresol: 1. Any one of three metameric substances, CH | 2. C6H | 3. OH, homologous with and resembling phenol. They are obtained from coal tar and wood tar, and are colorless, oily liquids or solids. Note:
dicalcic: 1. Having two atoms or equivalents of calcium to the molecule
munificence:
1. Means of defense | 2. Fortification.  Spenser.

The quality or state of being munificent | 3. A giving or bestowing with extraordinary liberality
crimeful: 1. Criminal | 2. Wicked | 3. Contrary to law, right, or dury.  Shak
tranation: 1. The act of swimming over.  Bailey
subtonic: 1. Applied to, or distinguishing, a speech element consisting of tone, or proper vocal sound, not pure as in the vowels, but dimmed and otherwise modified by some kind of obstruction in the oral or the nasal passage, and in some cases with a mixture of breath sound | 2. -- a term introduced by Dr. James Rush in | 3. See Guide to Pronunciation, §§155, 199-
celtic:
1. Of or pertaining to the Celts | 2. As, Celtic people, tribes, literature, tongue. 

The language of the Celts. Note: The remains of the old Celtic language are found in the Gaelic, the Erse or Irish the Manx, and the Welsh and its cognate dialects Cornish and Bas Breton
salicylous: 1. Pertaining to, or designating, a substance called salicylous acid, and now salicylal
himself: 1. An emphasized form of the third person masculine pronoun | 2. -- used as a subject usually with he | 3. As, he himself will bear the blame
bugaboo: 1. Something frightful, as a specter | 2. Anything imaginary that causes needless fright | 3. Something used to excite needless fear
athanor: 1. A digesting furnace, formerly used by alchemists. It was so constructed as to maintain uniform and durable heat. Chambers
mediate: 1. Being between the two extremes | 2. Middle | 3. Interposed
piedness: 1. The state of being pied. Shak
abstractiveness: 1. The quality of being abstractive | 2. Abstractive property
byname: 1. To give a nickname to. Camden
chimaeroid: 1. Related to, or like, the chimæra
hydrochloride: 1. A compound of hydrochloric acid with a base | 2. -- distinguished from a chloride, where only chlorine unites with the base
interstice: 1. That which intervenes between one thing and another | 2. Especially, a space between things closely set, or between the parts which compose a body | 3. A narrow chink
provencial: 1. Of or pertaining to Provence in France
councilist: 1. One who belong to a council | 2. One who gives an opinion.  I will in three months be an expert counsilist. Milton
enchoric: 1. Belonging to, or used in, a country | 2. Native | 3. Domestic
humerus: 1. The bone of the brachium, or upper part of the arm or fore limb. The part of the limb containing the humerus | 2. The brachium
poster: 1. A large bill or placard intended to be posted in public places | 2. One who posts bills | 3. A billposter
voyager: 1. One who voyages | 2. One who sails or passes by sea or water
wieldless: 1. Not to be wielded | 2. Unmanageable | 3. Unwieldy.  "Wieldless might." Spenser
protocercal: 1. Having a caudal fin extending around the end of the vertebral column, like that which is first formed in the embryo of fishes | 2. Diphycercal
ribbonwood: 1. A malvaceous tree of New Zealand, the bark of which is used for cordage
intervolution: 1. The state of being intervolved or coiled up | 2. A convolution | 3. As, the intervolutions of a snake. Hawthorne
crustiness: 1. The state or quality of having crust or being like crust | 2. Hardness | 3. The quality of being crusty or surly. Old Christy forgot his usual crustiness. W. Irving
rockrose: 1. A name given to any species of the genus Helianthemum, low shrubs or herbs with yellow flowers, especially the European H. vulgare and the American frostweed, H. Canadense. Cretan rockrose, a related shrub, one of the plants yielding the fragrant gum called ladanum
hoyman: 1. One who navigates a hoy | 2. A common hoyman to carry goods by water for hire. Hobart
punter:
1. One who punts | 2. Specifically, one who plays against the banker or dealer, as in baccara and faro. Hoyle.

One who punts a football | 3. Also, one who propels a punt
viscosity: 1. The quality or state of being viscous | 2. A quality analogous to that of a viscous fluid, supposed to be caused by internal friction, especially in the case of gases
bogy: 1. A specter | 2. A hobgoblin | 3. A bugbear. "Death's heads and bogies." J. H. Newman.  There are plenty of such foolish attempts at playing bogy in the history of savages. C. Kingsley
gonotheca: 1. A capsule developed on certain hydroids, inclosing the blastostyle upon which the medusoid buds or gonophores are developed | 2. -- called also gonangium, and teleophore. See Hydroidea, and Illust. of Campanularian
reforge: 1. To forge again or anew | 2. Hence, to fashion or fabricate anew | 3. To make over. Udall
ingravidation: 1. The state of being pregnant or impregnated
broncho: 1. A native or a Mexican horse of small size
vulcanite: 1. Hard rubber produced by vulcanizing with a large proportion of sulphur
paw: 1. The foot of a quadruped having claws, as the lion, dog, cat, etc | 2. The hand.  Dryden. Paw clam, the tridacna | 3. -- so called because shaped like an animal's paw
sire: 1. A lord, master, or other person in authority. See Sir.  Pain and distress, sickness and ire, And melancholy that angry sire, Be of her palace senators. Rom. of R | 2. A tittle of respect formerly used in speaking to elders and superiors, but now only in addressing a sovereign | 3. A father
fauteuil: 1. An armchair | 2. Hence, membership in the French Academy | 3. Chair of a presiding officer
oxlike: 1. Characteristic of, or like, an ox
metacenter: 1. The point of intersection of a vertical line through the center of gravity of the fluid displaced by a floating body which is tipped through a small angle from its position of equilibrium, and the inclined line which was vertical through the center of gravity of the body when in equilibrium. Note: When the metacenter is above the center of gravity, the position of the body is stable | 2. When below it, unstable
accuse: 1. Accusation.  Shak | 2. To charge with, or declare to have committed, a crime or offense | 3. To charge with an offense, judicially or by a public process
triobolar: 1. Of the value of three oboli | 2. Hence, mean | 3. Worthless.  It may pass current . . . for a triobolar ballad. Cheyne
biseptate: 1. With two partitions or septa. Gray
saporosity: 1. The quality of a body by which it excites the sensation of taste
subglacial: 1. Pertaining or belonging to the under side of a glacier | 2. Being beneath a glacier | 3. As, subglacial streams
rubescent: 1. Growing or becoming red | 2. Tending to redness
thrower: 1. One who throws. Specifically: One who throws or twists silk | 2. A throwster. One who shapes vessels on a throwing engine
photometrical: 1. Of or pertaining to photometry, or to a photometer
potatory: 1. Of or pertaining to drinking. Ld. Lytton
thimblerig: 1. A sleight-of-hand trick played with three small cups, shaped like thimbles, and a small ball or little pea | 2. To swindle by means of small cups or thimbles, and a pea or small ball placed under one of them and quickly shifted to another, the victim laying a wager that he knows under which cup it is | 3. Hence, to cheat by any trick
saturable: 1. Capable of being saturated | 2. Admitting of saturation. -- Sat`u*ra*bil"i*ty, n
cyanotype: 1. A photographic picture obtained by the use of a cyanide
sturiones: 1. An order of fishes including the sturgeons
cubhood: 1. The state of being a cub | 2. "From cubhood to old age." W. B. Dawkins
comanches: 1. A warlike, savage, and nomadic tribe of the Shoshone family of Indians, inhabiting Mexico and the adjacent parts of the United States | 2. -- called also Paducahs. They are noted for plundering and cruelty
filoselle: 1. A kind of silk thread less glossy than floss, and spun from coarser material. It is much used in embroidery instead of floss
dispope: 1. To refuse to consider as pope | 2. To depose from the popedom. One whom they disposed. Tennyson
plenum: 1. That state in which every part of space is supposed to be full of matter | 2. -- opposed to vacuum. G. Francis
curvirostral: 1. Having a crooked beak, as the crossbill
fetichistic: 1. Pertaining to, or involving, fetichism. A man of the fifteenth century, inheriting its strange web of belief and unbelief, of epicurean levity and fetichistic dread. G. Eliot
phloretic: 1. Pertaining to, or derived from, or designating, an organic acid obtained by the decomposition of phloretin
dubitate: 1. To doubt.  If he . . . were to loiter dubitating, and not come. Carlyle
rhizophora: 1. A genus of trees including the mangrove. See Mangrove
patriot:
1. One who loves his country, and zealously supports its authority and interests. Bp. Hall. Such tears as patriots shaed for dying laws. Pope.

Becoming to a patriot | 2. Patriotic
discrete: 1. Separate | 2. Distinct | 3. Disjunct. Sir M. Hale
unpen: 1. To release from a pen or from confinement. "If a man unpens another's water." Blackstone
platina: 1. Platinum. Platina mohr, platinum black. -- Platina yellow, a pigment prepared from platinum
paleontology: 1. The science which treats of the ancient life of the earth, or of fossils which are the remains of such life
ethically: 1. According to, in harmony with, moral principles or character
erythrochroism: 1. An unusual redness, esp | 2. In the plumage of birds, or hair of mammals, independently of age, sex, or season
protococcus: 1. A genus of minute unicellular algæ including the red snow plant

aphakial: 1. Pertaining to aphakia | 2. As, aphakial eyes
dragman: 1. A fisherman who uses a dragnet. Sir M. Hale
syringin: 1. A glucoside found in the bark of the lilac and extracted as a white crystalline substance | 2. -- formerly called also lilacin
aborticide: 1. The act of destroying a fetus in the womb | 2. Feticide
bah: 1. An exclamation expressive of extreme contempt. Twenty-five years ago the vile ejaculation, Bah! was utterly unknown to the English public. De Quincey
beestings:
1. Same as Biestings.

The first milk given by a cow after calving. B. Jonson. The thick and curdy milk . . . commonly called biestings. Newton.
ahriman: 1. The Evil Principle or Being of the ancient Persians | 2. The Prince of Darkness as opposer to Ormuzd, the King of Light
naik: 1. A chief | 2. A leader | 3. A Sepoy corporal. Balfour
finedrawn: 1. Drawn out with too much subtilty | 2. Overnice | 3. As, finedrawn speculations
oviferous: 1. Egg-bearing | 2. -- applied particularly to certain receptacles, as in Crustacea, that retain the eggs after they have been excluded from the formative organs, until they are hatched
enstamp: 1. To stamp | 2. To mark as It is the motive . . . which enstamps the character. Gogan
pterygopodium: 1. A specially modified part of the ventral fin in male elasmobranchs, which serves as a copulatory organ, or clasper
vocalist: 1. A singer, or vocal musician, as opposed to an instrumentalist
diluvial: 1. Of or pertaining to a flood or deluge, esp | 2. To the great deluge in the days of Noah | 3. Diluvian

Bog spavin, a soft swelling produced by distention of the capsular ligament of the hock | 3. -- called also blood spavin. -- Bone spavin, spavin attended with exostosis
successionist: 1. A person who insists on the importance of a regular succession of events, offices, etc | 2. Especially, one who insists that apostolic succession alone is valid
amphiarthrosis: 1. A form of articulation in which the bones are connected by intervening substance admitting slight motion | 2. Symphysis
disjunctively: 1. In a disjunctive manner | 2. Separately. Dr. H. More
triangle: 1. A figure bounded by three lines, and containing three angles. Note: A triangle is either plane, spherical, or curvilinear, according as its sides are straight lines, or arcs of great circles of a sphere, or any curved lines whatever. A plane triangle is designated as scalene, isosceles, or equilateral, according as it has no two sides equal, two sides equal, or all sides equal | 2. And also as right-angled, or oblique-angled, according as it has one right angle, or none | 3. And oblique-angled triangle is either acute-angled, or obtuse-angled, according as all the angles are acute, or one of them obtuse. The terms scalene, isosceles, equilateral, right-angled, acute-angled, and obtuse-angled, are applied to spherical triangles in the same sense as to plane triangles
malacozoic: 1. Of or pertaining to the Malacozoa
seerhand: 1. A kind of muslin of a texture between nainsook and mull
forerecited: 1. Named or recited before. "The forerecited practices." Shak
purparty: 1. A share, part, or portion of an estate allotted to a coparcener.  I am forced to eat all the game of your purparties, as well as my own thirds. Walpole
nitrite: 1. A salt of nitrous acid. Amyl nitrite, a yellow oily volatile liquid, used in medicine as a depressant and a vaso-dilator. Its inhalation produces an instantaneous flushing of the face
psilopaedic: 1. Having down upon the pterylæ only | 2. -- said of the young of certain birds
phthiriasis: 1. A disease consisting in the excessive multiplication of lice on the human body
pupivora: 1. A group of parasitic Hymenoptera, including the ichneumon flies, which destroy the larvæ and pupæ of insects
acclimatize: 1. To inure or habituate to a climate different from that which is natural | 2. To adapt to the peculiarities of a foreign or strange climate | 3. Said of man, the inferior animals, or plants
mintage: 1. The coin, or other production, made in a mint. Stamped in clay, a heavenly mintage. Sterling | 2. The duty paid to the mint for coining
wiggery: 1. A wig or wigs | 2. False hair.  A. Trollope | 3. Any cover or screen, as red-tapism.  Fire peels the wiggeries away from them  Carlyle
stoop:
1. Originally, a covered porch with seats, at a house door | 2. The Dutch stoep as introduced by the Dutch into New York. Afterward, an out-of-door flight of stairs of from seven to fourteen steps, with platform and parapets, leading to an entrance door some distance above the street | 3. The French perron. Hence, any porch, platform, entrance stairway, or small veranda, at a house door. 

A vessel of liquor
orthodoxical: 1. Pertaining to, or evincing, orthodoxy | 2. Orthodox
inbred: 1. Bred within | 2. Innate | 3. As, inbred worth. "Inbred sentiments." Burke
whahoo: 1. An American tree, the winged elm
divergence: 1. A receding from each other in moving from a common center | 2. The state of being divergent | 3. As, an angle is made by the divergence of straight lines. Rays come to the eye in a state of divergency
swinesty: 1. A sty, or pen, for swine
superficies: 1. The surface | 2. The exterior part, superficial area, or face of a thing | 3. Everything on the surface of a piece of ground, or of a building, so closely connected by art or nature as to constitute a part of it, as houses, or other superstructures, fences, trees, vines, etc
halma: 1. The long jump, with weights in the hands, -- the most important of the exercises of the Pentathlon
apopemptic: 1. Sung or addressed to one departing | 2. Valedictory | 3. As, apoplectic songs or hymns
christmas: 1. An annual church festival and in some States a legal holiday, in memory of the birth of Christ, often celebrated by a particular church service, and also by special gifts, greetings, and hospitality. Christmas box | 2. A box in which presents are deposited at Christmas. A present or small gratuity given to young people and servants at Christmas | 3. A Christmas gift. -- Christmas carol, a carol sung at, or suitable for, Christmas. -- Christmas day
changeableness: 1. The quality of being changeable | 2. Fickleness | 3. Inconstancy
fleeting: 1. Passing swiftly away | 2. Not durable | 3. Transient

stonecutter: 1. One whose occupation is to cut stone | 2. Also, a machine for dressing stone
pyuria: 1. A morbid condition in which pus is discharged in the urine
mesmerization: 1. The act of mesmerizing | 2. The state of being mesmerized
epiphora: 1. The watery eye | 2. A disease in which the tears accumulate in the eye, and trickle over the cheek | 3. The emphatic repetition of a word or phrase, at the end of several sentences or stanzas
denotation: 1. The marking off or separation of anything. Hammond
triumph: 1. A magnificent and imposing ceremonial performed in honor of a general who had gained a decisive victory over a foreign enemy. Note: The general was allowed to enter the city crowned with a wreath of laurel, bearing a scepter in one hand, and a branch of laurel in the other, riding in a circular chariot, of a peculiar form, drawn by four horses. He was preceded by the senate and magistrates, musicians, the spoils, the captives in fetters, etc., and followed by his army on foot in marching order. The procession advanced in this manner to the Capitoline Hill, where sacrifices were offered, and victorious commander entertained with a public feast | 2. Hence, any triumphal procession | 3. A pompous exhibition
syth: 1. See Sith, Sithe.  Chaucer. Piers Plowman
lotophagi: 1. A people visited by Ulysses in his wanderings. They subsisted on the lotus. See Lotus, and Lotus-eater
response: 1. The act of responding | 2. An answer or reply. Specifically: Reply to an objection in formal disputation. I. Watts. The answer of the people or congregation to the priest or clergyman, in the litany and other parts of divine service. A kind of anthem sung after the lessons of matins and some other parts of the office. A repetition of the given subject in a fugue by another part on the fifth above or fourth below. Busby
malvesie: 1. Malmsey wine. See Malmsey. " A jub of malvesye." Chaucer

swastica: 1. A symbol or ornament in the form of a Greek cross with the ends of the arms at right angles all in the same direction, and each prolonged to the height of the parallel arm of the cross. A great many modified forms exist, ogee and volute as well as rectilinear, while various decorative designs, as Greek fret or meander, are derived from or closely associated with it. The swastika is found in remains from the Bronze Age in various parts of Europe, esp | 2. At Hissarlik, and was in frequent use as late as the 10th century. It is found in ancient Persia, in India, where both Jains and Buddhists used it as religious symbol, in China and Japan, and among Indian tribes of North, Central, and South America. It is usually thought to be a charm, talisman, or religious token, esp | 3. A sign of good luck or benediction. Max MüLler distinguished from the swastika, with arms prolonged to the right, the suavastika, with arms prolonged to the left, but this distinction is not commonly recognized. Other names for the swastika are fylfot and gammadion

it: 1. The neuter pronoun of the third person, corresponding to the masculine pronoun he and the feminine she, and having the same plural. Note: The possessive form its is modern, being rarely found in the writings of Shakespeare and Milton, and not at all in the original King James's version of the Bible. During the transition from the regular his to the anomalous its, it was to some extent employed in the possessive without the case ending. See His, and He. In Dryden's time its had become quite established as the regular form. The day present hath ever inough to do with it owne grief. Genevan Test. Do, child, go to it grandam, child. Shak. It knighthood shall do worse. It shall fright all it friends with borrowing letters. B. Jonson. Note: In the course of time, the nature of the neuter sign i in it, the form being found in but a few words, became misunderstood. Instead of being looked upon as an affix, it passed for part of the original word. Hence was formed from it the anomalous genitive it, superseding the Saxon his | 2. Latham. muscle: 1. An organ which, by its contraction, produces motion. See Illust. of Muscles of the Human Body, in Appendix. The contractile tissue of which muscles are largely made up. Note: Muscles are of two kinds, striated and nonstriated. The striated muscles, which, in most of the higher animals, constitute the principal part of the flesh, exclusive of the fat, are mostly under the control of the will, or voluntary, and are made up of great numbers of elongated fibres bound together into bundles and inclosed in a sheath of connective tissue, the perimysium. Each fiber is inclosed in a delicate membrane, is made up of alternate segments of lighter and darker material which give it a transversely striated appearance, and contains, scattered through its substance, protoplasmic nuclei, the so-called muscle corpuscles. The nonstriated muscles are involuntary. They constitute a large part of the walls of the alimentary canal, blood vessels, uterus, and bladder, and are found also in the iris, skin, etc | 2. They are made up of greatly elongated cells, usually grouped in bundles or sheets | 3. Muscular strength or development

unprinciple: 1. To destroy the moral principles of

Internat. Cyc

Collimating eyepiece. See under Collimate. -- Negative, or Huyghenian, eyepiece, an eyepiece consisting of two plano-convex lenses with their curved surfaces turned toward the object glass, and separated from each other by about half the sum of their focal distances, the image viewed by the eye being formed between the two lenses. it was devised by Huyghens, who applied it to the telescope. Campani applied it to the microscope, whence it is sometimes called Campani's eyepiece. -- Positive eyepiece, an eyepiece consisting of two plano-convex lenses placed with their curved surfaces toward each other, and separated by a distance somewhat less than the focal distance of the one nearest eye, the image of the object viewed being beyond both lenses | 2. -- called also, from the name of the inventor, Ramsden's eyepiece. -- terrestrial, or Erecting eyepiece, an eyepiece used in telescopes for viewing terrestrial objects, consisting of three, or usually four, lenses, so arranged as to present the image of the object viewed in an erect position

A box with holes in its lid | 3. -- used for sprinkling flour, as on meat or a breadboard

As, there is an analogy between these objects, or one thing has an analogy to or with another. Note: Analogy is very commonly used to denote similarity or essential resemblance

To give the whetstone, to give a premium for extravagance in falsehood

1. Any one of several small species of herring which are commonly preserved in olive oil for food, especially the pilchard, or European sardine. The California sardine is similar. The American sardines of the Atlantic coast are mostly the young of the common herring and of the menhaden.

See Sardius

midshipman: 1. Formerly, a kind of naval cadet, in a ship of war, whose business was to carry orders, messages, reports, etc., between the officers of the quarter-deck and those of the forecastle, and render other services as required. In the English naval service, the second rank attained by a combatant officer after a term of service as naval cadet. Having served three and a half years in this rank, and passed an examination, he is eligible to promotion to the rank of lieutenant. In the United States navy, the lowest grade of officers in line of promotion, being graduates of the Naval Academy awaiting promotion to the rank of ensign | 2. An American marine fish of the genus Porichthys, allied to the toadfish. Cadet midshipman, formerly a title distinguishing a cadet line officer from a cadet engineer at the U. S. Naval Academy. See under Cadet. -- Cadet midshipman, formerly, a naval cadet who had served his time, passed his examinations, and was awaiting promotion | 3. -- now called, in the United States, midshipman
melopiano: 1. A piano having a mechanical attachment which enables the player to prolong the notes at will
oosporic: 1. Of or pertaining to an oöspore
blocking: 1. The act of obstructing, supporting, shaping, or stamping with a block or blocks | 2. Blocks used to support temporarily

talcous: 1. Of or pertaining to talc | 2. Composed of, or resembling, talc

pes: 1. The distal segment of the hind limb of vertebrates, including the tarsus and foot

bucolic:

aliethmoidal: 1. Pertaining to expansions of the ethmoid bone or

imp | 3. & p. p. of Reck. Chaucer

The ordeal by fire was performed, either by handling red-hot iron, or by walking barefoot and blindfold over red-hot plowshares, laid at unequal distances. If the person escaped unhurt, he was adjudged innocent | 2. Otherwise he was condemned as guilty. The ordeal by water was performed, either by plunging the bare arm to the elbow in boiling water, an escape from injury being taken as proof of innocence, or by casting the accused person, bound hand and foot, into a river or pond, when if he floated it was an evidence of guilt, but if he sunk he was acquitted. ladybird: 1. Any one of numerous species of small beetles of the genus Coccinella and allied genera | 2. -- called also ladybug, ladyclock, lady cow, lady fly, and lady beetle. wattling: 1. The act or process of binding or platting with twigs | 2. Also, the network so formed. Made with a wattling of canes or sticks. Dampier
perpetuation: 1. The act of making perpetual, or of preserving from extinction through an endless existence, or for an indefinite period of time | 2. Continuance. Sir T. Browne
morbidness: 1. The quality or state of being morbid | 2. Morbidity

slabbery: 1. Like, or covered with, slabber or slab | 2. Slippery | 3. Sloppy

octogild: 1. A pecuniary compensation for an injury, of eight times the value of the thing

cornist: 1. A performer on the cornet or horn

skutterudite: 1. A mineral of a bright metallic luster and tin-white to pale lead-gray color. It consist of arsenic and cobalt
denarcotize: 1. To deprive of narcotine | 2. As, to denarcotize opium. -- De*nar`co*ti*za"tion, n
hoe:
1. A tool chiefly for digging up weeds, and arranging the earth about plants in fields and gardens. Dutch hoe, one having the blade set for use in the manner of a spade. -- Horse hoe, a kind of cultivator.

To cut, dig, scrape, turn, arrange, or clean, with a hoe | 3. As, to hoe the earth in a garden
litho: 1. A combining form from Gr. stone
sojournment: 1. Temporary residence, as that of a stranger or a traveler

yank:
1. A jerk or twitch. 

To twitch | 2. To jerk. 

An abbreviation of Yankee

That branch of the science of mechanics which relates to fluids, or, as usually limited, which treats of the laws of motion and action of nonelastic fluids, whether as investigated mathematically, or by observation and experiment | 2. stichomancy: 1. Divination by lines, or passages of books, taken at hazard

sous: 1. A corrupt form of Sou.  Colman, the Elder
brattishing: 1. See Brattice, n | 2. Carved openwork, as of a shrine, battlement, or parapet
livering: 1. A kind of pudding or sausage made of liver or pork.  Chapman
jutlandish: 1. Of or pertaining to Jutland, or to the people of Jutland
boyau: 1. A winding or zigzag trench forming a path or communication from one siegework to another, to a magazine, etc

tai:
1. Designating, or pertaining to, the chief linguistic stock of Indo-China, including the peoples of Siamese and Shan speech.

A member of one of the tribes of the Tai stock. The Tais first appeared in history in Yunnan, and from thence they migrated into Upper Burma. The earliest swarms appear to have entered that tract about two thousand years ago, and were small in number. Census of India,
pentane: 1. Any one of the three metameric hydrocarbons, C5H12, of the methane or paraffin series. They are colorless, volatile liquids, two of which occur in petroleum. So called because of the five carbon atoms in the molecule
nesslerize: 1. To treat or test, as a liquid, with a solution of mercuric iodide in potassium iodide and potassium hydroxide, which is called Nessler's solution or Nessler's test, and is used to detect the presence of ammonia
stipulary: 1. Of or pertaining to stipules | 2. Stipular

unctuosity: 1. Quality or state of being unctuous. Sir T. Browne
bel: 1. The Babylonian name of the god known among the Hebrews as Baal. See Baal. Baruch vi

diiodide: 1. A compound of a binary type containing two atoms of iodine | 2. -- called also biniodide

botocudos: 1. A Brazilian tribe of Indians, noted for their use of poisons | 2. - - also called Aymborés
counterseal: 1. To seal or ratify with another or others. Shak

pennipotent: 1. Strong of wing | 2. Strong on the wing.  Davies

1. Same as Chronologist.

rearrangement: 1. The act of rearranging, or the state of being rearranged

clypeus: 1. The frontal plate of the head of an insect
paragenic: 1. Originating in the character of the germ, or at the first commencement of an individual | 2. -- said of peculiarities of structure, character, etc
proruption: 1. The act or state of bursting forth | 2. A bursting out | 3. Sir T. Browne
treacle: 1. A remedy against poison. See Theriac, | 2. We kill the viper, and make treacle of him | 3. Jer. Taylor

hesitancy: 1. The act of hesitating, or pausing to consider | 2. Slowness in deciding | 3. Vacillation
system: 1. An assemblage of objects arranged in regular subordination, or after some distinct method, usually logical or scientific | 2. add: 1. To give by way of increased possession | 2. To bestow. The Lord shall add to me another son | 3. Gen. xxx

When the muscles of the lower jaw are affected, it is called locked-jaw, or lickjaw, and it takes various names from the various incurvations of the body resulting from the spasm | 2. That condition of a muscle in which it is in a state of continued vibratory contraction, as when stimulated by a series of induction shocks
monomyary: 1. Of or pertaining to the Monomya. -- n.  One of the Monomya

respectful: 1. Marked or characterized by respect | 2. As, respectful deportment. With humble joi and with respectful fear. Prior. -- Re*spect"ful*ly, adv | 3. -- Re*spect"ful*ness, n
histohaematin: 1. One of a class of respiratory pigments, widely distributed in the animal kingdom, capable of ready oxidation and reduction
prairie: 1. An extensive tract of level or rolling land, destitute of trees, covered with coarse grass, and usually characterized by a deep, fertile soil. They abound throughout the Mississippi valley, between the Alleghanies and the Rocky mountains. From the forests and the prairies, From the great lakes of the northland. Longfellow | 2. A meadow or tract of grass | 3. Especially, a so called natural meadow. Prairie chicken, any American grouse of the genus Tympanuchus, especially T. Americanus, which inhabits the prairies of the central United States. Applied also to the sharp-tailed grouse. -- Prairie clover, any plant of the leguminous genus Petalostemon, having small rosy or white flowers in dense terminal heads or spikes. Several species occur in the prairies of the United States. -- Prairie dock, a coarse composite plant with large rough leaves and yellow flowers, found in the Western prairies. -- Prairie dog, a small American rodent allied to the marmots. It inhabits the plains west of the Mississippi. The prairie dogs burrow in the ground in large warrens, and have a sharp bark like that of a dog
sweepstake: 1. A winning of all the stakes or prizes. Heylin | 2. A complete removal or carrying away | 3. A clean sweep.  Bp. Hacket
recoinage: 1. The act of coining anew | 2. That which is coined anew
dioeciously: 1. In a dioecious manner. Dioeciously hermaphrodite, having flowers structurally perfect, but practically dioecious, -- those on one plant producing no pollen, and those on another no ovules
republication: 1. A second publication, or a new publication of something before published, as of a former will, of a volume already published, or the like | 2. Specifically, the publication in one country of a work first issued in another | 3. A reprint. If there be many testaments, the last overthrows all the former
teetee: 1. Any one of several species of small, soft-furred South American monkeys belonging to Callithrix, Chrysothrix, and allied genera | 2. As, the collared teetee, and the squirrel teetee. didactical: 1. Fitted or intended to teach | 2. Conveying instruction | 3. Preceptive
antisplenetic: 1. Good as a remedy against disease of the spleen. -- n.  An antisplenetic medicine
dakir: 1. A measure of certain commodities by number, usually ten or twelve, but sometimes twenty | 2. As, a daker of hides consisted of ten skins | 3. A daker of gloves of ten pairs. Burrill
obtund: 1. To reduce the edge, pungency, or violent action of | 2. To dull | 3. To blunt
ebon: 1. Consisting of ebony | 2. Like ebony, especially in color | 3. Black
clientship: 1. Condition of a client | 2. State of being under the protection of a patron. Dryden
intercommune: 1. To intercommunicate | 2. To have mutual communication or intercourse by conservation

hart: 1. A stag | 2. The male of the red deer. See the Note under Buck. Goodliest of all the forest, hart and hind. Milton

eructate: 1. To eject, as wind, from the stomach | 2. To belch.  Howell
domed: 1. Furnished with a dome | 2. Shaped like a dome
spanish:
1. Of or pertaining to Spain or the Spaniards. Spanish bayonet, a liliaceous plant with rigid spine-tipped leaves. The name is also applied to other similar plants of the Southwestern United States and mexico. Called also Spanish daggers. -- Spanish bean See the Note under Bean. -- Spanish black, a black pigment obtained by charring cork. Ure. -- Spanish broom, a leguminous shrub having many green flexible rushlike twigs. -- Spanish brown, a species of earth used in painting, having a dark reddish brown color, due to the presence of sesquioxide of iron. -- Spanish buckeye, a small tree of Texas, New Mexico, etc., related to the buckeye, but having pinnate leaves and a three-seeded fruit. -- Spanish burton, a purchase composed of two single blocks. A double Spanish burton has one double and two single blocks. Luce. -- Spanish chalk, a kind of steatite | 2. -- so called because obtained from Aragon in Spain. -- Spanish cress, a cruciferous plant, a species of peppergrass. -- Spanish curiew, the long-billed curlew.  -- Spanish daggers See Spanish bayonet. -- Spanish elm, a large West Indian tree furnishing hard and useful timber. -- Spanish feretto, a rich reddish brown pigment obtained by calcining copper and sulphur together in closed crucibles. -- Spanish flag, the California rockfish. It is conspicuously colored with bands of red and white. -- Spanish fly, a brilliant green beetle, common in the south of Europe, used for raising blisters. See Blister beetle under Blister, and Cantharis. -- Spanish fox, a yarn twisted against its lay | 3. -- Spanish grass. See Esparto. -- Spanish juice, licorice. -- Spanish leather. See Cordwain. -- Spanish mackerel. A species of mackerel found both in Europe and America. In America called chub mackerel, big-eyed mackerel, and bull mackerel. In the United States, a handsome mackerel having bright yellow round spots, highly esteemed as a food fish. The name is sometimes erroneously applied to other species. See Illust. under Mackerel. -- Spanish main, the name formerly given to the southern portion of the Caribbean Sea, together with the contiguous coast, embracing the route traversed by Spanish treasure ships from the New to the Old World. -- Spanish moss. See Tillandsia. -- Spanish needles, a composite weed having achenia armed with needlelike awns. -- Spanish nut, a bulbous plant of the south of Europe. -- Spanish potato, the sweet potato. See under Potato. -- Spanish red, an ocherous red pigment resembling Venetian red, but slightly yellower and warmer. Fairholt. -- Spanish reef, a knot tied in the head of a jib-headed sail. -- Spanish sheep, a merino. -- Spanish white, an impalpable powder prepared from chalk by pulverizing and repeated washings, -- used as a white pigment. -- Spanish windlass, a wooden roller, with a rope wound about it, into which a marline spike is thrust to serve as a lever.

septically: 1. In a septic manner | 2. In a manner tending to promote putrefaction

oenocyan: 1. The coloring matter of red wines
sternutatory: 1. Sternutative. -- n.  A sternutatory substance or medicine

fenugreek: 1. A plant cultivated for its strong- smelling seeds, which are "now only used for giving false importance to horse medicine and damaged hay." J. Smith
pneumography: 1. A description of the lungs. Dunglison
workwoman: 1. A woman who performs any work | 2. Especially, a woman skilled in needlework
barreled: 1. Having a barrel | 2. -- used in composition | 3. As, a double-barreled gun
landlock: 1. To inclose, or nearly inclose, as a harbor or a vessel, with land

epistoler: 1. One of the clergy who reads the epistle at the communion service | 2. An epistler
aliturgical: 1. Applied to those days when the holy sacrifice is not offered. Shipley
rock:
1. See Roc.

A distaff used in spinning | 2. The staff or frame about which flax is arranged, and from which the thread is drawn in spinning. Chapman. E. W. Gosse

burrhel: 1. The wild Himalayan, or blue, sheep

cabob:

trig:

The term Indonesian, introduced by Logan to designate the light- colored non-Malay inhabitants of the Eastern Archipelago, is now used as a convenient collective name for all the peoples of Malaysia and Polynesia who are neither Malay nor Papuans, but of Caucasic type.  . . . It is likewise a common constituent, either as the free acid or as a urate, of urinary or renal calculi and of the so-called gouty concretions. From acid urines, uric acid is frequently deposited, on standing in a cool place, in the form of a reddish yellow sediment, nearly always crystalline. Chemically, it is composed of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen, C5H4N4O3, and by decomposition yields urea, among other products. To speak for Buncombe, to speak for mere show, or popularly. Note: "The phrase originated near the close of the debate on the famous 'Missouri Question,' in the 16th Congress. It was then used by Felix Walker -- a naïve old mountaineer, who resided at Waynesville, in Haywood, the most western country of North Carolina, near the border of the adjacent country of Buncombe, which formed part of his district. The old man rose to speak, while the house was impatiently calling for the 'Question,' and several members gathered round him, begging him to desist. canton: 1. A song or canto  Write loyal cantons of contemned love. Shak | 2. A small portion | 3. A division
instroke: 1. An inward stroke | 2. Specif., in a steam or other engine, a stroke in which the piston is moving away from the crank shaft | 3. -- opposed to outstroke
mucronate: 1. Ending abruptly in a sharp point | 2. Abruptly tipped with a short and sharp point | 3. As, a mucronate leaf. -- Mu"cro*nate*ly, adv
paulownia: 1. A genus of trees of the order Scrophulariaceæ, consisting of one species, Paulownia imperialis. Note: The tree is native to Japan, and has immense heart-shaped leaves, and large purplish flowers in panicles. The capsules contain many little winged seeds, which are beautiful microscopic objects. The tree is hardy in America as far north as Connecticut
gulfy: 1. Full of whirlpools or gulfs. Chapman
deemster: 1. A judge in the Isle of Man who decides controversies without process. Cowell
eon: 1. An immeasurable or infinite space of time | 2. Eternity | 3. A long space of time

laughable: 1. Fitted to excite laughter | 2. As, a laughable story | 3. A laughable scene. Syn. -- Droll
sketchiness: 1. The quality or state of being sketchy | 2. Lack of finish | 3. Incompleteness
trender: 1. One whose business is to free wool from its filth
quicksand: 1. Sand easily moved or readily yielding to pressure | 2. Especially, a deep mass of loose or moving sand mixed with water, sometimes found at the mouth of a river or along some coasts, and very dangerous, from the difficulty of extricating a person who begins sinking into it. Life hath quicksands, -- Life hath snares! Longfellow

tricarballylic: 1. Of, pertaining to, or designating, a complex tribasic organic acid, C3H | 2. 3 occurring naturally in unripe beet roots, and produced artificially from glycerin as a white crystalline substance
underscore: 1. To draw a mark or line under | 2. To underline. J. Tucker
periodide: 1. An iodide containing a higher proportion of iodine than any other iodide of the same substance or series
reticularia: 1. An extensive division of rhizopods in which the pseudopodia are more or less slender and coalesce at certain points, forming irregular meshes. It includes the shelled Foraminifera, together with some groups which lack a true shell
ladyhood: 1. The state or quality of being a lady | 2. The personality of a lady
mysticism: 1. Obscurity of doctrine | 2. The doctrine of the Mystics, who professed a pure, sublime, and wholly disinterested devotion, and maintained that they had direct intercourse with the divine Spirit, and aquired a knowledge of God and of spiritual things unattainable by the natural intellect, and such as can not be analyzed or explained | 3. The doctrine that the ultimate elements or principles of knowledge or belief are gained by an act or process akin to feeling or faith
travail: 1. Labor with pain | 2. Severe toil or exertion. As everything of price, so this doth require travail. Hooker | 3. Parturition
ascertainable: 1. That may be ascertained. -- As`cer*tain"a*ble*ness, n. -- As`cer*tain"a*bly, adv
synchronical: 1. Happening at the same time | 2. Synchronous. Boyle. -- Syn*chron"ic*al*ly, adv
optocoelia: 1. The cavity of one of the optic lobes of the brain in many animals. B. G. Wilder
fielder: 1. A ball payer who stands out in the field to catch or stop balls
gloria: 1. A doxology, sung or said at the end of the Psalms in the service of the Roman Catholic and other churches. A portion of the Mass, and also of the communion service in some churches. In the Episcopal Church the version in English is used. The musical setting of a gloria

interrupter: 1. One who, or that which, interrupts | 2. A device for opening and closing an electrical circuit | 3. A vibrating spring or tuning fork, arranged to make and break a circuit at rapidly recurring intervals, by the action of the current itself
senile: 1. Of or pertaining to old age | 2. Proceeding from, or characteristic of, old age | 3. Affected with the infirmities of old age
clothes: 1. Covering for the human body | 2. Dress | 3. Vestments
migrant: 1. Migratory. Sir T. Browne. -- n.  A migratory bird or other animal
enlist: 1. To enter on a list | 2. To enroll | 3. To register
phycocyanine: 1. A blue coloring matter found in certain algæ
regardant: 1. Looking behind | 2. Looking backward watchfully.  turns thither his regardant eye | 3. Southey
anoa: 1. A small wild ox of Celebes, allied to the buffalo, but having long nearly straight horns
fortilage: 1. A little fort | 2. A blockhouse.  Spenser

necroscopic: 1. Or or relating to post-mortem examinations
impendent: 1. Impending | 2. Threatening. Impendent horrors, threatening hideous fall. Milton
