It is much used in Europe for hedges, and for standards in gardens. The American hawthorn is Cratægus cordata, which has the leaves but little lobed. Gives not the hawthorn bush a sweeter shade To shepherds Shak
jinx: 1. A person, object, influence, or supernatural being which is supposed to bring bad luck or to cause things to go wrong
orderable: 1. Capable of being ordered | 2. Tractable.  Being very orderable in all his sickness. Fuller
put:
1. A pit | 2. Chaucer.

3d pers. sing. pres. of Put, contracted from putteth. Chaucer.

A rustic | 3. A clown
palet:
1. Same as Palea.

A perpendicular band upon an escutcheon, one half the breadth of the pale
denticulate: 1. Furnished with denticles | 2. Notched into little toothlike projections | 3. As, a denticulate leaf of calyx. -- Den*tic"u*late*ly, adv
sympiesometer: 1. A sensitive kind of barometer, in which the pressure of the atmosphere, acting upon a liquid, as oil, in the lower portion of the instrument, compresses an elastic gas in the upper part. Note: The column of oil of a lower part BC of a glass tube compresses hydrogen gas in the upper part AB, and is thus measured on the scale pq by the position of a surface of the oil in the tube. The scale pq is adjustable, and its index must be set to the division on the scale rs corresponding to the temperature indicated by the termometer t, in order to correct for the effects of temperature on the gas | 2. It is sensitive, and convenient for use at sea, but inferior in accuracy to the mercurial barometer
bibliology: 1. An account of books | 2. Book lore | 3. Bibliography
linseed: 1. The seeds of flax, from which linseed oil is obtained.  Linseed cake, the solid mass or cake which remains when oil is expressed. -- Linseed meal, linseed cake reduced to powder. -- Linseed oil, oil obtained by pressure from flaxseed
parroter: 1. One who simply repeats what he has heard.  J. S. Mill
glide: 1. The glede or kite | 2. To move gently and smoothly | 3. To pass along without noise, violence, or apparent effort

alligate: 1. To tie | 2. To unite by some tie | 3. Instincts alligated to their nature. Sir M. Hale
orphanotrophy: 1. A hospital for orphans.  A. Chalmers | 2. The act of supporting orphans
cottised: 1. Set between two cottises, -- said of a bend | 2. Or between two barrulets, -- said of a bar or fess
decoctible: 1. Capable of being boiled or digested
kittiwake: 1. A northern gull, inhabiting the coasts of Europe and America. It is white, with black tips to the wings, and has but three toes
pulmotor: 1. An apparatus for producing artificial respiration by pumping oxygen or air or a mixture of the two into and out of the lungs, as of a person who has been asphyxiated by drowning, breathing poisonous gases, or the like, or of one who has been stunned by an electrical shock
promoter: 1. One who, or that which, forwards, advances, or promotes | 2. An encourager | 3. As, a promoter of charity or philosophy. Boyle
lardaceous: 1. Consisting of, or resembling, lard. Lardaceous degeneration, amyloid degeneration
fibrinoplastic: 1. Like fibrinoplastin | 2. Capable of forming fibrin when brought in contact with fibrinogen
junk: 1. A fragment of any solid substance | 2. A thick piece. See Chunk.  Lowell | 3. Pieces of old cable or old cordage, used for making gaskets, mats, swabs, etc., and when picked to pieces, forming oakum for filling the seams of ships

antipodal: 1. Pertaining to the antipodes | 2. Situated on the opposite side of the globe | 3. Diametrically opposite. His antipodal shadow." Lowell
whaling:
1. The hunting of whales.

Pertaining to, or employed in, the pursuit of whales | 2. As, a whaling voyage | 3. A whaling vessel

fourierist: 1. One who adopts the views of Fourier
employment: 1. The act of employing or using | 2. Also, the state of being employed | 3. That which engages or occupies

erogate: 1. To lay out, as money | 2. To deal out | 3. To expend

fortune: 1. The arrival of something in a sudden or unexpected manner | 2. Chance | 3. Accident

pretypify: 1. To prefigure | 2. To exhibit previously in a type. Bp. Pearson

fantique: 1. State of worry or excitment | 2. Fidget | 3. Ill humor.  Dickens
pici: 1. A division of birds including the woodpeckers and wrynecks

volapuk: 1. Literally, world's speech | 2. The name of an artificial language invented by Johan Martin Schleyer, of Constance, Switzerland, about

Any ruminant of the genus Rangifer, of the Deer family, found in the colder parts of both the Eastern and Western hemispheres, and having long irregularly branched antlers, with the brow tines palmate. Note: The common European species is domesticated in Lapland. The woodland reindeer or caribou is found in Canada and Maine The Barren Ground reindeer or caribou, of smaller size, is found on the shores of the Arctic Ocean, in both hemispheries. Reindeer moss, a gray branching lichen which forms extensive patches on the ground in arctic and even in north temperature regions. It is the principal food of the Lapland reindeer in winter. -- Reindeer period, a name sometimes given to a part of the Paleolithic era when the reindeer was common over Central Europe

endorse:
1. Same as Indorse. Note: Both endorse and indorse are used by good writers | 2. But the tendency is to the more general use of indorse and its derivatives indorsee, indorser, and indorsement.

A subordinary, resembling the pale, but of one fourth its width

laciniolate: 1. Consisting of, or abounding in, very minute laciniæ

marlitic: 1. Partaking of the qualites of marlite
embox: 1. To inclose, as in a box | 2. To imbox
conveyable: 1. Capable of being conveyed or transferred. Burke

impending: 1. Hanging over | 2. Overhanging | 3. Suspended so as to menace

Bather.  Chaucer. For lever had I die than see his deadly face. Spenser | 3. A rigid piece which is capable of turning about one point, or axis, and in which are two or more other points where forces are applied

beweep:
1. To weep over | 2. To deplore | 3. To bedew with tears. "His timeless death beweeping." Drayton.

juliform: 1. Having the shape or appearance of a julus or catkin

archaeography: 1. A description of, or a treatise on, antiquity or antiquities

submersed: 1. Being or growing under water, as the leaves of aquatic plants
apostrophic: 1. Pertaining to an apostrophe, grammatical or rhetorical
dowry: 1. A gift | 2. Endowment.  Spenser | 3. The money, goods, or estate, which a woman brings to her husband in marriage

1. Made less harsh or burdensome | 2. Alleviated.  Sir. T. Elyot.

Made smooth, as if polished

Equipments

Flexible sandstone, the finer-grained variety of itacolumite, which on account of the scales of mica in the lamination is quite flexible. -- Red sandstone, a name given to two extensive series of British rocks in which red sandstones predominate, one below, and the other above, the coal measures. mastodonsaurus: 1. A large extinct genus of labyrinthodonts, found in the European Triassic rocks

To sigh. 

Stunk
troyounce: 1. See Troy ounce, under Troy weight, above, and under Ounce
semimute:
1. Having the faculty of speech but imperfectly developed or partially lost.

A semimute person

padnag: 1. An ambling nag | 2. "An easy padnag." Macaulay

kydde: 1. Imp | 2. Of Kythe, to show.  Chaucer. Note: Spenser erroneously uses kydst to mean "knowest."
pillwort: 1. Any plant of the genus Pilularia | 2. Minute aquatic cryptograms, with small pill-shaped fruit | 3. -- sometimes called peppergrass
withstand: 1. To stand against | 2. To oppose | 3. To resist, either with physical or moral force
contractive: 1. Tending to contract | 2. Having the property or power or power of contracting
inopercular: 1. Having no operculum | 2. -- said of certain gastropod shells
probation: 1. The act of proving | 2. Also, that which proves anything | 3. Proof.  When by miracle God dispensed great gifts to the laity, . . . he gave probation that he intended that all should prophesy and preach. Jer. Taylor
rotor: 1. The rotating part of a generator or motor
idealistic: 1. Of or pertaining to idealists or their theories
legging:
1. A cover for the leg, like a long gaiter.

, from Leg, v. t
painty: 1. Unskillfully painted, so that the painter's method of work is too obvious | 2. Also, having too much pigment applied to the surface
bristliness: 1. The quality or state of having bristles
greenhouse: 1. A house in which tender plants are cultivated and sheltered from the weather
join: 1. To bring together, literally or figuratively | 2. To place in contact | 3. To connect
labyrinthine: 1. Pertaining to, or like, a labyrinth | 2. Labyrinthal
bullion: 1. Uncoined gold or silver in the mass. Note: Properly, the precious metals are called bullion, when smelted and not perfectly refined, or when refined, but in bars, ingots or in any form uncoined, as in plate. The word is often often used to denote gold and silver, both coined and uncoined, when reckoned by weight and in mass, including especially foreign, or uncurrent, coin | 2. Base or uncurrent coin.  And those which eld's strict doom did disallow, And damm for bullion, go for current now | 3. Sylvester
peptic: 1. Relating to digestion | 2. Promoting digestion | 3. Digestive
postglacial: 1. Formed or occurring after the last glacial epoch of the Pleistocene period, or at a locality within the area of Pleistocene glaciation after the final disappearance of the glacier from the locality. Of, pertaining to, or designating, an epoch after the last Glacial and before the Terrace epoch
direptitiously: 1. With plundering violence | 2. By violent injustice.  Strype
h: 1. The eighth letter of the English alphabet, is classed among the consonants, and is formed with the mouth organs in the same position as that of the succeeding vowel. It is used with certain consonants to form digraphs representing sounds which are not found in the alphabet, as sh, th, th, as in shall, thing, thine | 2. Also, to modify the sounds of some other letters, as when placed after c and p, with the former of which it represents a compound sound like that of tsh, as in charm, with the latter, the sound of f, as in phase, phantom. In some words, mostly derived or introduced from foreign languages, h following c and g indicates that those consonants have the hard sound before e, i, and y, as in chemistry, chiromancy, chyle, Ghent, Ghibelline, etc | 3. In some others, ch has the sound of sh, as in chicane. See Guide to Pronunciation, §§ 153, 179, 181-3, 237-
embroider: 1. To ornament with needlework | 2. As, to embroider a scarf. Thou shalt embroider the coat of fine linen. Ex. xxviii
rhabdite: 1. A minute smooth rodlike or fusiform structure found in the tissues of many Turbellaria | 2. One of the hard parts forming the ovipositor of insects
osmic: 1. Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, osmium | 2. Specifically, designating those compounds in which it has a valence higher than in other lower compounds | 3. As, osmic oxide. Osmic acid. Osmic tetroxide. Osmic acid proper, an acid analogous to sulphuric acid, not known in the free state, but forming a well-known and stable series of salts, which were formerly improperly called osmites. -- Osmic tetroxide, a white volatile crystalline substance, OsO4, the most stable and characteristic of the compounds of osmium. It has a burning taste, and gives off a vapor, which is a powerful irritant poison, violently attacking the eyes, and emitting a strong chlorinelike odor. Formerly improperly called osmic acid
corruptibility: 1. The quality of being corruptible | 2. The possibility or liability of being corrupted | 3. Corruptibleness. Burke
darbies: 1. Manacles | 2. Handcuffs.  Jem Clink will fetch you the darbies. Sir W. Scott. Note: In "The Steel Glass" by Gascoigne, printed in 1576, occurs the line "To binde such babes in father Derbies bands."
noetian: 1. One of the followers of Noetus, who lived in the third century. He denied the distinct personality of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
dilacerate: 1. To rend asunder | 2. To tear to pieces. Sir T. Browne
formed: 1. Arranged, as stars in a constellation | 2. As, formed stars | 3. Having structure
courtiery: 1. The manners of a courtier | 2. Courtliness.  B. Jonson
creat: 1. An usher to a riding master
pinnigrade: 1. An animal of the seal tribe, moving by short feet that serve as paddles
informant: 1. One who, or that which, informs, animates, or vivifies.  Glanvill | 2. One who imparts information or instruction | 3. One who offers an accusation
panderly: 1. Having the quality of a pander. "O, you panderly rascals." Shak
yard: 1. A rod | 2. A stick | 3. A staff.  P. Plowman. If men smote it with a yerde. Chaucer
chlorodyne: 1. A patent anodyne medicine, containing opium, chloroform, Indian hemp, etc
argent: 1. Silver, or money | 2. Whiteness | 3. Anything that is white. The polished argent of her breast. Tennyson
releasor: 1. One by whom a release is given
stratarithmetry: 1. The art of drawing up an army, or any given number of men, in any geometrical figure, or of estimating or expressing the number of men in such a figure
teil: 1. The lime tree, or linden | 2. -- called also teil tree
apodictically: 1. So as to be evident beyond contradiction
science: 1. Knowledge | 2. Lnowledge of principles and causes | 3. Ascertained truth of facts. If we conceive God's or science, before the creation, to be extended to all and every part of the world, seeing everything as it is, . . . his science or sight from all eternity lays no necessity on anything to come to pass. Hammond. Shakespeare's deep and accurate science in mental philosophy. Coleridge
splice: 1. To unite, as two ropes, or parts of a rope, by a particular manner of interweaving the strands, -- the union being between two ends, or between an end and the body of a rope | 2. Splice grafting.ee under Grafting. -- To splice the main brace, to give out, or drink, an extra allowance of spirits on occasion of special exposure to wet or cold, or to severe fatigue
commandment: 1. An order or injunction given by authority | 2. A command | 3. A charge
apogee: 1. That point in the orbit of the moon which is at the greatest distance from the earth. Note: Formerly, on the hypothesis that the earth is in the center of the system, this name was given to that point in the orbit of the sun, or of a planet, which was supposed to be at the greatest distance from the earth | 2. Fig.: The farthest or highest point | 3. Culmination
dedicatee: 1. One to whom a thing is dedicated | 2. -- correlative to dedicator
disruption: 1. The act or rending asunder, or the state of being rent asunder or broken in pieces | 2. Breach | 3. Rent
sesquioxide: 1. An oxide containing three atoms of oxygen with two atoms of some other substance | 2. Thus, alumina, Al2O3 is a sesquioxide
rehabilitation: 1. The act of rehabilitating, or the state of being rehabilitated. Bouvier. Walsh
gray: 1. White mixed with black, as the color of pepper and salt, or of ashes, or of hair whitened by age | 2. Sometimes, a dark mixed color | 3. As, the soft gray eye of a dove. These gray and dun colors may be also produced by mixing whites and blacks. Sir I. Newton
forth: 1. Forward | 2. Onward in time, place, or order | 3. In advance from a given point
considerer: 1. One who considers | 2. A man of reflection | 3. A thinker. Milton
textman: 1. One ready in quoting texts.  Bp. Sanderston
parabolism: 1. The division of the terms of an equation by a known quantity that is involved in the first term
evanid: 1. Liable to vanish or disappear | 2. Faint | 3. Weak
exulcerative: 1. Tending to cause ulcers | 2. Exulceratory. Holland
consentient: 1. Agreeing in mind | 2. Accordant. The consentient judgment of the church. Bp. Pearson
mucoid: 1. Resembling mucus. Dunglison. Mucoid degeneration, a form of degeneration in which the tissues are transformed into a semisolid substance resembling mucus. Quain
enticement: 1. The act or practice of alluring or tempting | 2. As, the enticements of evil companions | 3. That which entices, or incites to evil
polyeidism: 1. The quality or state of being polyeidic
semisoun: 1. A half sound | 2. A low tone.  "Soft he cougheth with a semisoun." Chaucer
shent:
1. Obs | 2. 3d pers. sing. pres. of Shend, for shendeth. Chaucer.

To shend.  Chaucer
testicond: 1. Having the testicles naturally concealed, as in the case of the cetaceans
companionship: 1. Fellowship | 2. Association | 3. The act or fact of keeping company with any one
sublobular: 1. Situated under, or at the bases of, the lobules of the liver
smalt: 1. A deep blue pigment or coloring material used in various arts. It is a vitreous substance made of cobalt, potash, and calcined quartz fused, and reduced to a powder
devest: 1. To divest | 2. To undress. Shak | 3. To take away, as an authority, title, etc., to deprive
scissile: 1. Capable of being cut smoothly | 2. Scissible.  Arbuthnot
heterosporous: 1. Producing two kinds of spores unlike each other
tubercled: 1. Having tubercles | 2. Affected with, tubercles | 3. Tuberculate
industrious: 1. Given to industry | 2. Characterized by diligence | 3. Constantly, regularly, or habitually occupied
traductive: 1. Capable of being deduced | 2. Derivable.  Bp. Warburton

agora: 1. An assembly | 2. Hence, the place of assembly, especially the market place, in an ancient Greek city
tricking:
1. Given to tricks | 2. Tricky. Sir W. Scott.

Dress | 3. Ornament. Shak
poonac: 1. A kind of oil cake prepared from the cocoanut. See Oil cake, under Cake

tiller: 1. One who tills | 2. A husbandman | 3. A cultivator
tradesman: 1. One who trades | 2. A shopkeeper | 3. A mechanic or artificer
chaffinch: 1. A bird of Europe, having a variety of very sweet songs, and highly valued as a cage bird | 2. -- called also copper finch

To make into a sandwich | 2. Also, figuratively, to insert between portions of something dissimilar | 3. To form of alternate parts or things, or alternating layers of a different nature
firstly: 1. In the first place | 2. Before anything else | 3. -- sometimes improperly used for first

frescade: 1. A cool walk | 2. Shady place.  Maunder
majestatic: 1. Majestic.  E. Pocock. Dr. J. Scott
aeroyacht: 1. A form of hydro-aëroplane | 2. A flying boat
hoven:
1. Affected with hoove | 2. As, hooven, or hoven, cattle.

p. p. of Heave.

Affected with the disease called hoove | 3. As, hoven cattle
counterirritation: 1. See Counter irritant, etc., under Counter, a
impracticability: 1. The state or quality of being impracticable | 2. Infeasibility. Goldsmith | 3. An impracticable thing
dusky: 1. Partially dark or obscure | 2. Not luminous | 3. Dusk

henceforth: 1. From this time forward | 2. Henceforward. I never from thy side henceforth to stray. Milton
angiology: 1. That part of anatomy which treats of blood vessels and lymphatics

Centrobaric method, a process invented for the purpose of measuring the area or the volume generated by the rotation of a line or surface about a fixed axis, depending upon the principle that every figure formed by the revolution of a line or surface about such an axis has for measure the product of the line or surface by the length of the path of its center of gravity | 2. -- sometimes called theorem of Pappus, also, incorrectly, Guldinus's properties. But the distinction of meaning between roasting and baking is not always observed

ethmotrubinal: 1. See Turbinal. -- n.  An ethmoturbinal bone

bechamel: 1. A rich, white sauce, prepared with butter and cream
bolometer: 1. An instrument for measuring minute quantities of radiant heat, especially in different parts of the spectrum | 2. -- called also actinic balance, thermic balance. S. P. Langley

outlet: 1. The place or opening by which anything is let out | 2. A passage out | 3. An exit
chinese: 1. Of or pertaining to China | 2. Peculiar to China. Chinese paper. See India paper, under India. -- Chinese wax, a snowy-wgite, waxlike substance brought from China. A native or natives of China, or one of that yellow race with oblique eyelids who live principally in China
cashmerette: 1. A kind of dress goods, made with a soft and glossy surface like cashmere

adulter: 1. To commit adultery | 2. To pollute.  B. Jonson
tull: 1. To allure | 2. To tole.  With empty hands men may no hawkes tull. Chaucer
yenite: 1. A silicate of iron and lime occurring in black prismatic crystals | 2. -- also called ilvaite
voltairism: 1. The theories or practice of Voltaire. J. Morley

monoclinal: 1. Having one oblique inclination | 2. -- applied to strata that dip in only one direction from the axis of elevation
latterkin: 1. A pointed wooden tool used in glazing leaden lattice
break: 1. To strain apart | 2. To sever by fracture | 3. To divide with violence

fleamy: 1. Bloody | 2. Clotted.  Foamy bubbling of a fleamy brain. Marston

necessary: 1. Such as must be | 2. Impossible to be otherwise | 3. Not to be avoided
pact: 1. An agreement | 2. A league | 3. A compact
knarl: 1. A knot in wood. See Gnarl

1. The province or seigniory of a palatine | 2. The dignity of a palatine. Howell.

To make a palatinate of.  Fuller
revulsion: 1. A strong pulling or drawing back | 2. Withdrawal. "Revulsions and pullbacks." SSir T. Brovne | 3. A sudden reaction
crawford: 1. A Crawford peach | 2. A well-known freestone peach, wich yellow flesh, first raised by Mr. William Crawford, of New Jersey
peri: 1. An imaginary being, male or female, like an elf or fairy, represented as a descendant of fallen angels, excluded from paradise till penance is accomplished. Moore
piassava: 1. A fibrous product of two Brazilian palm trees, -- used in making brooms, and for other purposes. Called also piaçaba and piasaba
lar:
1. A tutelary deity | 2. A deceased ancestor regarded as a protector of the family. The domestic Lares were the tutelar deities of a house | 3. Household gods. Hence, Eng.: Hearth or dwelling house. Nor will she her dear Lar forget, Victorious by his benefit. Lovelace. The Lars and Lemures moan with midnight plaint. Milton. Looking backward in vain toward their Lares and lands. Longfellow.

A species of gibbon, found in Burmah. Called also white-handed gibbon
amphipodous: 1. Of or pertaining to the Amphipoda
anhinga: 1. An aquatic bird of the southern United States | 2. The darter, or snakebird
disheritance: 1. The act of disinheriting or state of being disinherited | 2. Disinheritance.  Beau. & Fl
biauriculate: 1. Having two auricles, as the heart of mammals, birds, and reptiles | 2. Having two earlike projections at its base, as a leaf
gold: 1. An old English name of some yellow flower, -- the marigold, according to Dr. Prior, but in Chaucer perhaps the turnsole | 2. A metallic element, constituting the most precious metal used as a common commercial medium of exchange. cryptogram: 1. A cipher writing. Same as Cryptograph
edgeless: 1. Without an edge | 2. Not sharp | 3. Blunt

tailed: 1. Having a tail | 2. Having a tail or tails | 3. -- chiefly used in composition

A water-tight box, of timber or iron within which work is carried on in building foundations or structures below the water level. liturgy: 1. An established formula for public worship, or the entire ritual for public worship in a church which uses prescribed forms | 2. A formulary for public prayer or devotion. moveless: 1. Motionless | 2. Fixed. "Moveless as a tower." Pope
aroid: 1. Belonging to, or resembling, the Arum family of plants
cariole: 1. A small, light, open one-horse carriage. A covered cart. A kind of calash. See Carryall
phascolome: 1. A marsupial of the genus Phascolomys | 2. A wombat

remark: 1. To mark in a notable manner | 2. To distinquish clearly | 3. To make noticeable or conspicuous
tripartition: 1. A division by threes, or into three parts | 2. The taking of a third part of any number or quantity
barograph: 1. An instrument for recording automatically the variations of atmospheric pressure
motile: 1. Having powers of self-motion, though unconscious | 2. As, the motile spores of certain seaweeds | 3. Producing motion
stroud: 1. A kind of coarse blanket or garment used by the North American Indians
manipulative: 1. Of or pertaining to manipulation | 2. Performed by manipulation
shoppy: 1. Abounding with shops | 2. Of or pertaining to shops, or one's own shop or business | 3. As, shoppy talk.  Mrs. Gaskell

greillade: 1. Iron ore in coarse powder, prepared for reduction by the Catalan process

hippe: 1. A genus of marine decapod crustaceans, which burrow rapidly in the sand by pushing themselves backward | 2. -- called also bait bug | 3. See Illust. under Anomura
aldol: 1. A colorless liquid, C4H8O2, obtained by condensation of two molecules of acetaldehyde: CH3CHO + CH3CHO = H3CHCH2CO | 2. Also, any of various derivatives of this. The same reaction has been applied, under the name of aldol condensation, to the production of many compounds
scourger: 1. One who scourges or punishes | 2. One who afflicts severely. The West must own the scourger of the world. Byron
mohurrum: 1. The first month of the Mohammedan year. Whitworth | 2. A festival of the Shiah sect of the Mohammedans held during the first ten days of the month Mohurrum
ladylike: 1. Like a lady in appearance or manners | 2. Well-bred. She was ladylike, too, after the manner of the feminine gentility of those days. Hawthorne | 3. Becoming or suitable to a lady
woulding: 1. Emotion of desire | 2. Inclination | 3. Velleity.  Hammond
fornix: 1. An arch or fold | 2. As, the fornix, or vault, of the cranium | 3. The fornix, or reflection, of the conjuctiva. Esp., two longitudinal bands of white nervous tissue beneath the lateral ventricles of the brain
maselyn: 1. A drinking cup | 2. See 1st Maslin, | 3. Chaucer
suboctave: 1. Containing one part of eight | 2. Having the ratio of one to eight. Bp. Wilkins
jingoism: 1. The policy of the Jingoes, so called. See Jingo,
lexiphanic: 1. Using, or interlarded with, pretentious words | 2. Bombastic | 3. As, a lexiphanic writer or speaker
groundnut: 1. The fruit of the Arachis hypogæa | 2. The peanut | 3. The earthnut. A leguminous, twining plant, producing clusters of dark purple flowers and having a root tuberous and pleasant to the taste. The dwarf ginseng.  Gray. A European plant of the genus Bunium having an edible root of a globular shape aud sweet, aromatic taste
atramental: 1. Of or pertaining to ink | 2. Inky | 3. Black, like ink
succotash: 1. Green maize and beans boiled together. The dish is borrowed from the native Indians
fluffy: 1. Pertaining to, or resembling, fluff or nap | 2. Soft and downy. "The carpets were fluffy." Thackeray. The present Barnacle . . . had a youthful aspect, and the fluffiest little whisker, perhaps, that ever was seen. Dickens. -- Fluff"i*ness, n
gateman: 1. A gate keeper | 2. A gate tender
expulse: 1. To drive out | 2. To expel.  If charity be thus excluded and expulsed. Milton
taurocholic: 1. Pertaining to, or designating, a conjugate acid composed of taurine and cholic acid, present abundantly in human bile and in that of carnivora. It is exceedingly deliquescent, and hence appears generally as a thick, gummy mass, easily soluble in water and alcohol. It has a bitter taste
angiosperm: 1. A plant which has its seeds inclosed in a pericarp. Note: The term is restricted to exogenous plants, and applied to one of the two grand divisions of these species, the other division including gymnosperms, or those which have naked seeds. The oak, apple, beech, etc., are angiosperms, while the pines, spruce, hemlock, and the allied varieties, are gymnosperms
solertiousness: 1. The quality or state of being solert.  Bp. Hacket
unicity: 1. The condition of being united | 2. Quality of the unique | 3. Unification. Not unity, but what the schoolmen call unicity. De Quincey. The unicity we strive not to express, for that is impossible, but to designate by the nearest analogy. Coleridge
theoretical: 1. Pertaining to theory | 2. Depending on, or confined to, theory or speculation | 3. Speculative
hypogastrium: 1. The lower part of the abdomen
metatungstic: 1. Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid known only in its salts and properly called polytungstic, or pyrotungstic, acid
transaction: 1. The doing or performing of any business | 2. Management of any affair | 3. Performance
decker: 1. One who, or that which, decks or adorns | 2. A coverer | 3. As, a table decker
rhinopome: 1. Any old-world bat of the genus Rhinopoma. The rhinopomes have a long tail extending beyond the web, and inhabit caves and tombs
semen: 1. The seed of plants | 2. The seed or fecundating fluid of male animals | 3. Sperm. It is a white or whitish viscid fluid secreted by the testes, characterized by the presence of spermatozoids to which it owes its generative power. Semen contra, or Semen cinæ or cynæ, a strong aromatic, bitter drug, imported from Aleppo and Barbary, said to consist of the leaves, peduncles, and unexpanded flowers of various species of Artemisia
groundly: 1. Solidly | 2. Deeply | 3. Thoroughly.  Those whom princes do once groundly hate, Let them provide to die as sure us fate. Marston
estovers: 1. Necessaries or supples | 2. An allowance to a person out of an estate or other thing for support | 3. As of wood to a tenant for life, etc., of sustenance to a man confined for felony of his estate, or alimony to a woman divorced out of her husband's estate. Blackstone. Common of estovers. See under Common, n
trawl: 1. To take fish, or other marine animals, with a trawl | 2. A fishing line, often extending a mile or more, having many short lines bearing hooks attached to it. It is used for catching cod, halibut, etc | 3. A boulter
abacus: 1. A table or tray strewn with sand, anciently used for drawing, calculating, etc | 2. A calculating table or frame | 3. An instrument for performing arithmetical calculations by balls sliding on wires, or counters in grooves, the lowest line representing units, the second line, tens, etc
depository: 1. A place where anything is deposited for sale or keeping | 2. As, warehouse is a depository for goods | 3. A clerk's office is a depository for records
tibicinate: 1. To play on a tibia, or pipe
alinement: 1. Same as Alignment. Note: . New Eng. Dict.
atmology: 1. That branch of science which treats of the laws and phenomena of aqueous vapor. Whewell
affusion: 1. The act of pouring upon, or sprinkling with a liquid, as water upon a child in baptism. Specifically:  The act of pouring water or other fluid on the whole or a part of the body, as a remedy in disease. Dunglison
endue:
1. To invest. Latham. Tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high. Luke xxiv | 2. Endue them . . . with heavenly gifts. Book of Common Prayer.

An older spelling of Endow. Tillotson
amnesic: 1. Of or pertaining to amnesia. "Amnesic or coördinate defects." Quian
logographer: 1. A chronicler | 2. One who writes history in a condensed manner with short simple sentences | 3. One skilled in logography
ourselves: 1. Sing. Ourself (we | 2. Also, alone in the predicate, in the nominative or the objective case. We ourselves might distinctly number in words a great deal further then we usually do. Locke. Safe in ourselves, while on ourselves we stand. Dryden. Note: The form ourself is usec only in the regal or formal style after we or us, denoting a single person. Unless we would denude ourself of all force. Clarendon
knitchet: 1. A number of things tied or knit together | 2. A bundle | 3. A fagot.  Halliwell. When they  be dried, they ought to be made up into knitchets, or handfuls. Holland
bilalo: 1. A two-masted passenger boat or small vessel, used in the bay of Manila
perform: 1. To carry through | 2. To bring to completion | 3. To achieve
piggin: 1. A small wooden pail or tub with an upright stave for a handle, -- often used as a dipper
cathodegraph: 1. A picture produced by the Röntgen rays | 2. A radiograph
pollenize: 1. To supply with pollen | 2. To impregnate with pollen
folkething: 1. The lower house of the Danish Rigsdag, or Parliament. See Legislature, below
visa:
1. See Vis.

To indorse, after examination, with the word visé, as a passport | 2. To visé
platinochloric: 1. Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, an acid consisting of platinous chloride and hydrochloric acid, called platinochloric, or chloroplatinous, acid
highly: 1. In a high manner, or to a high degree | 2. Very much | 3. As, highly esteemed
shield: 1. A broad piece of defensive armor, carried on the arm, -- formerly in general use in war, for the protection of the body. See Buckler. Now put your shields before your hearts and fight, With hearts more proof than shields. Shak | 2. Anything which protects or defends | 3. Defense
discifloral: 1. Bearing the stamens on a discoid outgrowth of the receptacle | 2. - - said of a subclass of plants. Cf. Calycifloral
phycoxanthin: 1. A yellowish coloring matter found in certain algæ
coyotillo: 1. A low rhamnaceous shrub of the southwestern United States and Mexico. Its berries are said to be poisonous to the coyote
hydronephrosis: 1. An accumulation of urine in the pelvis of the kidney, occasioned by obstruction in the urinary passages
denominator: 1. One who, or that which, gives a name | 2. Origin or source of a name. This opinion that Aram . . . was the father and denomination of the Syrians in general. Sir W. Raleigh | 3. That number placed below the line in vulgar fractions which shows into how many parts the integer or unit is divided. Note: Thus, in denominator, showing that the integer is divided into five parts
canterbury: 1. A city in England, giving its name various articles. It is the seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury, and contains the shrine of Thomas à Becket, to which pilgrimages were formerly made | 2. A stand with divisions in it for holding music, loose papers, etc | 3. Canterbury ball, a species of Campanula of several varietes, cultivated for its handsome bell-shaped flowers. -- Canterbury gallop, a gentle gallop such as was used by pilgrims riding, to Canterbury
paracyanogen: 1. A polymeric modification of cyanogen, obtained as a brown or black amorphous residue by heating mercuric cyanide
corolla: 1. The inner envelope of a flower | 2. The part which surrounds the organs of fructification, consisting of one or more leaves, called petals. It is usually distinguished from the calyx by the fineness of its texture and the gayness of its colors. See the Note under Blossom
untowardly: 1. Perverse | 2. Froward | 3. Untoward. "Untowardly tricks and vices." Locke
pericardiac: 1. Of or pertaining to pericardium | 2. Situated around the heart. Pericardial fluid, a serous fluid of a pale yellow color contained in the pericardium
peerie: 1. Inquisitive | 2. Suspicious | 3. Sharp.  "Two peery gray eyes." Sir W. Scott
archencephala: 1. The division that includes man alone. R. Owen
conformist: 1. One who conforms or complies | 2. Esp., one who conforms to the Church of England, or to the Established Church, as distinguished from a dissenter or nonconformist. A cheeful conformist to your judgment. Jer.Taylor
cartogram: 1. A map showing geographically, by shades or curves, statistics of various kinds | 2. A statistical map
swivel: 1. A piece, as a ring or hook, attached to another piece by a pin, in such a manner as to permit rotation about the pin as an axis | 2. A small piece of ordnance, turning on a point or swivel | 3. -- called also swivel gun
unbalanced: 1. Not balanced | 2. Not in equipoise | 3. Having no counterpoise, or having insufficient counterpoise. Let Earth unbalanced from her orbit fly
bondmaid: 1. A female slave, or one bound to service without wages, as distinguished from a hired servant
argean: 1. Pertaining to the ship Argo. See Argo
dooring: 1. The frame of a door. Milton
carnify: 1. To form flesh | 2. To become like flesh. Sir M. Hale
excur: 1. To run out or forth | 2. To extend.  Harvey
semipellucid: 1. Half clear, or imperfectly transparent | 2. As, a semipellucid gem
kinaesthetic: 1. Of, pertaining to, or involving, kinæsthesis
dulse: 1. A seaweed of a reddish brown color, which is sometimes eaten, as in Scotland. The true dulse is Sarcophyllis edulis | 2. The common is Rhodymenia.  The crimson leaf of the dulse is seen To blush like a banner bathed in slaughter. Percival
ablins:
1. Perhaps. 

Perhaps | 2. Possibly.  Burns. AICH'S METAL Aich's met"al.  A kind of gun metal, containing copper, zinc, and iron, but no tin
ordovician: 1. Of or pertaining to a division of the Silurian formation, corresponding in general to the Lower Silurian of most authors, exclusive of the Cambrian. -- n.  The Ordovician formation
squad:
1. A small party of men assembled for drill, inspection, or other purposes | 2. Hence, any small party.

Sloppy mud | 3. Tennyson
altiscope: 1. An arrangement of lenses and mirrors which enables a person to see an object in spite of intervening objects
hetarism: 1. A supposed primitive state of society, in which all the women of a tribe were held in common. H. Spencer. -- Het`a*ris"tic, a
stinkwood: 1. A name given to several kinds of wood with an unpleasant smell, as that of the Foetidia Mauritiana of the Mauritius, and that of the South African Ocotea bullata
swaggerer: 1. One who swaggers | 2. A blusterer | 3. A bully
truffled: 1. Provided or cooked with truffles | 2. Stuffed with truffles | 3. As, a truffled turkey
proviso: 1. An article or clause in any statute, agreement, contract, grant, or other writing, by which a condition is introduced, usually beginning with the word provided | 2. A conditional stipulation that affects an agreement, contract, law, grant, or the like | 3. As, the contract was impaired by its proviso. He doth deny his prisoners, But with proviso and exception. Shak
inquiline: 1. A gallfly which deposits its eggs in galls formed by other insects
flume: 1. A stream | 2. Especially, a passage channel, or conduit for the water that drives a mill wheel | 3. Or an artifical channel of water for hydraulic or placer mining
shun: 1. To avoid | 2. To keep clear of | 3. To get out of the way of
endearment: 1. The act of endearing or the state of being endeared | 2. Also, that which manifests, excites, or increases, affection. "The great endearments of prudent and temperate speech." Jer. Taylor. Her first endearments twining round the soul. Thomson
conformation: 1. The act of conforming | 2. The act of producing conformity. The conformation of our hearts and lives to the duties of true religion and morality. I. Watts | 3. The state of being conformed
vermicular: 1. Of or pertaining to a worm or worms | 2. Resembling a worm | 3. Shaped like a worm
decembrist: 1. One of those who conspired for constitutional government against the Emperor Nicholas on his accession to the throne at the death of Alexander I., in December, 1825 | 2. -- called also Dekabrist. He recalls the history of the decembrists . . . that gallant band of revolutionists. G. Kennan
intellective: 1. Pertaining to, or produced by, the intellect or understanding | 2. Intellectual | 3. Having power to understand, know, or comprehend
toweling: 1. Cloth for towels, especially such as is woven in long pieces to be cut at will, as distinguished from that woven in towel lengths with borders, etc
septillion: 1. According to the French method of numeration, the number expressed by a unit with twenty-four ciphers annexed. According to the English method, the number expressed by a unit with forty-two ciphers annexed. See Numeration
politize: 1. To play the politician | 2. To dispute as politicians do.  Milton
sunbird: 1. Any one of numerous species of small brilliantly colored birds of the family Nectariniidæ, native of Africa, Southern Asia, the East Indies, and Australia. In external appearance and habits they somewhat resemble humming birds, but they are true singing birds. The sun bittern
spheric: 1. Having the form of a sphere | 2. Like a sphere | 3. Globular
decolorant: 1. A substance which removes color, or bleaches
gast: 1. To make aghast | 2. To frighten | 3. To terrify. See Aghast.  Chaucer. Shak
lamellicornia: 1. A group of lamellicorn, plant-eating beetles | 2. -- called also Lamellicornes
locally: 1. With respect to place | 2. In place | 3. As, to be locally separated or distant
hallucination: 1. The act of hallucinating | 2. A wandering of the mind | 3. Error
equirotal: 1. Having wheels of the same size or diameter | 2. Having equal rotation
gonorrhoea: 1. A contagious inflammatory disease of the genitourinary tract, affecting especially the urethra and vagina, and characterized by a mucopurulent discharge, pain in urination, and chordee | 2. Clap
sunniah: 1. One of the sect of Sunnites
furfurol: 1. A colorless oily liquid, C4H3O.CHO, of a pleasant odor, obtained by the distillation of bran, sugar, etc., and regarded as an aldehyde derivative of furfuran | 2. -- called also furfural
milliweber: 1. The thousandth part of one weber
feculent: 1. Foul with extraneous or impure substances | 2. Abounding with sediment or excrementitious matter | 3. Muddy
streek: 1. To stretch | 2. Also, to lay out, as a dead body. See Streak
critically: 1. In a critical manner | 2. With nice discernment | 3. Accurately
meter:
1. One who, or that which, metes or measures. See Coal-meter | 2. An instrument for measuring, and usually for recording automatically, the quantity measured. A line above or below a hanging net, to which the net is attached in order to strengthen it | 3. Rhythmical arrangement of syllables or words into verses, stanzas, strophes, etc
abatis: 1. A means of defense formed by felled trees, the ends of whose branches are sharpened and directed outwards, or against the enemy
lubrical: 1. Having a smooth surface | 2. Slippery | 3. Lascivious
nonphotobiotic: 1. Capable of living without light | 2. As, nonphotobiotic plant cells, or cells which habitually live in darkness
hairbrained: 1. See Harebrained. HAIRBREADTH | 2. HAIR'SBREADTH Hair"breadth`, Hair's"breadth`, a.  The diameter or breadth of a hair | 3. A very small distance
adaptation: 1. The act or process of adapting, or fitting | 2. Or the state of being adapted or fitted | 3. Fitness. "Adaptation of the means to the end." Erskine
antemural: 1. An outwork of a strong, high wall, with turrets, in front gateway, for defending the entrance
installment: 1. The act of installing | 2. Installation. Take oaths from all kings and magistrates at their installment, to do impartial justice by law | 3. Milton
reseau: 1. A system of lines forming small squares of standard size, which is photographed, by a separate exposure, on the same plate with star images to facilitate measurements, detect changes of the film, etc | 2. In lace, a ground or foundation of regular meshes, like network

horopter: 1. The line or surface in which are situated all the points which are seen single while the point of sight, or the adjustment of the eyes, remains unchanged. The sum of all the points which are seen single, while the point of sight remains unchanged, is called the horopter. J. Le Conte
tautologist: 1. One who uses tautological words or phrases
hellier: 1. One who heles or covers | 2. Hence, a tiler, slater, or thatcher.   Usher
inverted: 1. Changed to a contrary or counterchanged order | 2. Reversed | 3. Characterized by inversion
picine: 1. Of or pertaining to the woodpeckers, or to the Piciformes
urry: 1. A sort of blue or black clay lying near a vein of coal
embrocation: 1. The act of moistening and rubbing a diseased part with spirit, oil, etc | 2. The liquid or lotion with which an affected part is rubbed
goman: 1. A husband | 2. A master of a family
sprite: 1. A spirit | 2. A soul | 3. A shade
trichotomous: 1. Divided into three parts, or into threes | 2. Three-forked | 3. As, a trichotomous stem. Martyn
dandyize: 1. To make, or to act, like a dandy | 2. To dandify
overburden:
1. To load with too great weight or too much care, etc | 2. Sir P. Sidney.

The waste which overlies good stone in a quarry. Raymond
aerometric: 1. Of or pertaining to aërometry | 2. As, aërometric investigations
notidanian: 1. Any one of several species of sharks of the family Notidanidæ, or Hexanchidæ. Called also cow sharks. See Shark
year: 1. The time of the apparent revolution of the sun trough the ecliptic | 2. The period occupied by the earth in making its revolution around the sun, called the astronomical year | 3. squali: 1. The suborder of elasmobranch fishes which comprises the sharks
indult: 1. A privilege or exemption | 2. An indulgence | 3. A dispensation granted by the pope
inveigh: 1. To declaim or rail | 2. To utter censorious and bitter language | 3. To attack with harsh criticism or reproach, either spoken or written
transcendent: 1. Very excellent | 2. Superior or supreme in excellence | 3. Surpassing others
similative: 1. Implying or indicating likeness or resemblance.  In similative or instrumental relation to a pa. pple. , as almond-leaved, -scented, etc | 2. New English Dict
valsalvian: 1. Of or pertaining to Valsalva, an Italian anatomist of the 17th century. Valsalvian experiment, the process of inflating the middle ear by closing the mouth and nostrils, and blowing so as to puff out the cheeks

An hydraulic apparatus, or a system of works or fixtures, by which a supply of water is furnished for useful or ornamental purposes, including dams, sluices, pumps, aqueducts, distributing pipes, fountains, etc | 3. -- used chiefly in the plural
dissertation: 1. A formal or elaborate argumentative discourse, oral or written | 2. A disquisition | 3. An essay
duskish: 1. Somewhat dusky. " Duskish smoke." Spenser. -- Dusk"ish*ly, adv | 2. -- Dusk"ish*ness, n
decachordon: 1. An ancient Greek musical instrument of ten strings, resembling the harp | 2. Something consisting of ten parts. W. Watson
giggle:
1. To laugh with short catches of the breath or voice | 2. To laugh in a light, affected, or silly manner | 3. To titter with childish levity. Giggling and laughing with all their might At the piteous hap of the fairy wight. J. R. Drake.

A kind of laugh, with short catches of the voice or breath
barrio: 1. In Spain and countries colonized by Spain, a village, ward, or district outside a town or city to whose jurisdiction it belongs
fortunate: 1. Coming by good luck or favorable chance | 2. Bringing some good thing not foreseen as certain | 3. Presaging happiness
preventingly: 1. So as to prevent or hinder
pharyngeal:
1. Of or pertaining to the pharynx | 2. In the region of the pharynx.

A pharyngeal bone or cartilage | 3. Especially, one of the lower pharyngeals, which belong to the rudimentary fifth branchial arch in many fishes, or one of the upper pharyngeals, or pharyngobranchials, which are the dorsal elements in the complete branchial arches

plicidentine: 1. A form of dentine which shows sinuous lines of structure in a transverse section of the tooth
umbrageous: 1. Forming or affording a shade | 2. Shady | 3. Shaded
grassiness: 1. The state of abounding with grass | 2. A grassy state
ambulant: 1. Walking | 2. Moving from place to place. Gayton
infortunate: 1. Unlucky | 2. Unfortunate.  Shak. "A most infortynate chance." Howell. - In*for"tu*nate*ly, adv
patrocination: 1. The act of patrocinating or patronizing.  "Patrocinations of treason." Bp. Hall
momently: 1. For a moment | 2. In a moment | 3. Every moment

prodigality: 1. Extravagance in expenditure, particularly of money | 2. Excessive liberality | 3. Profusion
tartuffish: 1. Like a tartuffe | 2. Precise | 3. Hypocritical. Sterne
reviviscent: 1. Able or disposed to revive | 2. Reviving. E. Darwin
unlocated: 1. Not located or placed | 2. Not fixed in a place | 3. Not surveyed, or designated by marks, limits, or boundaries, as appropriated to some individual, company, or corporation
jurist: 1. One who professes the science of law | 2. One versed in the law, especially in the civil law | 3. A writer on civil and international law
grilly: 1. To broil | 2. To grill | 3. Hence, To harass.  Hudibras

The development of the young is the same as that of birds. Note: It is nearly related in many respects to Aves, or birds. The principal existing orders are Testidunata or Chelonia, Crocodilia, Lacertilla, Ophidia, and Rhynchocephala | 2. The chief extinct orders are Dinosauria, Theremorpha, Mosasauria, Pterosauria, Plesiosauria, Ichtyosauria
smiter: 1. One who smites. I give my back to the smiters. Isa. l
intromittent: 1. Throwing, or allowing to pass, into or within | 2. Used in copulation | 3. -- said of the external reproductive organs of the males of many animals, and sometimes of those of the females
isatropic: 1. Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained from atropine, and isomeric with cinnamic acid
semiquaver: 1. A note of half the duration of the quaver | 2. -- now usually called a sixsteenth note

whitling: 1. A young full trout during its second season

An accessory supposes a principal offender. One who is neither the chief actor in an offense, nor present at its performance, but accedes to or becomes involved in its guilt, either by some previous or subsequent act, as of instigating, encouraging, aiding, or concealing, etc., is an accessory. An accomplice is one who participates in the commission of an offense, whether as principal or accessory. undulatory: 1. Moving in the manner of undulations, or waves | 2. Resembling the motion of waves, which successively rise or swell rise or swell and fall | 3. Pertaining to a propagated alternating motion, similar to that of waves. Undulatory theory, or Wave theory, that theory which regards its various phenomena as due to undulations in an ethereal medium, propagated from the radiant with immense, but measurable, velocities, and producing different impressions on the retina according to their amplitude and frequency, the sensation of brightness depending on the former, that of color on the latter. The undulations are supposed to take place, not in the direction of propagation, as in the air waves constituting sound, but transversely, and the various phenomena of refraction, polarization, interference, etc., are attributable to the different affections of these undulations in different circumstances of propagation. It is computed that the frequency of the undulations corresponding to the several colors of the spectrum ranges from 458 millions of millions per second for the extreme red ray, to 727 millions of millions for the extreme violet, and their lengths for the same colors, from the thirty-eight thousandth to the sixty thousandth part of an inch. The theory of ethereal undulations is applicable not only to the phenomena of light, but also to those of heat

double:
1. Twofold; multiplied by two; increased by its equivalent; made twice as large or as much, etc. Let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me. 2 Kings ii. 9. Darkness and tempest make a double night. Dryden. 2. Being in pairs; presenting two of a kind, or two in a set together; coupled.  The swan, on still St. Mary's lake, Float double, swan and shadow. Wordsworth. 3. Divided into two; acting two parts, one openly and the other secretly; equivocal; deceitful; insincere. With a double heart do they speak. Ps. xii. 2. 4.  Having the petals in a flower considerably increased beyond the natural number, usually as the result of cultivation and the expense of the stamens, or stamens and pistils. The white water lily and some other plants have their blossoms naturally double. Note: Double is often used as the first part of a compound word, generally denoting two ways, or twice the number, quantity, force, etc., twofold, or having two. Double base, or Double bass, the largest and lowest-toned instrument in the violin form; the contrabasso or violone. -- Double convex. See under Convex. -- Double counterpoint, that species of counterpoint or composition, in which two of the parts may be inverted, by setting one of them an octave higher or lower. -- Double court, a court laid out for four players, two on each side. -- Double dagger, a reference mark ( | 2. ) next to the dagger ( | 3. ) in order; a diesis. -- Double drum, a large drum that is beaten at both ends. -- Double eagle, a gold coin of the United States having the value of 20 dollars. -- Double entry. See under Bookkeeping. -- Double floor, a floor in which binding joists support flooring joists above and ceiling joists below. See Illust. of Double-framed floor. -- Double flower. See Double, a., 4. -- Double-framed floor, a double floor having girders into which the binding joists are framed. -- Double fugue, a fugue on two subjects. -- Double letter. Two letters on one shank; a ligature. A mail requiring double postage. -- Double note, a note of double the length of the semibreve; a breve. See Breve. -- Double octave, an interval composed of two octaves, or fifteen notes, in diatonic progression; a fifteenth. -- Double pica. See under Pica. -- Double play, a play by which two players are put out at the same time. -- Double plea, a plea alleging several matters in answer to the declaration, where either of such matters alone would be a sufficient bar to the action. Stephen. -- Double point, a point of a curve at which two branches cross each other. Conjugate or isolated points of a curve are called double points, since they possess most of the properties of double points. They are also called acnodes, and those points where the branches of the curve really cross are called crunodes. The extremity of a cusp is also a double point. -- Double quarrel. See Duplex querela, under Duplex. -- Double refraction. See Refraction. -- Double salt. A mixed salt of any polybasic acid which has been saturated by different bases or basic radicals, as the double carbonate of sodium and potassium, NaKCO3.6H2O. A molecular combination of two distinct salts, as common alum, which consists of the sulphate of aluminium, and the sulphate of potassium or ammonium. -- Double shuffle, a low, noisy dance. -- Double standard, a double standard of monetary values; i. e., a gold standard and a silver standard, both of which are made legal tender. -- Double star, two stars so near to each other as to be seen separate only by means of a telescope. Such stars may be only optically near to each other, or may be physically connected so that they revolve round their common center of gravity, and in the latter case are called also binary stars. -- Double time. Same as Double-quick. -- Double window, a window having two sets of glazed sashes with an air space between them.

Twice; doubly. I was double their age. Swift.

1. To increase by adding an equal number, quantity, length, value, or the like; multiply by two; to double a sum of money; to double a number, or length. Double six thousand, and then treble that. Shak. 2. To make of two thicknesses or folds by turning or bending together in the middle; to fold one part upon another part of; as, to double the leaf of a book, and the like; to clinch, as the fist; -- often followed by up; as, to double up a sheet of paper or cloth. Prior. Then the old man Was wroth, and doubled up his hands. Tennyson. 3. To be the double of; to exceed by twofold; to contain or be worth twice as much as. Thus reënforced, against the adverse fleet, Still doubling ours, brave Rupert leads the way. Dryden. 4. To pass around or by; to march or sail round, so as to reverse the direction of motion. Sailing along the coast, the doubled the promontory of Carthage. Knolles. 5.  To unite, as ranks or files, so as to form one from each two.

1. To be increased to twice the sum, number, quantity, length, or value; to increase or grow to twice as much. 'T is observed in particular nations, that within the space of three hundred years, notwithstanding all casualties, the number of men doubles. T. Burnet. 2. To return upon one's track; to turn and go back over the same ground, or in an opposite direction. Doubling and turning like a hunted hare. Dryden. Doubling and doubling with laborious walk. Wordsworth. 3. To play tricks; to use sleights; to play false. What penalty and danger you accrue, If you be found to double. J. Webster. 4.  To set up a word or words a second time by mistake; to make a doublet. To double upon, to inclose between two fires.

1. Twice as much; twice the number, sum, quantity, length, value, and the like. If the thief be found, let him pay double. Ex. xxii. 7. 2. Among compositors, a doublet; among pressmen, a sheet that is twice pulled, and blurred. 3. That which is doubled over or together; a doubling; a plait; a fold. Rolled up in sevenfold double Of plagues. Marston. 4. A turn or circuit in running to escape pursues; hence, a trick; a shift; an artifice. These men are too well acquainted with the chase to be flung off by any false steps or doubles. Addison. 5. Something precisely equal or counterpart to another; a counterpart. Hence, a wraith. My charming friend . . . has, I am almost sure, a double, who preaches his afternoon sermons for him. Atlantic Monthly. 6. A player or singer who prepares to take the part of another player in his absence; a substitute. 7. Double beer; strong beer. 8.  A feast in which the antiphon is doubled, hat is, said twice, before and after the Psalms, instead of only half being said, as in simple feasts. Shipley. 9.  A game between two pairs of players; as, a first prize for doubles. 10.  An old term for a variation, as in Bach's Suites

r: 1. R, the eighteenth letter of the English alphabet, is a vocal consonant.  It is sometimes called a semivowel, and a liquid. See Guide to Pronunciation, §§ 178, 179, and 250- | 2. In words derived from the Greek language the letter h is generally written after r to represent the aspirated sound of the Greek "r, but does not affect the pronunciation of the English word, as rhapsody, rhetoric. The English letter derives its form from the Greek through the Latin, the Greek letter being derived from the Phonician, which, it is believed, is ultimately of Egyptian origin.
