Worthy of the palm | 2. Palmy | 3. Preëminent
dregginess: 1. Fullness of dregs or lees | 2. Foulness | 3. Feculence
aeroscopy: 1. The observation of the state and variations of the atmosphere
bimana: 1. Animals having two hands | 2. -- a term applied by Cuvier to man as a special order of Mammalia
mithridate: 1. An antidote against poison, or a composition in form of an electuary, supposed to serve either as a remedy or a preservative against poison | 2. An alexipharmic | 3. -- so called from King Mithridates, its reputed inventor.  a drop of the true elixir
insecta: 1. One of the classes of Arthropoda, including those that have one pair of antennæ, three pairs of mouth organs, and breathe air by means of tracheæ, opening by spiracles along the sides of the body. In this sense it includes the Hexapoda, or six-legged insects and the Myriapoda, with numerous legs. See Insect, n | 2. In a more restricted sense, the Hexapoda alone. See Hexapoda | 3. In the most general sense, the Hexapoda, Myriapoda, and Arachnoidea, combined. Note: The typical Insecta, or hexapod insects, are divided into several orders, viz.: Hymenoptera, as the bees and ants
metonymy: 1. A trope in which one word is put for another that suggests it | 2. As, we say, a man keeps a good table instead of good provisions | 3. We read Virgil, that is, his poems
memorializer: 1. One who petitions by a memorial. T. Hook
oscillometer: 1. An instrument for measuring the angle through which a ship rolls or pitches at sea
amarine: 1. A characteristic crystalline substance, obtained from oil of bitter almonds
gomphosis: 1. A form of union or immovable articulation where a hard part is received into the cavity of a bone, as the teeth into the jaws
joinder: 1. The act of joining | 2. A putting together | 3. Conjunction. Confirmed by mutual joinder of your hands. Shak
concession: 1. The act of conceding or yielding | 2. Usually implying a demand, claim, or request, and thus distinguished from giving, which is voluntary or spontaneous. By mutual concession the business was adjusted. Hallam | 3. A thing yielded
malodorous: 1. Offensive to the sense of smell | 2. Ill-smelling. -- Mal*o"dor*ous*ness. n. Carlyle
booker: 1. One who enters accounts or names, etc., in a book | 2. A bookkeeper
brevity: 1. Shortness of duration | 2. Briefness of time | 3. As, the brevity of human life
opprobrious: 1. Expressive of opprobrium | 2. Attaching disgrace | 3. Reproachful
magnetizer: 1. One who, or that which, imparts magnetism
overfront: 1. To confront | 2. To oppose | 3. To withstand.  Milton
pityroid: 1. Having the form of, or resembling, bran. Smart
tartaric:
1. Of or pertaining to Tartary in Asia, or the Tartars. Tartarian lamb, Scythian lamb. See Barometz.

Of or pertaining to tartar | 2. Derived from, or resembling, tartar. Tartaric acid. An acid widely diffused throughout the vegetable kingdom, as in grapes, mountain-ash berries, etc., and obtained from tartar as a white crystalline substance, C2H2 | 3. 2, having a strong pure acid taste. It is used in medicine, in dyeing, calico printing, photography, etc., and also as a substitute for lemon juice. Called also dextro-tartaric acid. By extension, any one of the series of isomeric acids of which tartaric acid proper is the type
unset: 1. Not set | 2. Not fixed or appointed
latah: 1. A convulsive tic or hysteric neurosis prevalent among Malays, similar to or identical with miryachit and jumping disease, the person affected performing various involuntary actions and making rapid inarticulate ejaculations in imitation of the actions and words of another person
ascospore: 1. One of the spores contained in the asci of lichens and fungi
eariness: 1. Fear or timidity, especially of something supernatural.  The sense of eariness, as twilight came on. De Quincey
turritelloid: 1. Of, pertaining to, or resembling, the turritellas
nodule: 1. A rounded mass or irregular shape | 2. A little knot or lump
neoplasty: 1. Restoration of a part by granulation, adhesive inflammation, or autoplasty
vitelligenous: 1. Producing yolk, or vitelline substance | 2. -- applied to certain cells formed in the ovaries of many insects, and supposed to supply nutriment to the developing ova
endocarp: 1. The inner layer of a ripened or fructified ovary
baize: 1. A coarse woolen stuff with a long nap | 2. -- usually dyed in plain colors. A new black baize waistcoat lined with silk. Pepys
sufflaminate: 1. To retard the motion of, as a carriage, by preventing one or more of its wheels from revolving, either by means of a chain or otherwise | 2. Hence, to stop | 3. To impede.  Barrow
harquebus: 1. A firearm with match holder, trigger, and tumbler, made in the second half of the 15th century. the barrel was about forty inches long. A form of the harquebus was subsequently called arquebus with matchlock
gismondite: 1. A native hydrated silicate of alumina, lime, and potash, first noticed near Rome
circumspect: 1. Attentive to all the circustances of a case or the probable consequences of an action | 2. Cautious | 3. Prudent
motherwort: 1. A labiate herb, of a bitter taste, used popularly in medicine | 2. Lion's tail. The mugwort. See Mugwort
dibranchiate: 1. Having two gills. -- n.  One of the Dibranchiata
rotalite: 1. Any fossil foraminifer of the genus Rotalia, abundant in the chalk formation. See Illust. under Rhizopod
unaidable: 1. Incapable of being aided. "Her unaidable estate." Shak
saccharify: 1. Toconvert into, or to impregnate with, sugar
administration: 1. The act of administering | 2. Government of public affairs | 3. The service rendered, or duties assumed, in conducting affairs
tether:
1. A long rope or chain by which an animal is fastened, as to a stake, so that it can range or feed only within certain limits.

To confine, as an animal, with a long rope or chain, as for feeding within certain limits. And by a slender cord was tethered to a stone. Wordsworth
surrebuter: 1. The reply of a plaintiff to a defendant's rebutter
tussicular: 1. Of or pertaining to a cough. Dunglison
procession: 1. The act of proceeding, moving on, advancing, or issuing | 2. Regular, orderly, or ceremonious progress | 3. Continuous course. Bp. Pearson. That the procession of their life might be More equable, majestic, pure, and free. Trench
balanoglossus: 1. A peculiar marine worm. See Enteropneusta, and Tornaria
unconcernment: 1. The state of being unconcerned, or of having no share or concern | 2. Unconcernedness.  South
assertory: 1. Affirming | 2. Maintaining. Arguments . . . assertory, not probatory. Jer. Taylor. An assertory, not a promissory, declaration. Bentham. A proposition is assertory, when it enounces what is known as actual. Sir W. Hamilton
rhachilla: 1. A branch of inflorescence | 2. The zigzag axis on which the florets are arranged in the spikelets of grasses
crookbill: 1. A New Zealand plover, remarkable for having the end of the beak abruptly bent to the right
wherein: 1. In which | 2. In which place, thing, time, respect, or the like | 3. -- used relatively. Her clothes wherein she was clad. Chaucer. There are times wherein a man ought to be cautious as well as innocent. Swift
sennit: 1. A braided cord or fabric formed by plaiting together rope yarns or other small stuff | 2. Plaited straw or palm leaves for making hats
shasta: 1. A mountain peak, etc., in California
inexorable: 1. Not to be persuaded or moved by entreaty or prayer | 2. Firm | 3. Determined
chloroplast: 1. A plastid containing chlorophyll, developed only in cells exposed to the light. Chloroplasts are minute flattened granules, usually occurring in great numbers in the cytoplasm near the cell wall, and consist of a colorless ground substance saturated with chlorophyll pigments. Under light of varying intensity they exhibit phototactic movements. In animals chloroplasts occur only in certain low forms
fricatrice: 1. A lewd woman | 2. A harlot.  B. Jonson
bilamellate: 1. Formed of two plates, as the stigma of the Mimulus | 2. Also, having two elevated ridges, as in the lip of certain flowers
songcraft: 1. The art of making songs or verse | 2. Metrical composition | 3. Versification. A half-effected inscription. Written with little skill of songcraft. Longfellow
impede: 1. To hinder | 2. To stop in progress | 3. To obstruct
buttercup: 1. A plant of the genus Ranunculus, or crowfoot, particularly R. bulbosus, with bright yellow flowers | 2. -- called also butterflower, golden cup, and kingcup. It is the cuckoobud of Shakespeare
fateful: 1. Having the power of serving or accomplishing fate. "The fateful steel." J. Barlow | 2. Significant of fate | 3. Ominous. The fateful cawings of the crow. Longfellow. -- Fate"ful*ly, adv.- Fate"ful*ness, n
retaker: 1. One who takes again what has been taken | 2. A recaptor. Kent
supramundane: 1. Being or situated above the world or above our system | 2. Celestial
chabasite: 1. A mineral occuring in glassy rhombohedral crystals, varying, in color from white to yellow or red | 2. It is essentially a hydrous silicate of alumina and lime. Called also chabasie
imaginal: 1. Characterized by imagination | 2. Imaginative | 3. Also, given to the use or rhetorical figures or imagins
committee:
1. One or more persons elected or appointed, to whom any matter or bussiness is referred, either by a legislative body, or by a court, or by any collective body of men acting together. Commitee of the whole , a committee, embracing all the members present, into which a legislative or deliberative body sometimes resolves itself, for the purpose of considering a particular measure under the operation of different rules from those governing the general legislative proceedings. The committee of the whole has its own chairman, and reports its action in the form of recommendations. -- Standing committee. See under Standing.

One to whom the charge of the person or estate of another, as of a lunatic, is committed by suitable authority | 2. A guardian
shank: 1. See Chank | 2. The part of the leg from the knee to the foot | 3. The shin
cerebroscopy: 1. Examination of the brain for the diagnosis of diseas | 2. Esp., the act or process of diagnosticating the condition of the brain by examination of the interior of the eye. Buck
memoria: 1. Memory. Memoria technica, technical memory | 2. A contrivance for aiding the memory
sextolet: 1. A double triplet | 2. A group of six equal notes played in the time of four
inisle: 1. To form into an island | 2. To surround.  Drayton
redbreast: 1. The European robin. The American robin. See Robin. The knot, or red-breasted snipe | 2. -- called also robin breast, and robin snipe. See Knot | 3. The long-eared pondfish. See Pondfish
unpolish: 1. To deprive of polish | 2. To make impolite
news: 1. A report of recent occurences | 2. Information of something that has lately taken place, or of something before unknown | 3. Fresh tindings
vein: 1. One of the vessels which carry blood, either venous or arterial, to the heart. See Artery, | 2. One of the similar branches of the framework of a leaf | 3. One of the ribs or nervures of the wings of insects. See Venation
aldermanly:
1. Pertaining to, or like, an alderman.

Pertaining to, or like, an alderman. "An aldermanly discretion." Swift
bushwhacking: 1. Traveling, or working a way, through bushes | 2. Pulling by the bushes, as in hauling a boat along the bushy margin of a stream.  T. Flint | 3. The crimes or warfare of bushwhackers
xenogenetic: 1. Of or pertaining to xenogenesis | 2. As, the xenogenetic origin of microzymes. Huxley
maculation: 1. The act of spotting | 2. A spot | 3. A blemish. Shak
historiographership: 1. The office of an historiographer. Saintsbury
gens: 1. A clan or family connection, embracing several families of the same stock, who had a common name and certain common religious rites | 2. A subdivision of the Roman curia or tribe | 3. A minor subdivision of a tribe, among American aborigines. It includes those who have a common descent, and bear the same totem
howell: 1. The upper stage of a porcelian furnace
tetrol: 1. A hypothetical hydrocarbon, C4H4, analogous to benzene | 2. -- so called from the four carbon atoms in the molecule. Tetrol phenol, furfuran
argilliferous: 1. Producing clay | 2. -- applied to such earths as abound with argil. Kirwan
flitch: 1. The side of a hog salted and cured | 2. A side of bacon. Swift | 3. One of several planks, smaller timbers, or iron plates, which are secured together, side by side, to make a large girder or built beam
laurin: 1. A white crystalline substance extracted from the fruit of the bay, and consisting of a complex mixture of glycerin ethers of several organic acids
conscientiousness: 1. The quality of being conscientious | 2. A scrupulous regard to the dictates of conscience
conterminant: 1. Having the same limits | 2. Ending at the same time | 3. Conterminous. Lamb
pornographic: 1. Of or pertaining to pornography | 2. Lascivious | 3. Licentious
aggeration: 1. A heaping up | 2. Accumulation | 3. As, aggerations of sand
heptandria: 1. A Linnæan class of plants having seven stamens
bottle: 1. A hollow vessel, usually of glass or earthenware, with a narrow neck or mouth, for holding liquids | 2. The contents of a bottle | 3. As much as a bottle contains
swad: 1. A cod, or pod, as of beans or pease.  Swad, in the north, is a peascod shell -- thence used for an empty, shallow-headed fellow. Blount | 2. A clown | 3. A country bumpkin.  "Country swains, and silly swads." Greene. There was one busy fellow was their leader, A blunt, squat swad, but lower than yourself. B. Jonson
cochineal: 1. A dyestuff consisting of the dried bodies of females of the Coccus cacti, an insect native in Mexico, Central America, etc., and found on several species of cactus, esp | 2. Opuntia cochinellifera. Note: These insects are gathered from the plant, killed by the application of heat, and exposed to the sun to dry | 3. When dried they resemble small, rough berries or seeds, of a brown or purple color, and form the cochineal of the shops, which is used for making carmine, and also as a red dye
attempt: 1. To make trial or experiment of | 2. To try | 3. To endeavor to do or perform
blackcock: 1. The male of the European black grouse | 2. - - so called by sportsmen. The female is called gray hen | 3. See Heath grouse
cowry: 1. A marine shell of the genus Cypræa. Note: There are numerous species, many of them ornamental. Formerly C. moneta and several other species were largely used as money in Africa and some other countries, and they are still so used to some extent. The value is always trifling, and varies at different places
dimissory: 1. Sending away | 2. Dismissing to another jurisdiction | 3. Granting leave to depart. Letters dimissory, letters given by a bishop dismissing a person who is removing into another diocese, and recommending him for reception there. Hook
bloody: 1. Containing or resembling blood | 2. Of the nature of blood | 3. As, bloody excretions
duckbill: 1. See Duck mole, under Duck, n
pentecost: 1. A solemn festival of the Jews | 2. -- so called because celebrated on the fiftieth day after the second day of the Passover | 3. -- hence called, also, the Feast of Weeks. At this festival an offering of the first fruits of the harvest was made. By the Jews it was generally regarded as commemorative of the gift of the law on the fiftieth day after the departure from Egypt
polychroite: 1. The coloring matter of saffron | 2. -- formerly so called because of the change of color on treatment with certain acids | 3. -- called also crocin, and safranin
photographer: 1. One who practices, or is skilled in, photography
volitient: 1. Exercising the will | 2. Acting from choice | 3. Willing, or having power to will. "What I do, I do volitient, not obedient." Mrs. Browning
geniality: 1. The quality of being genial | 2. Sympathetic cheerfulness | 3. Warmth of disposition and manners
hyads: 1. A cluster of five stars in the face of the constellation Taurus, supposed by the ancients to indicate the coming of rainy weather when they rose with the sun | 2. Thro' scudding drifts the rainy Hyaned Vext the dim sea | 3. Tennyson
thiophenol: 1. A colorless mobile liquid, C6H | 2. SH, of an offensive odor, and analogous to phenol | 3. -- called also phenyl sulphydrate
growan: 1. A decomposed granite, forming a mass of gravel, as in tin lodes in Cornwall
agog: 1. In eager desire | 2. Eager | 3. Astir. All agog to dash through thick and thin. Cowper
retentivity: 1. The power of retaining | 2. Retentive force | 3. As, the retentivity of a magnet
transpeciate: 1. To change from one species to another | 2. To transform.  Power to transpeciate a man into a horse. Sir T. Browne
draglink: 1. A link connecting the cranks of two shafts. A drawbar
antiseptic:
1. Counteracting or preventing putrefaction, or a putrescent tendency in the system | 2. Antiputrefactive. Antiseptic surgery, that system of surgical practice which insists upon a systematic use of antiseptics in the performance of operations and the dressing of wounds.

A substance which prevents or retards putrefaction, or destroys, or protects from, putrefactive organisms | 3. As, salt, carbolic acid, alcohol, cinchona
revers: 1. A part turned or folded back so as to show the inside, or a piece put on in imitation of such a part, as the lapel of a coat
unlawlike: 1. Not according to law | 2. Being or done in violation of law | 3. Unlawful. Milton
symposiast: 1. One engaged with others at a banquet or merrymaking. Sydney Smith
globuliferous: 1. Bearing globules | 2. In geology, used of rocks, and denoting a variety of concretionary structure, where the concretions are isolated globules and evenly distributed through the texture of the rock
pachonta: 1. A substance resembling gutta-percha, and used to adulterate it, obtained from the East Indian tree Isonandra acuminata
unctuous: 1. Of the nature or quality of an unguent or ointment | 2. Fatty | 3. Oily
underhonest: 1. Not entirely honest.  "We think him overproud and underhonest." Shak
debit: 1. A debt | 2. An entry on the debtor side of an account | 3. -- mostly used adjectively
bansshee: 1. A supernatural being supposed to warn a family of the approaching death of one of its members, by wailing or singing in a mournful voice
callosum: 1. The great band commissural fibers which unites the two cerebral hemispheres. See corpus callosum, under Carpus
boarish: 1. Swinish | 2. Brutal | 3. Cruel. In his anointed flesh stick boarish fangs. Shak
fairy: 1. Enchantment | 2. Illusion.  Chaucer. The God of her has made an end, And fro this worlde's fairy Hath taken her into company. Gower | 3. The country of the fays
coleorhiza: 1. A sheath in the embryo of grasses, inclosing the caulicle. Gray
neuropore: 1. An opening at either end of the embryonic neural canal
cycas: 1. A genus of trees, intermediate in character between the palms and the pines. The pith of the trunk of some species furnishes a valuable kind of sago
fantasied: 1. Filled with fancies or imaginations.  Shak
dignified: 1. Marked with dignity | 2. Stately | 3. As, a dignified judge
proteiform: 1. Changeable in form | 2. Resembling a Proteus, or an amoeba
infiltrate:
1. To enter by penetrating the pores or interstices of a substance | 2. To filter into or through something. The water infiltrates through the porous rock. Addison.

To penetrate gradually | 3. -- sometimes used reflexively. J. S. Mill
plausive: 1. Applauding | 2. Manifesting praise. Young | 3. Plausible, specious.  Shak
connivent: 1. Forbearing to see | 2. Designedly inattentive | 3. As, connivent justice.  Milton
scyphistoma: 1. The young attached larva of Discophora in the stage when it resembles a hydroid, or actinian
ellipsograph: 1. An instrument for describing ellipses | 2. -- called also trammel
steerer: 1. One who steers | 2. As, a boat steerer
dehisce: 1. To gape | 2. To open by dehiscence
ceratospongiae: 1. An order of sponges in which the skeleton consists of horny fibers. It includes all the commercial sponges
toadeater: 1. A fawning, obsequious parasite | 2. A mean sycophant | 3. A flatterer
xanthous: 1. Yellow | 2. Specifically, of or pertaining to those races of man which have yellowish, red, auburn, or brown hair
antiputrefactive: 1. Counteracting, or preserving from, putrefaction | 2. Antiseptic
apodeme: 1. One of the processes of the shell which project inwards and unite with one another, in the thorax of many Crustacea
animism: 1. The doctrine, taught by Stahl, that the soul is the proper principle of life and development in the body | 2. The belief that inanimate objects and the phenomena of nature are endowed with personal life or a living soul | 3. Also, in an extended sense, the belief in the existence of soul or spirit apart from matter. Tylor
granulous: 1. Full of grains | 2. Abounding with granular substances | 3. Granular
inquietude: 1. Disturbed state | 2. Uneasiness either of body or mind | 3. Restlessness
rely: 1. To rest with confidence, as when fully satisfied of the veracity, integrity, or ability of persons, or of the certainty of facts or of evidence | 2. To have confidence | 3. To trust
foraminiferous: 1. Having small openings, or foramina | 2. Pertaining to, or composed of, Foraminifera | 3. As, foraminiferous mud
lignification: 1. A change in the character of a cell wall, by which it becomes harder. It is supposed to be due to an incrustation of lignin
saracen: 1. Anciently, an Arab | 2. Later, a Mussulman | 3. In the Middle Ages, the common term among Christians in Europe for a Mohammedan hostile to the crusaders. Saracen's consound, a kind of ragewort, anciently used to heal wounds
chitter: 1. To chirp in a tremulous manner, as a bird.  Chaucer | 2. To shiver or chatter with cold.  Burns
ablation: 1. A carrying or taking away | 2. Removal. Jer. Taylor | 3. Extirpation. Dunglison
metronome: 1. An instrument consisting of a short pendulum with a sliding weight. It is set in motion by clockwork, and serves to measure time in music
tobacconist: 1. A dealer in tobacco | 2. Also, a manufacturer of tobacco | 3. A smoker of tobacco.  Sylvester
defalcate: 1. To cut off | 2. To take away or deduct a part of | 3. -- used chiefly of money, accounts, rents, income, etc
utraquist: 1. One who receives the eucharist in both kinds | 2. Esp., one of a body of Hussites who in the 15th century fought for the right to do this. Called also Calixtines
tendance: 1. The act of attending or waiting | 2. Attendance.  Spenser. The breath Of her sweet tendance hovering over him | 3. Tennyson
stratify: 1. To form or deposit in strata, or layers, as substances in the earth | 2. To arrange in strata
quake: 1. To be agitated with quick, short motions continually repeated | 2. To shake with fear, cold, etc | 3. To shudder
jabiru: 1. One of several large wading birds of the genera Mycteria and Xenorhynchus, allied to the storks in form and habits. Note: The American jabiru is white, with the head and neck black and nearly bare of feathers. The East Indian and Australian has the neck, head, and back covered with glossy, dark green feathers, changing on the head to purple. The African jabiru has the neck, head, wing coverts, and tail, black, and is called also saddle-billed stork
jejunity: 1. The quality of being jejune | 2. Jejuneness
umbrate: 1. To shade | 2. To shadow | 3. To foreshadow
ramenta: 1. Thin brownish chaffy scales upon the leaves or young shoots of some plants, especially upon the petioles and leaves of ferns. Gray
ineffectualness: 1. Want of effect, or of power to produce it | 2. Inefficacy. The ineffectualness of some men's devotion. Wake
nonjuror: 1. One of those adherents of James II. who refused to take the oath of allegiance to William and Mary, or to their successors, after the revolution of 1688 | 2. A Jacobite
breath: 1. The air inhaled and exhaled in respiration, air which, in the process of respiration, has parted with oxygen and has received carbonic acid, aqueous vapor, warmth, etc | 2. Melted as breath into the wind. Shak | 3. The act of breathing naturally or freely
pallidness: 1. The quality or state of being pallid | 2. Paleness | 3. Pallor
none: 1. No one | 2. Not one | 3. Not anything
prepotent: 1. Very powerful | 2. Superior in force, influence, or authority | 3. Predominant. Plaifere
helminth: 1. An intestinal worm, or wormlike intestinal parasite | 2. One of the Helminthes
forbearance: 1. The act of forbearing or waiting | 2. The exercise of patience. He soon shall findForbearance no acquittance ere day end | 3. Milton
bourbonist: 1. One who adheres to the house of Bourbon | 2. A legitimist
spectroscope: 1. An optical instrument for forming and examining spectra, so as to determine, from the position of the spectral lines, the composition of the substance
populist: 1. A member of the People's party. -- Pop`u*lis"tic, a
bahadur: 1. A title of respect or honor given to European officers in East Indian state papers, and colloquially, and among the natives, to distinguished officials and other important personages
outpour:
1. To pour out | 2. Milton.

A flowing out | 3. A free discharge
contraremonstrant: 1. One who remonstrates in opposition or answer to a remonstraint.  They did the synod wrong to make this distinction of contraremonstrants and remonstrants. Hales
nidulate: 1. To make a nest, as a bird.  Cockeram
enrapt: 1. Thrown into ecstasy | 2. Transported | 3. Enraptured. Shak
wreak: 1. To reck | 2. To care.  Shak | 3. To revenge
tulipomania: 1. A violent passion for the acquisition or cultivation of tulips | 2. -- a word said by Beckman to have been coined by Menage. Note: In Holland, in the first half of the 17th century, the cultivation of tulips became a mania. It began about the year 1634, and, like a violent epidemic, seized upon all classes of the community, leading to disasters and misery such as the records of commerce or of bankruptcies can scarcely parallel. In 1636, tulip marts had been established in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Haarlem, Leyden, and various other towns, where tulip bulbs were sold and resold in the same manner as stocks are on the Stock Exchange of London. Baird
prosody: 1. That part of grammar which treats of the quantity of syllables, of accent, and of the laws of versification or metrical composition
bask:
1. To lie in warmth | 2. To be exposed to genial heat. Basks in the glare, and stems the tepid wave. Goldsmith.

To warm by continued exposure to heat | 3. To warm with genial heat. Basks at the fire his hairy strength. Milton
cemetery: 1. A place or ground set apart for the burial of the dead | 2. A graveyard | 3. A churchyard
mineralogist: 1. One versed in mineralogy | 2. One devoted to the study of minerals | 3. A carrier shell
onus: 1. A burden | 2. An obligation. Onus probandi ( Etym: , obligation to furnish evidence to prove a thing | 3. The burden of proof
uplander: 1. One dwelling in the upland | 2. Hence, a countryman | 3. A rustic
tegula: 1. A small appendage situated above the base of the wings of Hymenoptera and attached to the mesonotum
cytula: 1. The fertilized egg cell or parent cell, from the development of which the child or other organism is formed. Hæckel
henhussy: 1. A cotquean | 2. A man who intermeddles with women's concerns
roast: 1. To cook by exposure to radiant heat before a fire | 2. As, to roast meat on a spit, or in an oven open toward the fire and having reflecting surfaces within | 3. Also, to cook in a close oven
peccable: 1. Liable to sin | 2. Subject to transgress the divine law | 3. "A frail and peccable mortal." Sir W. Scott
physicianed: 1. Licensed as a physician.  "A physicianed apothecary." Walpole
waddywood: 1. An Australian tree | 2. Also, its wood, used in making waddies
broadcast: 1. A casting or throwing seed in all directions, as from the hand in sowing | 2. Cast or dispersed in all directions, as seed from the hand in sowing | 3. Widely diffused
insaniate: 1. To render unsound | 2. To make mad | 3. Feltham
unrumple: 1. To free from rumples | 2. To spread or lay even,
drear:
1. Dismal | 2. Gloomy with solitude. "A drear and dying sound." Milton.

Sadness | 3. Dismalness.  Spenser
profile: 1. An outline, or contour | 2. As, the profile of an apple | 3. A human head represented sidewise, or in a side view
categoricalness: 1. The quality of being categorical, positive, or absolute. A. Marvell
craniologist: 1. One proficient in craniology | 2. A phrenologist
wriggler: 1. One who, or that which, wriggles. Cowper

As formed by Laplace, it supposed the matter of the solar system to have existed originally in the form of a vast, diffused, revolving nebula, which, gradually cooling and contracting, threw off, in obedience to mechanical and physical laws, succesive rings of matter, from which subsequently, by the same laws, were produced the several planets, satellites, and other bodies of the system. These words denote different degrees of complicity in some deed or crime. An abettor is one who incites or encourages to the act, without sharing in its performance. An accessory supposes a principal offender. One who is neither the chief actor in an offense, nor present at its performance, but accedes to or becomes involved in its guilt, either by some previous or subsequent act, as of instigating, encouraging, aiding, or concealing, etc., is an accessory. An accomplice is one who participates in the commission of an offense, whether as principal or accessory. Thus in treason, there are no abettors or accessories, but all are held to be principals or accomplices

Window tracery is imitated in many decorative objects, as panels of wood or metal either pierced or in relief. See also Stump tracery under Stump, and Fan tracery under Fan. The plant which yields pepper, an East Indian woody climber, with ovate leaves and apetalous flowers in spikes opposite the leaves. The berries are red when ripe. sipunculoidea: 1. Same as Gephyrea. In a restricted sense, same as Sipunculacea

flown:
1. P. of Fly | 2. -- often used with the auxiliary verb to be | 3. As, the birds are flown.

1. Provided with mandibles adapted for biting, as many insects.

An insect having mandibles

The brown hyena, and the spotted hyena, are found in Southern Africa. The extinct cave hyena inhabited England and France. Cave hyena. thickhead: 1. A thick-headed or stupid person | 2. Any one of several species of Australian singing birds of the genus Pachycephala. The males of some of the species are bright- colored. Some of the species are popularly called thrushes
desk: 1. A table, frame, or case, usually with sloping top, but often with flat top, for the use writers and readers. It often has a drawer or repository underneath | 2. A reading table or lectern to support the book from which the liturgical service is read, differing from the pulpit from which the sermon is preached | 3. Also (esp
condemnatory: 1. Condemning | 2. Containing or imposing condemnation or censure | 3. As, a condemnatory sentence or decree
concupiscible: 1. Exciting to, or liable to be affected by, concupiscence | 2. Provoking lustful desires. Shak | 3. Exciting desire, good or evil. The schools reduce all the passions to these two heads, the concupiscible and irascible appetite. South
about: 1. Around | 2. All round | 3. On every side of. "Look about you." Shak. "Bind them about thy neck." Prov. iii
colemanite: 1. A hydrous borate of lime occurring in transparent colorless or white crystals, also massive, in Southern California
assets: 1. Property of a deceased person, subject by law to the payment of his debts and legacies | 2. -- called assets because sufficient to render the executor or administrator liable to the creditors and legatees, so far as such goods or estate may extend. Story. Blackstone. Effects of an insolvent debtor or bankrupt, applicable to the payment of debts | 3. The entire property of all sorts, belonging to a person, a corporation, or an estate
twittering: 1. The act of one who, or that which, twitters | 2. A slight nervous excitement or agitation, such as is caused by desire, expectation, or suspense. A widow, who had a twittering towards a second husband, took a gossiping companion to manage the job | 3. L'Estrange
forcarve: 1. To cut completely | 2. To cut off | 3. Chaucer
hygrostatics: 1. The science or art of comparing or measuring degrees of moisture. Evelyn
pelfray: 1. Pelf | 2. Also, figuratively, rubbish | 3. Trash.  Cranmer
moringic: 1. Designating an organic acid obtained from oil of ben | 2. See Moringa
numbfish: 1. The torpedo, which numbs by the electric shocks which it gives
depredate: 1. To subject to plunder and pillage | 2. To despoil | 3. To lay waste
splenotomy: 1. Dissection or anatomy of the spleen. An incision into the spleen | 2. Removal of the spleen by incision
amphidromical: 1. Pertaining to an Attic festival at the naming of a child | 2. -- so called because the friends of the parents carried the child around the hearth and then named it
meracious: 1. Being without mixture or adulteration | 2. Hence, strong | 3. Racy
lindia: 1. A peculiar genus of rotifers, remarkable for the absence of ciliated disks. By some zoölogists it is thought to be like the ancestral form of the Arthropoda
astrography: 1. The art of describing or delineating the stars | 2. A description or mapping of the heavens
urohyal: 1. Of or pertaining to one or more median and posterior elements in the hyoidean arch of fishes. -- n.  A urohyal bone or cartilage
inseparability: 1. The quality or state of being inseparable | 2. Inseparableness. Locke
dioecious: 1. Having the sexes in applied to plants in which the female flowers occur on one individual and the male flowers on another of the same species, and to animals in which the ovum is produced by one individual and the sperm cell by another | 2. -- opposed to monoecious
accouple: 1. To join | 2. To couple.  The Englishmen accoupled themselves with the Frenchmen. Hall
browed: 1. Having a brow | 2. -- used in composition | 3. As, dark-browed, stern-browed
intact: 1. Untouched, especially by anything that harms, defiles, or the like | 2. Uninjured | 3. Undefiled
darkness: 1. The absence of light | 2. Blackness | 3. Obscurity
asteroid: 1. A starlike body | 2. Esp | 3. One of the numerous small planets whose orbits lie between those of Mars and Jupiter
glade: 1. An open passage through a wood | 2. A grassy open or cleared space in a forest. There interspersed in lawns and opening glades. Pope | 3. An everglade
ally: 1. To unite, or form a connection between, as between families by marriage, or between princes and states by treaty, league, or confederacy | 2. -- often followed by to or with. O chief! in blood, and now in arms allied. Pope | 3. To connect or form a relation between by similitude, resemblance, friendship, or love. These three did love each other dearly well, And with so firm affection were allied. Spenser. The virtue nearest to our vice allied. Pope. procuration: 1. The act of procuring | 2. Procurement | 3. The management of another's affairs
perichondrial: 1. Of or pertaining to the perichondrium | 2. Situated around cartilage
intercartilaginous: 1. Within cartilage | 2. Endochondral | 3. As, intercartilaginous ossification
rehabilitate: 1. To invest or clothe again with some right, authority, or dignity | 2. To restore to a former capacity | 3. To reinstate
injury: 1. Any damage or violation of, the person, character, feelings, rights, property, or interests of an individual | 2. That which injures, or occasions wrong, loss, damage, or detriment | 3. Harm
enshrine: 1. To inclose in a shrine or chest | 2. Hence, to preserve or cherish as something sacred | 3. As, to enshrine something in memory. We will enshrine it as holy relic. Massinger
showiness: 1. The quality or state of being showy | 2. Pompousness | 3. Great parade
chirp:
1. To make a shop, sharp, cheerful, as of small birds or crickets.

A short, sharp note, as of a bird or insect. "The chirp of flitting bird." Bryant
gaydiang: 1. A vessel of Anam, with two or three masts, lofty triangular sails, and in construction somewhat resembling a Chinese junk
intenible: 1. Incapable of holding or containing.  This captious and intenible sieve. Shak
sipunculoid: 1. Pertaining to the Sipunculoidea. -- n.  One of the Sipunculoidea
toret:
1. A Turret. 

A ring for fastening a hawk's leash to the jesses | 2. Also, a ring affixed to the collar of a dog, etc | 3. Chaucer
cachemia: 1. A degenerated or poisoned condition of the blood. --Ca*chæ"mic, Ca*che"mic, a
paregoric:
1. Mitigating | 2. Assuaging or soothing pain | 3. As, paregoric elixir.

A medicine that mitigates pain
flap: 1. Anything broad and limber that hangs loose, or that is attached by one side or end and is easily moved | 2. As, the flap of a garment. A cartilaginous flap upon the opening of the larynx. Sir T. Browne | 3. A hinged leaf, as of a table or shutter
miraculize: 1. To cause to seem to be a miracle.  Shaftesbury
solicitor: 1. One who solicits | 2. An attorney or advocate | 3. One who represents another in court
synepy: 1. The interjunction, or joining, of words in uttering the clauses of sentences
atavism: 1. The recurrence, or a tendency to a recurrence, of the original type of a species in the progeny of its varieties | 2. Resemblance to remote rather than to near ancestors | 3. Reversion to the original form. The recurrence of any peculiarity or disease of an ancestor in a subsequent generation, after an intermission for a generation or two
catechu: 1. A dry, brown, astringent extract, obtained by decoction and evaporation from the Acacia catechu, and several other plants growing in India. It contains a large portion of tannin or tannic acid, and is used in medicine and in the arts. It is also known by the names terra japonica, cutch, gambier, etc | 2. Ure. Dunglison
earthquake:
1. A shaking, trembling, or concussion of the earth, due to subterranean causes, often accompanied by a rumbling noise. The wave of shock sometimes traverses half a hemisphere, destroying cities and many thousand lives | 2. -- called also earthdin, earthquave, and earthshock. Earthquake alarm, a bell signal constructed to operate on the theory that a few seconds before the occurrence of an earthquake the magnet temporarily loses its power.

Like, or characteristic of, an earthquake | 3. Loud
reembark: 1. To put, or go, on board a vessel again | 2. To embark again
paradoxure: 1. Any species of Paradoxurus, a genus of Asiatic viverrine mammals allied to the civet, as the musang, and the luwack or palm cat. See Musang
unplume: 1. To strip of plumes or feathers | 2. Hence, to humiliate
gallican: 1. Of or pertaining to Gaul or France | 2. Gallic | 3. French
whippersnapper: 1. A diminutive, insignificant, or presumptuous person.  "Little whippersnappers like you." T. Hughes
predorsal: 1. Situated in front of the back | 2. Immediately in front, or on the ventral side the dorsal part of the vertebral column
positivism: 1. A system of philosophy originated by M. Auguste Comte, which deals only with positives. It excludes from philosophy everything but the natural phenomena or properties of knowable things, together with their invariable relations of coexistence and succession, as occurring in time and space. Such relations are denominated laws, which are to be discovered by observation, experiment, and comparison. This philosophy holds all inquiry into causes, both efficient and final, to be useless and unprofitable
longiloquence: 1. Long-windedness. American longiloquence in oratory. Fitzed. Hall
oddness: 1. The state of being odd, or not even. Take but one from three, and you not only destroy the oddness, but also the essence of that number. Fotherby | 2. Singularity | 3. Strangeness
ooesporangium: 1. An oögonium | 2. Also, a case containing oval or rounded spores of some other kind than oöspores
orphanage: 1. The state of being an orphan | 2. Orphanhood | 3. Orphans, collectively
enneagynous: 1. Having or producing nine pistils or styles | 2. -- said of a flower or plant
prosing: 1. Writing prose | 2. Speaking or writing in a tedious or prosy manner. Sir W. Scott
cashew: 1. A tree of the same family which the sumac. It is native in tropical America, but is now naturalized in all tropical countries. Its fruit, a kidney-shaped nut, grows at the extremity of an edible, pear-shaped hypocarp, about three inches long. Casbew nut, the large, kidney-shaped fruit of the cashew, which is edible after the caustic oil has been expelled from the shell by roasting the nut
hemorrhagic: 1. Pertaining or tending to a flux o
solatium: 1. Anything which alleviates or compensates for suffering or loss | 2. A compensation | 3. Esp., an additional allowance, as for injured feelings
ology: 1. A colloquial or humorous name for any science or branch of knowledge. He had a smattering of mechanics, of physiology, geology, mineralogy, and all other ologies whatsoever. De Quincey
whilk:
1. A kind of mollusk, a whelk | 2. The scoter. 

Which.  Note: Whilk is sometimes used in Chaucer to represent the Northern dialect
disdain: 1. A feeling of contempt and aversion | 2. The regarding anything as unworthy of or beneath one | 3. Scorn. How my soul is moved with just disdain! Pope. Note: Often implying an idea of haughtiness. Disdain and scorn ride sparkling in her eyes. Shak
grenadier: 1. Originaly, a soldier who carried and threw grenades | 2. Afterward, one of a company attached to each regiment or battalion, taking post on the right of the line, and wearing a peculiar uniform. In modern times, a member of a special regiment or corps | 3. As, a grenadier of the guard of Napoleon I. one of the regiment of Grenadier Guards of the British army, etc
horizontality: 1. The state or quality of being horizontal. Kirwan
tantalic: 1. Of or pertaining to tantalum | 2. Derived from, or containing, tantalum | 3. Specifically, designating any one of a series of acids analogous to nitric acid and the polyacid compounds of phosphorus
december: 1. The twelfth and last month of the year, containing thirty-one days. During this month occurs the winter solstice | 2. Fig.: With reference to the end of the year and to the winter season | 3. As, the December of his life
parataxis: 1. The mere ranging of propositions one after another, without indicating their connection or interdependence | 2. -- opposed to syntax. Brande & C
rashly: 1. In a rush manner | 2. With precipitation. He that doth anything rashly, must do it willingly | 3. For he was free to deliberate or not
salmonet: 1. A salmon of small size | 2. A samlet
fealty: 1. Fidelity to one's lord | 2. The feudal obligation by which the tenant or vassal was bound to be faithful to his lord | 3. The special oath by which this obligation was assumed
biaxal: 1. Having two axes | 2. As, biaxial polarization. Brewster. -- Bi*ax"i*al*ly, adv
sickler: 1. One who uses a sickle | 2. A sickleman | 3. A reaper
statical: 1. Resting | 2. Acting by mere weight without motion | 3. As, statical pressure
thecodont:
1. Having the teeth inserted in sockets in the alveoli of the jaws | 2. Of or pertaining to the thecodonts.

One of the Thecodontia
rebullition: 1. The act of boiling up or effervescing.  Sir H. Wotton
oology: 1. The science of eggs in relation to their coloring, size, shape, and number
rutilate: 1. To shine | 2. To emit rays of light.  Ure
kink: 1. A twist or loop in a rope or thread, caused by a spontaneous doubling or winding upon itself | 2. A close loop or curl | 3. A doubling in a cord
quarrel: 1. An arrow for a crossbow | 2. -- so named because it commonly had a square head.  To shoot with arrows and quarrel. Sir J. Mandeville. Two arblasts, . . . with windlaces and quarrels. Sir W. Scott | 3. Any small square or quadrangular member
scragginess: 1. The quality or state of being scraggy | 2. Scraggedness
eaglestone: 1. A concretionary nodule of clay ironstone, of the size of a walnut or larger, so called by the ancients, who believed that the eagle transported these stones to her nest to facilitate the laying of her eggs | 2. Aëtites
monogenesis: 1. Oneness of origin | 2. Esp | 3. , development of all beings in the universe from a single cell
great: 1. Large in space | 2. Of much size | 3. Big
wainbote: 1. See Cartbote. See also the Note under Bote
fluidal: 1. Pertaining to a fluid, or to its flowing motion. Fluidal structure, the structure characteristic of certain volcanic rocks in which the arrangement of the minute crystals shows the lines of flow of thew molten material before solidification | 2. -- also called fluxion structure
nor: 1. A negative connective or particle, introducing the second member or clause of a negative proposition, following neither, or not, in the first member or clause. Nor is also used sometimes in the first member for neither, and sometimes the neither is omitted and implied by the use of nor | 2. Provide neither gold nor silver, nor brass, in your purses, nor scrip for your journey. Matt. x. 9, | 3. Where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt. Matt. vi
ruberythrinic: 1. Pertaining to, or designating, an acid extracted from madder root. It is a yellow crystalline substance from which alizarin is obtained
humeral: 1. Of or pertaining to the humerus, or upper part of the arm | 2. Brachial. Humeral veil, a long, narrow veil or scarf of the same material as the vestments, worn round the shoulders by the officiating priest or his attendant at Mass, and used to protect the sacred vessels from contact with the hands
bellman: 1. A man who rings a bell, especially to give notice of anything in the streets. Formerly, also, a night watchman who called the hours. Milton
durst: 1. Of Dare. See Dare, v. i
harness: 1. Originally, the complete dress, especially in a military sense, of a man or a horse | 2. Hence, in general, armor. At least we 'll die witch harness on our back. Shak | 3. The equipment of a draught or carriage horse, for drawing a wagon, coach, chaise, etc
pseudomorph: 1. An irregular or deceptive form | 2. A pseudomorphous crystal, as a crystal consisting of quartz, but having the cubic form of fluor spar, the fluor crystal having been changed to quartz by a process of substitution
insisture: 1. A dwelling or standing on something | 2. Fixedness | 3. Persistence.  Shak
paddock: 1. A toad or frog. Wyclif. "Loathed paddocks." Spenser Paddock pipe, a hollow-stemmed plant of the genus Equisetum, especially E. limosum and the fruiting stems of E. arvense | 2. -- called also padow pipe and toad pipe. See Equisetum. -- Paddock stone. See Toadstone. -- Paddock stool,a toadstool | 3. A small inclosure or park for sporting
blessing: 1. The act of one who blesses | 2. A declaration of divine favor, or an invocation imploring divine favor on some or something | 3. A benediction
obfuscation: 1. The act of darkening or bewildering | 2. The state of being darkened. "Obfuscation of the cornea." E. Darwin
undertone: 1. A low or subdued tone or utterance | 2. A tone less loud than usual
tweeze: 1. A surgeon's case of instruments. Howell
corolliflorous: 1. Having the stamens borne on the petals, and the latter free from the calyx. Compare Calycifloral and Thalamifloral
guidage: 1. The reward given to a guide for services.  Ainsworth | 2. Guidance | 3. Lead
embattlement: 1. An intended parapet | 2. A battlement | 3. The fortifying of a building or a wall by means of battlements
unchancy: 1. Happening at a bad time | 2. Unseasonable | 3. Inconvenient. A. Trollope
ageless: 1. Without old age limits of duration | 2. As, fountains of ageless youth
geostatic: 1. Relating to the pressure exerted by earth or similar substance. Geostatic arch, an arch having a form adapted to sustain pressure similar to that exerted by earth. Rankine
unnun: 1. To remove from condition of being a nun | 2. Many did quickly unnun and disfriar themselves. Fuller
encapsulation: 1. The act of inclosing in a capsule | 2. The growth of a membrane around so as to inclose it in a capsule
arabesqued: 1. Ornamented in the style of arabesques
chaconne: 1. An old Spanish dance in moderate three-four measure, like the Passacaglia, which is slower. Both are used by classical composers as themes for variations
errantry: 1. A wandering | 2. A roving | 3. Esp., a roving in quest of adventures. Addison
mocha: 1. A seaport town of Arabia, on the Red Sea | 2. A variety of coffee brought from Mocha | 3. An Abyssinian weight, equivalent to a Troy grain. Mocha stone, moss agate
olitory: 1. Of or pertaining to, or produced in, a kitchen garden | 2. Used for kitchen purposes | 3. As, olitory seeds. At convenient distance towards the olitory garden. Evelyn
staphylomatous: 1. Of or pertaining to staphyloma | 2. Affected with staphyloma
amend: 1. To change or modify in any way for the better | 2. As, by simply removing what is erroneous, corrupt, superfluous, faulty, and the like | 3. By supplying deficiencies
eleatic: 1. Of or pertaining to a certain school of Greek philosophers who taught that the only certain science is that which owes nothing to the senses, and all to the reason. -- n.  A philosopher of the Eleatic school
sputum: 1. That which is expectorated | 2. A salival discharge | 3. Spittle
patten: 1. A clog or sole of wood, usually supported by an iron ring, worn to raise the feet from the wet or the mud | 2. The patten now supports each frugal dame. Gay | 3. A stilt.  Halliwell
nonvocal: 1. Not vocal | 2. Destitute of tone. -- n.  A nonvocal consonant
intertransverse: 1. Between the transverse processes of the vertebræ
sarcolemma: 1. The very thin transparent and apparently homogenous sheath which incloses a striated muscular fiber | 2. The myolemma
taotai: 1. In China, an official at the head of the civil and military affairs of a circuit, which consists of two or more fu, or territorial departments | 2. --called also, by foreigners, intendant of circuit. Foreign consuls and commissioners associated with taotais as superintendants of trade at the treaty ports are ranked with the taotai
bromidiom: 1. A conventional comment or saying, such as those characteristic of bromides
lusk:
1. Lazy | 2. Slothful. 

A lazy fellow | 3. A lubber.  T. Kendall.

To be idle or unemployed
outspend: 1. Outlay | 2. Expenditure.  A mere outspend of savageness. I. Taylor
paraclete: 1. An advocate | 2. One called to aid or support | 3. Hence, the Consoler, Comforter, or Intercessor
decompound: 1. To compound or mix with that is already compound | 2. To compound a second time | 3. To reduce to constituent parts
verticillate: 1. Arranged in a transverse whorl or whorls like the rays of a wheel | 2. As, verticillate leaves of a plant | 3. A verticillate shell
expletively: 1. In the manner of an expletive
sustentation: 1. The act of sustaining, or the state of being sustained | 2. Preservation from falling | 3. Support
emication: 1. A flying off in small particles, as heated iron or fermenting liquors | 2. A sparkling | 3. Scintillation. Sir T. Browne
submersion: 1. The act of submerging, or putting under water or other fluid, or of causing to be overflowed | 2. The act of plunging under water, or of drowning | 3. The state of being put under water or other fluid, or of being overflowed or drowned
candlewaster: 1. One who consumes candles by being up late for study or dissipation. A bookworm, a candlewaster. B. Jonson
eupepsia: 1. Soundness of the nutritive or digestive organs | 2. Good concoction or digestion | 3. -- opposed to dyspepsia
musar: 1. An itinerant player on the musette, an instrument formerly common in Europe
scutelliplantar: 1. Having broad scutella on the front, and small scales on the posterior side, of the tarsus | 2. -- said of certain birds
crunk: 1. To cry like a crane.  "The crane crunketh." Withals
irishism: 1. A mode of speaking peculiar to the Irish | 2. An Hibernicism
speaker: 1. One who speaks. Specifically: One who utters or pronounces a discourse | 2. Usually, one who utters a speech in public | 3. As, the man is a good speaker, or a bad speaker. One who is the mouthpiece of others
podophyllin: 1. A brown bitter gum extracted from the rootstalk of the May apple. It is a complex mixture of several substances
mediaevalist: 1. One who has a taste for, or is versed in, the history of the Middle Ages | 2. One in sympathy with the spirit or forms of the Middle Ages
immould: 1. To mold into shape, or form.  G. Fletcher
matrass: 1. A round-bottomed glass flask having a long neck | 2. A bolthead
wiliness: 1. The quality or state of being wily | 2. Craftiness | 3. Cunning
consolation: 1. The act of consoling | 2. The state of being consoled | 3. Allevation of misery or distress of mind
pain: 1. Punishment suffered or denounced | 2. Suffering or evil inflicted as a punishment for crime, or connected with the commission of a crime | 3. Penalty. Chaucer. We will, by way of mulct or pain, lay it upon him
diatessaron: 1. The interval of a fourth | 2. A continuous narrative arranged from the first four books of the New Testament | 3. An electuary compounded of four medicines
symphony: 1. A consonance or harmony of sounds, agreeable to the ear, whether the sounds are vocal or instrumental, or both. The trumpets sound, And warlike symphony in heard around. Dryden | 2. A stringed instrument formerly in use, somewhat resembling the virginal. With harp and pipe and symphony. Chaucer | 3. An elaborate instrumental composition for a full orchestra, consisting usually, like the sonata, of three or four contrasted yet inwardly related movements, as the allegro, the adagio, the minuet and trio, or scherzo, and the finale in quick time. The term has recently been applied to large orchestral works in freer form, with arguments or programmes to explain their meaning, such as the "symphonic poems" of Liszt. The term was formerly applied to any composition for an orchestra, as overtures, etc., and still earlier, to certain compositions partly vocal, partly instrumental. An instrumental passage at the beginning or end, or in the course of, a vocal composition
lexicographic: 1. Of or pertaining to, or according to, lexicography. -- Lex`i*co*graph"ic*al*ly, adv
pickerel: 1. A young or small pike.  Bet  is, quoth he, a pike than a pickerel. Chaucer | 2. Any one of several species of freshwater fishes of the genus Esox, esp | 3. The smaller species. The glasseye, or wall-eyed pike. See Wall-eye
devulgarize: 1. To free from what is vulgar, common, or narrow. Shakespeare and Plutarch's "Lives" are very devulgarizing books. E. A. Abbott
impanel: 1. To enter in a list, or on a piece of parchment, called a panel | 2. To form or enroll, as a list of jurors in a court of justice. Blackstone
postaxial: 1. Situated behind any transverse axis in the body of an animal | 2. Caudal | 3. Posterior
cyst: 1. A pouch or sac without opening, usually membranous and containing morbid matter, which is accidentally developed in one of the natural cavaties or in the substance of an organ. Eaton | 3. A small capsule or sac of the kind in which many immature entozoans exit in the tissues of living animals
embow: 1. To bend like a bow | 2. To curve. "Embowed arches."  Sir W. Scott. With gilded horns embowed like the moon. Spenser
roving: 1. The operatin of forming the rove, or slightly twisted sliver or roll of wool or cotton, by means of a machine for the purpose, called a roving frame, or roving machine | 2. A roll or sliver of wool or cotton drawn out and slightly twisted | 3. A rove. See 2d Rove,
akinesia: 1. Paralysis of the motor nerves | 2. Loss of movement. Foster
eve: 1. Evening.  Winter oft, at eve resumes the breeze. Thomson | 2. The evening before a holiday, -- from the Jewish mode of reckoning the day as beginning at sunset. not at midnight | 3. As, Christians eve is the evening before Christmas
corporeally: 1. In the body | 2. In a bodily form or manner
coniferin: 1. A glucoside extracted from the cambium layer of coniferous trees as a white crystalline substance
backwoods: 1. The forests or partly cleared grounds on the frontiers
unlovely: 1. Not lovely | 2. Not amiable | 3. Possessing qualities that excite dislike
alcoometry: 1. See Alcoholometry. Note: The chemists say alcomètre, alcoomètrie, doubtless by the suppression of a syllable in order to avoid a disagreeable sequence of sounds. Littré
battuta: 1. The measuring of time by beating
dechristianize: 1. To turn from, or divest of, Christianity
larviform: 1. Having the form or structure of a larva
woodstone: 1. A striped variety of hornstone, resembling wood in appearance
maieutics: 1. The art of giving birth to ideas, which are conceived as struggling for birth. Payne
soldo: 1. A small Italian coin worth a sou or a cent | 2. The twentieth part of a lira
rabato: 1. A kind of ruff for the neck | 2. A turned-down collar | 3. A rebato.  Shak
veranda: 1. An open, roofed gallery or portico, adjoining a dwelling house, forming an out-of-door sitting room. See Loggia. The house was of adobe, low, with a wide veranda on the three sides of the inner court. Mrs. H. H. Jackson
coralwort: 1. A cruciferous herb of certain species of Dentaria | 2. -- called also toothwort, tooth violet, or pepper root
anthropotomy: 1. The anatomy or dissection of the human body | 2. Androtomy. Owen
prosencephalon: 1. The anterior segment of the brain, including the cerebrum and olfactory lobes | 2. The forebrain. The cerebrum. Huxley
tethys: 1. A genus of a large naked mollusks having a very large, broad, fringed cephalic disk, and branched dorsal gills. Some of the species become a foot long and are brilliantly colored
ungrave: 1. To raise or remove from the grave | 2. To disinter | 3. To untomb
meedful: 1. Worthy of meed, reward, or recompense | 2. Meritorious. "Meedful works." Wiclif
albion: 1. An ancient name of England, still retained in poetry. In that nook-shotten isle of Albion. Shak
embryotroph: 1. The material from which an embryo is formed and nourished
locator: 1. One who locates, or is entitled to locate, land or a mining claim
mime:
1. A kind of drama in which real persons and events were generally represented in a ridiculous manner | 2. An actor in such representations.

To mimic.  -- Mim"er, n
ermined: 1. Clothed or adorned with the fur of the ermine. Pope
accrementition: 1. The process of generation by development of blastema, or fission of cells, in which the new formation is in all respect like the individual from which it proceeds
overply: 1. To ply to excess | 2. To exert with too much vigor | 3. To overwork. Milton

creosote:
1. Wood-tar oil | 2. An oily antiseptic liquid, of a burning smoky taste, colorless when pure, but usually colored yellow or brown by impurity or exposure. It is a complex mixture of various phenols and their ethers, and is obtained by the distillation of wood tar, especially that of beechwood. Note: It is remarkable as an antiseptic and deodorizer in the preservation of wood, flesh, etc., and in the prevention of putrefaction | 3. But it is a poor germicide, and in this respect has been overrated. Smoked meat, as ham, owes its preservation and taste to a small quantity of creosote absorbed from the smoke to which it is exposed. Carbolic acid is phenol proper, while creosote is a mixture of several phenols. Coal-tar creosote, a colorless or yellow, oily liquid, obtained in the distillation of coal tar, and resembling wood-tar oil, or creosote proper, in composition and properties.

To saturate or impregnate with creosote, as timber, for the prevention of decay

accorporate: 1. To unite | 2. To attach | 3. To incorporate.  Milton

unconcluding: 1. Inconclusive.  Locke. -- Un`con*clud"ing*ness, n.  Jer. Taylor

parochially: 1. In a parochial manner | 2. By the parish, or by parishes. Bp. Stillingfleet
atmologist: 1. One who is versed in atmology

smectite: 1. A hydrous silicate of alumina, of a greenish color, which, in certain states of humidity, appears transparent and almost gelatinous
gibber:
1. A balky horse. Youatt.

To speak rapidly and inarticulately. Shak
abduction: 1. The act of abducing or abducting | 2. A drawing apart | 3. A carrying away. Roget
frequenter: 1. One who frequents | 2. One who often visits, or resorts to customarily
fretum: 1. A strait, or arm of the sea
inconspicuous: 1. Not conspicuous or noticeable | 2. Hardly discernible. -- In`con*spic"u*ous*ly, adv | 3. -- In`con*spic"u*ous*ness, n. Boyle
longipennes: 1. A group of longwinged sea birds, including the gulls, petrels, etc

alcooemetry: 1. See Alcoholometry. Note: The chemists say alcomètre, alcoomètrie, doubtless by the suppression of a syllable in order to avoid a disagreeable sequence of sounds. Littré
grandevous: 1. Of great age | 2. Aged | 3. Longlived.  Bailey

quadricipital: 1. Of or pertaining to the quadriceps
polite: 1. Smooth | 2. Polished.  Rays of light falling on a polite surface. Sir I. Newton | 3. Smooth and refined in behavior or manners

tanate: 1. An Asiatic wild dog, native of Japan and adjacent countries. It has a short, bushy tail. Called also raccoon dog
excitant:
1. Tending to excite | 2. Exciting.

gemmiparity: 1. Reproduction by budding | 2. Gemmation. See Budding
unflower: 1. To strip of flowers.  G. Fletcher

narrator: 1. One who narrates | 2. One who relates a series of events or transactions

fletcher: 1. One who fletches of feathers arrows | 2. A manufacturer of bows and arrows.  Mortimer

A kind of compass saw or fret saw
mooncalf: 1. A monster | 2. A false conception | 3. A mass of fleshy matter, generated in the uterus
pinnatiped:
1. Having the toes bordered by membranes | 2. Fin-footed, as certain birds.

Any bird which has the toes bordered by membranes
arbitrarily: 1. In an arbitrary manner | 2. By will only | 3. Despotically

uxoricidal: 1. Of or pertaining to uxoricide | 2. Tending to uxoricide
custard: 1. A mixture of milk and eggs, sweetened, and baked or boiled. coralloidal: 1. Resembling coral | 2. Coralloid. Sir T. browne
asteriated: 1. Radiated, with diverging rays | 2. As, asteriated sapphire

foregoer: 1. One who goes before another | 2. A predecessor | 3. Hence, an ancestor' a progenitor

ellwand: 1. Formerly, a measuring rod an ell long

kittle:
1. To bring forth young, as a cat | 2. To kitten | 3. To litter. 

To tickle.   Halliwell. Jamieson.

Ticklish

To play the casuist. Milton

proximally: 1. On or toward a proximal part | 2. Proximad

The feeding and reproductive zooids hang down from the under side of the disk

chronographic: 1. Of or pertaining to a chronograph

1. To form a plot or scheme | 2. To contrive to accomplish a purpose by secret artifice | 3. To carry on a secret and illicit love or amour.

To fill with artifice and duplicity

1. Delay.  Bp. Hall.

1. A figure by which arguments are placed in various points of view, and then turned to one point. Smart.

A dark green or bronze-colored laminated variety of pyroxene, common in certain igneous rocks

1. See Coellac.

The cipher multiplying everything by two, as in common arithmetic by ten

nonterm: 1. A vacation between two terms of a court

retuse: 1. Having the end rounded and slightly indented | 2. As, a retuse leaf

A plant of the order Labiatæ

1. To wind or collect into a ball | 2. Hence, to gather into a mass or anything like a mass. Where he builds the agglomerated pile. Cowper.

serolin: 1. A peculiar fatty substance found in the blood, probably a mixture of fats, cholesterin, etc | 2. A body found in fecal matter and thought to be formed in the intestines from the cholesterin of the bile | 3. -- called also stercorin, and stercolin
estrade: 1. A portion of the floor of a room raised above the general level, as a place for a bed or a throne | 2. A platform | 3. A dais. He  himself should have his desk on a mounted estrade or platform. J. G. Fitch
metathesis: 1. Transposition, as of the letters or syllables of a word | 2. As, pistris for pristis | 3. Meagre for meager
pleasantry: 1. That which denotes or promotes pleasure or good humor | 2. Cheerfulness | 3. Gayety
seismograph: 1. An apparatus for registering the shocks and undulatory motions of earthquakes
equally: 1. In an equal manner or degree in equal shares or proportion | 2. With equal and impartial justice | 3. Without difference
tap: 1. To strike with a slight or gentle blow | 2. To touch gently | 3. To rap lightly
pedality: 1. The act of measuring by paces.  Ash
manual: 1. Of or pertaining to the hand | 2. Done or made by the hand | 3. As, manual labor
quip: 1. A smart, sarcastic turn or jest | 2. A taunt | 3. A severe retort
varietas: 1. A variety | 2. -- used in giving scientific names, and often abbreviated to var
exacuate: 1. To whet or sharpen.  B. Jonson. -- Ex*ac`u*a"tion, n
nectarine:
1. Nectareous.  Milton.

A smooth-skinned variety of peach. Spanish nectarine, the plumlike fruit of the West Indian tree Chrysobalanus Icaco | 2. -- also called cocoa plum. it is made into a sweet conserve which a largely exported from Cuba
tachymeter: 1. An instrument, esp | 2. A transit or theodolite with stadia wires, for determining quickly the distances, bearings, and elevations of distant objects | 3. A speed indicator
perciformes: 1. An extensive tribe or suborder of fishes, including the true perches | 2. The pondfishes | 3. The sciænoids
cirrobranchiata: 1. A division of Mollusca having slender, cirriform appendages near the mouth | 2. The Scaphopoda
usherdom: 1. The office or position of an usher | 2. Ushership | 3. Also, ushers, collectively
elemi: 1. A fragrant gum resin obtained chiefly tropical trees of the genera Amyris and Canarium. A. elemifera yields Mexican elemi | 2. Commune, the Manila elemi. It is used in the manufacture of varnishes, also in ointments and plasters
romany: 1. A gypsy | 2. The language spoken among themselves by the gypsies
inveiglement: 1. The act of inveigling, or the state of being inveigled | 2. That which inveigles | 3. Enticement
rectilineal: 1. Straight | 2. Consisting of a straight line or lines | 3. Bounded by straight lines
reducent: 1. Tending to reduce. -- n.  A reducent agent
hine: 1. A servant | 2. A farm laborer | 3. A peasant
toothsome: 1. Grateful to the taste | 2. Palable. -- Tooth"some*ly, adv | 3. -- Tooth"some*ness, n. Though less toothsome to me, they were more wholesome for me. Fuller
halfen: 1. Wanting half its due qualities.  Spencer
tubicolous: 1. Inhabiting a tube | 2. As, tubicolous worms
langrage: 1. A kind of shot formerly used at sea for tearing sails and rigging. It consisted of bolts, nails, and other pieces of iron fastened together or inclosed in a canister
titanium: 1. An elementary substance found combined in the minerals manaccanite, rutile, sphene, etc., and isolated as an infusible iron- gray amorphous powder, having a metallic luster. It burns when heated in the air | 2. Symbol Ti. Atomic weight
tattling: 1. Given to idle talk | 2. Apt to tell tales. -- Tat"tling*ly, adv
intensifier: 1. One who or that which intensifies or strengthens | 2. In photography, an agent used to intensify the lights or shadows of a picture
gambrel:
1. The hind leg of a horse | 2. A stick crooked like a horse's hind leg | 3. -- used by butchers in suspending slaughtered animals. Gambrel roof, a curb roof having the same section in all parts, with a lower steeper slope and an upper and flatter one, so that each gable is pentagonal in form.

To truss or hang up by means of a gambrel. Beau. & Fl
polypite: 1. One of the feeding zooids, or polyps, of a coral, hydroid, or siphonophore | 2. A hydranth. See Illust. of Campanularian. Sometimes, the manubrium of a hydroid medusa | 3. A fossil coral
terrorism: 1. The act of terrorizing, or state of being terrorized | 2. A mode of government by terror or intimidation. Jefferson.  The practise of coercing governments to accede to political demands by committing violence on civilian targets | 3. Any similar use of violence to achieve goals
corypheus: 1. The conductor, chief, or leader of the dramatic chorus | 2. Hence, the chief or leader of a party or interest. That noted corypheus  of the Independent faction. South
deductible: 1. Capable of being deducted, taken away, or withdrawn. Not one found honestly deductible From any use that pleased him | 2. Mrs. Browning | 3. Deducible
capsquare: 1. A metal covering plate which passes over the trunnions of a cannon, and holds it in place
cockswain: 1. The steersman of a boat | 2. A petty officer who has charge of a boat and its crew
exhaustless: 1. Not be exhausted | 2. Inexhaustible | 3. As, an exhaustless fund or store
feudalize: 1. To reduce toa feudal tenure | 2. To conform to feudalism
suffrage: 1. A vote given in deciding a controverted question, or in the choice of a man for an office or trust | 2. The formal expression of an opinion | 3. Assent
hereditable: 1. Capable of being inherited. See Inheritable. Locke | 2. Qualified to inherit | 3. Capable of inheriting
polluting: 1. Adapted or tending to pollute | 2. Causing defilement or pollution. -- Pol*lut"ing*ly, adv
reclusory: 1. The habitation of a recluse | 2. A hermitage
isospondylous: 1. Of or pertaining to the Isospondyli | 2. Having the anterior vertebræ separate and normal
lustrous: 1. Bright | 2. Shining | 3. Luminous. " Good sparks and lustrous." Shak. -- Lus"trous*ly, adv
echinate: 1. Set with prickles | 2. Prickly, like a hedgehog | 3. Bristled
cubism: 1. A movement or phase in post-impressionism. - - Cu"bist, n
whitewall: 1. The spotted flycatcher | 2. -- so called from the white color of the under parts
awork: 1. At work | 2. In action. "Set awork." Shak
hackberry: 1. A genus of trees related to the elm, but bearing drupes with scanty, but often edible, pulp. C. occidentalis is common in the Eastern United States. Gray
transubstantiate: 1. To change into another substance.  The spider love which transubstantiates all, And can convert manna to gall. Donne | 2. To change, as the sacramental elements, bread and wine, into the flesh and blood of Christ
marquess: 1. A marquis. Lady marquess, a marchioness.  Shak
tower: 1. A mass of building standing alone and insulated, usually higher than its diameter, but when of great size not always of that proportion. A projection from a line of wall, as a fortification, for purposes of defense, as a flanker, either or the same height as the curtain wall or higher. A structure appended to a larger edifice for a special purpose, as for a belfry, and then usually high in proportion to its width and to the height of the rest of the edifice | 2. As, a church tower | 3. A citadel
apagogical: 1. Proving indirectly, by showing the absurdity, or impossibility of the contrary. Bp. Berkeley
warfare: 1. Military service | 2. Military life | 3. Contest carried on by enemies
unicellular: 1. Having, or consisting of, but a single cell | 2. As, a unicellular organism
reseat: 1. To seat or set again, as on a chair, throne, etc | 2. Dryden | 3. To put a new seat, or new seats, in
hogging: 1. Drooping at the ends | 2. Arching | 3. -in distinction from sagging. Hogging frame. See Hogframe
troll: 1. A supernatural being, often represented as of diminutive size, but sometimes as a giant, and fabled to inhabit caves, hills, and like places | 2. A witch. Troll flower. Same as Globeflower | 3. To move circularly or volubly
nidgery: 1. A trifle | 2. A piece of foolery.  Skinner
flour: 1. The finely ground meal of wheat, or of any other grain | 2. Especially, the finer part of meal separated by bolting | 3. Hence, the fine and soft powder of any substance
albuminoid: 1. Resembling albumin. -- n.  One of a class of organic principles which form the main part of organized tissues. Brunton
temperament: 1. Internal constitution | 2. State with respect to the relative proportion of different qualities, or constituent parts. The common law . . . has reduced the kingdom to its just state and temperament. Sir M. Hale | 3. Due mixture of qualities
inwall:
1. To inclose or fortify as with a wall. Spenser.

An inner wall | 2. Specifically, the inner wall, or lining, of a blast furnace
languaged: 1. Having a language | 2. Skilled in language | 3. -- chiefly used in composition. " Manylanguaged nations." Pope
agility: 1. The quality of being agile | 2. The power of moving the limbs quickly and easily | 3. Nimbleness
saengerfest: 1. A festival of singers | 2. A German singing festival
launderer: 1. One who follows the business of laundering
shorthorn: 1. One of a breed of large, heavy domestic cattle having short horns. The breed was developed in England
smutch:
1. A stain | 2. A dirty spot. B. Jonson.

To blacken with smoke, soot, or coal.  B. Jonson
specificness: 1. The quality or state of being specific
tuckahoe: 1. A curious vegetable production of the Southern Atlantic United States, growing under ground like a truffle and often attaining immense size. The real nature is unknown. Called also Indian bread, and Indian loaf
jacobean: 1. Of or pertaining to a style of architecture and decoration in the time of James the First, of England. "A Jacobean table." C. L. Eastlake
wolverine: 1. The glutton | 2. A nickname for an inhabitant of Michigan
figurate: 1. Of a definite form or figure. Plants are all figurate and determinate, which inanimate bodies are not | 2. Bacon | 3. Figurative
nuddle: 1. To walk quickly with the head bent forward | 2. -- often with along
streamlet: 1. A small stream | 2. A rivulet | 3. A rill
barker: 1. An animal that barks | 2. Hence, any one who clamors unreasonably | 3. One who stands at the doors of shops to urg
cerused: 1. Washed with a preparation of white lead | 2. As, cerused face. Beau. & Fl
officialism: 1. The state of being official | 2. A system of official government | 3. Also, adherence to office routine
lant:
1. Urine.  Nares.

Any one of several species of small, slender, marine fishes of the genus Ammedytes. The common European species and the American species live on sandy shores, buried in the sand, and are caught in large quantities for bait. Called also launce, and sand eel | 2. See Lanterloo.  Halliwell
earthwards: 1. Toward the earth | 2. -- opposed to heavenward or skyward
kirsome: 1. Christian | 2. Christened.  I am a true kirsome woman. Beau. & Fl
pucelle: 1. A maid | 2. A virgin.   Lady or pucelle, that wears mask or fan | 3. Jonson. La Pucelle, the Maid of Orleans, Joan of Arc
matchmaking:
1. The act or process of making matches for kindling or burning | 2. The act or process of trying to bring about a marriage for others.

Busy in making or contriving marriages | 3. As, a matchmaking woman
chlorate: 1. A salt of chloric acid | 2. As, chlorate of potassium
gonorrhea: 1. A contagious inflammatory disease of the genitourinary tract, affecting especially the urethra and vagina, and characterized by a mucopurulent discharge, pain in urination, and chordee | 2. Clap
underlaid: 1. Laid or placed underneath | 2. Also, having something laid or lying underneath
fourche: 1. Having the ends forked or branched, and the ends of the branches terminating abruptly as if cut off | 2. -- said of an ordinary, especially of a cross
canine: 1. Of or pertaining to the family Canidæ, or dogs and wolves | 2. Having the nature or qualities of a dog | 3. Like that or those of a dog
luggage: 1. That which is lugged | 2. Anything cumbrous and heavy to be carried | 3. Especially, a traveler's trunks, baggage, etc., or their contents. I am gathering up my luggage, and preparing for my journey. Swift. What do you mean, To dote thus on such luggage! Shak. Syn. -- Plunder
sumach: 1. Any plant of the genus Rhus, shrubs or small trees with usually compound leaves and clusters of small flowers. The powdered leaves, peduncles, and young branches of certain species of the sumac plant, used in tanning and dyeing. Poison sumac. See under Poison
cataplexy: 1. A morbid condition caused by an overwhelming shock or extreme fear and marked by rigidity of the muscles. -- Cat`a*plec"tic, a
concealed: 1. Hidden | 2. Kept from sight | 3. Secreted. -- Con*ceal"ed*ly (, adv
milkful: 1. Full of milk | 2. Abounding with food.  "Milkful vales." Sylvester
renownful: 1. Having great renown | 2. Famous. "Renownful Scipio." Marston
suspensor: 1. A suspensory | 2. The cord which suspends the embryo | 3. And which is attached to the radicle in the young state
oldness: 1. The state or quality of being old | 2. Old age
delightful: 1. Highly pleasing | 2. Affording great pleasure and satisfaction. "Delightful bowers." Spenser. "Delightful fruit." Milton. Syn. -- Delicious | 3. Charming. See Delicious. -- De*light"ful*ly, adv
secretary: 1. One who keeps, or is intrusted with, secrets | 2. A person employed to write orders, letters, dispatches, public or private papers, records, and the like | 3. An official scribe, amanuensis, or writer
stay: 1. A large, strong rope, employed to support a mast, by being extended from the head of one mast down to some other, or to some part of the vessel. Those which lead forward are called fore-and-aft stays | 2. Those which lead to the vessel's side are called backstays. See Illust. of Ship. In stays, or Hove in stays, in the act or situation of staying, or going about from one tack to another. R. H. Dana, Jr. -- Stay holes, openings in the edge of a staysail through which the hanks pass which join it to the stay. -- Stay tackle, a tackle attached to a stay and used for hoisting or lowering heavy articles over the side. -- To miss stays, to fail in the attempt to go about. Totten. -- Triatic stay, a rope secured at the ends to the heads of the foremast and mainmast with thimbles spliced to its bight into which the stay tackles hook | 3. To stop from motion or falling
foresignify: 1. To signify beforehand | 2. To foreshow | 3. To typify. Milton
metabasis: 1. A transition from one subject to another | 2. Same as Metabola
wankle: 1. Not to be depended on | 2. Weak | 3. Unstable.  Grose
dopper: 1. An Anabaptist or Baptist.  B. Jonson
usufruct: 1. The right of using and enjoying the profits of an estate or other thing belonging to another, without impairing the substance. Burrill
volt:
1. A circular tread | 2. A gait by which a horse going sideways round a center makes two concentric tracks | 3. A sudden movement to avoid a thrust.

The unit of electro-motive force
illegal: 1. Not according to, or authorized by, law | 2. Specif., contrary to, or in violation of, human law | 3. Unlawful

jujitsu: 1. The Japanese art of self-defense without weapons, now widely used as a system of physical training. It depends for its efficiency largely upon the principle of making use of an opponent's strength and weight to disable or injure him, and by applying pressure so that his opposing movement will throw him out of balance, dislocate or break a joint, etc | 2. It opposes knowledge and skill to brute strength, and demands an extensive practical knowledge of human anatomy

adeptness: 1. The quality of being adept | 2. Skill
