redolency: 1. The quality of being redolent | 2. Sweetness of scent | 3. Pleasant odor
chamfer: 1. The surface formed by cutting away the arris, or angle, formed by two faces of a piece of timber, stone, etc | 2. To cut a furrow in, as in a column | 3. To groove
coenosarc: 1. The common soft tissue which unites the polyps of a compound hydroid. See Hydroidea
brocaded: 1. Woven or worked, as brocade, with gold and silver, or with raised flowers, etc | 2. Brocaded flowers o'er the gay mantua shine. Gay | 3. Dressed in brocade
hirtellous: 1. Pubescent with minute and somewhat rigid hairs
susurration: 1. A whispering | 2. A soft murmur. "Soft susurrations of the trees." Howell
cranked: 1. Formed with, or having, a bend or crank | 2. As, a cranked axle
dammar: 1. An oleoresin used in making varnishes | 2. Dammar gum | 3. Dammara resin. It is obtained from certain resin trees indigenous to the East Indies, esp
wheedle: 1. To entice by soft words | 2. To cajole | 3. To flatter
foliosity: 1. The ponderousness or bulk of a folio | 2. Voluminousness.  De Quincey

photism: 1. A luminous image or appearance of a hallucinatory character

oceanic: 1. Of or pertaining to the ocean | 2. Found or formed in or about, or produced by, the ocean | 3. Frequenting the ocean, especially mid-ocean. Petrels are the most aërial and oceanic of birds. Darwin
prandial: 1. Of or pertaining to a repast, especially to dinner
mesencephalon: 1. The middle segment of the brain | 2. The midbrain. Sometimes abbreviated to mesen. See Brain
lorikeet: 1. Any one numerous species of small brush-tongued parrots or lories, found mostly in Australia, New Guinea and the adjacent islands, with some forms in the East Indies. monton: 1. A heap of ore | 2. A mass undergoing the process of amalgamation
porringer: 1. A porridge dish | 2. Esp., a bowl or cup from which children eat or are fed | 3. As, a silver porringer. Wordsworth
cummin: 1. Same as Cumin. Ye pay tithe of mint, and cummin. Matt. xxiii
inextinguishably: 1. So as not to be extinguished | 2. In an inextinguishable manner
congenite: 1. Congenital | 2. Connate | 3. Inborn. See Congenital.  Many conclusions, of moral and intellectual truths, seem . . . to be congenite with us. Sir M. Hale

selective: 1. Selecting | 2. Tending to select. This selective providence of the Almighty. Bp. Hall
directness: 1. The quality of being direct | 2. Straightness | 3. Straightforwardness
salvor: 1. One who assists in saving a ship or goods at sea, without being under special obligation to do so. Wheaton

requisitionist: 1. One who makes or signs a requisition

campana: 1. A church bell | 2. The pasque flower. Drayton | 3. Same as Gutta
unsitting: 1. Not sitting well | 2. Unbecoming.  "Unsitting words." Sir T. More
sanative: 1. Having the power to cure or heal | 2. Healing | 3. Tending to heal

uncipher: 1. To decipher | 2. As, to uncipher a letter.  Sir W. Temple

delapsion: 1. A falling down, or out of place | 2. Prolapsion
pica: 1. The genus that includes the magpies | 2. A vitiated appetite that craves what is unfit for food, as chalk, ashes, coal, etc | 3. Chthonophagia
nidification: 1. The act or process of building a nest
avulse: 1. To pluck or pull off | 2. Shenstone
earthward: 1. Toward the earth | 2. -- opposed to heavenward or skyward
uncreated: 1. Deprived of existence | 2. Annihilated. Beau. & Fl | 3. Not yet created
hoistway: 1. An opening for the hoist, or
supersensitive: 1. Excessively sensitive | 2. Morbidly sensitive. -- Su`per*sen"si*tive*ness, n
duplicative: 1. Having the quality of duplicating or doubling | 2. Having the quality of subdividing into two by natural growth. "Duplicative subdivision." Carpenter
subservience: 1. The quality or state of being subservient | 2. Instrumental fitness or use | 3. Hence, willingness to serve another's purposes
pedesis: 1. Same as Brownian movement, under Brownian
turgent: 1. Rising into a tumor, or a puffy state | 2. Swelling | 3. Tumid
prox: 1. "The ticket or list of candidates at elections, presented to the people for their votes."  Bartlett
wane: 1. To be diminished | 2. To decrease | 3. -- contrasted with wax, and especially applied to the illuminated part of the moon. Like the moon, aye wax ye and wane. Waning moons their settled periods keep. Addison

colossus: 1. A statue of gigantic size. The name was especially applied to certain famous statues in antiquity, as the Colossus of Nero in Rome, the Colossus of Apollo at Rhodes. Smith | 2. Any man or beast of gigantic size
renneted: 1. Provided or treated with rennet.  "Pressed milk renneted." Chapman
sulphureity: 1. The quality or state of being sulphureous.  B. Jonson

thymate: 1. A compound of thymol analogous to a salt | 2. As, sodium thymate
nystagmus: 1. A rapid involuntary oscillation of the eyeballs

disesteem: 1. Want of esteem | 2. Low estimation, inclining to dislike | 3. Disfavor
personalize: 1. To make personal. "They personalize death." H. Spencer
wormseed: 1. Any one of several plants, as Artemisia santonica, and Chenopodium anthelminticum, whose seeds have the property of expelling worms from the stomach and intestines. Wormseed mustard, a slender, cruciferous plant having small lanceolate leaves

shako: 1. A kind of military cap or headress

bahaudur: 1. A title of respect or honor given to European officers in East Indian state papers, and colloquially, and among the natives, to distinguished officials and other important personages
incremental: 1. Pertaining to, or resulting from, the process of growth | 2. As, the incremental lines in the dentine of teeth
eupeptic: 1. Of or pertaining to good digestion | 2. Easy of digestion | 3. Having a good digestion
flint: 1. A massive, somewhat impure variety of quartz, in color usually of a gray to brown or nearly black, breaking with a conchoidal fracture and sharp edge. It is very hard, and strikes fire with steel | 2. A piece of flint for striking fire | 3. -- formerly much used, esp

perspicuous: 1. Capable of being through | 2. Transparent | 3. Translucent

multicipital: 1. Having many heads or many stems from one crown or root. Gray

neodymium: 1. An elementary substance which forms one of the constituents of didymium. Symbol Nd. Atomic weight
eudaemonism: 1. That system of ethics which defines and enforces moral obligation by its relation to happiness or personal well-being
hustings: 1. A court formerly held in several cities of England | 2. hexactinellid: 1. Having six-rayed spicules | 2. Belonging to the Hexactinellinæ

sandwort: 1. Any plant of the genus Arenaria, low, tufted herbs (order Caryophyllace\'

dictionary: 1. A book containing the words of a language, arranged alphabetically, with explanations of their meanings | 2. A lexicon | 3. A vocabulary
meteorometer: 1. An apparatus which transmits automatically to a central station atmospheric changes as marked by the anemometer, barometer, thermometer, etc
zilla: 1. A low, thorny, suffrutescent, crucifeous plant found in the deserts of Egypt. Its leaves are boiled in water, and eaten, by the Arabs
decerniture: 1. A decree or sentence of a court. Stormonth
adagial: 1. Pertaining to an adage | 2. Proverbial. "Adagial verse." Barrow
gowany: 1. Having, abounding in, or decked with, daisies.  Sweeter than gowany glens or new-mown hay | 2. Ramsay
misbecoming: 1. Unbecoming. Milton. -- Mis`be*com"ing*ly, adv | 2. -- Mis`be*com"ing*ness, n. Boyle
perjured: 1. Guilty of perjury | 2. Having sworn falsely | 3. Forsworn. Shak. "Perjured persons." 1 Tim. i
sparlyre: 1. The calf of the leg | 2. Wyclif
reparel: 1. A change of apparel | 2. A second or different suit.  Beau & Fl
leech:
1. See 2d Leach.

See Leach, v. t.

The border or edge at the side of a sail.  Leech line, a line attached to the leech ropes of sails, passing up through blocks on the yards, to haul the leeches by. Totten. -- Leech rope, that part of the boltrope to which the side of a sail is sewed | 2. Physician or surgeon | 3. A professor of the art of healing.   Spenser. Leech, heal thyself. Wyclif
rapped:
1. Imp | 2. & p. p. of Rap, to strike.

imp | 3. & p. p. of Rap, to snatch away
shebang: 1. A jocosely depreciative name for a dwelling or shop
indefinitude: 1. Indefiniteness | 2. Vagueness | 3. Also, number or quantity not limited by our understanding, though yet finite.  Sir M . Hale
xenomi: 1. A suborder of soft-rayed fresh-water fishes of which the blackfish of Alaska is the type
sphygmograph: 1. An instrument which, when applied over an artery, indicates graphically the movements or character of the pulse. See Sphygmogram
fibrinogen: 1. An albuminous substance existing in the blood, and in other animal fluids, which either alone or with fibrinoplastin or paraglobulin forms fibrin, and thus causes coagulation
flagship: 1. The vessel which carries the commanding officer of a fleet or squadron and flies his distinctive flag or pennant
zebu: 1. A bovine mammal extensively domesticated in India, China, the East Indies, and East Africa. It usually has short horns, large pendulous ears, slender legs, a large dewlap, and a large, prominent hump over the shoulders | 2. But these characters vary in different domestic breeds, which range in size from that of the common ox to that of a large mastiff. Note: Some of the varieties are used as beasts of burden, and some fore for riding, while others are raised for their milk and flesh. The Brahmin bull, regarded as sacred by the Hindoos, also belongs to this species. The male is called also Indian bull, Indian ox, Madras ox, and sacred bull
agister: 1. Formerly, an officer of the king's forest, who had the care of cattle agisted, and collected the money for the same | 2. -- hence called gisttaker, which in England is corrupted into guest-taker. Now, one who agists or takes in cattle to pasture at a certain rate | 3. A pasturer. Mozley & W
blink: 1. To wink | 2. To twinkle with, or as with, the eye | 3. One eye was blinking, and one leg was lame. Pope

hallow: 1. To make holy | 2. To set apart for holy or religious use | 3. To consecrate
conure: 1. An American parrakeet of the genus Conurus. Many species are known. See Parrakeet
stormwind: 1. A heavy wind | 2. A wind that brings a storm | 3. The blast of a storm. Longfellow
piepowder: 1. An ancient court of record in England, formerly incident to every fair and market, of which the steward of him who owned or had the toll was the judge. Blackstone
thermometrograph: 1. An instrument for recording graphically the variations of temperature, or the indications of a thermometer
errhine: 1. A medicine designed to be snuffed up the nose, to promote discharges of mucus | 2. A sternutatory. Coxe. -- a.  Causing or increasing secretion of nasal mucus

exegetical: 1. Pertaining to exegesis | 2. Tending to unfold or illustrate | 3. Explanatory
menstruum: 1. Any substance which dissolves a solid body | 2. A solvent. The proper menstruum to dissolve metal. Bacon. mynchery: 1. A nunnery | 2. -- a term still applied to the ruins of certain nunneries in England
allayment: 1. An allaying | 2. That which allays | 3. Mitigation.  The like allayment could I give my grief. Shak
irony: 1. Made or consisting of iron | 2. Partaking of iron | 3. Iron
producibility: 1. The quality or state of being producible. Barrow
hanukkah: 1. The Jewish Feast of the Dedication, instituted by Judas Maccabæus, his brothers, and the whole congregation of Israel, in 165 b. c., to commemorate the dedication of the new altar set up at the purification of the temple of Jerusalem to replace the altar which had been polluted by Antiochus Epiphanes. The feast, which is mentioned in John x. 22, is held for eight days, and is celebrated everywhere, chiefly as a festival of lights, by the Jews

erlking: 1. A personification, in German and Scandinavian mythology, of a spirit natural power supposed to work mischief and ruin, esp | 2. To children

Any one of numerous species of flounders more or less related to the true turbots, as the American plaice, or summer flounder, the halibut, and the diamond flounder of California. The filefish | 2. -- so called in Bermuda. The trigger fish. Spotted turbot. See Windowpane
inhiation: 1. A gaping after | 2. Eager desire | 3. Craving.  Bp. Hall
brill: 1. A fish allied to the turbot, much esteemed in England for food | 2. -- called also bret, pearl, prill. See Bret
japhetic: 1. Pertaining to, or derived from, Japheth, one of the sons of Noah | 2. As, Japhetic nations, the nations of Europe and Northern Asia | 3. Japhetic languages
pleurodynia: 1. A painful affection of the side, simulating pleurisy, usually due to rheumatism
libbard: 1. A leopard.  Spenser. Keats. LIBBARD'S BANE Lib"bard's bane`  . Leopard's bane
perigynium: 1. Some unusual appendage about the pistil, as the bottle-shaped body in the sedges, and the bristles or scales in some other genera of the Sedge family, or Cyperaceæ

The spikenard of the ancients is the Nardostachys Jatamansi, a native of the Himalayan region. From its blackish roots a perfume for the hair is still prepared in India | 2. A fragrant essential oil, as that from the Nardostachys Jatamansi
vincetoxin: 1. A glucoside extracted from the root of the white swallowwort as a bitter yellow amorphous substance | 2. -- called also asclepiadin, and cynanchin
surrebound: 1. To give back echoes | 2. To reëcho.  Chapman
flavine: 1. A yellow, crystalline, organic base, C13H12N2O, obtained artificially
codfish: 1. A kind of fish. Same as Cod
engaging: 1. Tending to draw the attention or affections | 2. Attractive | 3. As, engaging manners or address. -- En*ga"ging*ly, adv
wyla: 1. A helmeted Australian cockatoo | 2. -- called also funeral cockatoo
analcime: 1. A white or flesh-red mineral, of the zeolite, occurring in isometric crystals. By friction, it acquires a weak electricity | 2. Hence its name
discalceate: 1. To pull off shoes or sandals from.  Cockeram
oryctognosy: 1. Mineralogy.  -- Or`yc*tog*nos"tic, a. -- Or`yc*tog*nos"tic*al, a.  -- Or`yc*tog*nos"tic*al*ly, adv
recount:
1. To count or reckon again.

A counting again, as of votes.

To tell over | 2. To relate in detail | 3. To recite
oxamethylane: 1. Methyl oxamate, obtained as a pearly white crystalline substance
poristical: 1. Of or pertaining to a porism | 2. Of the nature of a porism
doubtfulness: 1. State of being doubtful | 2. Uncertainty of meaning | 3. Ambiguity
capacify: 1. To quality.  The benefice he is capacified and designed for | 2. Barrow
airling: 1. A thoughtless, gay person.  "Slight airlings." B. Jonson
nimbleness: 1. The quality of being nimble | 2. Lightness and quickness in motion | 3. Agility
phlogosis: 1. Inflammation of external parts of the body | 2. Erysipelatous inflammation
molle: 1. Lower by a semitone | 2. Flat | 3. As, E molle, that is, E flat

huke: 1. An outer garment worn in Europe in the Middle Ages.   Bacon
antimonsoon: 1. The upper, contrary-moving current of the atmosphere over a monsoon
disprofess: 1. To renounce the profession or pursuit of. His arms, which he had vowed to disprofess. Spenser
ministerially: 1. In a ministerial manner | 2. In the character or capacity of a minister
tinny: 1. Pertaining to, abounding with, or resembling, tin | 2. "The tinny strand." Drayton
desinent: 1. Ending | 2. Forming an end | 3. Lowermost.  "Their desinent parts, fish." B. Jonson
seaman:
1. A merman | 2. The male of the mermaid.  "Not to mention mermaids or seamen." Locke.

One whose occupation is to assist in the management of ships at sea | 3. A mariner
carat: 1. The weight by which precious stones and pearls are weighed. Note: The carat equals three and one fifth grains Troy, and is divided into four grains, sometimes called carat grains. Diamonds and other precious stones are estimated by carats and fractions of carats, and pearls, usually, by carat grains. Titfany | 2. A twenty-fourth part | 3. -- a term used in estimating the proportionate fineness of gold. Note: A mass of metal is said to be so many carats fine, according to the number of twenty-fourths of pure gold which it contains
burnoose: 1. A cloaklike garment and hood woven in one piece, worn by Arabs | 2. A combination cloak and hood worn by women
uplift: 1. To lift or raise aloft | 2. To raise | 3. To elevate
trituberculy: 1. A theory of the development of mammalian molar teeth. The primitive stage is that of simple cones, as in reptiles. The simple cone then developed a smaller cone in front and another behind. Next, a cingulum was developed, and the three cones became arranged in a triangle, the two smaller cusps having moved to the outer side in upper and to the inner in lower molars. This primitive triangle is called the trigon or trigonid and this stage the tritubercular or trigonodont. The trigon being a cutting apparatus, an extension of the posterior part of the crown was developed in lower molars for crushing, and a smaller corresponding part appeared in upper molars. Another large cone then arose, usually from the cingulum. In more complex forms, smaller intermediate cusps appeared
potulent: 1. Fit to drink | 2. Potable.  Johnson | 3. Nearly drunk

hobnail: 1. A short, sharp-pointed, large-headed nail, -- used in shoeing houses and for studding the soles of heavy shoes | 2. A clownish person | 3. A rustic. Milton. Hobnail liver, a disease in which the liver is shrunken, hard, and covered with projections like hobnails
redness: 1. The quality or state of being red | 2. Red color

As, hernia of the brain, of the lung, or of the bowels. Hernia of the abdominal viscera in most common. Called also rupture. Strangulated hernia, a hernia so tightly compressed in some part of the channel through which it has been protruded as to arrest its circulation, and produce swelling of the protruded part. It may occur in recent or chronic hernia, but is more common in the latter
haustellata: 1. An artificial division of insects, including all those with a sucking proboscis

1. To throw with a jerk | 2. To throw edge foremost.   Addison.

See Squir
regratiatory: 1. A returning or giving of thanks.  Skelton

To infect with the pox, or syphilis

tight: 1. P. of Tie. Spenser | 2. Firmly held together | 3. Compact
addition: 1. The act of adding two or more things together | 2. -- opposed to subtraction or diminution. "This endless addition or addibility of numbers." Locke | 3. Anything added
gripple:
1. A grasp | 2. A gripe.  Spenser.

urea: 1. A very soluble crystalline body which is the chief constituent of the urine in mammals and some other animals. Chemically it is carbamide, CO2, and when heated with strong acids or alkalies is decomposed into carbonic acid and ammonia. It unites with acids to form salts, as nitrate of urea, and it can be made synthetically from ammonium cyanate, with which it is isomeric. Urea ferment, a soluble ferment formed by certain bacteria, which, however, yield the ferment from the body of their cells only after they have been killed by alcohol. It causes urea to take up water and decompose into carbonic acid and ammonia. Many different bacteria possess this property, especially Bacterium ureæ and Micrococcus ureæ, which are found abundantly in urines undergoing alkaline fermentation

photosynthesis: 1. The process of constructive metabolism by which carbohydrates are formed from water vapor and the carbon dioxide of the air in the chlorophyll-containing tissues of plants exposed to the action of light. It was formerly called assimilation, but this is now commonly used as in animal physiology. The details of the process are not yet clearly known. Baeyer's theory is that the carbon dioxide is reduced to carbon monoxide, which, uniting with the hydrogen of the water in the cell, produces formaldehyde, the latter forming various sugars through polymerization. Vines suggests that the carbohydrates are secretion products of the chloroplasts, derived from decomposition of previously formed proteids. The food substances are usually quickly translocated, those that accumulate being changed to starch, which appears in the cells almost simultaneously with the sugars. The chloroplasts perform photosynthesis only in light and within a certain range of temperature, varying according to climate. This is the only way in which a plant is able to organize carbohydrates. All plants without a chlorophyll apparatus, as the fungi, must be parasitic or saprophytic. --Pho`to*syn*thet"ic, a. -- Pho`to*syn*thet"ic*al*ly, adv

spectrum: 1. An apparition | 2. A specter | 3. The several colored and other rays of which light is composed, separated by the refraction of a prism or other means, and observed or studied either as spread out on a screen, by direct vision, by photography, or otherwise. See Illust. of Light, and Spectroscope. A luminous appearance, or an image seen after the eye has been exposed to an intense light or a strongly illuminated object. When the object is colored, the image appears of the complementary color, as a green image seen after viewing a red wafer lying on white paper. Called also ocular spectrum. Absorption spectrum, the spectrum of light which has passed through a medium capable of absorbing a portion of the rays. It is characterized by dark spaces, bands, or lines. -- Chemical spectrum, a spectrum of rays considered solely with reference to their chemical effects, as in photography. These, in the usual photogrophic methods, have their maximum influence at and beyond the violet rays, but are not limited to this region. -- Chromatic spectrum, the visible colored rays of the solar spectrum, exhibiting the seven principal colors in their order, and covering the central and larger portion of the space of the whole spectrum. -- Continous spectrum, a spectrum not broken by bands or lines, but having the colors shaded into each other continously, as that from an incandescent solid or liquid, or a gas under high pressure. -- Diffraction spectrum, a spectrum produced by diffraction, as by a grating. -- Gaseous spectrum, the spectrum of an incandesoent gas or vapor, under moderate, or especially under very low, pressure. It is characterized by bright bands or lines. -- Normal spectrum, a representation of a spectrum arranged upon conventional plan adopted as standard, especially a spectrum in which the colors are spaced proportionally to their wave lengths, as when formed by a diffraction grating. -- Ocular spectrum. See Spectrum, 2, above. -- Prismatic spectrum, a spectrum produced by means of a prism. -- Solar spectrum, the spectrum of solar light, especially as thrown upon a screen in a darkened room. It is characterized by numerous dark lines called Fraunhofer lines. -- Spectrum analysis, chemical analysis effected by comparison of the different relative positions and qualities of the fixed lines of spectra produced by flames in which different substances are burned or evaporated, each substance having its own characteristic system of lines. -- Thermal spectrum, a spectrum of rays considered solely with reference to their heating effect, especially of those rays which produce no luminous phenomena

In addition there may be wasting of the muscles, falling out of the hair and nails, and distortion of the hands and feet with destruction of the bones and joints. It is incurable, and is probably contagious.Mycobacterium leprae, curable in most cases by therapy with a combination of antibiotics, but cases resistant to therapy are increasing. Note: The disease now called leprosy, also designated as Lepra or Lepra Arabum, and Elephantiasis Græcorum, is not the same as the leprosy of the ancients. The latter was, indeed, a generic name for many varieties of skin disease, some of which, among the Hebrews, rendered a person ceremonially unclean. A variety of leprosy of the Hebrews was characterized by the presence of smooth, shining, depressed white patches or scales, the hair on which participated in the whiteness while the skin and adjacent flesh became insensible. It was incurable disease

The venom causes great pain, but is unattended either with redness or swelling, except in the axillary or inguinal glands, when an extremity is affected. It is seldom if ever destructive of life. Scorpions are found widely dispersed in the warm climates of both the Old and New Worlds | 2. The pine or gray lizard | 3. The scorpene
gonfanon: 1. The ensign or standard in use by certain princes or states, such as the mediæval republics of Italy, and in more recent times by the pope | 2. A name popularly given to any flag which hangs from a crosspiece or frame instead of from the staff or the mast itself. Standards and gonfalons, 'twixt van and rear, Stream in the air | 3. Milton
artful: 1. Performed with, or characterized by, art or skill.  "Artful strains." "Artful terms." Milton | 2. Artificial | 3. Imitative. Addison
juiciness: 1. The state or quality of being juicy | 2. Succulence plants
interesting: 1. Engaging the attention | 2. Exciting, or adapted to excite, interest, curiosity, or emotion | 3. As, an interesting story
subocular: 1. Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the eye
invalidation: 1. The act of inavlidating, or the state of being invalidated. So many invalidations of their right. Burke
fumatorium: 1. An air-tight compartment in which vapor may be generated to destroy germs or insects | 2. Esp., the apparatus used to destroy San José scale on nursery stock, with hydrocyanic acid vapor
instrument: 1. That by means of which any work is performed, or result is effected | 2. A tool | 3. A utensil
follower: 1. One who follows | 2. A pursuer | 3. An attendant
titter:
1. To laugh with the tongue striking against the root of the upper teeth | 2. To laugh with restraint, or without much noise | 3. To giggle. A group of tittering pages ran before. Longfellow.

A restrained laugh. "There was a titter of . . . delight on his countenance." Coleridge.

To seesaw. See Teeter
glomerous: 1. Gathered or formed into a ball or round mass.  Blount
torrent: 1. A violent stream, as of water, lava, or the like | 2. A stream suddenly raised and running rapidly, as down a precipice. The roaring torrent is deep and wide. Longfellow | 3. Fig.: A violent or rapid flow
ichthyolatry: 1. Worship of fishes, or of fish-shaped idols. Layard
maraschino: 1. A liqueur distilled from fermented cherry juice, and flavored with the pit of a variety of cherry which grows in Dalmatia
conterminous: 1. Having the same bounds, or limits | 2. Bordering upon | 3. Contiguous. This conformed so many of them as were conterminous to the colonies and garrisons, to the Roman laws. Sir M. Hale
sprinkling: 1. The act of one who, or that which, sprinkles. Baptism may well enough be performed by sprinkling or effusion of water. Ayliffe | 2. A small quantity falling in distinct drops or particles | 3. As, a sprinkling of rain or snow
ergotic: 1. Pertaining to, or derived from, ergot | 2. As, ergotic acid
unabridged: 1. Not abridged, or shortened | 2. Full | 3. Complete
rummer: 1. A large and tall glass, or drinking cup | 2. Philips
pulpited: 1. Placed in a pulpit.  Sit . . . at the feet of a pulpited divine. Milton
autohypnotism: 1. Hypnotism of one's self by concentration of the attention on some object or idea
eland: 1. A species of large South African antelope. It is valued both for its hide and flesh, and is rapidly disappearing in the settled districts | 2. -- called also Cape elk | 3. The elk or moose
foolery: 1. The practice of folly | 2. The behavior of a fool | 3. Absurdity. Folly in fools bears not so strong a note, As foolery in the wise, when wit doth dote. Shak
sarcoptid: 1. Any species of the genus Sarcoptes and related genera of mites, comprising the itch mites and mange mites. -- a.  Of or pertaining to the itch mites
proconsulary: 1. Of or pertaining of a proconsul | 2. As, proconsular powers | 3. Under the government of a proconsul
harten: 1. To hearten | 2. To encourage | 3. To incite.  Spenser
vermeology: 1. A discourse or treatise on worms | 2. That part of zoölogy which treats of worms | 3. Helminthology
novatianism: 1. The doctrines or principles of the Novatians. Milner
timorsome: 1. Easily frightened | 2. Timorous.   Sir W. Scott
impeople: 1. To people | 2. To give a population to.  Thou hast helped to impeople hell. Beaumont
mockable: 1. Such as can be mocked. Shak
improviso: 1. Not prepared or mediated beforehand | 2. Extemporaneous.  Jonhson
trance: 1. A tedious journey.  Halliwell | 2. A state in which the soul seems to have passed out of the body into another state of being, or to be rapt into visions | 3. An ecstasy. And he became very hungry, and would have eaten
dismission: 1. The act dismissing or sending away | 2. Permission to leave | 3. Leave to depart
camlet: 1. A woven fabric originally made of camel's hair, now chiefly of goat's hair and silk, or of wool and cotton.  Note: They have been made plain and twilled, of sigle warp and weft, of double warp, and sometimes with double weft also, with thicker yarn. Beck
unrip: 1. To rip | 2. To cut open. Bacon
cerebropathy: 1. A hypochondriacal condition verging upon insanity, occurring in those whose brains have been unduly taxed | 2. -- called also brain fag
ling:
1. A large, marine, gadoid fish of Northern Europe and Greenland. It is valued as a food fish and is largely salted and dried. Called also drizzle. The burbot of Lake Ontario. An American hake of the genus Phycis. A New Zealand food fish of the genus Genypterus. The name is also locally applied to other fishes, as the cultus cod, the mutton fish, and the cobia.

Heather. Ling honey, a sort of wild honey, made from the flowers of the heather. Holland
stovain: 1. A substance, C14H22O2NCl, the hydrochloride of an amino compound containing benzol, used, in solution with strychnine, as a local anæsthetic, esp | 2. By injection into the sheath of the spinal cord, producing anæsthesia below the point of introduction
stelography: 1. The art of writing or inscribing characters on pillars.  Stackhouse
accumbency: 1. The state of being accumbent or reclining
cephalic:
1. Of or pertaining to the head. See the Note under Anterior. Cephalic index, the ratio of the breadth of the cranium to the length, which is taken as the standard, and equal to 100 | 2. The breadth index. -- Cephalic vein, a large vein running from the back of the head alond the arm | 3. -- so named because the ancients used to open it for disorders of the head. Dunglison.

A medicine for headache, or other disorder in the head
haggard: 1. Wild or intractable | 2. Disposed to break away from duty | 3. Untamed
spignet: 1. An aromatic plant of America. See Spikenard
simmer:
1. To boil gently, or with a gentle hissing | 2. To begin to boil. I simmer as liquor doth on the fire before it beginneth to boil. Palsgrave.

To cause to boil gently | 3. To cook in liquid heated almost or just to the boiling point
dropt: 1. Imp | 2. & p. p. of Drop, v. G. Eliot
boroughmonger: 1. One who buys or sells the parliamentary seats of boroughs
nictitate: 1. To wink | 2. To nictate. Nictitating membrance, a thin membrance, found in many animals at the inner angle, or beneath the lower lid, of the eye, and capable of being drawn across the eyeball | 3. The third eyelid
quatorze: 1. The four aces, kings, queens, knaves, or tens, in the game of piquet | 2. -- so called because quatorze counts as fourteen points
hobblebush: 1. A low bush having long, straggling branches and handsome flowers. It is found in the Northern United States. Called also shinhopple
ironmongery: 1. Hardware | 2. A general name for all articles made of iron. Gwilt
hammochrysos: 1. A stone with spangles of gold color in it
inextricable: 1. Incapable of being extricated, untied, or disentangled | 2. Hopelessly intricate, confused, or obscure | 3. As, an inextricable knot or difficulty
chylopoetic: 1. Concerned in the formation of chyle | 2. As, the chylopoetic organs
disown: 1. To refuse to own or acknowledge as belonging to one's self | 2. To disavow or deny, as connected with one's self personally | 3. As, a parent can hardly disown his child
abluent: 1. Washing away | 2. Carrying off impurities | 3. Detergent. -- n.  A detergent
neighboring: 1. Living or being near | 2. Adjacent | 3. As, the neighboring nations or countries
buffy: 1. Resembling, or characterized by, buff. Buffy coat, the coagulated plasma of blood when the red corpuscles have so settled out that the coagulum appears nearly colorless. This is common in diseased conditions where the corpuscles run together more rapidly and in denser masses than usual. Huxley
moan: 1. To make a low prolonged sound of grief or pain, whether articulate or not | 2. To groan softly and continuously. Unpitied and unheard, where misery moans. Thomson. Let there bechance him pitiful mischances, To make him moan. Shak | 3. To emit a sound like moan
orthography: 1. The art or practice of writing words with the proper letters, according to standard usage | 2. Conventionally correct spelling | 3. Also, mode of spelling
yeldrin: 1. The yellow-hammer | 2. -- called also yeldrock, and yoldrin
annunciative: 1. Pertaining to annunciation | 2. Announcing.  Dr. H. More
gressorial: 1. Adapted for walking | 2. Anisodactylous | 3. As the feet of certain birds and insects. See Illust. under Aves
outway: 1. A way out | 2. Exit.  In divers streets and outways multiplied. P. Fletcher
searchless: 1. Impossible to be searched | 2. Inscrutable | 3. Impenetrable
charras: 1. The gum resin of the hemp plant. Same as Churrus. Balfour
autumnal: 1. Of, belonging to, or peculiar to, autumn | 2. As, an autumnal tint | 3. Produced or gathered in autumn
ichnite: 1. A fossil footprint | 2. As, the ichnites in the Triassic sandstone. Page
cobwall: 1. A wall made of clay mixed with straw
triptych: 1. Anything in three parts or leaves. Specifically: -- A writing tablet in three parts, two of which fold over on the middle part. A picture or altarpiece in three compartments
nutritive: 1. Of or pertaining to nutrition | 2. As, the nutritive functions | 3. Having the quality of nourishing
subtartarean: 1. Being or living under Tartarus | 2. Infernal. "Subtartarean powers." Pope
complaint: 1. Expression of grief, regret, pain, censure, or resentment | 2. Lamentation | 3. Murmuring
subpulmonary: 1. Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the lungs
gage: 1. A pledge or pawn | 2. Something laid down or given as a security for the performance of some act by the person depositing it, and forfeited by nonperformance | 3. Security. Nor without gages to the needy lend. Sandys
ostensible: 1. Capable of being shown | 2. Proper or intended to be shown.  Walpole | 3. Shown
caterwaul:
1. To cry as cats in rutting time | 2. To make a harsh, offensive noise. Coleridge.

A caterwauling
diseaseful: 1. Causing uneasiness.  Disgraceful to the king and diseaseful to the people. Bacon | 2. Abounding with disease | 3. Producing diseases
noise: 1. Sound of any kind. The heavens turn about in a most rapid motion without noise to us perceived. Bacon. Note: Noise is either a sound of too short a duration to be determined, like the report of a cannon | 2. Or else it is a confused mixture of many discordant sounds, like the rolling of thunder or the noise of the waves. Nevertheless, the difference between sound and noise is by no means precise. Ganot | 3. Especially, loud, confused, or senseless sound
replaceable: 1. Capable or admitting of being put back into a place | 2. Admitting of having its place supplied by a like thing or an equivalent | 3. As, the lost book is replaceable
floppy: 1. Having a tendency to flop or flap | 2. As, a floppy hat brim. G. Eliot
nighness: 1. The quality or state of being nigh.  "Nighness of blood." Holished
recovery: 1. The act of recovering, regaining, or retaking possession | 2. Restoration from sickness, weakness, faintness, or the like | 3. Restoration from a condition of mistortune, of fright, etc
astroscope: 1. An old astronomical instrument, formed of two cones, on whose surface the constellations were delineated
laurentian: 1. Pertaining to, or near, the St. Lawrence River | 2. As, the Laurentian hills. Laurentian period, the lower of the two divisions of the Archæan age | 3. -- called also the Laurentian
churning: 1. The act of one who churns | 2. The quantity of butter made at one operation
firearm: 1. A gun, pistol, or any weapon from a shot is discharged by the force of an explosive substance, as gunpowder
binomial: 1. An expression consisting of two terms connected by the sign plus or minus | 2. As, a+b, or 7- | 3. Consisting of two terms
xanthose: 1. An orange-yellow substance found in pigment spots of certain crabs
discomfiture: 1. The act of discomfiting, or the state of being discomfited | 2. Rout | 3. Overthrow
inadmissibility: 1. The state or quality of being inadmissible, or not to be received
thankworthy: 1. Deserving thanks | 2. Worthy of gratitude | 3. Mreitorious. For this thankworthy, if a man, for conscience toward God, endure grief, suffering wrongfully. 1 Pet. ii
gambroon: 1. A kind of twilled linen cloth for lining. Simmonds
brachycephalic: 1. Having the skull short in proportion to its breadth | 2. Shortheaded | 3. -- in distinction from dolichocephalic
eldest: 1. Oldest | 2. Longest in duration. Shak | 3. Born or living first, or before the others, as a son, daughter, brother, etc
silicide: 1. A binary compound of silicon, or one regarded as binary.  Hydrogen silicide, a colorless, spontaneously inflammable gas, SiH4, produced artifically from silicon, and analogous to methane | 2. -- called also silico-methane, silicon hydride, and formerly siliciureted hydrogen
subarytenoid: 1. Situated under the arytenoid cartilage of the larynx
excitement: 1. The act of exciting, or the state of being roused into action, or of having increased action | 2. Impulsion | 3. Agitation
surfboat: 1. A boat intended for use in heavy surf. It is built with a pronounced sheer, and with a view to resist the shock of waves and of contact with the beach
doorga: 1. A Hindoo divinity, the consort of Siva, represented with ten arms.  Malcom
refashion: 1. To fashion anew | 2. To form or mold into shape a second time. MacKnight
arch: 1. Any part of a curved line | 2. Usually a curved member made up of separate wedge-shaped solids, with the joints between them disposed in the direction of the radii of the curve | 3. Used to support the wall or other weight above an opening. In this sense arches are segmental, round, or pointed. A flat arch is a member constructed of stones cut into wedges or other shapes so as to support each other without rising in a curve. Note: Scientifically considered, the arch is a means of spanning an opening by resolving vertical pressure into horizontal or diagonal thrust
duly: 1. In a due, fit, or becoming manner | 2. As it ought to be | 3. Properly
molly:
1. Same as Mollemoke.

A pet or colloquial name for Mary. Molly cottontail. See Cottontail. -- Molly Maguire | 2. Pl. Molly Maguires. A member of a secret association formed among the tenantry in Ireland about 1843, principally for the purpose of intimidating law officers and preventing the service of legal writs. Its members disguised themselves in the dress of women. A member of a similar association of Irishmen organized in the anthracite coal region of Pennsylvania, about 1854, for the purpose of intimidating employers and officers of the law, and for avenging themselves by murder on persons obnoxious to them. The society was broken up by criminal prosecutions in
pseudodox: 1. Not true in opinion or doctrine | 2. False. -- n.  A false opinion or doctrine. "To maintain the atheistical pseudodox which judgeth evil good, and darkness light." T. Adams
vaccary: 1. A cow house, dairy house, or cow pasture.  Wright
hepatogenous: 1. Arising from the liver | 2. Due to a condition of the liver | 3. As, hepatogenic jaundice
rosland: 1. Heathy land | 2. Land full of heather | 3. Moorish or watery land
ultrazodiacal: 1. Outside the zodiac | 2. Being in that part of the heavens that is more than eight degrees from the ecliptic | 3. As, ultrazodiacal planets, that is, those planets which in part of their orbits go beyond the zodiac
downweigh: 1. To weigh or press down. A different sin downweighs them to the bottom. Longfellow
bilberry: 1. The European whortleberry | 2. Also, its edible bluish black fruit. There pinch the maids as blue as bilberry. Shak | 3. Any similar plant or its fruit
booster: 1. An instrument for regulating the electro-motive force in an alternating-current circuit | 2. -- so called because used to "boost", or raise, the pressure in the circuit
alcove: 1. A recessed portion of a room, or a small room opening into a larger one | 2. Especially, a recess to contain a bed | 3. A lateral recess in a library
gruel: 1. A light, liquid food, made by boiling meal of maize, oatmeal, or fiour in water or milk | 2. Thin porridge
scythe:
1. An instrument for mowing grass, grain, or the like, by hand, composed of a long, curving blade, with a sharp edge, made fast to a long handle, called a snath, which is bent into a form convenient for use | 2. The sharp-edged scythe shears up the spiring grass. Dryden. The scythe of Time mows down. Milton | 3. A scythe-shaped blade attached to ancient war chariots.

To cut with a scythe
puzzlement: 1. The state of being puzzled | 2. Perplexity. Miss Mitford
kanacka: 1. A native of the Sandwich Islands
supraglotic: 1. Situated above the glottis | 2. -- applied to that part of the cavity of the larynx above the true vocal cords
zoopraxiscope: 1. An instrument similar to, or the same as, the, the phenakistoscope, by means of which pictures projected upon a screen are made to exhibit the natural movements of animals, and the like
biblist: 1. One who makes the Bible the sole rule of faith | 2. A biblical scholar | 3. A biblicist. I. Taylor
shop: 1. Imp | 2. Of Shape. Shaped. Chaucer | 3. A building or an apartment in which goods, wares, drugs, etc., are sold by retail. From shop to shop Wandering, and littering with unfolded silks The polished counter. Cowper
backwardly: 1. Reluctantly | 2. Slowly | 3. Aversely.  Sir P. Sidney
stot: 1. A horse.  Chaucer. Thorold Rogers | 2. A young bull or ox, especially one three years old
hepta: 1. A combining form from Gr. "epta`, seven
saxifragant: 1. Breaking or destroying stones | 2. Saxifragous.  -- n.  That which breaks or destroys stones
soffit: 1. The under side of the subordinate parts and members of buildings, such as staircases, entablatures, archways, cornices, or the like. See Illust. of Lintel
synchronism: 1. The concurrence of events in time | 2. Simultaneousness | 3. The tabular arrangement of historical events and personages, according to their dates
prostitution: 1. The act or practice of prostituting or offering the body to an indiscriminate intercourse with men | 2. Common lewdness of a woman | 3. The act of setting one's self to sale, or of devoting to infamous purposes what is in one's power
daisied: 1. Full of daisies | 2. Adorned with daisies. "The daisied green." Langhorne. The grass all deep and daisied. G. Eliot
racketer: 1. One who makes, or engages in, a racket
retroversion: 1. A turning or bending backward | 2. Also, the state of being turned or bent backward | 3. Displacement backwards
paraphrastic: 1. Paraphrasing | 2. Of the nature of paraphrase | 3. Explaining, or translating in words more clear and ample than those of the author
buoyant: 1. Having the quality of rising or floating in a fluid | 2. Tending to rise or float | 3. As, iron is buoyant in mercury. "Buoyant on the flood." Pope
apis: 1. A genus of insects of the order Hymenoptera, including the common honeybee and other related species. See Honeybee
carrion: 1. The dead and putrefying body or flesh of an animal | 2. Flesh so corrupted as to be unfit for food. They did eat the dead carrions. Spenser | 3. A contemptible or worthless person
pointed: 1. Sharp | 2. Having a sharp point | 3. As, a pointed rock
liquidity: 1. The state or quality of being liquid
thialol: 1. A colorless oily liquid,2S2, having a strong garlic odor | 2. -- called also ethyl disulphide. By extension, any one of the series of related compounds
pronate: 1. Somewhat prone | 2. Inclined | 3. As, pronate trees. Kane
familist: 1. One of afanatical Antinomian sect originating in Holland, and existing in England about 1580, called the Family of Love, who held that religion consists wholly in love
firstborn: 1. First brought forth | 2. First in the order of nativity | 3. Eldest
engrail:
1. To variegate or spot, as with hail. A caldron new engrailed with twenty hues. Chapman | 2. To indent with small curves. See Engrailed.

To form an edging or border | 3. To run in curved or indented lines. Parnell
oxybromic: 1. Pertaining to, or designating, certain compounds of oxygen and bromine
groggy: 1. Overcome with grog | 2. Tipsy | 3. Unsteady on the legs
hote: 1. To command | 2. To enjoin.  Piers Plowman | 3. To promise.  Chaucer
piperaceous: 1. Of or pertaining to the order of plants of which the pepper is the type. There are about a dozen genera and a thousand species, mostly tropical plants with pungent and aromatic qualities
apophyge: 1. The small hollow curvature given to the top or bottom of the shaft of a column where it expands to meet the edge of the fillet | 2. -- called also the scape. Parker
phenanthridine: 1. A nitrogenous hydrocarbon base, C13H9N, analogous to phenanthrene and quinoline
causerie: 1. Informal talk or discussion, as about literary matters | 2. Light conversation | 3. Chat
tonnihood: 1. The female of the bullfinch | 2. -- called also tonyhoop
sapid: 1. Having the power of affecting the organs of taste | 2. Possessing savor, or flavor. Camels, to make the water sapid, do raise the mud with their feet. Sir T. Browne
dissolute: 1. With nerves unstrung | 2. Weak.  Spenser | 3. Loosed from restraint
vividity: 1. The quality or state of being vivid | 2. Vividness
pinna: 1. A leaflet of a pinnate leaf. See Illust. of Bipinnate leaf, under Bipinnate. One of the primary divisions of a decompound leaf | 2. One of the divisions of a pinnate part or organ | 3. Etym: [L. pinna, akin to Gr.  Any species of Pinna, a genus of large bivalve mollusks found in all warm seas. bawcock: 1. A fine fellow | 2. -- a term of endearment.  "How now, my bawcock " Shak

wormling: 1. A little worm. O dusty wormling! dost thou strive and stand With heaven's high monarch Sylvester
auditorship: 1. The office or function of auditor
blindfold: 1. To cover the eyes of, as with a bandage | 2. To hinder from seeing. And when they had blindfolded him, they struck him on the face. Luke xxii | 3. Having the eyes covered
fontanel: 1. An issue or artificial ulcer for the discharge of humors from the body. Wiseman | 2. One of the membranous intervals between the incompleted angles of the parietal and neighboring bones of a fetal or young skull | 3. -- so called because it exhibits a rhythmical pulsation. humorism: 1. The theory founded on the influence which the humors were supposed to have in the production of disease | 2. Galenism. Dunglison | 3. The manner or disposition of a humorist
nigrosine: 1. A dark blue dyestuff, of the induline group | 2. -- called also azodiphenyl blue
doubtfully: 1. In a doubtful manner. Nor did the goddess doubtfully declare. Dryden
clypeate: 1. Shaped like a round buckler or shield | 2. Scutate | 3. Furnished with a shield, or a protective plate or shell
exigible: 1. That may be exacted | 2. Repairable.  A. Smith
assenting: 1. Giving or implying assent. -- As*sent"ing*ly, adv
luddite: 1. One of a number of riotous persons in England, who for six years tried to prevent the use of labor-saving machinery by breaking it, burning factories, etc | 2. -- so called from Ned Lud, a half-witted man who some years previously had broken stocking frames. J. & H. Smith. H. Martineau
curare: 1. A black resinoid extract prepared by the South American Indians from the bark of several species of Strychnos. It sometimes has little effect when taken internally, but is quickly fatal when introduced into the blood, and used by the Indians as an arrow poison
encrinic: 1. Relating to encrinites | 2. Containing encrinites, as certain kinds of limestone

puerility: 1. The quality of being puerile | 2. Childishness | 3. Puerileness. Sir T. Browne
labial: 1. Of or pertaining to the lips or labia | 2. As, labial veins | 3. Furnished with lips
shaver: 1. One who shaves | 2. One whose occupation is to shave | 3. One who is close in bargains
byssaceous: 1. Byssuslike | 2. Consisting of fine fibers or threads, as some very delicate filamentous algæ
blasting: 1. A blast | 2. Destruction by a blast, or by some pernicious cause. I have smitten you with blasting and mildew. Amos iv | 3. The act or process of one who, or that which, blasts
majuscule: 1. A capital letter | 2. Especially, one used in ancient manuscripts. See Majusculæ. Majuscule writing, writing composed wholly of capital letters, especially the style which prevailed in Europe from the third to the sixth century
cystic: 1. Having the form of, or living in, a cyst | 2. As, the cystic entozoa | 3. Containing cysts
peculiar: 1. One's own | 2. Belonging solely or especially to an individual | 3. Not possessed by others
duffel: 1. A kind of coarse woolen cloth, having a thick nap or frieze.  Good duffel gray and flannel fine. Wordsworth

moldboard: 1. A curved plate of iron back of the share of a plow, which turns over the earth in plowing | 2. A follow board
binotonous: 1. Consisting of two notes | 2. As, a binotonous cry
cuneate: 1. Wedge-shaped | 2. , wedge-shaped, with the point at the base | 3. As, a cuneate leaf

banderillero: 1. One who thrusts in the banderillas in bullfighting.  W. D. Howells
belvedere: 1. A small building, or a part of a building, more or less open, constructed in a place commanding a fine prospect
membranology: 1. The science which treats of membranes
sarmentose: 1. Long and filiform, and almost naked, or having only leaves at the joints where it strikes root | 2. As, a sarmentose stem. Bearing sarments | 3. Sarmentaceous
swiftness: 1. The quality or state of being swift | 2. Speed | 3. Quickness
chooser: 1. One who chooses | 2. One who has the power or right of choosing | 3. An elector. Burke
geranium: 1. A genus of plants having a beaklike tours or receptacle, around which the seed capsules are arranged, and membranous projections, or stipules, at the joints. Most of the species have showy flowers and a pungent odor. Called sometimes crane's-bill | 2. A cultivated pelargonium. Note: Many plants referred to the genus Geranium by the earlier botanists are now separated from it under the name of Pelargonium, which includes all the commonly cultivated "geraniums", mostly natives of South Africa

pulley:
1. A wheel with a broad rim, or grooved rim, for transmitting power from, or imparting power to, the different parts of machinery, or for changing the direction of motion, by means of a belt, cord, rope, or chain. Note: The pulley, as one of the mechanical powers, consists, in its simplest form, of a grooved wheel, called a sheave, turning within a movable frame or block, by means of a cord or rope attached at one end to a fixed point. The force, acting on the free end of the rope, is thus doubled, but can move the load through only half the space traversed by itself. The rope may also pass over a sheave in another block that is fixed. The end of the rope may be fastened to the movable block, instead of a fixed point, with an additional gain of power, and using either one or two sheaves in the fixed block. Other sheaves may be added, and the power multiplied accordingly. Such an apparatus is called by workmen a block and tackle, or a fall and tackle. See Block. A single fixed pulley gives no increase of power, but serves simply for changing the direction of motion. Band pulley, or Belt pulley, a pulley with a broad face for transmitting power between revolving shafts by means of a belt, or for guiding a belt. -- Cone pulley. See Cone pulley. -- Conical pulley, one of a pair of belt pulleys, each in the shape of a truncated cone, for varying velocities. -- Fast pulley, a pulley firmly attached upon a shaft. -- Loose pulley, a pulley loose on a shaft, to interrupt the transmission of motion in machinery. See Fast and loose pulleys, under Fast. Parting pulley, a belt pulley made in semicircular halves, which can be bolted together, to facilitate application to, or removal from, a shaft. -- Pulley block. Same as Block, n | 2. -- Pulley stile, the upright of the window frame into which a pulley is fixed and along which the sash slides. Split pulley, a parting pulley.

asterisk: 1. The figure of a star, thus,

reliable: 1. Suitable or fit to be relied on | 2. Worthy of dependance or reliance | 3. Trustworthy. "A reliable witness to the truth of the miracles." A. Norton. The best means, and most reliable pledge, of a higher object. Coleridge. According to General Livingston's humorous account, his own village of Elizabethtown was not much more reliable, being peopled in those agitated times by "unknown, unrecommended strangers, guilty-looking Tories, and very knavish Whigs." W. Irving. Note: Some authors take exception to this word, maintaining that it is unnecessary, and irregular in formation. It is, however, sanctioned by the practice of many careful writers as a most convenient substitute for the phrase to be relied upon, and a useful synonym for trustworthy, which is by preference applied to persons, as reliable is to things, such as an account, statement, or the like. The objection that adjectives derived from neuter verbs do not admit of a passive sense is met by the citation of laughable, worthy of being laughed at, from the neuter verb to laugh

telegraph:
1. An apparatus, or a process, for communicating intelligence rapidly between distant points, especially by means of preconcerted visible or audible signals representing words or ideas, or by means of words and signs, transmitted by electrical action. Note: The instruments used are classed as indicator, type-printing, symbol-printing, or chemical-printing telegraphs, according as the intelligence is given by the movements of a pointer or indicator, as in Cooke & Wheatstone's, or by impressing, on a fillet of paper, letters from types, as in House's and Hughe's, or dots and marks from a sharp point moved by a magnet, as in Morse's, or symbols produced by electro-chemical action, as in Bain's. In the offices in the United States the recording instrument is now little used, the receiving operator reading by ear the combinations of long and short intervals of sound produced by the armature of an electro-magnet as it is put in motion by the opening and breaking of the circuit, which motion, in registering instruments, traces upon a ribbon of paper the lines and dots used to represent the letters of the alphabet. See Illustration in Appendix. Acoustic telegraph. See under Acoustic. -- Dial telegraph, a telegraph in which letters of the alphabet and numbers or other symbols are placed upon the border of a circular dial plate at each station, the apparatus being so arranged that the needle or index of the dial at the receiving station accurately copies the movements of that at the sending station. -- Electric telegraph, or Electro-magnetic telegraph, a telegraph in which an operator at one station causes words or signs to be made at another by means of a current of electricity, generated by a battery and transmitted over an intervening wire. -- Facsimile telegraph. See under Facsimile. -- Indicator telegraph. See under Indicator. -- Pan-telegraph, an electric telegraph by means of which a drawing or writing, as an autographic message, may be exactly reproduced at a distant station. -- Printing telegraph, an electric telegraph which automatically prints the message as it is received at a distant station, in letters, not signs. -- Signal telegraph, a telegraph in which preconcerted signals, made by a machine, or otherwise, at one station, are seen or heard and interpreted at another | 2. A semaphore. -- Submarine telegraph cable, a telegraph cable laid under water to connect stations separated by a body of water. -- Telegraph cable, a telegraphic cable consisting of several conducting wires, inclosed by an insulating and protecting material, so as to bring the wires into compact compass for use on poles, or to form a strong cable impervious to water, to be laid under ground, as in a town or city, or under water, as in the ocean. -- Telegraph plant, a leguminous plant native of the East Indies. The leaflets move up and down like the signals of a semaphore.

A follower of Pythagoras | 2. One of the school of philosophers founded by Pythagoras

1. Any one of numerous species of regularly scaled harmless lizards of the family Scincidæ, common in the warmer parts of all the continents. Note: The officinal skink inhabits the sandy plains of South Africa. It was believed by the ancients to be a specific for various diseases. A common slender species of Southern Europe was formerly believed to produce fatal diseases in cattle by mere contact. The American skinks include numerous species of the genus Eumeces, as the blue-tailed skink of the Eastern United States. The ground skink, or ground lizard inhabits the Southern United States.

To draw or serve, as drink.  Bacchus the wine them skinketh all about. Chaucer. Such wine as Ganymede doth skink to Jove. Shirley.

To serve or draw liquor. 

Drink | 2. Also, pottage.  Bacon

myrtle: 1. A species of the genus Myrtus, especially Myrtus communis. The common myrtle has a shrubby, upright stem, eight or ten feet high. Its branches form a close, full head, thickly covered with ovate or lanceolate evergreen leaves. It has solitary axillary white or rosy flowers, followed by black several-seeded berries. The ancients considered it sacred to Venus. The flowers, leaves, and berries are used variously in perfumery and as a condiment, and the beautifully mottled wood is used in turning. Note: The name is also popularly but wrongly applied in America to two creeping plants, the blue-flowered periwinkle and the yellow- flowered moneywort. thorite: 1. A mineral of a brown to black color, or, as in the variety orangite, orange-yellow. It is essentially a silicate of thorium
pontoon: 1. A wooden flat-bottomed boat, a metallic cylinder, or a frame covered with canvas, India rubber, etc., forming a portable float, used in building bridges quickly for the passage of troops | 2. A low, flat vessel, resembling a barge, furnished with cranes, capstans, and other machinery, used in careening ships, raising weights, drawing piles, etc., chiefly in the Mediterranean | 3. A lighter. Pontoon bridge, a bridge formed with pontoons. -- Pontoon train, the carriages of the pontoons, and the materials they carry for making a pontoon bridge. Note: The French spelling ponton often appears in scientific works, but pontoon is more common form
trumpetweed: 1. An herbaceous composite plant, often having hollow stems, and bearing purplish flowers in small corymbed heads. The sea trumpet
receivership: 1. The state or office of a receiver
endaspidean: 1. Having the anterior scutes extending around the tarsus on the inner side | 2. -- said of certain birds
mealy: 1. Having the qualities of meal | 2. Resembling meal | 3. Soft, dry, and friable
sarment: 1. A prostrate filiform stem or runner, as of the strawbwrry. See Runner
tantalite: 1. A heavy mineral of an iron-black color and submetallic luster. It is essentially a tantalate of iron
ethos: 1. The character, sentiment, or disposition of a community or people, considered as a natural endowment | 2. The spirit which actuates manners and customs | 3. Also, the characteristic tone or genius of an institution or social organization
slaver: 1. A vessel engaged in the slave trade | 2. A slave ship | 3. A person engaged in the purchase and sale of slaves
bactrian: 1. Of or pertaining to Bactria in Asia. -- n.  A native of Bactria. Bactrian camel, the two-humped camel
voter: 1. One who votes | 2. One who has a legal right to vote, or give his suffrage | 3. An elector
gamma: 1. The third letter of the Greek alphabet
gladiatorism: 1. The art or practice of a gladiator
encaustic:
1. Prepared by means of heat | 2. Burned in. Encaustic painting, painting by means of wax with which the colors are combined, and which is afterwards fused with hot irons, thus fixing the colors. -- Encaustic tile, an earthenware tile which has a decorative pattern and is not wholly of one color.

The method of painting in heated wax, or in any way where heat is used to fix the colors
pelargonium: 1. A large genus of plants of the order Geraniaceæ, differing from Geranium in having a spurred calyx and an irregular corolla. Note: About one hundred and seventy species are known, nearly all of them natives of South Africa, and many having very beautiful blossoms. See the Note under Geranium
cycloidal: 1. Pertaining to, or resembling, a cycloid | 2. As, the cycloidal space is the space contained between a cycloid and its base. Cycloidal engine. See Geometric lathe
elflock: 1. Hair matted, or twisted into a knot, as if by elves
chilopoda: 1. One of the orders of myriapods, including the centipeds. They have a single pair of elongated legs attached laterally to each segment | 2. Well developed jaws | 3. And a pair of thoracic legs converted into poison fangs. They are insectivorous, very active, and some species grow to the length of a foot
columbin: 1. A white, crystalline, bitter substance. See Calumbin
palladian: 1. Of, pertaining to, or designating, a variety of the revived classic style of architecture, founded on the works of Andrea Palladio, an Italian architect of the 16th century
mudar: 1. Either one of two asclepiadaceous shrubs, which furnish a strong and valuable fiber. The acrid milky juice is used medicinally
kieselguhr: 1. Siliceous earth | 2. Specifically, porous infusorial earth, used as an absorbent of nitroglycerin in the manufacture of dynamite
orgeat: 1. A sirup in which, formerly, a decoction of barley entered, but which is now prepared with an emulsion of almonds, -- used to flavor beverages or edibles
phasemeter: 1. A device for measuring the difference in phase of two alternating currents of electromotive forces
original: 1. Pertaining to the origin or beginning | 2. Preceding all others | 3. First in order
britisher: 1. An Englishman | 2. A subject or inhabitant of Great Britain, esp | 3. One in the British military or naval service
auriculate: 1. Having ears or appendages like ears | 2. Eared. Esp.: Having lobes or appendages like the ear | 3. Shaped like the ear
zooegraphical: 1. Of or pertaining to the description of animals
asian: 1. Of or pertaining to Asia | 2. Asiatic. "Asian princes." Jer. Taylor. -- n.  An Asiatic
offerable: 1. Capable of being offered | 2. Suitable or worthy to be offered
scoter: 1. Any one of several species of northern sea ducks of the genus Oidemia. Note: The European scoters are Oidemia nigra, called also black duck, black diver, surf duck | 2. And the velvet, or double, scoter. The common American species are the velvet, or white-winged, scoter, called also velvet duck, white-wing, bull coot, white- winged coot | 3. The black scoter, called also black coot, butterbill, coppernose

mensal:
1. Belonging to the table | 2. Transacted at table | 3. As, mensa conversation.

Occurring once in a month
abolition: 1. The act of abolishing, or the state of being abolished | 2. An annulling | 3. Abrogation
squir: 1. To throw with a jerk | 2. To throw edge foremost.   Addison
snowcap: 1. A very small humming bird native of New Grenada. Note: The feathers of the top of the head are white and snining, the body blue black with a purple and bronzy luster. The name is applied also to Microchæra parvirostris of Central America, which is similar in color
indicatory: 1. Serving to show or make known | 2. Showing | 3. Indicative
beadsnake: 1. A small poisonous snake of North America, banded with yellow, red, and black
roumanian:
1. Of or pertaining to Roumania.

An inhabitant of Roumania | 2. Also, the language of Roumania, one of the Romance or Romanic languages descended from Latin, but containing many words from other languages, as Slavic, Turkish, and Greek
brief: 1. Short in duration. How brief the life of man | 2. Shak | 3. Concise
microcoustic:
1. Pertaining, or suited, to the audition of small sounds | 2. Fitted to assist hearing.

An instrument for making faint sounds audible, as to a partially deaf person
vermeil: 1. Vermilion | 2. Also, the color of vermilion, a bright, beautiful red | 3. In her cheeks the vermeil red did show Like roses in a bed of lilies shed. Spenser
bipyramidal: 1. Consisting of two pyramids placed base to base | 2. Having a pyramid at each of the extremities of a prism, as in quartz crystals
hydrastine: 1. An alkaloid, found in the rootstock of the golden seal, and extracted as a bitter, white, crystalline substance. It is used as a tonic and febrifuge
romantic: 1. Of or pertaining to romance | 2. Involving or resembling romance | 3. Hence, fanciful
salsuginous: 1. Growing in brackish places or in salt marches
styracin: 1. A white crystalline tasteless substance extracted from gum storax, and consisting of a salt of cinnamic acid with cinnamic alcohol
mennonist: 1. One of a small denomination of Christians, so called from Menno Simons of Friesland, their founder. They believe that the New Testament is the only rule of faith, that there is no original sin, that infants should not be baptized, and that Christians ought not to take oath, hold office, or render military service
portage:
1. A sailor's wages when in port. The amount of a sailor's wages for a voyage.

A porthole.  Shak | 2. The act of carrying or transporting | 3. The price of carriage
nomenclature: 1. A name.  Bacon | 2. A vocabulary, dictionary, or glossary | 3. The technical names used in any particular branch of science or art, or by any school or individual
affirm: 1. To make firm | 2. To confirm, or ratify | 3. Esp
thoroughness: 1. The quality or state of being thorough | 2. Completeness
abeyance: 1. Expectancy | 2. Condition of being undetermined. Note: When there is no person in existence in whom an inheritance can vest, it is said to be in abeyance, that is, in expectation | 3. The law considering it as always potentially existing, and ready to vest whenever a proper owner appears. Blackstone
former: 1. One who forms | 2. A maker | 3. A creator
magnifier: 1. One who, or that which, magnifies
farinose: 1. Yielding farinaa | 2. As, farinose substances | 3. Civered with a sort of white, mealy powder, as the leaves of some poplars, and the body of certain insects
reasoning: 1. The act or process of adducing a reason or reasons | 2. Manner of presenting one's reasons | 3. That which is offered in argument
woaded: 1. Colored or stained with woad. "Man tattoed or woaded, winter- clad in skins." Tennyson
caucasian: 1. Of or pertaining to the Caucasus, a mountainous region between the Black and Caspian seas | 2. Of or pertaining to the white races of mankind, of whom the people about Mount Caucasus were formerly taken as the type | 3. A native or inhabitant of the Caucasus, esp
inland: 1. Within the land | 2. More or less remote from the ocean or from open water | 3. Interior
liveried: 1. Wearing a livery. See Livery, | 2. The liveried servants wait. Parnell
trippingly: 1. In a tripping manner | 2. With a light, nimble, quick step | 3. With agility
arcual: 1. Of or pertaining to an arc | 2. Arcual measure of an angle, that in which the unit angle has its measuring arc equal to the radius of the circle
cervelat: 1. An ancient wind instrument, resembling the bassoon in tone
cinctured: 1. Having or wearing a cincture or gridle
canape: 1. A sofa or divan | 2. A slice or piece of bread fried in butter or oil, on which anchovies, mushrooms, etc., are served
coleopteral: 1. Having wings covered with a case or sheath | 2. Belonging to the Coleoptera
keratogenous: 1. Producing horn | 2. As, the keratogenous membrane within the horny hoof of the horse
literalize: 1. To make literal | 2. To interpret or put in practice according to the strict meaning of the words | 3. -- opposed to spiritualize
atheism: 1. The disbelief or denial of the existence of a God, or supreme intelligent Being. Atheism is a ferocious system, that leaves nothing above us to excite awe, nor around us to awaken tenderness. R. Hall. Atheism and pantheism are often wrongly confounded. Shipley | 2. Godlessness
bestiality: 1. The state or quality of being bestial | 2. Unnatural connection with a beast
reformado: 1. A monk of a reformed order.  Weever | 2. An officer who, in disgrace, is deprived of his command, but retains his rank, and sometimes his pay
grandmotherly: 1. Like a grandmother in age or manner | 2. Kind | 3. Indulgent
unbe: 1. To cause not to be | 2. To cause to be another.  How oft, with danger of the field beset, Or with home mutinies, would he unbe Himself! Old Pay

amassment: 1. An amassing | 2. A heap collected | 3. A large quantity or number brought together
saccharose: 1. Cane sugar | 2. Sucrose | 3. Also, in general, any one of the group of which saccharose, or sucrose proper, is the type. See Sucrose
vodka: 1. A Russian drink distilled from rye

They are communistic, opposed to any violence, and unwilling to use the labor of animals. Driven out of Russia proper, many have emigrated to Cyprus and Canada. See Raskolnik, below
fiddledeedee: 1. An exclamatory word or phrase, equivalent to nonsense!
royalty: 1. The state of being royal | 2. The condition or quality of a royal person | 3. Kingship
baldhead: 1. A person whose head is bald. 2 Kings ii | 2. A white-headed variety of pigeon
hulled: 1. Deprived of the hulls. Hulled corn, kernels of maize prepared for food by removing the hulls
subtly: 1. In a subtle manner | 2. Slyly | 3. Artfully
banter: 1. To address playful good-natured ridicule to, -- the person addressed, or something pertaining to him, being the subject of the jesting | 2. To rally | 3. As, he bantered me about my credulity. Hag-ridden by my own fancy all night, and then bantered on my haggard looks the next day
percale: 1. A fine cotton fabric, having a linen finish, and often printed on one side, -- used for women's and children's wear
quadrifid: 1. Divided, or deeply cleft, into four parts | 2. As, a quadrifid perianth | 3. A quadrifid leaf
impregn: 1. To impregnate | 2. To make fruitful.  His perniciousss words, impregned With reason. Milton. Semele doth Bacchus bear Impregned of Jove. Dr. H. More
oboe: 1. One of the higher wind instruments in the modern orchestra, yet of great antiquity, having a penetrating pastoral quality of tone, somewhat like the clarinet in form, but more slender, and sounded by means of a double reed | 2. A hautboy. Oboe d'amore Etym: , and Oboe di caccia Etym: , are names of obsolete modifications of the oboe, often found in the scores of Bach and Handel
synangium: 1. The divided part beyond the pylangium in the aortic trunk of the amphibian heart. -- Syn*an"gi*al, a
gas: 1. An aëriform fluid | 2. -- a term used at first by chemists as synonymous with air, but since restricted to fluids supposed to be permanently elastic, as oxygen, hydrogen, etc., in distinction from vapors, as steam, which become liquid on a reduction of temperature. In present usage, since all of the supposed permanent gases have been liquified by cold and pressure, the term has resumed nearly its original signification, and is applied to any substance in the elastic or aëriform state | 3. A complex mixture of gases, of which the most important constituents are marsh gas, olefiant gas, and hydrogen, artificially produced by the destructive distillation of gas coal, or sometimes of peat, wood, oil, resin, etc
coagulability: 1. The quality of being coagulable | 2. Capacity of being coagulated. Ure
mythopoeic: 1. Making or producing myths | 2. Giving rise to mythical narratives. The mythopoeic fertility of the Greeks. Grote
whosoever: 1. Whatsoever person | 2. Any person whatever that | 3. Whoever. Whosoever will, let him take . . . freely. Rev. xxii
justify: 1. To prove or show to be just | 2. To vindicate | 3. To maintain or defend as conformable to law, right, justice, propriety, or duty. That to the height of this great argument I may assert eternal providence, And justify the ways of God to men
grudgingness: 1. The state or quality of grudging, or of being full of grudge or unwillingness
phylogenetic: 1. Relating to phylogenesis, or the race history of a type of organism. -- Phy*lo*ge*net"ic*al*ly, adv
fame: 1. Public report or rumor. The fame thereof was heard in Pharaoh's house. Gen. xlv | 2. Report or opinion generally diffused | 3. Renown
corundum: 1. The earth alumina, as found native in a crystalline state, including sapphire, which is the fine blue variety | 2. The oriental ruby, or red sapphire | 3. The oriental amethyst, or purple sapphire
muscadel: 1. See Muscatel, n. Quaffed off the muscadel. Shak
expurgate: 1. To purify | 2. To clear from anything noxious, offensive, or erroneous | 3. To cleanse
provocative:
1. Serving or tending to provoke, excite, or stimulate | 2. Exciting.

Anything that is provocative | 3. A stimulant
ascus: 1. A small membranous bladder or tube in which are inclosed the seedlike reproductive particles or sporules of lichens and certain fungi
chilostomata: 1. An extensive suborder of marine Bryozoa, mostly with calcareous shells. They have a movable lip and a lid to close the aperture of the cells
rubus: 1. A genus of rosaceous plants, including the raspberry and blackberry

tintinnabulum: 1. A bell | 2. Also, a set or combination of bells or metal plates used as a musical instrument or as a toy
significatory: 1. Significant. -- n.  That which is significatory
lazaret: 1. A public building, hospital, or pesthouse for the reception of diseased persons, particularly those affected with contagious diseases

cannonade: 1. The act of discharging cannon and throwing ball, shell, etc., for the purpose of destroying an army, or battering a town, ship, or fort | 2. -- usually, an attack of some continuance. rhabdosphere: 1. A minute sphere composed of rhabdoliths
sheading: 1. A tithing, or division, in the Isle of Man, in which there is a coroner, or chief constable. The island is divided into six sheadings
uniquity: 1. The quality or state of being unique | 2. Uniqueness.  Walpole
unconstitutional: 1. Not constitutional | 2. Not according to, or consistent with, the terms of a constitution of government | 3. Contrary to the constitution
puttee: 1. Same as Putty, a kind of gaiter
stigmatic: 1. A notorious profligate or criminal who has been branded | 2. One who bears the marks of infamy or punishment.  Bullokar | 3. A person who is marked or deformed by nature. Shak
hairtail: 1. Any species of marine fishes of the genus Trichiurus | 2. Esp., T. lepterus of Europe and America. They are long and like a band, with a slender, pointed tail. Called also bladefish
cotemporaneous: 1. Living or being at the same time | 2. Contemporaneous. -- Co*tem`po*ra"ne*ous*ly, adv | 3. -- Co*tem`po*ra"ne*ous*ness, n
imesatin: 1. A dark yellow, crystalline substance, obtained by the action of ammonia on isatin
coincider: 1. One who coincides with another in an opinion
erogation: 1. The act of giving out or bestowing.  Sir T. Elyot
greenbacker: 1. One of those who supported greenback or paper money, and opposed the resumption of specie payments
preorbital: 1. Situated in front or the orbit
sesquibasic: 1. Containing, or acting as, a base in the proportions of a sesqui compound
undershapen: 1. Under the usual shape or size | 2. Small | 3. Dwarfish.  His dwarf, a vicious undershapen thing. Tennyson
embogue: 1. To disembogue | 2. To discharge, as a river, its waters into the sea or another river
parry: 1. To ward off | 2. To stop, or to turn aside | 3. As, to parry a thrust, a blow, or anything that means or threatens harm. Locke. Vice parries wide The undreaded volley with a sword of straw. Cowper
endome: 1. To cover as with a dome
originary: 1. Causing existence | 2. Productive.  The production of animals, in the originary way, requires a certain degree of warmth. Cheyne | 3. Primitive

feeler: 1. One who, or that which, feels | 2. One of the sense organs or certain animals, which are used in testing objects by touch and in searching for food | 3. An antenna
inmate: 1. One who lives in the same house or apartment with another | 2. A fellow lodger | 3. Esp.,one of the occupants of an asylum, hospital, or prison
isologous: 1. Having similar proportions, similar relations, or similar differences of composition | 2. -- said specifically of groups or series which differ by a constant difference | 3. As, ethane, ethylene, an acetylene, or their analogous compounds, form an isologous series
pedestrian:
1. Going on foot | 2. Performed on foot | 3. As, a pedestrian journey.

A walker
societarian: 1. Of or pertaining to society | 2. Social. The all-sweeping besom of societarian reformation. Lamb
streaming: 1. Sending forth streams | 2. The act or operation of that which streams | 3. The act of that which sends forth, or which runs in, streams
durante: 1. During | 2. As, durante vita, during life | 3. Durante bene placito, during pleasure
season: 1. One of the divisions of the year, marked by alternations in the length of day and night, or by distinct conditions of temperature, moisture, etc., caused mainly by the relative position of the earth with respect to the sun | 2. In the north temperate zone, four seasons, namely, spring, summer, autumn, and winter, are generally recognized. Some parts of the world have three seasons, -- the dry, the rainy, and the cold | 3. Other parts have but two, -- the dry and the rainy. The several seasons of the year in their beauty. Addison
copying: 1. From Copy, v. Copying ink | 2. See under Ink. -- Copying paper, thin unsized paper used for taking copies of letters, etc., in a copying press. -- Copying press, a machine for taking by pressure, an exact copy of letters, etc., written in copying ink

camembert: 1. A kind of soft, unpressed cream cheese made in the vicinity of Camembert, near Argentan, France | 2. Also, any cheese of the same type, wherever made
haycock: 1. A conical pile or hear of hay in the field. The tanned haycock in the mead. Milton
lam: 1. To beat soundly | 2. To thrash.  Beau. & Fl
propyl: 1. The hypothetical radical C3H7, regarded as the essential residue of propane and related compounds
blacks: 1. The name of a kind of in used in copperplate printing, prepared from the charred husks of the grape, and residue of the wine press | 2. Soot flying in the air | 3. Black garments, etc

quiescent: 1. Being in a state of repose | 2. At rest | 3. Still
malonyl: 1. A hydrocarbon radical, CH | 2. 2, from malonic acid

coyly: 1. In a coy manner | 2. With reserve
interplace: 1. To place between or among | 2. As, to interplace a name.  Daniel

obsess: 1. To besiege | 2. To beset. Sir T. Elyot

milliampere: 1. The thousandth part of one ampère
mischief: 1. Harm | 2. Damage | 3. Esp., disarrangement of order

encave: 1. To hide in, or as in, a cave or recess. "Do but encave yourself." Shak
hackney: 1. A horse for riding or driving | 2. A nag | 3. A pony. Chaucer

pawn:
1. See Pan, the masticatory.

iodhydrin: 1. One of a series of compounds containing iodine, and analogous to the chlorhydrins
