rong:
1. Imp | 2. & p. p. of Ring. Chaucer.

Rung.  Chaucer
jehad: 1. A religious war against infidels or Mohammedan heretics | 2. Also, any bitter war or crusade for a principle or belief.  courage in war . . . had not, like that of the Mohammedan dervishes of the Sudan, or of Mohammedans anywhere engaged in a jehad, a religious motive and the promise of future bliss behind it. James Bryce
amphiuma: 1. A genus of amphibians, inhabiting the Southern United States, having a serpentlike form, but with four minute limbs and two persistent gill openings | 2. The Congo snake
nautch: 1. An entertainment consisting chiefly of dancing by professional dancing girls
dapple:
1. One of the spots on a dappled animal. He has . . . as many eyes on his body as my gray mare hath dapples. Sir P. Sidney.

Marked with spots of different shades of color | 2. Spotted | 3. Variegated
pycnometer: 1. A specific gravity bottle | 2. A standard flask for measuring and comparing the densities of liquids

1. Not either | 2. Not the one or the other. Which of them shall I take Both one or neither Neither can be enjoyed, If both remain alive. Shak. He neither loves, Nor either cares for him | 3. Shak.

not either

1. Making warm | 2. Heating.

The early, immature form of any animal when more or less of a metamorphosis takes place, before the assumption of the mature shape

silversides: 1. Any one of several species of small fishes of the family Atherinidæ, having a silvery stripe along each side of the body. The common species of the American coast is very abundant. Called also silverside, sand smelt, friar, tailor, and tinker. Brook silversides, a small fresh-water North American fish related to the marine silversides
tartronyl: 1. A hypothetical radical constituting the characteristic residue of tartronic acid and certain of its derivatives
deter: 1. To prevent by fear | 2. Hence, to hinder or prevent from action by fear of consequences, or difficulty, risk, etc | 3. Addison. Potent enemies tempt and deter us from our duty. Tillotson. My own face deters me from my glass. Prior
hotcockles: 1. A childish play, in which one covers his eyes, and guesses who strikes him or his hand placed behind him
extraparochial: 1. Beyond the limits of a parish. -- Ex`tra*pa*ro"chi*al*ly, adv
docimastic: 1. Proving by experiments or tests. Docimastic art, metallurgy, or the art of assaying metals | 2. The art of separating metals from foreign matters, and determining the nature and quantity of metallic substances contained in any ore or mineral
majorcan: 1. Of or pertaining to Majorca. -- n.  A native or inhabitant of Majorca
commutative: 1. Relative to exchange | 2. Interchangeable | 3. Reciprocal. -- Com*mut"a*tive"ly, adv
hexdecylic: 1. Pertaining to, or derived from, hexdecyl or hecdecane | 2. As, hexdecylic alcohol
commonty: 1. A common | 2. A piece of land in which two or more persons have a common right. Bell
expirable: 1. That may expire | 2. Capable of being brought to an end
dudder:
1. To confuse or confound with noise. Jennings.

To shiver or tremble | 2. To dodder. I dudder and shake like an aspen leaf. Ford.

A peddler or hawker, especially of cheap and flashy goods pretended to be smuggled | 3. A duffer
piningly: 1. In a pining manner | 2. Droopingly. Poe
arachnology: 1. The department of zoölogy which treats of spiders and other Arachnida
scrobiculate: 1. Having numerous small, shallow depressions or hollows | 2. Pitted
desiccation: 1. The act of desiccating, or the state of being desiccated
beeswing: 1. The second crust formed in port and some other wines after long keeping. It consists of pure, shining scales of tartar, supposed to resemble the wing of a bee
escapade: 1. The fling of a horse, or ordinary kicking back of his heels | 2. A gambol | 3. Act by which one breaks loose from the rules of propriety or good sense
silicon: 1. A nonmetalic element analogous to carbon. It always occurs combined in nature, and is artificially obtained in the free state, usually as a dark brown amorphous powder, or as a dark crystalline substance with a meetallic luster. Its oxide is silica, or common quartz, and in this form, or as silicates, it is, next to oxygen, the most abundant element of the earth's crust. Silicon is characteristically the element of the mineral kingdom, as carbon is of the organic world. Symbol Si. Atomic weight | 2. Called also silicium
probationary: 1. Of or pertaining to probation | 2. Serving for trial. To consider this life . . . as a probationary state. Paley
nigraniline: 1. The complex, nitrogenous, organic base and dyestuff called also aniline black
coffeepot: 1. A covered pot im which coffee is prepared,
burn: 1. To consume with fire | 2. To reduce to ashes by the action of heat or fire | 3. -- frequently intensified by up: as, to burn up wood. "We'll burn his body in the holy place." Shak
insolubility: 1. The quality or state of being insoluble or not dissolvable, as in a fluid | 2. The quality of being inexplicable or insolvable
enlimn: 1. To adorn by illuminating or ornamenting with colored and decorated letters and figures, as a book or manuscript.  Palsgrave
ingroove: 1. To groove in | 2. To join in or with a groove. Tennyson
schoolship: 1. A vessel employed as a nautical training school, in which naval apprentices receive their education at the expense of the state, and are trained for service as sailors. Also, a vessel used as a reform school to which boys are committed by the courts to be disciplined, and instructed as mariners
confederate: 1. United in a league | 2. Allied by treaty | 3. Engaged in a confederacy
oxamethane: 1. Ethyl oxamate, obtained as a white scaly crystalline powder
dimmish: 1. Somewhat dim | 2. As, dimmish eyes. "Dimmy clouds." Sir P. Sidney
irrigate: 1. To water | 2. To wet | 3. To moisten with running or dropping water
fraudless: 1. Free from fraud. -- Fraud"less*ly, adv | 2. -- Fraud"less*ness, n
trepidation: 1. An involuntary trembling, sometimes an effect of paralysis, but usually caused by terror or fear | 2. Quaking | 3. Quivering
rectilinearity: 1. The quality or state of being rectilinear. Coleridge
internationally: 1. In an international manner | 2. From an international point of view
ordnance: 1. Heavy weapons of warfare | 2. Cannon, or great guns, mortars, and howitzers | 3. Artillery
quillwort: 1. Any plant or species of the genus Isoetes, cryptogamous plants with a cluster of elongated four-tubed rushlike leaves, rising from a corm, and containing spores in their enlarged and excavated bases. There are about seventeen American species, usually growing in the mud under still, shallow water. So called from the shape of the shape of the leaves
interstellar: 1. Between or among the stars | 2. As, interstellar space. Bacon
wigwag: 1. To signal by means of a flag waved from side to side according to a code adopted for the purpose
anther: 1. That part of the stamen containing the pollen, or fertilizing dust, which, when mature, is emitted for the impregnation of the ovary. -- An"ther*al, a
scarab: 1. Any one of numerous species of lamellicorn beetles of the genus Scarabæus, or family Scarabæidæ, especially the sacred, or Egyptian, species
molluscan: 1. Of or pertaining to mollusks. -- n.  A mollusk | 2. One of the Mollusca
reprimand: 1. Severe or formal reproof | 2. Reprehension, private or public. Goldsmith gave his landlady a sharp reprimand for her treatment of him | 3. Macaulay
volley: 1. A flight of missiles, as arrows, bullets, or the like | 2. The simultaneous discharge of a number of small arms. Fiery darts in flaming volleys flew. Milton. Each volley tells that thousands cease to breathe. Byron | 3. A burst or emission of many things at once
knowledge: 1. The act or state of knowing | 2. Clear perception of fact, truth, or duty | 3. Certain apprehension
aventail: 1. The movable front to a helmet | 2. The ventail
verticil: 1. A circle either of leaves or flowers about a stem at the same node | 2. A whorl
robbin:
1. A kind of package in which pepper and other dry commodities are sometimes exported from the East Indies. The robbin of rice in Malabar weighs about 84 pounds. Simmonds.

See Ropeband
wrestling: 1. Act of one who wrestles | 2. Specif., the sport consisting of the hand-to-hand combat between two unarmed contestants who seek to throw each other. The various styles of wrestling differ in their definition of a fall and in the governing rules. In Greco-Roman wrestling, tripping and taking hold of the legs are forbidden, and a fall is gained, by the contestant who pins both his opponent's shoulders to the ground. In catch-as-catch-can wrestling, all holds are permitted except such as may be barred by mutual consent, and a fall is defined as in Greco-Roman style. Lancashire style wrestling is essentially the same as catch-as-catch- can | 3. In Cumberland and Westmorland wrestling the contestants stand chest to chest, grasping each other around the body. The one first losing his hold, or touching the ground with any part of his body except his feet, loses the bout. If both fall to the ground at the same time, it is a dogfall, and must be wrestled over. In the Cornwall and Devon wrestling, the wrestlers complete in strong loose linen jackets, catching hold of the jacket, or anywhere above the waist. Two shoulders and one hip, or two hips and one shoulder, must touch the ground to constitute a fall, and if a man is thrown otherwise than on his back the contestants get upon their feet and the bout recommences
sesterce: 1. A Roman coin or denomination of money, in value the fourth part of a denarius, and originally containing two asses and a half, afterward four asses, -- equal to about two pence sterling, or four cents. Note: The sestertium was equivalent to one thousand sesterces, equal to £8 17s 1d. sterling, or about $43, before the reign of Augustus. After his reign its value was about £7 16s. 3d. sterling. The sesterce was originally coined only in silver, but later both in silver and brass
further: 1. To a greater distance | 2. In addition | 3. Moreover. See Farther. Carries us, I know not how much further, into familiar company. M. Arnold. They sdvanced us far as Eleusis and Thria
yis: 1. Yes.  "Yis, sir," quod he, "yis, host." Chaucer
depolishing: 1. The process of removing the vitreous glaze from porcelain, leaving the dull luster of the surface of ivory porcelian. Knight
catholicly: 1. In a catholic manner | 2. Generally | 3. Universally. Sir L. Cary
varix: 1. A uneven, permanent dilatation of a vein. Note: Varices are owing to local retardation of the venous circulation, and in some cases to relaxation of the parietes of the veins. They are very common in the superficial veins of the lower limbs. Dunglison | 2. One of the prominent ridges or ribs extending across each of the whorls of certain univalve shells. Note: The varices usually indicate stages of growth, each one showing a former position of the outer lip of the aperture
ventage: 1. A small hole, as the stop in a flute | 2. A vent. Shak
hypotarsus: 1. A process on the posterior side of the tarsometatarsus of many birds | 2. The calcaneal process. -- Hy`po*tar"sal, a
bewitchedness: 1. The state of being bewitched. Gauden
sinupalliate: 1. Having a pallial sinus. See under Sinus
translavation: 1. A laving or lading from one vessel to another.  Holland
sarcolactic: 1. Relating to muscle and milk | 2. As, sarcolactic acid. See Lactic acid, under Lactic
roger: 1. A black flag with white skull and crossbones, formerly used by pirates | 2. -- called also Jolly Roger
conceit: 1. That which is conceived, imagined, or formed in the mind | 2. Idea | 3. Thought
monanthous: 1. Having but one flower | 2. One-flowered. Gray
ceriph: 1. One of the fine lines of a letter, esp | 2. One of the fine cross strokes at the top and bottom of letters.  Savage
heracleonite: 1. A follower of Heracleon of Alexandria, a Judaizing Gnostic, in the early history of the Christian church
rhusma: 1. A mixtire of caustic lime and orpiment, or tersulphide of arsenic, -- used in the depilation of hides. Knight
demulce: 1. To soothe | 2. To mollify | 3. To pacify
forfered: 1. Excessively alarmed | 2. In great fear.  "Forfered of his death." Chaucer
bizet: 1. The upper faceted portion of a brilliant-cut diamond, which projects from the setting and occupies the zone between the girdle and the table. See Brilliant, n
bullirag: 1. To intimidate by bullying | 2. To rally contemptuously | 3. To badger
alethoscope: 1. An instrument for viewing pictures by means of a lens, so as to present them in their natural proportions and relations
clerical: 1. Of or pertaining to the clergy | 2. Suitable for the clergy. "A clerical education." Burke | 3. Of or relating to a clerk or copyist, or to writing. "Clerical work." E. Everett. A clerical error, an error made in copying or writing
impacable: 1. Not to be appeased or quieted.  Spenser. -- Im*pa"ca*bly, adv
manducable: 1. Such as can be chewed | 2. Fit to be eaten.  Any manducable creature. Sir T. Herbert
episcopally: 1. By episcopal authority | 2. In an episcopal manner
prolegomenon: 1. A preliminary remark or observation | 2. An introductory discourse prefixed to a book or treatise. D. Stokes. Sir W. Scott
swashy: 1. Soft, like fruit that is too ripe | 2. Quashy | 3. Swash

potamology: 1. A scientific account or discussion of rivers | 2. A treatise on rivers | 3. Potamography
iliad: 1. A celebrated Greek epic poem, in twenty-four books, on the destruction of Ilium, the ancient Troy. The Iliad is ascribed to Homer

The gadflies of the horse produce the intestinal parasites called bots. See Botfly, and Bots. The true horseflies are often erroneously called gadflies, and the true gadflies are sometimes incorrectly called breeze flies. Gadfly petrel, one of several small petrels of the genus Oestrelata
sensuous: 1. Of or pertaining to the senses, or sensible objects | 2. Addressing the senses | 3. Suggesting pictures or images of sense. To this poetry would be made precedent, as being less subtle and fine, but more simple, sensuous, and passionate. Milton

austromancy: 1. Soothsaying, or prediction of events, from observation of the winds

Noisy demagogues who had been accused of sedition. Macaulay

downstream: 1. Down the stream | 2. As, floating downstream
sauroidichnite: 1. The fossil track of a saurian
disendowment: 1. The act of depriving of an endowment or endowments.  disendowment of the Irish Church. G. B. Smith
epigaeous: 1. Growing on, or close to, the ground

radically: 1. In a radical manner | 2. At, or from, the origin or root | 3. Fundamentally

calcic: 1. Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, calcium or lime
colloid: 1. Resembling glue or jelly | 2. Characterized by a jellylike appearance | 3. Gelatinous
engallant: 1. To make a gallant of.  B. Jonson

A white crystalline nitrogenous substance present in small amount in the pancreas and spleen, and formed in large quantity from the decomposition of proteid matter by various means, -- as by pancreatic digestion, by putrefaction as of cheese, by the action of boiling acids, etc | 2. sate: 1. To satisfy the desire or appetite of | 2. To satiate | 3. To glut
tribolet: 1. A goldsmith's tool used in making rings. Ainsworth | 2. A steel cylinder round which metal is drawn in the process of forming tubes. Tomlinson | 3. A tapering mandrel
gallivant: 1. To play the beau | 2. To wait upon the ladies | 3. Also, to roam about for pleasure without any definite plan.  Dickens
furioso: 1. With great force or vigor | 2. Vehemently

jess: 1. A short strap of leather or silk secured round the leg of a hawk, to which the leash or line, wrapped round the falconer's hand, was attached when used. See Illust. of Falcon. Like a hawk, which feeling freed From bells and jesses which did let her flight. Spenser

unwilled: 1. Deprived of the faculty of will or volition. Mrs. Browning

lour: 1. An Asiatic sardine, valued for its oil

officiant: 1. The officer who officiates or performs an office, as the burial office. Shipley
bowge:
1. To swell out | 2. See Bouge. 

To cause to leak.  See Bouge
baroko: 1. A form or mode of syllogism of which the first proposition is a universal affirmative, and the other two are particular negative
dogcart: 1. A light one-horse carriage, commonly two-wheeled, patterned after a cart. The original dogcarts used in England by sportsmen had a box at the back for carrying dogs
nodding: 1. Curved so that the apex hangs down | 2. Having the top bent downward
dogdraw: 1. The act of drawing after, or pursuing, deer with a dog | 2. Cowell
amenity: 1. The quality of being pleasant or agreeable, whether in respect to situation, climate, manners, or disposition | 2. Pleasantness | 3. Civility
ewry: 1. An office or place of household service where the ewers were formerly kept.  Parker

furthest:
1. Superl. Most remote | 2. Most in advance | 3. Farthest. See Further, a.

At the greatest distance
monacid: 1. Having one hydrogen atom replaceable by a negative or acid atom or radical | 2. Capable of neutralizing a monobasic acid | 3. -- said of bases, and of certain metals
thankworthiness: 1. The quality or state of being thankworthy
eucharistic: 1. Giving thanks | 2. Expressing thankfulness | 3. Rejoicing.  The eucharistical part of our daily devotions. Ray
mahori: 1. One of the dark race inhabiting principally the islands of Eastern Polynesia. Also used adjectively
malebranchism: 1. The philosophical system of Malebranche, an eminent French metaphysician. The fundamental doctrine of his system is that the mind can not have knowledge of anything external to itself except in its relation to God
coroneted: 1. Wearing, or entitled to wear, a coronet | 2. Of noble birth or rank
scribbler:
1. One who scribles | 2. A literary hack. The scribbler, pinched with hunger, writes to dine. Granville.

A scribbling machine

zoonic: 1. Of or pertaining to animals | 2. Obtained from animal substances
emersed: 1. Standing out of, or rising above, water. Gray
plication: 1. A folding or fold | 2. A plait. Richardson
connate: 1. Born with another | 2. Being of the same birth | 3. Congenital

bud: 1. A small protuberance on the stem or branches of a plant, containing the rudiments of future leaves, flowers, or stems | 2. An undeveloped branch or flower | 3. A small protuberance on certain low forms of animals and vegetables which develops into a new organism, either free or attached. See Hydra. Bud moth, a lepidopterous insect of several species, which destroys the buds of fruit trees
appreciatory: 1. Showing appreciation | 2. Appreciative | 3. As, appreciatory commendation. -- Ap*pre"ci*a*to*ri*ly, adv

term: 1. That which limits the extent of anything | 2. Limit | 3. Extremity
disyoke: 1. To unyoke | 2. To free from a yoke | 3. To disjoin.  R. Browning
steady: 1. Firm in standing or position | 2. Not tottering or shaking | 3. Fixed
unstock: 1. To deprive of a stock | 2. To remove the stock from | 3. To loose from that which fixes, or holds fast
abbreviature: 1. An abbreviation | 2. An abbreviated state or form | 3. An abridgment
microbarograph: 1. An instrument for recording minor fluctuations of atmospheric pressure, as opposed to general barometric surges
carolus: 1. An English gold coin of the value of twenty or twenty-three shillings. It was first struck in the reign of Charles I. Told down the crowns and Caroluses. Macawlay
putrescible:
1. Capable of putrefaction | 2. Liable to become putrid | 3. As, putrescible substances.

A substance, usually nitrogenous, which is liable to undergo decomposition when in contact with air and moisture at ordinary temperatures
inquisition: 1. The act of inquiring | 2. Inquiry | 3. Search
cliented: 1. Supplied with clients.  The least cliented pettifiggers. R. Carew
scrapepenny: 1. One who gathers and hoards money in trifling sums | 2. A miser
visored: 1. Wearing a visor | 2. Masked. Visored falsehood and base forgery. Milton
dishouse: 1. To deprive of house or home. "Dishoused villagers." James White
birkie: 1. A lively or mettlesome fellow.  Burns
altrices: 1. Nursers, -- a term applied to those birds whose young are hatched in a very immature and helpless condition, so as to require the care of their parents for some time | 2. -- opposed to præcoces
provisionally: 1. By way of provision for the time being | 2. Temporarily. Locke
duncish: 1. Somewhat like a dunce.  -- Dun"cish*ness, n
ergotine: 1. A powerful astringent alkaloid extracted from ergot as a brown, amorphous, bitter substance. It is used to produce contraction of the uterus
acrolein: 1. A limpid, colorless, highly volatile liquid, obtained by the dehydration of glycerin, or the destructive distillation of neutral fats containing glycerin. Its vapors are intensely irritating. Watts
curviserial: 1. Distributed in a curved line, as leaves along a stem
plaid:
1. A rectangular garment or piece of cloth, usually made of the checkered material called tartan, but sometimes of plain gray, or gray with black stripes. It is worn by both sexes in Scotland | 2. Goods of any quality or material of the pattern of a plaid or tartan | 3. A checkered cloth or pattern.

Having a pattern or colors which resemble a Scotch plaid
polygon: 1. A plane figure having many angles, and consequently many sides | 2. Esp., one whose perimeter consists of more than four sides | 3. Any figure having many angles. Polygon of forces, a polygonal figure, the sides of which, taken successively, represent, in length and direction, several forces acting simultaneously upon one point, so that the side necessary to complete the figure represents the resultant of those forces. Cf. Parallelogram of forces, under Parallelogram

dag: 1. A dagger | 2. A poniard.  Johnson | 3. A large pistol formerly used.  The Spaniards discharged their dags, and hurt some. Foxe. A sort of pistol, called dag, was used about the same time as hand guns and harquebuts. Grose
sen:
1. A Japanese coin, worth about one half of a cent.

Since
ischial: 1. Of or pertaining to the ischium or hip | 2. Ischiac | 3. Ischiadic
gluey: 1. Viscous | 2. Glutinous | 3. Of the nature of, or like, glue
folly: 1. The state of being foolish | 2. Want of good sense | 3. Levity, weakness, or derangement of mind
torricellian: 1. Of or pertaining to Torricelli, an Italian philosopher and mathematician, who, in 1643, discovered that the rise of a liquid in a tube, as in the barometer, is due to atmospheric pressure. See Barometer. Torricellian tube, a glass tube thirty or more inches in length, open at the lower end and hermetically sealed at the upper, such as is used in the barometer. -- Torricellian vacuum, a vacuum produced by filling with a fluid, as mercury, a tube hermetically closed at one end, and, after immersing the other end in a vessel of the same fluid, allowing the inclosed fluid to descend till it is counterbalanced by the pressure of the atmosphere, as in the barometer. Hutton
ewer: 1. A kind of widemouthed pitcher or jug | 2. Esp., one used to hold water for the toilet. Basins and ewers to lave her dainty hands. Shak
republicanize: 1. To change, as a state, into a republic | 2. To republican principles | 3. As, France was republicanized
substance: 1. That which underlies all outward manifestations | 2. Substratum | 3. The permanent subject or cause of phenomena, whether material or spiritual
writability: 1. Ability or capacity to write.  Walpole
calligrapher: 1. One skilled in calligraphy | 2. A good penman
colly:
1. The black grime or soot of coal.  Burton.

To render black or dark, as of with coal smut | 2. To begrime.  Thou hast not collied thy face enough. B. Jonson. Brief as the lighting in the collied night. Shak.

A kind of dog | 3. See Collie
delirium: 1. A state in which the thoughts, expressions, and actions are wild, irregular, and incoherent | 2. Mental aberration | 3. A roving or wandering of the mind, -- usually dependent on a fever or some other disease, and so distinguished from mania, or madness
uranyl: 1. The radical UO2, conveniently regarded as a residue of many uranium compounds
mangosteen: 1. A tree of the East Indies of the genus Garcinia. The tree grows to the height of eighteen feet, and bears fruit also called mangosteen, of the size of a small apple, the pulp of which is very delicious food

fissuration: 1. The act of dividing or opening | 2. The state of being fissured
sardel:
1. A sardine. 

A precious stone. See Sardius
nidget: 1. A fool | 2. An idiot, a coward.  Camden
athink: 1. To repent | 2. To displease | 3. To disgust.  Chaucer
pilidium: 1. The free-swimming, hat-shaped larva of certain nemertean worms. It has no resemblance to its parent, and the young worm develops in its interior
belling: 1. A bellowing, as of a deer in rutting time. Johnson
broomy: 1. Of or pertaining to broom | 2. Overgrowing with broom | 3. Resembling broom or a broom. If land grow mossy or broomy. Mortimer
pyrexical: 1. Of or pertaining to fever | 2. Feverish
vaporer: 1. One who vapors | 2. A braggart. Vaporer moth. See Orgyia
wishbone: 1. The forked bone in front of the breastbone in birds | 2. -- called also merrythought, and wishing bone. See Merrythought, and Furculum
macropinacoid: 1. One of the two planes of an orthorhombic crystal which are parallel to the vertical and longer lateral axes
converging: 1. Tending to one point | 2. Approaching each other | 3. Convergent

sham: 1. That which deceives expectation | 2. Any trick, fraud, or device that deludes and disappoint | 3. A make-believe
platycoelian: 1. Flat at the anterior and concave at the posterior end | 2. -- said of the centra of the vertebræ of some extinct dinouaurs

diverting: 1. Amusing | 2. Entertaining. -- Di*vert"ing*ly, adv | 3. -- Di*vert"ing*ness, n
pterygopalatine: 1. Of or pertaining to the pterygoid processes and the palatine bones

piacularity: 1. The quality or state of being piacular | 2. Criminality | 3. Wickedness. De Quincey

teleological: 1. Of or pertaining to teleology, or the doctrine of design. -- Te`le*o*log"ic*al*ly, adv

anger: 1. Trouble | 2. Vexation | 3. Also, physical pain or smart of a sore, etc

spirometry: 1. The act or process of measuring the chest capacity by means of a spirometer
spaniard: 1. A native or inhabitant of Spain
coverside: 1. A region of country having covers | 2. A hunting country
invoke: 1. To call on for aid or protection | 2. To invite earnestly or solemnly | 3. To summon
polycrotic: 1. Of or pertaining to polycrotism | 2. Manifesting polycrotism | 3. As, a polycrotic pulse
execrable: 1. Deserving to be execrated | 2. Accursed | 3. Damnable
beyond: 1. On the further side of | 2. In the same direction as, and further on or away than. Beyond that flaming hill. G. Fletcher | 3. At a place or time not yet reached

The body is long, flat, and composed of numerous segments or proglottids varying in shape, those toward the end of the body being much larger and longer than the anterior ones, and containing the fully developed sexual organs. The head is small, destitute of a mouth, but furnished with two or more suckers, and sometimes, also, with hooks for adhesion to the walls of the intestines of the animals in which they are parasitic. The larvæ live in the flesh of various creatures, and when swallowed by another animal of the right species develop into the mature tapeworm in its intestine. See Illustration in Appendix. Note: Three species are common parasites of man: the pork tapeworm, the larva of which is found in pork | 2. The beef tapeworm, the larva of which lives in the flesh of young cattle | 3. And the broad tapeworm which is found chiefly in the inhabitants of the mountainous regions of Europe and Asia. See also Echinococcus, Cysticercus, Proglottis, and 2d Measles,
tipstaff: 1. A staff tipped with metal. Bacon | 2. An officer who bears a staff tipped with metal | 3. A constable. Macaulay

deprecative: 1. Serving to deprecate | 2. Deprecatory. -- Dep"re*ca*tive*ly, adv
pill:
1. The peel or skin.  "Some be covered over with crusts, or hard pills, as the locusts." Holland.

To be peeled | 2. To peel off in flakes | 3. To deprive of hair

rid: 1. Imp | 2. & p. p. of Ride, v. i.  He rid to the end of the village, where he alighted. Thackeray | 3. To save

unregeneracy: 1. The quality or state of being unregenerate. Glanvill

tallow: 1. The suet or fat of animals of the sheep and ox kinds, separated from membranous and fibrous matter by melting. M. communis, from the West Indies, is often cultivated, and sometimes called Turk's cap

springhalt: 1. A kind of lameness in horse. See Stringhalt. Shak
vulneration: 1. The act of wounding, or the state of being wounded

posology: 1. The science or doctrine of doses | 2. Dosology
begum: 1. In the East Indies, a princess or lady of high rank. Malcom

noils: 1. Waste and knots of wool removed by the comb | 2. Combings

1. Having the form or structure of flies of the genus Musca, or family Muscidæ.

floreal: 1. The eight month of the French republican calendar. It began April 20, and ended May | 2. See Vendémiare

To form or shape on an anvil
fetation: 1. The formation of a fetus in the womb | 2. Pregnancy

preputial: 1. Of or pertaining to the prepuce

Note: Plants are divided by their structure and methods of reproduction into two series, phænogamous or flowering plants, which have true flowers and seeds, and cryptogamous or flowerless plants, which have no flowers, and reproduce by minute one-celled spores. In both series are minute and simple forms and others of great size and complexity. As to their mode of nutrition, plants may be considered as self-supporting and dependent. Self-supporting plants always contain chlorophyll, and subsist on air and moisture and the matter dissolved in moisture, and as a general rule they excrete oxygen, and use the carbonic acid to combine with water and form the material for their tissues. Dependent plants comprise all fungi and many flowering plants of a parasitic or saprophytic nature. As a rule, they have no chlorophyll, and subsist mainly or wholly on matter already organized, thus utilizing carbon compounds already existing, and not excreting oxygen. But there are plants which are partly dependent and partly self-supporting. The movements of climbing plants, of some insectivorous plants, of leaves, stamens, or pistils in certain plants, and the ciliary motion of zoöspores, etc., may be considered a kind of voluntary motion | 3. swietenia: 1. A genus of meliaceous trees consisting of one species, the mahogany tree

1. Procurable.  Sir T. Browne.

A comparison | 2. A similitude | 3. Specifically, a short fictitious narrative of something which might really occur in life or nature, by means of which a moral is drawn

A biennial climbing plant with elegant feathery leaves and large clusters of pretty white or pinkish flowers looking like grains of rice
countercurrent:
1. Running in an opposite direction.

A current running in an opposite direction to the main current

funky: 1. Pertaining to, or characterized by, great fear, or funking
nationally: 1. In a national manner or way | 2. As a nation. "The jews ... being nationally espoused to God by covenant." South

blunderer: 1. One who is apt to blunder

doting: 1. That dotes | 2. Silly | 3. Excessively fond. -- Dot"ing*ly, adv

Contractile vacuole, a pulsating cavity in the interior of a protozoan, supposed to be excretory in function. There may be one, two, or more

fanal: 1. A lighthouse, or the apparatus placed in it for giving light

zooetrophic: 1. Of or pertaining to the nourishment of animals

Wolfish | 2. Ravenous. Gauden

1. To tie or bind together. The pieces of isinglass are colligated in rows. Nicholson | 2. To bring together by colligation | 3. To sum up in a single proposition. He had discovered and colligated a multitude of the most wonderful . . . phenomena. Tundall.

Bound together

1. Imp | 2. Of Ding.

1. Having different essential qualities | 2. Of a different nature.

Having, or afflicted with, murrain

With thirst, with cold, with hunger so confounded. Chaucer

kite: 1. Any raptorial bird of the subfamily Milvinæ, of which many species are known. They have long wings, adapted for soaring, and usually a forked tail. Note: The European species are Milvus ictinus and M. govinda | 2. The sacred or Brahmany kite of India is Haliastur Indus | 3. The American fork-tailed kite is the Nauclerus furcatus
paraconic: 1. Pertaining to, or designating, an organic acid obtained as a deliquescent white crystalline substance, and isomeric with itaconic, citraconic, and mesaconic acids
spinster: 1. A woman who spins, or whose occupation is to spin. She spake to spinster to spin it out | 2. Piers Plowman. The spinsters and the knitters in the sun | 3. Shak
lactam: 1. One of a series of anhydrides of an amido type, analogous to the lactones, as oxindol
secundine: 1. The second coat, or integument, of an ovule, lying within the primine. Note: In the ripened seed the primine and secundine are usually united to form the testa, or outer seed coat. When they remain distinct the secundine becomes the mesosperm, as in the castor bean | 2. Etym:   The afterbirth, or placenta and membranes | 3. -- generally used in the plural
kingly: 1. Belonging to, suitable to, or becoming, a king | 2. Characteristic of, resembling, a king | 3. Directed or administered by a king
inarch: 1. To graft by uniting, as a scion, to a stock, without separating either from its root before the union is complete | 2. -- also called to graft by approach. P. Miler
boom: 1. A long pole or spar, run out for the purpose of extending the bottom of a particular sail | 2. As, the jib boom, the studding-sail boom, etc | 3. A long spar or beam, projecting from the mast of a derrick, from the outer end of which the body to be lifted is suspended
snite:
1. A snipe.  Carew.

To blow, as the nose | 2. To snuff, as a candle
casern: 1. A lodging for soldiers in garrison towns, usually near the rampart | 2. Barracks. Bescherelle
harshly: 1. In a harsh manner | 2. Gratingly | 3. Roughly
fetus: 1. The young or embryo of an animal in the womb, or in the egg | 2. Often restricted to the later stages in the development of viviparous and oviparous animals, embryo being applied to the earlier stages
anthropopathy: 1. The ascription of human feelings or passions to God, or to a polytheistic deity. In its recoil from the gross anthropopathy of the vulgar notions, it falls into the vacuum of absolute apathy. Hare
alaternus: 1. An ornamental evergreen shrub belonging to the buckthorns
mammillated: 1. Having small nipples, or small protuberances like nipples or mammæ | 2. Bounded like a nipple | 3. -- said of the apex of some shells
rissole: 1. A small ball of rich minced meat or fish, covered with pastry and fried
malediction: 1. A proclaiming of evil against some one | 2. A cursing | 3. Imprecation
doxologize: 1. To give glory to God, as in a doxology | 2. To praise God with doxologies
delimit: 1. To fix the limits of | 2. To demarcate | 3. To bound
lunette: 1. A fieldwork consisting of two faces, forming a salient angle, and two parallel flanks. See Bastion | 2. A half horseshoe, which wants the sponge | 3. A kind of watch crystal which is more than ordinarily flattened in the center
prelatize:
1. To bring under the influence of prelacy. Palfrey.

To uphold or encourage prelacy | 2. To exercise prelatical functions. An episcopacy that began then to prelatize. Milton
psalm:
1. A sacred song | 2. A poetical composition for use in the praise or worship of God. Humus devout and holy psalms Singing everlastingly. Milton | 3. Especially, one of the hymns by David and others, collected into one book of the Old Testament, or a modern metrical version of such a hymn for public worship.

To extol in psalms
pencel: 1. A small, narrow flag or streamer borne at the top of a lance | 2. - - called also pennoncel.  Piers Plowman. Chaucer
sparger: 1. A vessel with a perforated cover, for sprinkling with a liquid | 2. A sprinkler
ironwork: 1. Anything made of iron | 2. -- a general name of such parts or pieces of a building, vessel, carriage, etc., as consist of iron
eloign: 1. To remove afar off | 2. To withdraw.  From worldly cares he did himself eloign. Spenser | 3. To convey to a distance, or beyond the jurisdiction, or to conceal, as goods liable to distress. The sheriff may return that the goods or beasts are eloigned. Blackstone
hermaphroditic: 1. Partaking of the characteristics of both sexes | 2. Characterized by hermaphroditism. -- Her*maph`ro*dit"ic*al*ly, adv
insistence: 1. The quality of insisting, or being urgent or pressing | 2. The act of dwelling upon as of special importance | 3. Persistence
honeydew: 1. A sweet, saccharine substance, found on the leaves of trees and other plants in small drops, like dew | 2. Two substances have been called by this name | 3. One exuded from the plants, and the other secreted by certain insects, esp
subscription: 1. The act of subscribing | 2. That which is subscribed. Specifically: A paper to which a signature is attached. The signature attached to a paper. Consent or attestation by underwriting the name. Sum subscribed | 3. Amount of sums subscribed
ungored:
1. Not stained with gore | 2. Not bloodied. Sylvester.

Not gored or pierced
arctisca: 1. A group of Arachnida. See Illust. in Appendix
antiquity: 1. The quality of being ancient | 2. Ancientness | 3. Great age
reenter:
1. To enter again | 2. To cut deeper, as engraved lines on a plate of metal, when the engraving has not been deep enough, or the plate has become worn in printing.

To enter anew or again. Reëntering angle, an angle of a polygon pointing inward, as a, in the cut | 3. -- Reëntering polygon, a polygon having one or more reëntering angles
rereward: 1. The rear quard of an army
apprizer: 1. An appraiser | 2. A creditor for whom an appraisal is made. Sir W. Scott
fifty: 1. Five times ten | 2. As, fifty men | 3. The sum of five tens
pianograph: 1. A form of melodiograph applied to a piano
gite: 1. A gown.  She came often in a gite of red | 2. Chaucer
sherry: 1. A Spanish light-colored dry wine, made in Andalusia. As prepared for commerce it is colored a straw color or a deep amber by mixing with it cheap wine boiled down. Sherry cobbler, a beverage prepared with sherry wine, water, lemon or orange, sugar, ice, etc., and usually imbided through a straw or a glass tube
microseism: 1. A feeble earth tremor not directly perceptible, but detected only by means of specially constructed apparatus. -- Mi`cro*seis"mic, *seis"mic*al, a
guidance: 1. The act or result of guiding | 2. The superintendence or assistance of a guide | 3. Direction
blunderbuss: 1. A short gun or firearm, with a large bore, capable of holding a number of balls, and intended to do execution without exact aim | 2. A stupid, blundering fellow
lyncean: 1. Of or pertaining to the lynx
emancipation: 1. The act of setting free from the power of another, from slavery, subjection, dependence, or controlling influence | 2. Also, the state of being thus set free | 3. Liberation
votaress: 1. A woman who is a votary. Shak
outlay: 1. To lay out | 2. To spread out | 3. To display.  Drayton
pseudospore: 1. A peculiar reproductive cell found in some fungi
tippler: 1. One who keeps a tippling-house.  Latimer | 2. One who habitually indulges in the excessive use of spirituous liquors, whether he becomes intoxicated or not
genitive:
1. Of or pertaining to that case which expresses source or possession. It corresponds to the possessive case in English.

The genitive case. Genitive absolute, a construction in Greek similar to the ablative absolute in Latin. See Ablative absolute
perimetry: 1. The art of using the perimeter | 2. Measurement of the field of vision
systematical: 1. Of or pertaining to system | 2. Consisting in system | 3. Methodical
duelist: 1. One who fights in single combat.  A duelist . . . always values himself upon his courage, his sense of honor, his fidelity and friendship. Hume
dell: 1. A small, retired valley | 2. A ravine. In dells and dales, concealed from human sight. Tickell | 3. A young woman
proudling: 1. A proud or haughty person. Sylvester
contrist: 1. To make sad | 2. To deject and contrist myself. Sterne
eyne: 1. Plural of eye | 2. Obsolete, or used only in poetry. Shak. With such a plaintive gaze their eyne Are fastened upwardly on mine. Mrs. Browning
frost: 1. The act of freezing | 2. -- applied chiefly to the congelation of water | 3. Congelation of fluids
vulcan: 1. The god of fire, who presided over the working of metals | 2. -- answering to the Greek Hephæstus
flobert: 1. A small cartridge designed for target shooting | 2. -- sometimes called ball cap | 3. Flobert rifle, a rifle adapted to the use of floberts
nowadays: 1. In these days | 2. At the present time. What men of spirit, nowadays, Come to give sober judgment of new plays Garrick
doubter: 1. One who doubts | 2. One whose opinion is unsettled | 3. One who scruples
hobble: 1. To walk lame, bearing chiefly on one leg | 2. To walk with a hitch or hop, or with crutches. The friar was hobbling the same way too | 3. Dryden
reddendum: 1. A clause in a deed by which some new thing is reserved out of what had been granted before | 2. The clause by which rent is reserved in a lease. Cruise
molestation: 1. The act of molesting, or the state of being molested | 2. Disturbance | 3. Annoyance
volery: 1. A flight of birds.  Locke | 2. A large bird cage | 3. An aviary
insult: 1. The act of leaping on | 2. Onset | 3. Attack.  Dryden
linguistic: 1. Of or pertaining to language | 2. Relating to linguistics, or to the affinities of languages
columella: 1. An axis to which a carpel of a compound pistil may be attached, as in the case of the geranium | 2. Or which is left when a pod opens. A columnlike axis in the capsule of mosses | 3. A term applied to various columnlike parts
patchouli: 1. A mintlike plant of the East Indies, yielding an essential oil from which a highly valued perfume is made | 2. The perfume made from this plant. Patchouly camphor, a substance homologous with and resembling borneol, found in patchouly oil
slurred: 1. Marked with a slur | 2. Performed in a smooth, gliding style, like notes marked with a slur
evanesce: 1. To vanish away | 2. To because dissipated and disappear, like vapor. I believe him to have evanesced or evaporated. De Quincey
abloom: 1. In or into bloom | 2. In a blooming state. Masson
audition: 1. The act of hearing or listening | 2. Hearing. Audition may be active or passive | 3. Hence the difference between listening and simple hearing. Dunglison
pergolo: 1. A continuous colonnade or arcade | 2. -- applied to the decorative groups of windows, as in Venetian palazzi
floral: 1. Pertaining to Flora, or to flowers | 2. Made of flowers | 3. As, floral games, wreaths
fumette: 1. The stench or high flavor of game or other meat when kept long. Swift
thrave: 1. Twenty-four sheaves of wheat | 2. A shock, or stook | 3. The number of two dozen
ectoparasite: 1. Any parasite which lives on the exterior of animals | 2. -- opposed to endoparasite. -- Ec`to*par`a*sit"ic, a
musette: 1. A small bagpipe formerly in use, having a soft and sweet tone | 2. An air adapted to this instrument | 3. Also, a kind of rustic dance
curarine: 1. A deadly alkaloid extracted from the curare poison and from the Strychnos toxifera. It is obtained in crystalline colorless salts
malmsey: 1. A kind of sweet wine from Crete, the Canary Islands, etc | 2. Shak
adz:
1. To cut with an adz | 2. Carlyle.

A carpenter's or cooper's tool, formed with a thin arching blade set at right angles to the handle. It is used for chipping or slicing away the surface of wood
juvenile: 1. Young | 2. Youthful | 3. As, a juvenile appearance. "A juvenile exercitation." Glanvill
tiptoe: 1. The end, or tip, of the toe | 2. He must . . . stand on his typtoon . Chaucer. Upon his tiptoes stalketh stately by. Spenser. To be, or To stand, a tiptoe or on tiptoe, to be awake or alive to anything | 3. To be roused
dander:
1. Dandruff or scurf on the head | 2. Anger or vexation | 3. Rage  Halliwell.

To wander about
ballahou: 1. A fast-sailing schooner, used in the Bermudas and West Indies
fingered: 1. Having fingers | 2. Having leaflets like fingers | 3. Digitate

hamamelis: 1. A genus of plants which includes the witch-hazel, a preparation of which is used medicinally

spiroscope: 1. A wet meter used to determine the breathing capacity of the lungs
terret: 1. One of the rings on the top of the saddle of a harness, through which the reins pass
leader: 1. One who, or that which, leads or conducts | 2. A guide | 3. A conductor. Especially: One who goes first. One having authority to direct
node: 1. A knot, a knob | 2. A protuberance | 3. A swelling

tumulus: 1. An artificial hillock, especially one raised over a grave, particularly over the graves of persons buried in ancient times | 2. A barrow
imaginational: 1. Pertaining to, involving, or caused by, imagination
gyrate:
1. Winding or coiled round | 2. Curved into a circle | 3. Taking a circular course.

To revolve round a central point

discoloration: 1. The act of discoloring, or the state of being discolored | 2. Alteration of hue or appearance. Darwin | 3. A discolored spot
perfectional: 1. Of or pertaining to perfection | 2. Characterized by perfection.  Bp. Pearson
hatte: 1. Pres. & imp | 2. Sing. & pl. of Hote, to be called. See Hote.  Chaucer. A full perilous place, purgatory it hatte. Piers Plowman
principle: 1. Beginning | 2. Commencement.  Doubting sad end of principle unsound. Spenser | 3. A source, or origin
gunstome: 1. A cannon ball | 2. -- so called because originally made of stone.  Shak
jamaicine: 1. An alkaloid said to be contained in the bark of Geoffroya inermis, a leguminous tree growing in Jamaica and Surinam | 2. -- called also jamacina. Watts
indecorousness: 1. The quality of being indecorous | 2. Want of decorum
diclinic: 1. Having two of the intersections between the three axes oblique. See Crystallization

electropathy: 1. The treatment of disease by electricity
marrowish: 1. Of the nature of, or like, marrow
steamer: 1. A vessel propelled by steam | 2. A steamship or steamboat | 3. A steam fire engine. See under Steam
purgation: 1. The act of purging | 2. The act of clearing, cleansing, or putifying, by separating and carrying off impurities, or whatever is superfluous | 3. The evacuation of the bowels

vibrio: 1. A genus of motile bacteria characterized by short, slightly sinuous filaments and an undulatory motion | 2. Also, an individual of this genus
ageratum: 1. A genus of plants, one species of which has lavender-blue flowers in dense clusters

tical: 1. A bean-shaped coin of Siam, worth about sixty cents | 2. Also, a weight equal to 236 grains troy. Malcom | 3. A money of account in China, reckoning at about $

adelphous: 1. Having coalescent or clustered filaments | 2. -- said of stamens | 3. As, adelphous stamens. Usually in composition
jerking: 1. The act of pulling, pushing, or throwing, with a jerk. -- Jerk"ing*ly, adv

supralunar: 1. Beyond the moon | 2. Hence, very lofty
gemmation: 1. The formation of a new individual, either animal or vegetable, by a process of budding | 2. An asexual method of reproduction | 3. Gemmulation
friendly: 1. Having the temper and disposition of a friend | 2. Disposed to promote the good of another | 3. Kind
coinsurance: 1. Insurance jointly with another or others | 2. grid: 1. A grating of thin parallel bars, similar to a gridiron

Savannahs are clear pieces land without woods. Dampier. Savanna flower, a West Indian name for several climbing apocyneous plants of the genus Echites. -- Savanna sparrow, an American sparrow of which several varieties are found on grassy plains from Alaska to the Eastern United States. -- Savanna wattle, a name of two West Indian trees of the genus Citharexylum
toughen: 1. To grow or make tough, or tougher

lampic: 1. Pertaining to, or produced by, a lamp | 2. -- formerly said of a supposed acid
ken: 1. A house | 2. Esp., one which is a resort for thieves | 3. To know

multiparous: 1. Producing many, or more than one, at a birth

bereft: 1. Of Bereave. BERENICE'S HAIR Ber`e*ni"ce's Hair`.  See Coma Berenices, under Coma

jamb:

lilt:
1. To do anything with animation and quickness, as to skip, fly, or hop | 2. Wordsworth | 3. To sing cheerfully.

horal: 1. Of or pertaining to an hour, or to hours. Prior

element: 1. One of the simplest or essential parts or principles of which anything consists, or upon which the constitution or fundamental powers of anything are based. 2. One of the ultimate, undecomposable constituents of any kind of matter. Specifically: A substance which cannot be decomposed into different kinds of matter by any means at present employed; as, the elements of water are oxygen and hydrogen. Note: The elements are naturally classified in several families or groups, as the group of the alkaline elements, the halogen group, and the like. They are roughly divided into two great classes, the metals, as sodium, calcium, etc., which form basic compounds, and the nonmetals or metalloids, as oxygen, sulphur, chlorine, which form acid compounds; but the distinction is only relative, and some, as arsenic, tin, aluminium, etc., form both acid and basic compounds. The essential fact regarding every element is its relative atomic weight or equivalent. When the elements are tabulated in the order of their ascending atomic weights, the arrangement constitutes the series of the Periodic law of Mendelejeff. See Periodic law, under Periodic. This Periodic law enables us to predict the qualities of unknown elements. The number of elements known is about seventy-five, but the gaps in the Periodic law indicate the possibility of many more. Many of the elements with which we are familiar, as hydrogen, carbon, iron, gold, etc., have been recognized, by means of spectrum analysis, in the sun and the fixed stars. From certain evidence it appears that the chemical elements probably may not be simple bodies, but only very stable compounds of some simpler body or bodies. In formulas, the elements are designated by abbreviations of their names in Latin or New Latin. The Elements -------------------------------------------------------- ----Name | 2. Sym- | 3. 1. Originally, a small, sharp-built vessel, with two topsails on one or both masts and was called a topsail schooner. About 1840, longer vesels with three masts, fore-and-aft rigged, came into use, and since that time vesels with four masts and even with six masts, so rigged, are built. Schooners with more than two masts are designated three-masted schooners, four-masted schooners, etc | 2. See Illustration in Appendix. Note: The fist schooner ever constructed is said to have between built in Gloucester, Massachusetts, about theyar 1713, by a Captain Andrew Robinson, and to have received its name from the following trivial circumstance: When the vessel went off the stocks into the water, a bystander cried out,"O, how she scoons!" Robinson replied, " A scooner let her be | 3. " and, from that time, vessels thus masted and rigged have gone by this name. The word scoon is popularly used in some parts of New England to denote the act of making stones skip along the surface of water. The Scottish scon means the same thing. Both words are probably allied to the Icel. skunda, skynda, to make haste, hurry, AS. scunian to avoid, shun, Prov. E. scun. In the New England records, the word appears to have been originally written scooner. Babson, in his "History of Gloucester," gives the following extract from a letter written in that place Sept. 25, 1721, by Dr. Moses Prince, brother of the Rev. Thomas Prince, the annalist of New England: "This gentleman was first contriver of schooners, and built the first of that sort about eight years since."

To speak for Buncombe, to speak for mere show, or popularly. Note: "The phrase originated near the close of the debate on the famous 'Missouri Question,' in the 16th Congress. It was then used by Felix Walker -- a naïve old mountaineer, who resided at Waynesville, in Haywood, the most western country of North Carolina, near the border of the adjacent country of Buncombe, which formed part of his district. The old man rose to speak, while the house was impatiently calling for the 'Question,' and several members gathered round him, begging him to desist. He preserved, however, for a while, declaring that the people of his district expected it, and that he was bound to 'make a speech for Buncombe.'" W. Darlington.
