dripping: 1. A falling in drops, or the sound so made | 2. That which falls in drops, as fat from meat in roasting. Dripping pan, a pan for receiving the fat which drips from meat in roasting
dysluite: 1. A variety of the zinc spinel or gahnite
enervation: 1. The act of weakening, or reducing strength | 2. The state of being weakened | 3. Effeminacy. Bacon
gadder: 1. One who roves about idly, a rambling gossip
dynameter: 1. A dynamometer | 2. An instrument for determining the magnifying power of telescopes, consisting usually of a doubleimage micrometer applied to the eye end of a telescope for measuring accurately the diameter of the image of the object glass there formed | 3. Which measurement, compared with the actual diameter of the glass, gives the magnifying power
bliss: 1. Orig., blithesomeness | 2. Gladness | 3. Now, the highest degree of happiness
backbiter: 1. One who backbites | 2. A secret calumniator or detractor
jaguar: 1. A large and powerful feline animal, ranging from Texas and Mexico to Patagonia. It is usually brownish yellow, with large, dark, somewhat angular rings, each generally inclosing one or two dark spots. It is chiefly arboreal in its habits. Called also the American tiger
calamitous: 1. Suffering calamity | 2. Wretched | 3. Miserable.  Ten thousands of calamitous persons. South
maccabees: 1. The name given in later times to the Asmonæans, a family of Jewish patriots, who headed a religious revolt in the reign of Antiochus IV., 168-161 B. C., which led to a period of freedom for Israel. Schaff-Herzog | 2. The name of two ancient historical books, which give accounts of Jewish affairs in or about the time of the Maccabean princes, and which are received as canonical books in the Roman Catholic Church, but are included in the Apocrypha by Protestants. Also applied to three books, two of which are found in some MSS. of the Septuagint
comelily: 1. In a suitable or becoming manner.  Sherwood
judaization: 1. The act of Judaizing | 2. A conforming to the Jewish religion or ritual
turncoat: 1. One who forsakes his party or his principles | 2. A renegade | 3. An apostate. He is a turncoat, he was not true to his profession. Bunyan
worser: 1. Worse.  Thou dost deserve a worser end | 2. Beau. & Fl. From worser thoughts which make me do amiss. Bunyan. A dreadful quiet felt, and, worser far Than arms, a sullen interval of war | 3. Dryden. Note: This old and redundant form of the comparative occurs occasionally in the best authors, although commonly accounted a vulgarism. It has, at least, the analogy of lesser to sanction its issue. See Lesser. "The experience of man's worser nature, which intercourse with ill-chosen associates, by choice or circumstance, peculiarly teaches." Hallam
gallinacean: 1. One of the Gallinae or gallinaceous birds
procoelia:
1. Same as Procoele.

A division of Crocodilia, including the true crocodiles and alligators, in which the dorsal vertebræ are concave in front
elastin: 1. A nitrogenous substance, somewhat resembling albumin, which forms the chemical basis of elastic tissue. It is very insoluble in most fluids, but is gradually dissolved when digested with either pepsin or trypsin
logotype: 1. A single type, containing two or more letters | 2. As, æ, Æ, fi, fl, ffl, etc | 3. -- called also ligature
pellagrin: 1. One who is afficted with pellagra. Chambers's Encyc
proudly: 1. In a proud manner | 2. With lofty airs or mien | 3. Haughtily
scintillate: 1. To emit sparks, or fine igneous particles. As the electrical globe only scintillates when rubbed against its cushion. Sir W. Scott | 2. To sparkle, as the fixed stars
mannite: 1. A white crystalline substance of a sweet taste obtained from a so-called manna, the dried sap of the flowering ash | 2. -- called also mannitol, and hydroxy hexane. Cf. Dulcite. HO.CH | 3. OH = D-mannitol
inorganic: 1. Not organic | 2. Without the organs necessary for life | 3. Devoid of an organized structure
crinoline: 1. A kind of stiff cloth, used chiefly by women, for underskirts, to expand the gown worn over it | 2. -- so called because originally made of hair | 3. A lady's skirt made of any stiff material
lithochromics: 1. The art of printing colored pictures on canvas from oil paintings on stone
promulger: 1. One who promulges or publishes what was before unknown. Atterbury
cotangent: 1. The tangent of the complement of an arc or angle. See Illust. of Functions
indiscerpibility: 1. The state or quality of being indiscerpible.  Dr. H. More
predy: 1. Cleared and ready for engagement, as a ship. Smart
confutative: 1. Adapted or designed to confute.  Bp. Warburton
zohar: 1. A Jewish cabalistic book attributed by tradition to Rabbi Simon ben Yochi, who lived about the end of the 1st century, a. d. Modern critics believe it to be a compilation of the 13th century. Encyc. Brit
arab: 1. One of a swarthy race occupying Arabia, and numerous in Syria, Northern Africa, etc | 2. Street Arab, a homeless vagabond in the streets of a city, particularly and outcast boy or girl. Tylor. The ragged outcasts and street Arabs who are shivering in damp doorways. Lond. Sat. Rev
bailey: 1. The outer wall of a feudal castle | 2. The space immediately within the outer wall of a castle or fortress | 3. A prison or court of justice
swede: 1. A native or inhabitant of Sweden | 2. A Swedish turnip. See under Turnip
humorously: 1. Capriciously | 2. Whimsically. We resolve rashly, sillily, or humorously. Calamy | 3. Facetiously
courtliness: 1. The quality of being courtly | 2. Elegance or dignity of manners
galvanoplasty: 1. The art or process of electrotypy
greeze: 1. A step. See Gree, a step.  The top of the ladder, or first greeze, is this. Latimer
thaumatolatry: 1. Worship or undue admiration of wonderful or miraculous things.  The thaumatolatry by which our theology has been debased for more than a century. Hare
fuchsine: 1. Aniline red | 2. An artificial coal-tar dyestuff, of a metallic green color superficially, resembling cantharides, but when dissolved forming a brilliant dark red | 3. It consists of a hydrochloride or acetate of rosaniline. See Rosaniline
empanel:
1. A list of jurors | 2. A panel.  Cowell.

See Impanel
sibyl: 1. A woman supposed to be endowed with a spirit of prophecy. Note: The number of the sibyls is variously stated by different authors | 2. But the opinion of Varro, that there were ten, is generally adopted. They dwelt in various parts of Persia, Greece, and Italy | 3. A female fortune teller
hunch: 1. A hump | 2. A protuberance | 3. A lump
forkbeard: 1. A European fish, having a large flat head | 2. -- also called tadpole fish, and lesser forked beard. The European forked hake or hake's-dame | 3. -- also called great forked beard
repercussion: 1. The act of driving back, or the state of being driven back | 2. Reflection | 3. Reverberation
stylaster: 1. Any one of numerous species of delicate, usually pink, calcareous hydroid corals of the genus Stylaster
whelk: 1. Any one numerous species of large marine gastropods belonging to Buccinum and allied genera | 2. Especially, Buccinum undatum, common on the coasts both of Europe and North America, and much used as food in Europe. Whelk tingle, a dog whelk. See under Dog | 3. A papule
poenamu: 1. A variety of jade or nephrite, -- used in New Zealand for the manufacture of axes and weapons
balneal: 1. Of or pertaining to a bath. Howell
impossible: 1. Not possible | 2. Incapable of being done, of existing, etc | 3. Unattainable in the nature of things, or by means at command
bombazine: 1. A twilled fabric for dresses, of which the warp is silk, and the weft worsted. Black bombazine has been much used for mourning garments.  Tomlinson
arsenious: 1. Pertaining to, consisting of, or containing, arsenic | 2. As, arsenious powder or glass | 3. Pertaining to, or derived from, arsenic, when having an equivalence next lower than the highest
lappaceous: 1. Resembling the capitulum of burdock | 2. Covered with forked points
encyclopedist: 1. The compiler of an encyclopedia, or one who assists in such compilation | 2. Also, one whose knowledge embraces the whole range of the sciences. The Encyclopedists, the writers of the great French encyclopedia which appeared in 1751- | 3. The editors were Diderot and D'Alembert. Among the contributors were Voltaire and Rousseau
perispore: 1. The outer covering of a spore
firms: 1. The principal rafters of a roof, especially a pair of rafters taken together
bison: 1. The aurochs or European bison. The American bison buffalo, a large, gregarious bovine quadruped with shaggy mane and short black horns, which formerly roamed in herds over most of the temperate portion of North America, but is now restricted to very limited districts in the region of the Rocky Mountains, and is rapidly decreasing in numbers
adopter: 1. One who adopts | 2. A receiver, with two necks, opposite to each other, one of which admits the neck of a retort, and the other is joined to another receiver. It is used in distillations, to give more space to elastic vapors, to increase the length of the neck of a retort, or to unite two vessels whose openings have different diameters
renunciation: 1. The act of renouncing | 2. Formal declination to take out letters of administration, or to assume an office, privilege, or right. Syn. -- Renouncement | 3. Disownment
antitypical: 1. Of or pertaining to an antitype | 2. Explaining the type. -- An`ti*typ"ic*al*ly, adv
bewitch: 1. To gain an ascendency over by charms or incantations | 2. To affect (esp | 3. To injure) by witchcraft or sorcery. See how I am bewitched
bending: 1. The marking of the clothes with stripes or horizontal bands.  Chaucer
grandinous: 1. Consisting of hail | 2. Abounding in hail.  Bailey
islamize: 1. To conform, or cause to conform, to the religion of Islam
calipee: 1. A part of a turtle which is attached to the lower shell. It contains a fatty and gelatinous substance of a light yellowish color, much esteemed as a delicacy. Thackeray
lollard: 1. One of a sect of early reformers in Germany. One of the followers of Wyclif in England.  By Lollards all know the Wyclifities are meant, so called from Walter Lollardus, one of their teachers in Germany. Fuller
tridiapason: 1. A triple octave, or twenty-second. Busby
estuate: 1. To boil up | 2. To swell and rage | 3. To be agitated. Bacon
noil: 1. A short or waste piece or knot of wool separated from the longer staple by combing | 2. Also, a similar piece or shred of waste silk
minx: 1. A pert or a wanton girl. Shak | 2. A she puppy | 3. A pet dog
conducibility: 1. The state or quality of being conducible | 2. Conducibleness. Bp. Wilkins
ghoulish: 1. Characteristic of a ghoul | 2. Vampirelike | 3. Hyenalike
tympanohyal: 1. Of or pertaining to the tympanum and the hyoidean arch. -- n.  The proximal segment in the hyoidean arch, becoming a part of the styloid process of the temporal bone in adult man
shrive: 1. To hear or receive the confession of | 2. To administer confession and absolution to | 3. -- said of a priest as the agent. That they should shrive their parishioners. Piers Plowman. Doubtless he shrives this woman, . . . Else ne'er could he so long protract his speech. Shak. Till my guilty soul be shriven. Longfellow
mingle: 1. To mix | 2. Intermix | 3. To combine or join, as an individual or part, with other parts, but commonly so as to be distinguishable in the product
effigy: 1. The image, likeness, or representation of a person, whether a full figure, or a part | 2. An imitative figure | 3. -- commonly applied to sculptured likenesses, as those on monuments, or to those of the heads of princes on coins and medals, sometimes applied to portraits. To burn, or To hang, in effigy, to burn or to hang an image or picture of a person, as a token of public odium
nouthe: 1. Just now | 2. At present.  But thereof needeth not to speak as nouthe. Chaucer
passacaglia: 1. An old Italian or Spanish dance tune, in slow three-four measure, with divisions on a ground bass, resembling a chaconne
appellate:
1. Pertaining to, or taking cognizance of, appeals. "Appellate jurisdiction." Blackstone. "Appellate judges." Burke. Appelate court, a court having cognizance of appeals.

A person or prosecuted for a crime.  See Appellee
poi: 1. A national food of the Hawaiians, made by baking and pounding the kalo root, and reducing it to a thin paste, which is allowed to ferment
ere: 1. Before | 2. Sooner than.  Myself was stirring ere the break of day | 3. Shak. Ere sails were spread new oceans to explore. Dryden. Sir, come down ere my child die
unionistic: 1. Of or pertaining to union or unionists | 2. Tending to promote or preserve union
towned: 1. Having towns | 2. Containing many towns.  Hakluyt
washerwoman: 1. A woman who washes clothes, especially for hire, or for others | 2. The pied wagtail | 3. -- so called in allusion to its beating the water with its tail while tripping along the leaves of water plants
pug: 1. To mix and stir when wet, as clay for bricks, pottery, etc | 2. To fill or stop with clay by tamping | 3. To fill in or spread with mortar, as a floor or partition, for the purpose of deadening sound. See Pugging,
declaration: 1. The act of declaring, or publicly announcing | 2. Explicit asserting | 3. Undisguised token of a ground or side taken on any subject
sliver: 1. To cut or divide into long, thin pieces, or into very small pieces | 2. To cut or rend lengthwise | 3. To slit
biannual: 1. Occurring twice a year | 2. Half-yearly | 3. Semiannual
devata: 1. A deity | 2. A divine being | 3. A good spirit
accroach: 1. To hook, or draw to one's self as with a hook | 2. To usurp, as jurisdiction or royal prerogatives. They had attempted to accroach to themselves royal power. Stubbs
quietus: 1. Final discharge or acquittance, as from debt or obligation | 2. That which silences claims | 3. Rest
abysm: 1. An abyss | 2. A gulf. "The abysm of hell." Shak
glycyrrhiza: 1. A genus of papilionaceous herbaceous plants, one species of which, is the licorice plant, the roots of which have a bittersweet mucilaginous taste | 2. The root of Glycyrrhiza glabra, used as a demulcent, etc
equiponderant: 1. Being of the same weight. A column of air . . . equiponderant to a column of quicksilver. Locke
zaerthe:
1. Same as Zärthe.

A European bream
sigillaria:
1. Little images or figures of earthenware exposed for sale, or given as presents, on the last two days of the Saturnalia | 2. Hence, the last two, or the sixth and seventh, days of the Saturnalia.

A genus of fossil trees principally found in the coal formation | 3. -- so named from the seallike leaf scars in vertical rows on the surface
disclose: 1. To unclose | 2. To open | 3. -- applied esp
rightward: 1. Toward the right. Rightward and leftward rise the rocks. Southey
recompenser: 1. One who recompenses. A thankful recompenser of the benefits received. Foxe
flaunt: 1. To throw or spread out | 2. To flutter | 3. To move ostentatiously
histrionicism: 1. The histronic art | 2. Stageplaying. W. Black
uterovaginal: 1. Pertaining to both the uterus and the vagina
affectionate: 1. Having affection or warm regard | 2. Loving | 3. Fond
intolerability: 1. The quality of being intolerable | 2. Intolerableness
moreover: 1. Beyond what has been said | 2. Further | 3. Besides
placer:
1. One who places or sets. Spenser.

A deposit of earth, sand, or gravel, containing valuable mineral in particles, especially by the side of a river, or in the bed of a mountain torrent
fascia: 1. A band, sash, or fillet | 2. Especially, in surgery, a bandage or roller | 3. A flat member of an order or building, like a flat band or broad fillet
abortifacient: 1. Producing miscarriage. -- n.  A drug or an agent that causes premature delivery
disrepute: 1. Loss or want of reputation | 2. Ill character | 3. Disesteem
anywise: 1. In any wise or way | 2. At all | 3. "Anywise essential." Burke
crase: 1. To break in pieces | 2. To crack.  "The pot was crased." Chaucer
aunter:
1. Adventure | 2. Hap | 3. In aunters, perchance.

To venture
prejudicate:
1. Formed before due examination. "Ignorance and prejudicate opinions." Jer. Taylor | 2. Biased by opinions formed prematurely | 3. Prejudiced. "Prejudicate readers." Sir T. Browne.

To determine beforehand, especially to disadvantage
haematology: 1. The science which treats of the blood. Same as Hematology
vined: 1. Having leaves like those of the vine | 2. Ornamented with vine leaves. "Vined and figured columns." Sir H. Wotton
syncarp: 1. A kind of aggregate fruit in which the ovaries cohere in a solid mass, with a slender receptacle, as in the magnolia | 2. Also, a similar multiple fruit, as a mulberry
mouthful: 1. As much as is usually put into the mouth at one time | 2. Hence, a small quantity
holyday: 1. A religious festival | 2. A secular festival | 3. A holiday. Note: Holiday is the preferable and prevailing spelling in the second sense. The spelling holy day or holyday in often used in the first sense
desquamate: 1. To peel off in the form of scales | 2. To scale off, as the skin in certain diseases
requisitive:
1. Expressing or implying demand.  Harris.

One who, or that which, makes requisition | 2. A requisitionist
hemispheroidal: 1. Resembling, or approximating to, a hemisphere in form
distrainor: 1. One who distrains | 2. The party distraining goods or chattels. Blackstone
lituite: 1. Any species of ammonites of the genus Lituites. They are found in the Cretaceous formation
plunk: 1. To pluck and release quickly | 2. To twang | 3. To throw, push, drive heavily, plumply, or suddenly
jactation: 1. A throwing or tossing of the body | 2. A shaking or agitation. Sir. W. Temple
harry: 1. To strip | 2. To lay waste | 3. As, the Northmen came several times and harried the land. To harry this beautiful region. W. Irving. A red squirrel had harried the nest of a wood thrush. J. Burroughs
malformation: 1. Ill formation | 2. Irregular or anomalous formation | 3. Abnormal or wrong conformation or structure
manesheet: 1. A covering placed over the upper part of a horse's head
unfoldment: 1. The acct of unfolding, or the state of being unfolded. The extreme unfoldment of the instinctive powers. C. Morris
carrier: 1. One who, or that which, carries or conveys | 2. A messenger. The air which is but . . . a carrier of the sounds. Bacon | 3. One who is employed, or makes it his business, to carry goods for others for hire
brashy: 1. Resembling, or of the nature of, brash, or broken fragments | 2. Broken | 3. Crumbly. Our progress was not at all impeded by the few soft, brashy floes that we encountered. F. T. Bullen
placophora: 1. A division of gastropod Mollusca, including the chitons. The back is covered by eight shelly plates. Called also Polyplacophora. See Illust. under Chiton, and Isopleura
squeamish: 1. Having a stomach that is easily or nauseated | 2. Hence, nice to excess in taste | 3. Fastidious
isopathy: 1. The system which undertakes to cure a disease by means of the virus of the same disease. The theory of curing a diseased organ by eating the analogous organ of a healthy animal. Mayne. The doctrine that the power of therapeutics is equal to that of the causes of disease
cephalometry: 1. The measurement of the heads of living persons. -- Ceph`a*lo*met"ric,a
stoneware: 1. A species of coarse potter's ware, glazed and baked
estray:
1. To stray.  Daniel.

Any valuable animal, not wild, found wandering from its owner | 2. A stray. Burrill
beldam: 1. Grandmother | 2. -- corresponding to belsire. To show the beldam daughters of her daughter. Shak | 3. An old woman in general
mantra: 1. A prayer | 2. An invocation | 3. A religious formula
predicrotic: 1. A term applied to the pulse wave sometimes seen in a pulse curve or sphygmogram, between the apex of the curve and the dicrotic wave. The predicrotic or tidal wave is best marked in a hard pulse, i. e., where the blood pressure is high. Landois & Stirling
bever:
1. A light repast between meals | 2. A lunch.  Beau. & Fl.

To take a light repast between meals
disclaim: 1. To renounce all claim to deny | 2. Ownership of, or responsibility for | 3. To disown
adventuresome: 1. Full of risk | 2. Adventurous | 3. Venturesome. -- Ad*ven"ture*some*ness, n
glazing: 1. The act or art of setting glass | 2. The art of covering with a vitreous or glasslike substance, or of polishing or rendering glossy | 3. The glass set, or to be set, in a sash, frame. etc
italic: 1. Relating to Italy or to its people | 2. Applied especially to a kind of type in which the letters do not stand upright, but slope toward the right | 3. -- so called because dedicated to the States of Italy by the inventor, Aldus Manutius, about the year
agrostology: 1. That part of botany which treats of the grasses
scheme: 1. A combination of things connected and adjusted by design | 2. A system. The appearance and outward scheme of things. Locke. Such a scheme of things as shall at once take in time and eternity. Atterbury. Arguments . . . sufficient to support and demonstrate a whole scheme of moral philosophy. J. Edwards. The Revolution came and changed his whole scheme of life. Macaulay | 3. A plan or theory something to be done
natchnee: 1. An annual grass, cultivated in India as a food plant
myrmidon: 1. One of a fierce tribe or troop who accompained Achilles, their king, to the Trojan war | 2. A soldier or a subordinate civil officer who executes cruel orders of a superior without protest or pity | 3. -- sometimes applied to bailiffs, constables, etc
lepidomelane: 1. An iron-potash mica, of a raven-black color, usually found in granitic rocks in small six-sided tables, or as an aggregation of minute opaque scales. See Mica
unbend: 1. To free from flexure | 2. To make, or allow to become, straight | 3. To loosen
antares: 1. The principal star in Scorpio: -- called also the Scorpion's Heart
nucleated: 1. Having a nucleus | 2. Nucleate | 3. As, nucleated cells
coucher: 1. One who couches | 2. One who couches paper | 3. Etym: A factor or agent resident in a country for traffic. Blount. The book in which a corporation or other body registers its particular acts.  Cowell
cacotechny: 1. A corruption or corrupt state of art
exogen: 1. A plant belonging to one of the greater part of the vegetable kingdom, and which the plants are characterized by having c wood bark, and pith, the wood forming a layer between the other two, and increasing, if at all, by the animal addition of a new layer to the outside next to the bark. The leaves are commonly netted-veined, and the number of cotyledons is two, or, very rarely, several in a whorl. Cf. Endogen. Gray
paries: 1. The triangular middle part of each segment of the shell of a barnacle
hagberry: 1. A plant of the genus Prunus | 2. The bird cherry
translucency: 1. The quality or state of being translucent | 2. Clearness | 3. Partial transparency. Sir T. Browne
chain: 1. A series of links or rings, usually of metal, connected, or fitted into one another, used for various purposes, as of support, of restraint, of ornament, of the exertion and transmission of mechanical power, etc | 2. Put a chain of gold about his neck. Dan. v | 3. That which confines, fetters, or secures, as a chain
queencraft: 1. Craft or skill in policy on the part of a queen. Elizabeth showed much queencraft in procuring the votes of the nobility. Fuller
weakishness: 1. Quality or state of being weakish
cinnamon: 1. The inner bark of the shoots of Cinnamomum Zeylanicum, a tree growing in Ceylon. It is aromatic, of a moderately pungent taste, and is one of the best cordial, carminative, and restorative spices. Cassia. Cinnamon stone, a variety of garnet, of a cinnamon or hyacinth red color, sometimes used in jewelry. -- Oil of cinnamon, a colorless aromatic oil obtained from cinnamon and cassia, and consisting essentially of cinnamic aldehyde, C6H | 2. C2H | 3. CHO. -- Wild cinnamon. See Canella
enrockment: 1. A mass of large stones thrown into water at random to form bases of piers, breakwaters, etc
lure: 1. A contrivance somewhat resembling a bird, and often baited with raw meat | 2. -- used by falconers in recalling hawks. Shak | 3. Any enticement
cockup: 1. A large, highly esteemed, edible fish of India | 2. -- also called begti
linguacious: 1. Given to the use of the tongue | 2. Loquacious
bulbul: 1. The Persian nightingale. The name is also applied to several other Asiatic singing birds, of the family Timaliidæ. The green bulbuls belong to the Chloropsis and allied genera
gubernatorial: 1. Pertaining to a governor, or to government
meath: 1. A sweet liquor | 2. Mead.  Chaucer. Milton
grasp: 1. To seize and hold by clasping or embracing with the fingers or arms | 2. To catch to take possession of. Thy hand is made to grasp a palmer's staff. Shak | 3. To lay hold of with the mind
scorn: 1. Extreme and lofty contempt | 2. Haughty disregard | 3. That disdain which aprings from the opinion of the utter meanness and unworthiness of an object. Scorn at first makes after love the more. Shak. And wandered backward as in scorn, To wait an æon to be born. Emerson
alsatian:
1. Pertaining to Alsatia.

An inhabitant of Alsatia or Alsace in Germany, or of Alsatia or White Friars in London
misvalue: 1. To value wrongly or too little | 2. To undervalue. But for I am so young, I dread my work Wot be misvalued both of old and young. W. Browne
remember: 1. To have come into the mind again, as previously perceived, known, or felt | 2. To have a renewed apprehension of | 3. To bring to mind again
cantoris: 1. Of or pertaining to a cantor | 2. As, the cantoris side of a choir | 3. A cantoris stall. Shipley
monkey: 1. In the most general sense, any one of the Quadrumana, including apes, baboons, and lemurs. Any species of Quadrumana, except the lemurs. Any one of numerous species of Quadrumana (esp | 2. Such as have a long tail and prehensile feet) exclusive of apes and baboons. Note: The monkeys are often divided into three groups: Catarrhines, or Simidæ. These have an oblong head, with the oblique flat nostrils near together. Some have no tail, as the apes. All these are natives of the Old World. Platyrhines, or Cebidæ. These have a round head, with a broad nasal septum, so that the nostrils are wide apart and directed downward. The tail is often prehensile, and the thumb is short and not opposable. These are natives of the New World. Strepsorhines, or Lemuroidea. These have a pointed head with curved nostrils. They are natives of Southern Asia, Africa, and Madagascar | 3. A term of disapproval, ridicule, or contempt, as for mischievous child. This is the monkey's own giving out
dismail: 1. To divest of coat of mail. Spenser
pteropodous: 1. Of or pertaining to the Pteropoda
kee: 1. See Kie, Ky, and Kine.  Gay
predeterminate: 1. Determined beforehand | 2. As, the predeterminate counsel of God
dulcet: 1. Sweet to the taste | 2. Luscious.  She tempers dulcet creams. Milton | 3. Sweet to the ear
prepose: 1. To place or set before | 2. To prefix.  Fuller
diagnostics: 1. That part of medicine which has to do with ascertaining the nature of diseases by means of their symptoms or signs. His rare skill in diagnostics. Macaulay
lippitude: 1. Soreness of eyes | 2. The state of being blear-eyes | 3. Blearedness
microfarad: 1. The millionth part of a farad
shog:
1. A shock | 2. A jog | 3. A violent concussion or impulse. 

To shake
window: 1. An opening in the wall of a building for the admission of light and air, usually closed by casements or sashes containing some transparent material, as glass, and capable of being opened and shut at pleasure. I leaped from the window of the citadel. Shak. Then to come, in spite of sorrow, And at my window bid good morrow. Milton | 2. The shutter, casement, sash with its fittings, or other framework, which closes a window opening | 3. A figure formed of lines crossing each other.  Till he has windows on his bread and butter. King. French window, a casement window in two folds, usually reaching to the floor

Disappearing carriage, a carriage for heavy coast guns on which the gun is raised above the parapet for firing and upon discharge is lowered behind the parapet for protection. The levers are pivoted at their middle points, which are, with the top carriage, permitted restrained motion along the slightly inclined chassis rails. The counterweight is held in place by a pawl and ratchet. When the gun is loaded the pawl is released and the counterweight sinks, raising the gun to the firing position above the parapet. mechanics: 1. That science, or branch of applied mathematics, which treats of the action of forces on bodies. Note: That part of mechanics which considers the action of forces in producing rest or equilibrium is called statics | 2. That which relates to such action in producing motion is called dynamics. The term mechanics includes the action of forces on all bodies, whether solid, liquid, or gaseous. It is sometimes, however, and formerly was often, used distinctively of solid bodies only: The mechanics of liquid bodies is called also hydrostatics, or hydrodynamics, according as the laws of rest or of motion are considered. The mechanics of gaseous bodies is called also pneumatics. The mechanics of fluids in motion, with special reference to the methods of obtaining from them useful results, constitutes hydraulics. Animal mechanics, that portion of physiology which has for its object the investigation of the laws of equilibrium and motion in the animal body. The most important mechanical principle is that of the lever, the bones forming the arms of the levers, the contractile muscles the power, the joints the fulcra or points of support, while the weight of the body or of the individual limbs constitutes the weight or resistance. -- Applied mechanics, the principles of abstract mechanics applied to human art | 3. Also, the practical application of the laws of matter and motion to the construction of machines and structures of all kinds

overwet: 1. Excessive wetness.  Another ill accident is, overwet at sowing time. Bacon

tachygrapher: 1. One who writes shorthand | 2. A stenographer | 3. Esp., an ancient Greek or Roman notary
trope: 1. The use of a word or expression in a different sense from that which properly belongs to it | 2. In his frequent, long, and tedious speeches, it has been said that a trope never passed his lips. Bancroft. Note: Tropes are chiefly of four kinds: metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche, and irony. mesotheca: 1. The middle layer of the gonophore in the Hydrozoa

sugar: 1. A sweet white crystalline substance, of a sandy or granular consistency, obtained by crystallizing the evaporated juice of certain plants, as the sugar cane, sorghum, beet root, sugar maple, etc | 2. It is used for seasoning and preserving many kinds of food and drink. Ordinary sugar is essentially sucrose. See the Note below. Note: The term sugar includes several commercial grades, as the white or refined, granulated, loaf or lump, and the raw brown or muscovado. In a more general sense, it includes several distinct chemical compounds, as the glucoses, or grape sugars, and the sucroses, or true sugars. All sugars are carbohydrates. See Carbohydrate. The glucoses, or grape sugars, are ketone alcohols of the formula C6H12O6, and they turn the plane of polarization to the right or the left. They are produced from the amyloses and sucroses, as by the action of heat and acids of ferments, and are themselves decomposed by fermentation into alcohol and carbon dioxide. The only sugar as yet produced artificially belongs to this class. The sucroses, or cane sugars, are doubled glucose anhydrides of the formula C12H22O | 3. They are usually not fermentable as such, and they act on polarized light

falsetto: 1. A false or artificial voice | 2. That voice in a man which lies above his natural voice | 3. The male counter tenor or alto voice. See Head voice, under Voice
propagulum: 1. A runner terminated by a germinating bud
tabular: 1. Having the form of, or pertaining to, a table. Specifically: -- Having a flat surface | 2. As, a tabular rock. Formed into a succession of flakes | 3. Laminated. Nodules . . . that are tabular and plated. Woodward. Set in squares. Arranged in a schedule
uncase: 1. To take out of a case or covering | 2. To remove a case or covering from | 3. To uncover. L'Estrange
alkanet: 1. A dyeing matter extracted from the roots of Alkanna tinctoria, which gives a fine deep red color | 2. A boraginaceous herb yielding the dye | 3. Orchanet. The similar plant Anchusa officinalis
metamerism: 1. The symmetry of a metameric structure | 2. Serial symmetry | 3. The state of being made up of metameres
harmony: 1. The just adaptation of parts to each other, in any system or combination of things, or in things, or things intended to form a connected whole | 2. Such an agreement between the different parts of a design or composition as to produce unity of effect | 3. As, the harmony of the universe
pax: 1. The kiss of peace | 2. Also, the embrace in the sanctuary now substituted for it at High Mass in Roman Catholic churches | 3. A tablet or board, on which is a representation of Christ, of the Virgin Mary, or of some saint and which, in the Mass, was kissed by the priest and then by the people, in mediæval times
chime: 1. See Chine, n., | 2. The harmonious sound of bells, or of musical instruments. Instruments that made melodius chime. Milton | 3. A set of bells musically tuned to each other
working: 1. A & n. from Work. The word must cousin be to the working. Chaucer. Working beam. See Beam, n | 2. -- Working class, the class of people who are engaged in manual labor, or are dependent upon it for support | 3. Laborers
rapiered: 1. Wearing a rapier. "Scarletcoated, rapiered figures." Lowell
genoese: 1. Of or pertaining to Genoa, a city of Italy. -- n. sing. & pl.  A native or inhabitant of Genoa | 2. Collectively, the people of Genoa
diffission: 1. Act of cleaving or splitting.  Bailey
ammoniacal: 1. Of or pertaining to ammonia, or possessing its properties | 2. As, an ammoniac salt | 3. Ammoniacal gas
hellespont: 1. A narrow strait between Europe and Asia, now called the Daradanelles. It connects the Ægean Sea and the sea of Marmora
afterthought: 1. Reflection after an act | 2. Later or subsequent thought or expedient
bridler: 1. One who bridles | 2. One who restrains and governs, as with a bridle. Milton
campanula: 1. A large genus of plants bearing bell-shaped flowers, often of great beauty | 2. -- also called bellflower
secessionist: 1. One who upholds secession | 2. One who holds to the belief that a State has the right to separate from the Union at its will
stereotype: 1. A plate forming an exact faximile of a page of type or of an engraving, used in printing books, etc | 2. Specifically, a plate with type-metal face, used for printing. Note: A stereotype, or stereotypr plate, is made by setting movable type as for ordinary printing | 3. From these a cast is taken in plaster of Paris, paper pulp, or the like, and upon this cast melted type metal is poured, which, when hardened, makes a solid page or column, from which the impression is taken as from type
souterly: 1. Of or pertaining to a cobbler or cobblers | 2. Like a cobbler | 3. Hence, vulgar
thorax: 1. The part of the trunk between the neck and the abdomen, containing that part of the body cavity the walls of which are supported by the dorsal vertebræ, the ribs, and the sternum, and which the heart and lungs are situated | 2. The chest. Note: In mammals the thoracic cavity is completely separated from the abdominal by the diaphragm, but in birds and many reptiles the separation is incomplete, while in other reptiles, and in amphibians and fishes, there is no marked separation and no true thorax | 3. The middle region of the body of an insect, or that region which bears the legs and wings. It is composed of three united somites, each of which is composed of several distinct parts. See Illust. in Appendix. and Illust. of Coleoptera. The second, or middle, region of the body of a crustacean, arachnid, or other articulate animal. In the case of decapod Crustacea, some writers include under the term thorax only the three segments bearing the maxillipeds
gaidic: 1. Pertaining to hypogeic acid | 2. -- applied to an acid obtained from hypogeic acid
anomuran:
1. Irregular in the character of the tail or abdomen | 2. As, the anomural crustaceans. 

One of the Anomura
braying: 1. Making a harsh noise | 2. Blaring. "Braying trumpets." Shak
thunderous: 1. Producing thunder.  How he before the thunderous throne doth lie | 2. Milton | 3. Making a noise like thunder
beblood: 1. To make bloody | 2. To stain with blood.  Sheldon
toreumatography: 1. A description of sculpture such as bas-relief in metal
gaudery: 1. Finery | 2. Ornaments | 3. Ostentatious display.  "Tarnished gaudery." Dryden
redwithe: 1. A west Indian climbing shrub with slender reddish branchlets
interdiction: 1. The act of interdicting | 2. Prohibition | 3. Prohibiting decree
slade: 1. A little dell or valley | 2. A flat piece of low, moist ground.  Drayton | 3. The sole of a plow
roughly: 1. In a rough manner | 2. Unevenly | 3. Harshly
zooephyta: 1. An extensive artificial and heterogeneous group of animals, formerly adopted by many zoölogists. It included the coelenterates, echinoderms, sponges, Bryozoa, Protozoa, etc | 2. Note: Sometimes the name is restricted to the Coelentera, or to the Anthozoa
granny: 1. A grandmother | 2. A grandam | 3. Familiarly, an old woman. Granny's bend, or Granny's knot, a kind of insecure knot or hitch
mort:
1. A great quantity or number.  There was a mort of merrymaking. Dickens.

A woman | 2. A female.  Male gypsies all, not a mort among them. B. Jonson.

A salmon in its third year | 3. Death
gnide: 1. To rub | 2. To bruise | 3. To break in pieces.  Note: This word is found in Tyrwhitt's Chaucer, but improperly. The woed, though common in Old English, does not occur in Chaucer. T. R. Lounsbury
myrtaceous: 1. Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a large and important natural order of trees and shrubs, of which the myrtle is the type. It includes the genera Eucalyptus, Pimenta, Lechythis, and about seventy more
resultance: 1. The act of resulting | 2. That which results | 3. A result. Donne
sanhedrin: 1. The great council of the Jews, which consisted of seventy members, to whom the high priest was added. It had jurisdiction of religious matters
systematic: 1. Of or pertaining to system | 2. Consisting in system | 3. Methodical
hyperplastic: 1. Of or pertaining to hyperplasia | 2. Tending to excess of formative action
haulabout: 1. A bargelike vessel with steel hull, large hatchways, and coal transporters, for coaling war vessels from its own hold or from other colliers
lithotriptor: 1. An instrument for triturating the stone in the bladder | 2. A lithotrite
asyndeton: 1. A figure which omits the connective | 2. As, I came, I saw, I conquered. It stands opposed to polysyndeton
apollonic: 1. Of, pertaining to, or resembling, Apollo
filacer: 1. A former officer in the English Court of Common Pleas | 2. -- so called because he filed the writs on which he made out process.  Burrill
orchestian: 1. Any species of amphipod crustacean of the genus Orchestia, or family Orchestidæ. See Beach flea, under Beach
ensear: 1. To sear | 2. To dry up.  Ensear thy fertile and conceptious womb. Shak
kam: 1. Crooked | 2. Awry.  "This is clean kam." Shak
picot: 1. One of many small loops, as of thread, forming an ornamental border, as on a ribbon
assassin:
1. One who kills, or attempts to kill, by surprise or secret assault | 2. One who treacherously murders any one unprepared for defense.

To assassinate.  Stillingfleet
dinmont: 1. A wether sheep between one and two years old
front: 1. The forehead or brow, the part of the face above the eyes | 2. Sometimes, also, the whole face. Bless'd with his father's front, his mother's tongue. Pope. Grim-visaged war hath smoothed his wrinkled front. Shak. His front yet threatens, and his frowns command. Prior | 3. The forehead, countenance, or personal presence, as expressive of character or temper, and especially, of boldness of disposition, sometimes of impudence
encashment: 1. The payment in cash of a note, draft, etc
sight: 1. The act of seeing | 2. Perception of objects by the eye | 3. View
euphuist: 1. One who affects excessive refinement and elegance of language | 2. -- applied esp | 3. To a class of writers, in the age of Elizabeth, whose productions are marked by affected conceits and high-flown diction
bijoutry: 1. Small articles of virtu, as jewelry, trinkets, etc
imputability: 1. The quality of being imputable | 2. Imputableness
sublumbar: 1. Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the lumbar region of the vertebral column
wandering: 1. & n. from Wander, v. Wandering albatross, the great white albatross. See Illust. of Albatross. -- Wandering cell, an animal cell which possesses the power of spontaneous movement, as one of the white corpuscles of the blood. -- Wandering Jew, any one of several creeping species of Tradescantia, which have alternate, pointed leaves, and a soft, herbaceous stem which roots freely at the joints. They are commonly cultivated in hanging baskets, window boxes, etc | 2. -- Wandering kidney, a morbid condition in which one kidney, or, rarely, both kidneys, can be moved in certain directions | 3. -- called also floating kidney, movable kidney. -- Wandering liver, a morbid condition of the liver, similar to wandering kidney. -- Wandering mouse, the whitefooted, or deer, mouse. See Illust. of Mouse. -- Wandering spider, any one of a tribe of spiders that wander about in search of their prey
blancmanger: 1. A sort of fricassee with white sauce, variously made of capon, fish, etc | 2. Chaucer
feller:
1. One who, or that which, fells, knocks or cuts down | 2. A machine for felling trees.

An appliance to a sewing machine for felling a seam
decastere: 1. A measure of capacity, equal to ten steres, or ten cubic meters
hertzian: 1. Of or pert. to the German physicist Heinrich Hertz. Hertzian telegraphy, telegraphy by means of the Hertzian waves | 2. Wireless telegraphy. -- H. waves, electric waves | 3. -- so called because Hertz was the first to investigate them systematically. His apparatus consisted essentially in an oscillator for producing the waves, and a resonator for detecting them. The waves were found to have the same velocity as light, and to undergo reflection, refraction, and polarization
forficate: 1. Deeply forked, as the tail of certain birds
teaming: 1. The act or occupation of driving a team, or of hauling or carrying, as logs, goods, or the like, with a team | 2. Contract work.  Knight
drudge:
1. To perform menial work | 2. To labor in mean or unpleasant offices with toil and fatigue. He gradually rose in the estimation of the booksellers for whom he drudged. Macaulay.

To consume laboriously | 3. -- with away. Rise to our toils and drudge away the day
nuclein: 1. A constituent of the nuclei of all cells. It is a colorless amorphous substance, readily soluble in alkaline fluids and especially characterized by its comparatively large content of phosphorus. It also contains nitrogen and sulphur
stereotomic: 1. Of or pertaining to stereotomy | 2. Performed by stereotomy
peddle: 1. To travel about with wares for sale | 2. To go from place to place, or from house to house, for the purpose of retailing goods | 3. As, to peddle without a license
gelation: 1. The process of becoming solid by cooling | 2. A cooling and solidifying
homoioptoton: 1. A figure in which the several parts of a sentence end with the same case, or inflection generally
lymphography: 1. A description of the lymphatic vessels, their origin and uses
dextronic: 1. Pertaining to, or derived from, dextrose | 2. As, dextronic acid. Dextronic acid, a sirupy substance obtained by the partial oxidation of various carbohydrates, as dextrose, etc
achromatin: 1. Tissue which is not stained by fluid dyes. W. Flemming
noblesse: 1. Dignity | 2. Greatness | 3. Noble birth or condition.  Chaucer. Spenser. B. Jonson
plangent: 1. Beating | 2. Dashing, as a wave.  "The plangent wave." H. Taylor
legislatorship: 1. The office of a legislator. Halifax
wort:
1. A plant of any kind. Note: This word is now chiefly used in combination, as in colewort, figwort, St. John's-wort, woundwort, etc | 2. Pl.  Cabbages.

An infusion of malt which is unfermented, or is in the act of fermentation | 3. The sweet infusion of malt, which ferments and forms beer
proteid: 1. One of a class of amorphous nitrogenous principles, containing, as a rule, a small amount of sulphur | 2. An albuminoid, as blood fibrin, casein of milk, etc | 3. Proteids are present in nearly all animal fluids and make up the greater part of animal tissues and organs. They are also important constituents of vegetable tissues. See 2d Note under Food. -- Pro"te*id, a
bipupillate: 1. Having an eyelike spot on the wing, with two dots within it of a different color, as in some butterflies
castellated: 1. Inclosed within a building | 2. As, a fountain or cistern castellated.  Johnson | 3. Furnished with turrets and battlements, like a castle
variolite: 1. A kind of diorite or diabase containing imbedded whitish spherules, which give the rock a spotted appearance
defile: 1. To march off in a line, file by file | 2. To file off | 3. Same as Defilade
adjunction: 1. The act of joining | 2. The thing joined or added
catamite: 1. A boy kept for unnatural purposes
boer: 1. A colonist or farmer in South Africa of Dutch descent
archership: 1. The art or skill of an archer
shamoying: 1. A process used in preparing certain kinds of leather, which consists in frizzing the skin, and working oil into it to supply the place of the astringent ordinarily used in tanning
clarification: 1. The act or process of making clear or transparent, by freeing visible impurities | 2. As, the clarification of wine | 3. The act of freeing from obscurities. The clarification of men's ideas. Whewell
inosculate: 1. To unite by apposition or contact, as two tubular vessels at their extremities | 2. To anastomose | 3. To intercommunicate
parget: 1. To coat with parget | 2. To plaster, as walls, or the interior of flues | 3. As, to parget the outside of their houses. Sir T. Herbert. The pargeted ceiling with pendants. R. L. Stevenson
bucker: 1. One who bucks ore | 2. A broad-headed hammer used in bucking ore | 3. A horse or mule that bucks
twit: 1. To vex by bringing to notice, or reminding of, a fault, defect, misfortune, or the like | 2. To revile | 3. To reproach
shoreless: 1. Having no shore or coast | 2. Of indefinite or unlimited extent | 3. As, a shoreless ocean. Young
rhynchonella: 1. A genus of brachiopods of which some species are still living, while many are found fossil
anglicanism: 1. Strong partiality to the principles and rites of the Church of England | 2. The principles of the established church of England | 3. Also, in a restricted sense, the doctrines held by the high-church party
vocalization: 1. The act of vocalizing, or the state of being vocalized | 2. The formation and utterance of vocal sounds
dashing: 1. Bold | 2. Spirited | 3. Showy. The dashing and daring spirit is preferable to the listless. T. Campbell
tritheistical: 1. Of or pertaining to tritheism. Bolingbroke
lungfish: 1. Any fish belonging to the Dipnoi | 2. -- so called because they have both lungs and gills
taproom: 1. A room where liquors are kept on tap | 2. A barroom. The ambassador was put one night into a miserable taproom, full of soldiers smoking. Macaulay
sworder: 1. One who uses, or fights with, a sword | 2. A swordsman | 3. A soldier
cytoplasm: 1. The substance of the body of a cell, as distinguished from the karyoplasma, or substance of the nucleus. -- Cy`to*plas"mic (-pl, a
forebrace: 1. A rope applied to the fore yardarm, to change the position of the foresail
alt: 1. The higher part of the scale. See Alto. To be in alt, to be in an exalted state of mind
sagittary: 1. A centaur | 2. A fabulous being, half man, half horse, armed with a bow and quiver. Shak | 3. The Arsenal in Venice
dimmy: 1. Somewhat dim | 2. As, dimmish eyes. "Dimmy clouds." Sir P. Sidney
epidotic: 1. Related to, resembling, or containing epidote | 2. As, an epidotic granite
westwards: 1. Toward the west | 2. As, to ride or sail westward. Westward the course of empire takes its way | 3. Berkeley
monotriglyph: 1. A kind of intercolumniation in an entablature, in which only one triglyph and two metopes are introduced
wasite: 1. A variety of allanite from Sweden supposed to contain wasium
adherency: 1. The state or quality of being adherent | 2. Adherence | 3. That which adheres.  Dr. H. More
liken: 1. To allege, or think, to be like | 2. To represent as like | 3. To compare
entoplastic: 1. Pertaining to, or composed of, entoplasm | 2. As, the entoplastic products of some Protozoa, or the entoplastic modification of the cell protoplasm, by which a nucleus is produced
tergal: 1. Of or pertaining to back, or tergum. See Dorsal
socialist:
1. One who advocates or practices the doctrines of socialism.

Pertaining to, or of the nature of, socialism
polyporus: 1. A genus of fungi having the under surface full of minute pores | 2. Also, any fungus of this genus. Note: Polyporus fomentarius was formerly dried and cut in slices for tinder, called amadou. P. betulinus is common in America, and forms very large thick white semicircular excrescences on birch trees. Several species of Polyporous are considered edible
anthroponomics: 1. The science of the laws of the development of the human organism in relation to other organisms and to environment. -- An`thro*po*nom"ic*al, a
logical: 1. Of or pertaining to logic | 2. Used in logic | 3. As, logical subtilties. Bacon
acceptance: 1. The act of accepting | 2. A receiving what is offered, with approbation, satisfaction, or acquiescence | 3. Esp., favorable reception
ineptly: 1. Unfitly | 2. Unsuitably | 3. Awkwardly. None of them are made foolishly or ineptly. Dr. H. More
install: 1. To set in a seat | 2. To give a place to | 3. Establish in a place. She installed her guest hospitably by the fireside. Sir W. Scott
ineffectively: 1. In an ineffective manner | 2. Without effect | 3. Inefficiently
forester: 1. One who has charge of the growing timber on an estate | 2. An officer appointed to watch a forest and preserve the game | 3. An inhabitant of a forest. Wordsworth
mediaevalism: 1. The method or spirit of the Middle Ages | 2. Devotion to the institutions and practices of the Middle Ages | 3. A survival from the Middle Ages
littoral: 1. Of or pertaining to a shore, as of the sea | 2. Inhabiting the seashore, esp | 3. The zone between high-water and low-water mark
aggrege: 1. To make heavy | 2. To aggravate.  Chaucer
tripudiary: 1. Of or pertaining to dancing | 2. Performed by dancing.  " Tripudiary augurations." Sir T. Browne
ostosis: 1. Bone formation | 2. Ossification. See Ectostosis, and Endostosis
aband: 1. To abandon.  Enforced the kingdom to aband. Spenser | 2. To banish | 3. To expel.  Mir. for Mag
thermolysis: 1. The resolution of a compound into parts by heat | 2. Dissociation by heat
islam: 1. The religion of the Mohammedans | 2. Mohammedanism | 3. Islamism. Their formula of faith is: There is no God but Allah, and Mohammed is his prophet
emotionalize: 1. To give an emotional character to. Brought up in a pious family where religion was not talked about emotionalized, but was accepted as the rule of thought and conduct. Froude
retranslate: 1. To translate anew | 2. Especially, to translate back into the original language
maniac: 1. Raving with madness | 2. Raging with disordered intellect | 3. Affected with mania
pomologist: 1. One versed in pomology | 2. One who culticvates fruit trees
achromatization: 1. The act or process of achromatizing
ringer:
1. One who, or that which, rings | 2. Especially, one who rings chimes on bells | 3. A crowbar. Simmonds.

A horse that is not entitled to take part in a race, but is fraudulently got into it
twig: 1. To twitch | 2. To pull | 3. To tweak
endways: 1. On end | 2. Erectly | 3. In an upright position
unagreeable: 1. Disagreeable | 2. Not agreeing or consistent | 3. Unsuitable. Shak. -- Un`a*gree"a*ble*ness, n. -- Un`a*gree"a*bly, adv
stingray: 1. Any one of numerous rays of the family Dasyatidæ, syn | 2. Trygonidæ, having one or more large sharp barbed dorsal spines, on the whiplike tail, capable of inflicting severe wounds. Some species reach a large size, and some, esp., on the American Pacific coast, are very destructive to oysters
steeper: 1. A vessel, vat, or cistern, in which things are steeped
beating: 1. The act of striking or giving blows | 2. Punishment or chastisement by blows | 3. Pulsation
neocosmic: 1. Of or pertaining to the universe in its present state | 2. Specifically, pertaining to the races of men known to history
transported: 1. Conveyed from one place to another | 2. Figuratively, carried away with passion or pleasure | 3. Entranced. -- Trans*port"ed*ly, adv
clean: 1. Free from dirt or filth | 2. As, clean clothes | 3. Free from that which is useless or injurious
corded: 1. Bound or fastened with cords | 2. Piled in a form for measurement by the cord | 3. Made of cords.  "A corded ladder." Shak
lithoclast: 1. An instrument for crushing stones in the bladder
reconnoissance: 1. The act of reconnoitering | 2. Preliminary examination or survey. Specifically: An examination or survey of a region in reference to its general geological character.  An examination of a region as to its general natural features, preparatory to a more particular survey for the purposes of triangulation, or of determining the location of a public work. An examination of a territory, or of an enemy's position, for the purpose of obtaining information necessary for directing military operations | 3. A preparatory expedition. Reconnoissance in force, a demonstration or attack by a large force of troops for the purpose of discovering the position and strength of an enemy
infection: 1. The act or process of infecting. There was a strict order against coming to those pits, and that was only to prevent infection. De Foe | 2. That which infects, or causes the communicated disease | 3. Any effluvium, miasm, or pestilential matter by which an infectious disease is caused. And that which was still worse, they that did thus break out spread the infection further by their wandering about with the distemper upon them. De Foe
dislink: 1. To unlink | 2. To disunite | 3. To separate.  Tennyson
propaedeutics: 1. The preliminary learning connected with any art or science | 2. Preparatory instruction
perdix: 1. A genus of birds including the common European partridge. Formerly the word was used in a much wider sense to include many allied genera
shovelboard: 1. A board on which a game is played, by pushing or driving pieces of metal or money to reach certain marks | 2. Also, the game itself. Called also shuffleboard, shoveboard, shovegroat, shovelpenny | 3. A game played on board ship in which the aim is to shove or drive with a cue wooden disks into divisions chalked on the deck
ferruminate: 1. To solder or unite, as metals.  Coleridge
unmingle: 1. To separate, as things mixed. Bacon
gratitude: 1. The state of being grateful | 2. Warm and friendly feeling toward a benefactor | 3. Kindness awakened by a favor received
sinistrality: 1. The quality or state of being sinistral
donax: 1. A canelike grass of southern Europe, used for fishing rods, etc
ruly: 1. Orderly | 2. Easily restrained | 3. -- opposed to Ant: unruly.  Gascoigne
waspish: 1. Resembling a wasp in form | 2. Having a slender waist, like a wasp | 3. Quick to resent a trifling affront
tenant: 1. One who holds or possesses lands, or other real estate, by any kind of right, whether in fee simple, in common, in severalty, for life, for years, or at will | 2. Also, one who has the occupation or temporary possession of lands or tenements the title of which is in another | 3. -- correlative to landlord. See Citation from Blackstone, under Tenement,
breathful: 1. Full of breath | 2. Full of odor | 3. Fragrant
eulogist: 1. One who eulogizes or praises | 2. Panegyrist | 3. Encomiast. Buckle
immolation: 1. The act of immolating, or the state of being immolated, or sacrificed. Sir. T. Browne | 2. That which is immolated | 3. A sacrifice
thawy: 1. Liquefying by heat after having been frozen | 2. Thawing | 3. Melting
decrepitude: 1. The broken state produced by decay and the infirmities of age | 2. Infirm old age
dinoceras: 1. A genus of large extinct Eocene mammals from Wyoming | 2. -- called also Uintatherium. See Illustration in Appendix. Note: They were herbivorous, and remarkable for three pairs of hornlike protuberances on the skull. The males were armed with a pair of powerful canine tusks
loaf:
1. Any thick lump, mass, or cake | 2. Especially, a large regularly shaped or molded mass, as of bread, sugar, or cake. Bacon. Loaf sugar, refined sugar that has been formed into a conical loaf in a mold.

To spend time in idleness | 3. To lounge or loiter about. " Loafing vagabonds." W. Black.

To spend in idleness
proneness: 1. The quality or state of being prone, or of bending downward | 2. As, the proneness of beasts is opposed to the erectness of man | 3. The state of lying with the face down
racy: 1. Having a strong flavor indicating origin | 2. Of distinct characteristic taste | 3. Tasting of the soil
cantharidin: 1. The active principe of the cantharis, or Spanish fly, a volatile, acrid, bitter solid, crystallizing in four-sided prisms
nibelungenlied: 1. A great medieval German epic of unknown authorship containing traditions which refer to the Burgundians at the time of Attila and mythological elements pointing to heathen times
ho:
1. Who.  In some Chaucer MSS.

A stop | 2. A halt | 3. A moderation of pace. There is no ho with them. Decker
irrelavant: 1. Not relevant | 2. Not applicable or pertinent | 3. Not bearing upon or serving to support
sicken: 1. To make sick | 2. To disease. Raise this strength, and sicken that to death. Prior | 3. To make qualmish
subeditor: 1. An assistant editor, as of a periodical or journal
acclivity: 1. A slope or inclination of the earth, as the side of a hill, considered as ascending, in opposition to declivity, or descending | 2. An upward slope | 3. Ascent
ped: 1. A basket | 2. A hammer | 3. A pannier.  Halliwell
anthorism: 1. A description or definition contrary to that which is given by the adverse party
circumference: 1. The line that goes round or encompasses a circular figure | 2. A periphery. Millon | 3. A circle
landowning: 1. The owning of land. -- a.  Having property in land | 2. Of or pertaining to landowners
insubjection: 1. Want of subjection or obedience | 2. A state of disobedience, as to government
histophyly: 1. The tribal history of cells, a division of morphophyly. Haeckel
posit: 1. To dispose or set firmly or fixedly | 2. To place or dispose in relation to other objects. Sir M. Hale | 3. To assume as real or conceded
jaina: 1. One of a numerous sect in British India, holding the tenets of Jainism
purpurogenous: 1. Having the power to produce a purple color | 2. As, the purpurogenous membrane, or choroidal epithelium, of the eye | 3. See Visual purple, under Visual
context:
1. Knit or woven together | 2. Close | 3. Firm.  The coats, without, are context and callous. Derham.

The part or parts of something written or printed, as of Scripture, which precede or follow a text or quoted sentence, or are so intimately associated with it as to throw light upon its meaning. According to all the light that the contexts afford. Sharp.

To knit or bind together
laundry: 1. A laundering | 2. A washing | 3. A place or room where laundering is done
tripalmitate: 1. A palmitate derived from three molecules of palmitic acid
flittermouse: 1. A bat | 2. -- called also flickermouse, flindermouse, and flintymouse
victimize: 1. To make a victim of, esp | 2. By deception | 3. To dupe
spellwork: 1. Power or effect of magic | 2. That which is wrought by magic | 3. Enchantment. Like those Peri isles of light That hang by spellwork in the air
pernor: 1. One who receives the profits, as of an estate
canonship: 1. Of pertaining to Canopus in egypt | 2. As, the Canopic vases, used in embalming
cockneydom: 1. The region or home of cockneys | 2. Cockneys, collectively. Thackeray

Each of these cells is filled with, fluid, and contains a long, slender, often barbed, hollow thread coiled up within it. When the cell contracts the thread is quickly ejected, being at the same time turned inside out | 3. leaf: 1. A colored, usually green, expansion growing from the side of a stem or rootstock, in which the sap for the use of the plant is elaborated under the influence of light | 2. Note: Such leaves usually consist of a blade, or lamina , supported upon a leafstalk or petiole, which, continued through the blade as the midrib, gives off woody ribs and veins that support the cellular texture. The petiole has usually some sort of an appendage on each side of its base, which is called the stipule. The green parenchyma of the leaf is covered with a thin epiderm pierced with closable microscopic openings, known as stomata | 3. A special organ of vegetation in the form of a lateral outgrowth from the stem, whether appearing as a part of the foliage, or as a cotyledon, a scale, a bract, a spine, or a tendril. disfurnish: 1. To deprive of that with which anything is furnished | 2. To strip | 3. To render destitute
pectous: 1. Of, pertaining to, or consisting of, pectose
humanity: 1. The quality of being human | 2. The peculiar nature of man, by which he is distinguished from other beings | 3. Mankind collectively
unmeasurable: 1. Immeasurable. Swift. -- Un*meas"ur*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*meas"ur*a*bly, adv
refringent: 1. Pertaining to, or possessing, refringency | 2. Refractive | 3. Refracting
compart: 1. To divide | 2. To mark out into parts or subdivisions.  The crystal surface is comparted all In niches verged with rubies. Glover
hotchpot: 1. A mingled mass | 2. A confused mixture | 3. A stew of various ingredients
venetian: 1. Of or pertaining to Venice in Italy.
