The pattern is therefore commonly made up of simple stripes. -- Venetian chalk, a white compact or steatite, used for marking on cloth, etc | 3. -- Venetian door, a door having long, narrow windows or panes of glass on the sides. -- Venetian glass, a kind of glass made by the Venetians, for decorative purposes, by the combination of pieces of glass of different colors fused together and wrought into various ornamental patterns. -- Venetian red, a brownish red color, prepared from sulphate of iron
frankly: 1. In a frank manner | 2. Freely. Very frankly he confessed his treasons. Shak. Syn. -- Openly | 3. Ingenuously
diablerie: 1. Devilry | 2. Sorcery or incantation | 3. A diabolical deed
overcast: 1. To cast or cover over | 2. Hence, to cloud | 3. To darken. Those clouds that overcast your morn shall fly
anisopoda: 1. A division of Crustacea, which, in some its characteristics, is intermediate between Amphipoda and Isopoda
voltairean: 1. Of or relating to Voltaire, the French author. J. Morley
actinoid: 1. Having the form of rays | 2. Radiated, as an actinia
pleurocarpic: 1. Side-fruited | 2. -- said of those true mosses in which the pedicels or the capsules are from lateral archegonia | 3. -- opposed to Ant: acrocarpous
tapish: 1. To lie close to the ground, so as to be concealed | 2. To squat | 3. To crouch
verbena: 1. A genus of herbaceous plants of which several species are extensively cultivated for the great beauty of their flowers | 2. Vervain. Note: Verbena, or vervain, was used by the Greeks, the Romans, and the Druids, in their sacred rites. Brewer. Essence of verbena, Oil of verbena, a perfume prepared from the lemon verbena | 3. Also, a similar perfume properly called grass oil
paging: 1. The marking or numbering of the pages of a book
pomander: 1. A perfume to be carried with one, often in the form of a ball. A box to contain such perfume, formerly carried by ladies, as at the end of a chain | 2. -- more properly pomander box | 3. Bacon
achromatopsy: 1. Color blindness | 2. Inability to distinguish colors | 3. Daltonism
inlapidate: 1. To convert into a stony substance | 2. To petrity.  Bacon
coalmouse: 1. A small species of titmouse, with a black head | 2. The coletit
plowbote: 1. Wood or timber allowed to a tenant for the repair of instruments of husbandry. See Bote
shuttlecock:
1. A cork stuck with feathers, which is to be struck by a battledoor in play | 2. Also, the play itself.

To send or toss to and fro | 3. To bandy
subaudition: 1. The act of understanding, or supplying, something not expressed | 2. Also, that which is so understood or supplied. Trench
nugify: 1. To render trifling or futile | 2. To make silly.  Coleridge
ehlite: 1. A mineral of a green color and pearly luster | 2. A hydrous phosphate of copper
downward: 1. From a higher place to a lower | 2. In a descending course | 3. As, to tend, move, roll, look, or take root, downward or downwards. "Looking downwards." Pope. Their heads they downward bent. Drayton
vicinal: 1. Near | 2. Vicine. T. Warton. Vicinal planes, subordinate planes on a crystal, which are very near to the fundamental planes in angles, and sometimes take their place. They have in general very complex symbols
careen:
1. To cause to lean over so that she floats on one side, leaving the other side out of water and accessible for repairs below the water line | 2. To case to be off the keel.

To incline to one side, or lie over, as a ship when sailing on a wind | 3. To be off the keel
mease: 1. Five hundred | 2. As, a mease of herrings
traitor: 1. One who violates his allegiance and betrays his country | 2. One guilty of treason | 3. One who, in breach of trust, delivers his country to an enemy, or yields up any fort or place intrusted to his defense, or surrenders an army or body of troops to the enemy, unless when vanquished
cirrigerous: 1. Having curled locks of hair | 2. Supporting cirri, or hairlike appendages
chucklehead: 1. A person with a large head | 2. A numskull | 3. A dunce.  Knowles
pedimental: 1. Of or pertaining to a pediment
stramonium: 1. A poisonous plant | 2. Stinkweed. See Datura, and Jamestown weed
power: 1. Same as Poor, the fish | 2. Ability to act, regarded as latent or inherent | 3. The faculty of doing or performing something
unboot: 1. To take off the boots from
gillie: 1. A boy or young man | 2. A manservant | 3. A male attendant, in the Scottish Highlands. Sir W. Scott
placoganoidei: 1. A division of ganoid fishes including those that have large external bony plates and a cartilaginous skeleton
alisanders: 1. A name given to two species of the genus Smyrnium, formerly cultivated and used as celery now is | 2. -- called also horse parsely
trousering: 1. Cloth or material for making trousers
ectoprocta: 1. An order of Bryozoa in which the anus lies outside the circle of tentacles
advertise: 1. To give notice to | 2. To inform or apprise | 3. To notify
kindliness: 1. Natural inclination | 2. Natural course.  Milton | 3. The quality or state of being kindly
baboon: 1. One of the Old World Quadrumana, of the genera Cynocephalus and Papio | 2. The dog-faced ape | 3. Baboons have dog-like muzzles and large canine teeth, cheek pouches, a short tail, and naked callosities on the buttocks. They are mostly African. See Mandrill, and Chacma, and Drill an ape
roomless: 1. Being without room or rooms. Udall
stalactitiform: 1. Having the form of a stalactite | 2. Stalactiform
apodes: 1. An order of fishes without ventral fins, including the eels. A group of holothurians destitute of suckers. See Apneumona
veratrine: 1. A poisonous alkaloid obtained from the root hellebore and from sabadilla seeds as a white crystalline powder, having an acrid, burning taste. It is sometimes used externally, as in ointments, in the local treatment of neuralgia and rheumatism. Called also veratria, and veratrina
syrup:
1. A thick and viscid liquid made from the juice of fruits, herbs, etc., boiled with sugar | 2. A thick and viscid saccharine solution of superior quality | 3. Specifically, in pharmacy and often in cookery, a saturated solution of sugar and water, or such a solution flavored or medicated. Lucent sirups tinct with cinnamon. Keats. Mixing sirup. See the Note under Dextrose.

Same as Sirup, Sirupy
officeholder: 1. An officer, particularly one in the civil service | 2. A placeman
persulphide: 1. A sulphide containing more sulphur than some other compound of the same elements | 2. As, iron pyrites is a persulphide | 3. -- formerly called persulphuret
faction: 1. One of the divisions or parties of charioteers in the games of the circus | 2. A party, in political society, combined or acting in union, in opposition to the government, or state | 3. -- usually applied to a minority, but it may be applied to a majority
ishmaelite: 1. A descendant of Ishmael, of whom it was said, "His hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him." Gen. xvi | 2. One at enmity with society | 3. A wanderer
gynophore: 1. The pedicel raising the pistil or ovary above the stamens, as in the passion flower. Lindley | 2. One of the branches bearing the female gonophores, in certain Siphonophora
serpula: 1. Any one of numerous species of tubicolous annelids of the genus Serpula and allied genera of the family Serpulidæ. They secrete a calcareous tube, which is usually irregularly contorted, but is sometimes spirally coiled. The worm has a wreath of plumelike and often bright-colored gills around its head, and usually an operculum to close the aperture of its tube when it retracts
discretive: 1. Marking distinction or separation | 2. Disjunctive. Discretive proposition, one that expresses distinction, opposition, or variety, by means of discretive particles, as but, though, yet, etc | 3. As, travelers change their climate, but not their temper
jehovistic: 1. Relating to, or containing, Jehovah, as a name of God | 2. -- said of certain parts of the Old Testament, especially of the Pentateuch, in which Jehovah appears as the name of the Deity. See Elohistic
facinorous: 1. Atrociously wicked.  Jer. Taylor. -- Fa*cin"o*rous*ness, n
sorbition: 1. The act of drinking or sipping
columbite: 1. A mineral of a black color, submetallic luster, and high specific specific gravity. It is a niobate of iron and manganese, containing tantalate of iron | 2. -- first found in New England
gerbille: 1. One of several species of small, jumping, murine rodents, of the genus Gerbillus. In their leaping powers they resemble the jerboa. They inhabit Africa, India, and Southern Europe
swearer: 1. One who swears | 2. One who calls God to witness for the truth of his declaration | 3. A profane person
glower: 1. To look intently | 2. To stare angrily or with a scowl. Thackeray
nosing: 1. That part of the treadboard of a stair which projects over the riser | 2. Hence, any like projection, as the projecting edge of a molding
drone: 1. The male of bees, esp | 2. Of the honeybee. It gathers no honey. See Honeybee. All with united force combine to drive The lazy drones from the laborious hive. Dryden | 3. One who lives on the labors of others
quadruply: 1. To a fourfold quantity | 2. So as to be, or cause to be, quadruple | 3. As, to be quadruply recompensed
prosector: 1. One who makes dissections for anatomical illustration | 2. Usually, the assistant of a professional anatomist
temporalty: 1. The laity | 2. Secular people.  Abp. Abbot | 3. A secular possession
quantitive: 1. Estimable according to quantity | 2. Quantitative. Sir K. Digby
virtuosity: 1. The quality or state of being a virtuoso | 2. In a bad sense, the character of one in whom mere artistic feeling or æsthetic cultivation takes the place of religious character | 3. Sentimentalism. This famous passage . . . over which the virtuosity of modern times, rejoicing in evil, has hung so fondly. C. Kingsley
copepoda: 1. An order of Entomastraca, including many minute Crustacea, both freshwater and marine. Note: They have a distinct carapace. The eggs are carried in a pair of external pouches. Some are parasites of fishes
specificate: 1. To show, mark, or designate the species, or the distinguishing particulars of | 2. To specify.  ir M. Hale
hypermetropia: 1. A condition of the eye in which, through shortness of the eyeball or fault of the refractive media, the rays of light come to a focus behind the retina | 2. Farsightedness | 3. -- called also hyperopia. Cf. Emmetropia. Note: In hypermetropia, vision for distant objects, although not better absolutely, is better than that for near objects, and hence, the individual is said to be farsighted. It is corrected by the use of convex glasses. -- Hy`per*me*trop"ic, a
observe: 1. To take notice of by appropriate conduct | 2. To conform one's action or practice to | 3. To keep
spectacular: 1. Of or pertaining to a shows | 2. Of the nature of a show. "Spectacular sports." G. Hickes | 3. Adapted to excite wonder and admiration by a display of pomp or of scenic effects
exarch: 1. A viceroy | 2. In Ravenna, the title of the viceroys of the Byzantine emperors | 3. In the Eastern Church, the superior over several monasteries
extension: 1. The act of extending or the state of being extended | 2. A stretching out | 3. Enlargement in breadth or continuation of length
cordelle: 1. A twisted cord | 2. A tassel. Halliwell
millet: 1. The name of several cereal and forage grasses which bear an abundance of small roundish grains. The common millets of Germany and Southern Europe are Panicum miliaceum, and Setaria Italica. Note: Arabian millet is Sorghum Halepense. -- Egyptian or East Indian, millet is Penicillaria spicata. -- Indian millet is Sorghum vulgare. -- Italian millet is Setaria Italica, a coarse, rank-growing annual grass, valuable for fodder when cut young, and bearing nutritive seeds | 2. -- called also Hungarian grass. -- Texas millet is Panicum Texanum. -- Wild millet, or Millet grass, is Milium effusum, a tail grass growing in woods
seaming: 1. The act or process of forming a seam or joint | 2. The cord or rope at the margin of a seine, to which the meshes of the net are attached. Seaming machine, a machine for uniting the edges of sheet-metal plates by bending them and pinching them together
pickle: 1. See Picle | 2. A solution of salt and water, in which fish, meat, etc., may be preserved or corned | 3. Brine. Vinegar, plain or spiced, used for preserving vegetables, fish, eggs, oysters, etc
toxicant: 1. A poisonous agent or drug, as opium | 2. An intoxicant
push: 1. A pustule | 2. A pimple.  Bacon | 3. To press against with force
menhir: 1. A large stone set upright in olden times as a memorial or monument. Many, of unknown date, are found in Brittany and throughout Northern Europe
intellectualist: 1. One who overrates the importance of the understanding.  Bacon | 2. One who accepts the doctrine of intellectualism
tolerate: 1. To suffer to be, or to be done, without prohibition or hindrance | 2. To allow or permit negatively, by not preventing | 3. Not to restrain
interatomic: 1. Between atoms | 2. Situated, or acting, between the atoms of bodies | 3. As, interatomic forces
hedonism: 1. The doctrine of the Hedonic sect | 2. The ethical theory which finds the explanation and authority of duty in its tendency to give pleasure
pernoctation: 1. The act or state of passing the whole night | 2. A remaining all night. "Pernoctation in prayer." Jer. Taylor
neathouse: 1. A building for the shelter of neat cattle.  Massinger
besetment: 1. The act of besetting, or the state of being beset | 2. Also, that which besets one, as a sin | 3. "Fearing a besetment." Kane
caribbee:
1. Of or pertaining to the Caribs, to their islands, or to the sea lying between those islands and Central America.

A Carib
emanate: 1. To issue forth from a source | 2. To flow out from more or less constantly | 3. As, fragrance emanates from flowers
confer: 1. To bring together for comparison | 2. To compare.  If we confer these observations with others of the like nature, we may find cause to rectify the general opinion. Boyle | 3. To grant as a possession
discouragement: 1. The act of discouraging, or the state of being discouraged | 2. Depression or weakening of confidence | 3. Dejection
lithotriptist: 1. One skilled in breaking and extracting stone in the bladder
spongilla: 1. A genus of siliceous spongea found in fresh water
retail:
1. The sale of commodities in small quantities or parcels | 2. -- opposed to wholesale | 3. Sometimes, the sale of commodities at second hand.

Done at retail
omphalomesenteric: 1. Of or pertaining to the umbilicus and mesentery | 2. Omphalomesaraic | 3. As, the omphalomesenteric arteries and veins of a fetus
pup:
1. A young dog | 2. A puppy. a young seal.

To bring forth whelps or young, as the female of the canine species
sophisticated: 1. Adulterated | 2. Not pure | 3. Not genuine. So truth, while only one supplied the state, Grew scare and dear, and yet sophisticate. Dryden
oculina: 1. A genus of tropical corals, usually branched, and having a very volid texture
polyhedron: 1. A body or solid contained by many sides or planes | 2. A polyscope, or multiplying glass
cymoscope: 1. Any device for detecting the presence of electric waves. The influence of electric waves on the resistance of a particular kind of electric circuit, on the magnetization of steel, on the polarization of an electrolytic cell, or on the electric condition of a vacuum has been applied in the various cymoscopes
deftness: 1. The quality of being deft. Drayton
lamelliferous: 1. Bearing, or composed of, lamellæ, or thin layers, plates, or scales | 2. Foliated
bevel: 1. Any angle other than a right angle | 2. The angle which one surface makes with another when they are not at right angles | 3. The slant or inclination of such surface
knight: 1. A young servant or follower | 2. A military attendant | 3. In feudal times, a man-at-arms serving on horseback and admitted to a certain military rank with special ceremonies, including an oath to protect the distressed, maintain the right, and live a stainless life. One on whom knighthood, a dignity next below that of baronet, is conferred by the sovereign, entitling him to be addressed as Sir
leisurable: 1. Leisurely.  Hooker | 2. Vacant of employment | 3. Not occupied
warrantise:
1. Authority | 2. Security | 3. Warranty.  Shak.

To warrant.  Hakluyt
mislike: 1. To dislike | 2. To disapprove of | 3. To have aversion to
customableness: 1. Quality of being customable | 2. Conformity to custom
jervine: 1. A poisonous alkaloid resembling veratrine, and found with it in white hellebore | 2. -- called also jervina
pericellular: 1. Surrounding a cell | 2. As, the pericellular lymph spaces surrounding ganglion cells
diamide: 1. Any compound containing two amido groups united with one or more acid or negative radicals, -- as distinguished from a diamine. Cf. Amido acid, under Amido, and Acid amide, under Amide
permissive: 1. Permitting | 2. Granting leave or liberty. "By his permissive will." Milton | 3. Permitted
metasomatism: 1. An alteration in a mineral or rock mass when involving a chemical change of the substance, as of chrysolite to serpentine | 2. -- opposed to ordinary metamorphism, as implying simply a recrystallization. -- Met`a*so*mat"ic, a
defective: 1. Wanting in something | 2. Incomplete | 3. Lacking a part
inheritance: 1. The act or state of inheriting | 2. As, the inheritance of an estate | 3. The inheritance of mental or physical qualities
allusion: 1. A figurative or symbolical reference | 2. A reference to something supposed to be known, but not explicitly mentioned | 3. A covert indication
hairen: 1. Hairy.  His hairen shirt and his ascetic diet. J. Taylor
frankincense: 1. A fragrant, aromatic resin, or gum resin, burned as an incense in religious rites or for medicinal fumigation. The best kinds now come from East Indian trees, of the genus Boswellia | 2. A commoner sort, from the Norway spruce and other coniferous trees. The frankincense of the ancient Jews is still unidentified
umbrella: 1. A shade, screen, or guard, carried in the hand for sheltering the person from the rays of the sun, or from rain or snow. It is formed of silk, cotton, or other fabric, extended on strips of whalebone, steel, or other elastic material, inserted, or fastened to, a rod or stick by means of pivots or hinges, in such a way as to allow of being opened and closed with ease. See Parasol. Underneath the umbrella's oily shed. Gay | 2. The umbrellalike disk, or swimming bell, of a jellyfish | 3. Any marine tectibranchiate gastropod of the genus Umbrella, having an umbrella-shaped shell
epagoge: 1. The adducing of particular examples so as to lead to a universal conclusion | 2. The argument by induction
morbid: 1. Not sound and healthful | 2. Induced by a diseased or abnormal condition | 3. Diseased
purpura: 1. A disease characterized by livid spots on the skin from extravasated blood, with loss of muscular strength, pain in the limbs, and mental dejection | 2. The purples. Dunglison | 3. A genus of marine gastropods, usually having a rough and thick shell. Some species yield a purple dye
heliotype: 1. A picture obtained by the process of heliotypy
glooming: 1. Twilight | 2. The gloaming. When the faint glooming in the sky First lightened into day | 3. Trench. The balmy glooming, crescent-lit
embattle: 1. To arrange in order of battle | 2. To array for battle | 3. Also, to prepare or arm for battle
pigg: 1. A piggin. See 1st Pig. Sir W. Scott
zoophytological: 1. Of or pertaining to zoöphytology | 2. As, zoöphytological observations
ataunto: 1. Fully rigged, as a vessel | 2. With all sails set | 3. Set on end or set right
enunciatory: 1. Pertaining to, or containing, enunciation or utterance
blowzed: 1. Having high color from exposure to the weather | 2. Ruddy-faced | 3. Blowzy
exit: 1. He goes out, or retires from view | 2. As, exit Macbeth. Note: The Latin words exit, and exeunt, are used in dramatic writings to indicate the time of withdrawal from the stage of one or more of the actors | 3. The departure of a player from the stage, when he has performed his part. They have their exits and their entrances. Shak
coldly: 1. In a cold manner | 2. Without warmth, animation, or feeling | 3. With indifference
zoography: 1. A description of animals, their forms and habits
hodgepodge: 1. A mixed mass | 2. A medley. See Hotchpot. Johnson. HODGKIN'S DISEASE Hodg`kin's dis*ease".  A morbid condition characterized by progressive anæmia and enlargement of the lymphatic glands | 3. -- first described by Dr. Hodgkin, an English physician
ripple: 1. An implement, with teeth like those of a comb, for removing the seeds and seed vessels from flax, broom corn, etc | 2. To remove the seeds from, by means of a ripple | 3. Hence, to scratch or tear. Holland
teleseme: 1. A system of apparatus for electric signals providing for automatic transmission of a definite number of different signals or calls, as in connection with hotel annunciators
acquisitive: 1. Acquired.  He died not in his acquisitive, but in his native soil. Wotton | 2. Able or disposed to make acquisitions | 3. Acquiring
appositive: 1. Of or relating to apposition | 2. In apposition. -- n.  A noun in apposition. -- Ap*pos"i*tive*ly, adv | 3. Appositive to the words going immediately before. Knatchbull
statecraft: 1. The art of conducting state affairs | 2. State management | 3. Statesmanship
bookmark: 1. Something placed in a book to guide in finding a particular page or passage | 2. Also, a label in a book to designate the owner | 3. A bookplate
sophister: 1. A sophist. See Sophist.  Hooker | 2. A student who is advanced beyond the first year of his residence. Note: The entire course at the university consists of three years and one term, during which the students have the titles of first-year men, or freshmen | 3. Second-year men or junior sophs or sophisters
impaction: 1. The driving of one fragment of bone into another so that the fragments are not movable upon each other | 2. As, impaction of the skull or of the hip | 3. An immovable packing
sappho: 1. Any one of several species of brilliant South American humming birds of the genus Sappho, having very bright-colored and deeply forked tails | 2. -- called also firetail
hagiarchy: 1. A sacred government | 2. By holy orders of men | 3. Southey
decumbent: 1. Lying down | 2. Prostrate | 3. Recumbent. The decumbent portraiture of a woman. Ashmole
siccity: 1. Dryness | 2. Aridity | 3. Destitution of moisture.  The siccity and dryness of its flesh. Sir T. Browne
mammonism: 1. Devotion to the pursuit of wealth | 2. Worldliness. Carlyle
symptomatical: 1. Of or pertaining to symptoms | 2. Happening in concurrence with something | 3. Being a symptom
indiction: 1. Declaration | 2. Proclamation | 3. Public notice or appointment.  "Indiction of a war." Bacon. Secular princes did use to indict, or permit the indiction of, synods of bishops. Jer. Taylor
termination: 1. The act of terminating, or of limiting or setting bounds | 2. The act of ending or concluding | 3. As, a voluntary termination of hostilities
milvus: 1. A genus of raptorial birds, including the European kite
semifluid: 1. Imperfectly fluid. -- n.  A semifluid substance
monogamous: 1. Upholding, or practicing, monogamy | 2. Same as Monogamian | 3. Mating with but one of the opposite sex
doubleminded: 1. Having different minds at different times | 2. Unsettled | 3. Undetermined. A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways. Jas. i
subserviency: 1. The quality or state of being subservient | 2. Instrumental fitness or use | 3. Hence, willingness to serve another's purposes
salmis: 1. A ragout or partky roasted game stewed with sauce, wine, bread, and condiments suited to provoke appetite
echinococcus: 1. A parasite of man and of many domestic and wild animals, forming compound cysts or tumors in various organs, but especially in the liver and lungs, which often cause death. It is the larval stage of the Tænia echinococcus, a small tapeworm peculiar to the dog
chrysophanic: 1. Pertaining to, or derived from, or resembling, chrysophane. Chrysophanic acid, a yellow crystalline substance extracted from rhubarb, yellow dock, sienna, chrysarobin, etc., and shown to be a derivative of an anthracene. It is used in the treatment of skin diseases | 2. -- called also rhein, rheic acid, rhubarbarin, etc
chancre: 1. A venereal sore or ulcer | 2. Specifically, the initial lesion of true syphilis, whether forming a distinct ulcer or not | 3. -- called also hard chancre, indurated chancre, and Hunterian chancre. Soft chancre. A chancroid. See Chancroid
ambulator: 1. One who walks about | 2. A walker | 3. A beetle of the genus Lamia. A genus of birds, or one of this genus
guaiacol: 1. A colorless liquid, C7H8O2, with a peculiar odor. It is the methyl ether of pyrocatechin, and is obtained by distilling guaiacum from wood-tar creosote, and in other ways. It has been used in treating pulmonary tuberculosis
cosmography: 1. A description of the world or of the universe | 2. Or the science which teaches the constitution of the whole system of worlds, or the figure, disposition, and relation of all its parts
imperturbability: 1. The state or quality of being imperturbable
legislate: 1. To make or enact a law or laws. Solon, in legislating for the Athenians, had an idea of a more perfect constitution than he gave them. Bp. Watson
parametritis: 1. Inflammation of the cellular tissue in the vicinity of the uterus
putrefaction: 1. The act or the process of putrefying | 2. The offensive decay of albuminous or other matter. Note: Putrefaction is a complex phenomenon involving a multiplicity of chemical reactions, always accompanied by, and without doubt caused by, bacteria and vibriones | 3. Hence, putrefaction is a form of fermentation, and is sometimes called putrefaction fermentative. Putrefaction is not possible under conditions that preclude the development of living organisms. Many of the products of putrefaction are powerful poisons, and are called cadaveric poisons, or ptomaïnes
ris: 1. A bough or branch | 2. A twig.  As white as is the blossom upon the ris | 3. Chaucer
tangible: 1. Perceptible to the touch | 2. Tactile | 3. Palpable. Bacon
urdu: 1. The language more generally called Hindoostanee
decrease: 1. To grow less, -- opposed to increase | 2. To be diminished gradually, in size, degree, number, duration, etc., or in strength, quality, or excellence | 3. As, they days decrease in length from June to December. He must increase, but I must decrease. John iii
commensal:
1. One who eats at the same table | 2. An animal, not truly parasitic, which lives in with, or on, another, partaking usually of the same food. Both species may be benefited by the association.

Having the character of a commensal
pedantical: 1. Of or pertaining to a pedant | 2. Characteristic of, or resembling, a pedant | 3. Ostentatious of learning
lionism: 1. An attracting of attention, as a lion | 2. Also, the treating or regarding as a lion
microspore: 1. One of the exceedingly minute spores found in certain flowerless plants, as Selaginella and Isoetes, which bear two kinds of spores, one very much smaller than the other. Cf. Macrospore
dystome: 1. Cleaving with difficulty. Note: Datolite was called dystome spar by Mohs
hierourgy: 1. A sacred or holy work or worship.  Waterland
allanite: 1. A silicate containing a large amount of cerium. It is usually black in color, opaque, and is related to epidote in form and composition
foreappoint: 1. To set, order, or appoint, beforehand. Sherwood

ratify: 1. To approve and sanction | 2. To make valid | 3. To establish

Any one of numerous species of Unio, and related fresh-water genera

pachydactyl: 1. A bird or other animal having thick toes
northeastern: 1. Of or pertaining to the northeast | 2. Northeasterly

enmist: 1. To infold, as in a mist

prosiphon: 1. A minute tube found in the protocon
suitability: 1. The quality or state of being suitable | 2. Suitableness

fineer:
1. To run in dept by getting goods made up in a way unsuitable for the use of others, and then threatening not to take them except on credit.  Goldsmith.

To veneer

sibylist: 1. One who believes in a sibyl or the sibylline prophecies. Cudworth
cubiform: 1. Of the form of a cube
interstratified: 1. Stratified among or between other bodies | 2. As, interstratified rocks
mailclad: 1. Protected by a coat of mail | 2. Clad in armor. Sir W. Scott

pectinibranch: 1. One of the Pectinibranchiata. Also used adjectively
protestator: 1. One who makes protestation | 2. A protester
yarwhip: 1. The European bar-tailed godwit | 2. -- called also yardkeep, and yarwhelp. See Godwit

polish: 1. Of or pertaining to Poland or its inhabitants. -- n.  The language of the Poles | 2. To make smooth and glossy, usually by friction | 3. To burnish

transmogrification: 1. The act of transmogrifying, or the state of being transmogrified | 2. Transformation.  Clive, who wrote me about the transmogrification of our schoolfellow, an attorney's son | 3. Thackeray

cholinic: 1. Pertaining to, or obtained from, the bile. Cholic acid, a complex organic acid found as a natural constituent of taurocholic and glycocholic acids in the bile, and extracted as a resinous substance, convertible under the influence of ether into white crystals
dyas: 1. A name applied in Germany to the Permian formation, there consisting of two principal groups
liquate:
1. To melt | 2. To become liquid.  Woodward.

To separate by fusion, as a more fusible from a less fusible material

collimator: 1. A telescope arranged and used to determine errors of collimation, both vertical and horizontal. Nichol | 2. A tube having a convex lens at one end and at the other a small opening or slit which is at the principal focus of the lens, used for producing a beam of parallel rays | 3. Also, a lens so used
paranymphal: 1. Bridal | 2. Nuptial.  At some paranymphal feast. Ford
extirpable: 1. Capable of being extirpated or eradicated | 2. As, an extirpable plant. Evelyn
duplication: 1. The act of duplicating, or the state of being duplicated | 2. A doubling | 3. A folding over

resignee: 1. One to whom anything is resigned, or in whose favor a resignation is made

turbellarian: 1. One of the Turbellaria. Also used adjectively
foraminous: 1. Having foramina | 2. Full of holes | 3. Porous. Bacon
fluctuability: 1. The capacity or ability to fluctuate.  H. Walpole
ohm: 1. The standard unit in the measure of electrical resistance, being the resistance of a circuit in which a potential difference of one volt produces a current of one ampére. As defined by the International Electrical Congress in 1893, and by United States Statute, it is a resistance substantially equal to 109 units of resistance of the C.G.S. system of electro-magnetic units, and is represented by the resistance offered to an unvarying electric current by a column of mercury at the temperature of melting ice | 2. 4521 grams in mass, of a constant cross-sectional area, and of the length of | 3. 3 centimeters. As thus defined it is called the international ohm
quipu: 1. A contrivance employed by the ancient Peruvians, Mexicans, etc., as a substitute for writing and figures, consisting of a main cord, from which hung at certain distances smaller cords of various colors, each having a special meaning, as silver, gold, corn, soldiers. etc | 2. Single, double, and triple knots were tied in the smaller cords, representing definite numbers. It was chiefly used for arithmetical purposes, and to register important facts and events.  Tylor. The mysterious science of the quipus . . . supplied the Peruvians with the means of communicating their ideas to one another, and of transmitting them to future generations. Prescott
awake: 1. To rouse from sleep | 2. To wake | 3. To awaken. Where morning's earliest ray . . . awake her
vertebra: 1. One of the serial segments of the spinal column. Note: In many fishes the vertebræ are simple cartilaginous disks or short cylinders, but in the higher vertebrates they are composed of many parts, and the vertebræ in different portions of the same column vary very greatly. A well-developed vertebra usually consists of a more or less cylindrical and solid body, or centrum, which is surmounted dorsally by an arch, leaving an opening which forms a part of the canal containing the spinal cord. From this dorsal, or neural, arch spring various processes, or apophyses, which have received special names: a dorsal, or neural, spine, spinous process, or neurapophysis, on the middle of the arch | 2. Two anterior and two posterior articular processes, or zygapophyses | 3. And one or two transverse processes on each side. In those vertebræ which bear well- developed ribs, a tubercle near the end of the rib articulates at a tubercular facet on the transverse process, while the end, or head, of the rib articulates at a more ventral capitular facet which is sometimes developed into a second, or ventral, transverse process. In vertebrates with well-developed hind limbs, the spinal column is divided into five regions in each of which the vertebræ are specially designated: those vertebræ in front of, or anterior to, the first vertebra which bears ribs connected with the sternum are cervical
somersault: 1. A leap in which a person turns his heels over his head and lights upon his feet | 2. A turning end over end | 3. "The vaulter's sombersalts." Donne. Now I'll only Make him break his neck in doing a sommerset. Beau. & Fl
astroite: 1. A radiated stone or fossil | 2. Star-stone
musculosity: 1. The quality or state of being musculous | 2. Muscularity
orthomorphic: 1. Having the right form. Orthomorphic projection, a projection in which the angles in the figure to be projected are equal to the corresponding angles in the projected figure
bellic: 1. Of or pertaining to war | 2. Warlike | 3. Martial.  "Bellic Cæsar." Feltham
judiciousness: 1. The quality or state of being judicious | 2. Sagacity
retection: 1. Act of disclosing or uncovering something concealed.  Boyle
cholate: 1. A salt of cholic acid | 2. As, sodium cholate
sphene: 1. A mineral found usually in thin, wedge-shaped crystals of a yellow or green to black color. It is a silicate of titanium and calcium | 2. Titanite
bab: 1. Lit., gate | 2. -- a title given to the founder of Babism, and taken from that of Bab-ud-Din, assumed by him
eggar: 1. Any bombycid moth of the genera Eriogaster and Lasiocampa | 2. As, the oak eggar of Europe
ploc: 1. A mixture of hair and tar for covering the bottom of a ship
mandoline: 1. A small and beautifully shaped instrument resembling the lute
bipectinated: 1. Having two margins toothed like a comb
iridal: 1. Of or pertaining to the iris or rainbow | 2. Prismatic | 3. As, the iridal colors. Whewell
larrikin: 1. A rowdy street loafer | 2. A rowdyish or noisy ill-bred fellow | 3. -- variously applied, as to a street blackguard, a street Arab, a youth given to horse-play, etc

apogeotropic: 1. Bending away from the ground | 2. -- said of leaves, etc | 3. Darwin

Mermaid fish the angel fish. -- Mermaid's glove, a British branched sponge somewhat resembling a glove. -- Mermaid's head, a European spatangoid sea urchin having some resemblance to a skull. -- Mermaid weed, an aquatic herb with dentate or pectinate leaves
multiform: 1. Having many forms, shapes, or appearances. A plastic and multiform unit. Hare
oxide: 1. A binary compound of oxygen with an atom or radical, or a compound which is regarded as binary | 2. As, iron oxide, ethyl oxide, nitrogen oxide, etc | 3. Note: In the chemical nomenclature adopted by Guyton de Morveau, Lavoisier,and their associates, the term oxides was made to include all compounds of oxygen which had no acid properties, as contrasted with the acid, all of which were at that time supposed to contain oxygen. The orthography oxyde, oxyd, etc., was afterwards introduced in ignorance or disregard of the true etymology, but these forms are now obsolete in English. The spelling oxid is not common

It has an acrid, bitter taste, a strong, unpleasant smell, and is used for medical purposes, also in the arts, as in the manufacture of varnish
another: 1. One more, in addition to a former number | 2. A second or additional one, similar in likeness or in effect. Another yet! -- a seventh! I 'll see no more. Shak. Would serve to scale another Hero's tower. Shak | 3. Not the same

witherling: 1. A withered person | 2. One who is decrepit.  Chapman

death: 1. The cessation of all vital phenomena without capability of resuscitation, either in animals or plants. By the former is implied the absolute cessation of the functions of the brain, the circulatory and the respiratory organs

standing: 1. Remaining erect | 2. Not cut down | 3. As, standing corn
discreditable: 1. Not creditable | 2. Injurious to reputation | 3. Disgraceful
indoin: 1. A substance resembling indigo blue, obtained artificially from certain isatogen compounds
emeer:
1. Same as Emir.

ion: 1. One of the elements which appear at the respective poles when a body is subjected to electro-chemical decomposition. Cf. Anion, Cation

cha: 1. Tea | 2. -- the Chinese name, used generally in early works of travel, and now for a kind of rolled tea used in Central Asia. A pot with hot water . . . made with the powder of a certain herb called chaa, which is much esteemed. Tr. J. Van Linschoten's Voyages

pulas: 1. The East Indian leguminous tree Butea frondosa. See Gum Butea, under Gum

periplast: 1. Same as Periblast. -- Per`i*plas"tic, a. Huxley

See Bail, v. t., to lade | 3. Misery
babel: 1. The city and tower in the land of Shinar, where the confusion of languages took place. Therefore is the name of it called Babel. Gen. xi | 2. shepen: 1. A stable | 2. A shippen.  The shepne brenning with the blacke smoke. Chaucer

sorter: 1. One who, or that which, sorts

koodoo: 1. A large South African antelope. The males have graceful spiral horns, sometimes four feet long. The females are hornless. Called also nellut

Cylindrical lens, a lens having one, or more than one, cylindrical surface. -- Cylindric, or Cylindrical, surface, a surface described by a straight line that moves according to any law, but so as to be constantly parallel to a given line. -- Cylindrical vault. lattermath: 1. The latter, or second, mowing | 2. The aftermath

reve:
1. To reave.  Chaucer.

A plant of the genus Scorpiurus, with pods resembling caterpillars. Caterpillar catcher, or Caterpillar eater, a bird belonging to the family of Shrikes, which feeds on caterpillars. hyetography: 1. The branch of physical science which treats of the geographical distribution of rain

incensation: 1. The offering of incense.  Encyc. Brit
peristeromorphous: 1. Like or pertaining to the pigeons or Columbæ

sultanry: 1. The dominions of a sultan. Bacon
scraber: 1. The Manx shearwater. The black guillemot
birlaw: 1. A law made by husbandmen respecting rural affairs | 2. A rustic or local law or by-law
impreventability: 1. The state or quality of being impreventable
prelatess: 1. A woman who is a prelate | 2. The wife of a prelate. Milton
sorrel:
1. Of a yellowish or redish brown color | 2. As, a sorrel horse.

A yellowish or redish brown color.

spuminess: 1. The quality or condition of being spumy | 2. Spumescence

p. p. of Twitch. Chaucer

pangenesis: 1. An hypothesis advanced by Darwin in explanation of heredity. Note: The theory rests on the assumption, that the whole organization, in the sense of every separate atom or unit, reproduces itself, the cells throwing off minute granules called gemmules, which circulate freely throughout the system and multiply by subdivision. These gemmules collect in the reproductive organs and products, or in buds, so that the egg or bud contains gemmules from all parts of the parent or parents, which in development give rise to cells in the offspring similar to those from which they were given off in the parent. The hypothesis also assumes that these gemmules need not in all cases develop into cells, but may lie dormant, and be transmitted from generation to generation without producing a noticeable effect until a case of atavism occurs

eclipse: 1. An interception or obscuration of the light of the sun, moon, or other luminous body, by the intervention of some other body, either between it and the eye, or between the luminous body and that illuminated by it. A lunar eclipse is caused by the moon passing through the earth's shadow | 2. A solar eclipse, by the moon coming between the sun and the observer. A satellite is eclipsed by entering the shadow of its primary. The obscuration of a planet or star by the moon or a planet, though of the nature of an eclipse, is called an occultation. The eclipse of a small portion of the sun by Mercury or Venus is called a transit of the planet. Note: In ancient times, eclipses were, and among unenlightened people they still are, superstitiously regarded as forerunners of evil fortune, a sentiment of which occasional use is made in literature. That fatal and perfidious bark, Built in the eclipse, and rigged with curses dark. Milton | 3. The loss, usually temporary or partial, of light, brilliancy, luster, honor, consciousness, etc
